paragraphs.text: The Spirit sometimes showed the prophet what was being revealed so plainly that no allegorical figures were needed to interpret the words, and only the bare words themselves were used. At other times it showed them through symbols drawn from other things, with expressive words and names that suggest a different meaning. So too in Joseph's dreams, stars, eleven in number, seemed to bow down to him, and this was how his brothers were indicated; and another time he saw his brothers gathering ears of grain, which was how the famine was hinted at. In the same way most of what was prophesied to the present prophet was seen through symbols, and a great deal is also said in an interwoven manner, with some things meant literally and others figuratively woven together in the same passage. The same is found in the Savior's teachings, in which he is recorded as saying: "Do you not say, 'There are four months yet, and then the harvest comes'? Lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for harvest." Part of this is literal, and part is meant figuratively, and you could find countless other examples. So it is with the prophet we have in hand. In him you could find words to be understood literally, such as: "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings," and what follows. And these are to be taken only figuratively: "My beloved had a vineyard on a horn, in a fertile place," and what follows.

By "vision" he does not mean an ordinary vision, or one that falls under bodily eyes. He means a prophetic vision that beholds things which would happen long afterward. Someone might look at a great painted panel showing an enemy attack, the ravaging of a land, sieges and enslavements, all depicted in bright colors. In the same way the prophet seems to have seen the vision while awake and not in sleep, as the divine Spirit shone its light upon his soul.

Isaiah did not set out from schools, nor did he gain from formal teaching. He came from the field, and from a life that most people would think obscure and neglected, and he received divine inspiration and wisdom. Isaiah must also be called an evangelist, since he performed the same ministry as the evangelists. In a remarkable way he proclaims the Son of God: at times he speaks of his divinity, at times he foretells his passage into heaven, and he announces beforehand the birth of Emmanuel from a virgin and the resurrection. He must also be called an apostle, for his own scripture establishes this when it says: "And the Lord said, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said, Here I am; send me."

He teaches that the whole subject is directed against the nation of the Jews. This is true not only in the reign of the first king listed but also in those of the second, the third and the fourth. In each of the reigns mentioned you will find him reproving the nation of the Jews and making predictions against them, right up to the very end of their kingdom. This means either the nation of the Jews or the land, and Jerusalem, the city.

Why does he begin with Judea, when he is also going to speak against Babylon and the Egyptians? Because he begins with those who seemed to be dedicated to God, as is said elsewhere: "Begin from my holy ones," and "the mighty will be mightily tested."

He marked the time of the kings because the state of affairs among the Jews was different then. Things that the people of that time could not have imagined or even suspected were going to come to pass long afterward. This too must be noted: the whole book seems to be one continuous work, but the prophet spoke it piece by piece, on different occasions and over long intervals of time. So anyone who means to divide the contents, assign their meaning to their periods, and match the prophecy to the events of each reign needs much precise knowledge. For the time of the kings listed covers fifty whole years, and the contents of the entire book were spoken during that time.

The divine Spirit filled the prophet's soul with its own power and uttered these words through the prophet's mouth as through an instrument. In this way it prepared listeners for the words the Lord was speaking, which is why it says: "For the Lord has spoken." Then it goes on to show the very word the Lord spoke, saying in the person of the Lord: "I have begotten sons and raised them up." So the Lord spoke the word. The prophetic Spirit heard the voice of the Lord and, through the prophet as through an instrument, delivered to human ears the word it had heard the Lord speak. It summoned to this lesson the parts that hold the universe together: heaven, which has received the divine powers, and earth, the dwelling place of mortals. It bids heaven to hear and earth to give ear. There are several possible reasons. It may treat them as having souls, since some say that a soul governs both the heavenly body and the element of earth alike. It may be calling on the invisible powers through them. It may address its word to things that endure because what was prophesied would come to pass long afterward, and mortal nature lasts only a short time. Or it may summon heaven and earth because the Jews are not worthy. It assigns "hearing" to heaven, meaning understanding, as the higher faculty, and "giving ear" to earth, meaning hearing through the ears, which is more bodily.
He says "I have begotten sons" because, through the rational soul, they came to be in his image, and also because the first of them received a special privilege.

By saying "The ox knows its owner," he hints that the nations, which before were in no way different from irrational beasts, will understand, but Israel will not understand. "Did not understand" stands for "will not understand." The ox and the donkey recognize those who feed them by natural instinct. But God gave these people such great care that they were not only made rational but were also counted worthy to be called the people of God and honored with the name of sons. Yet they did not even do what irrational animals do and know the Lord who begot and reared them, honored and exalted them. I think these words also point prophetically to God's Christ, who is himself the Lord. When he came to them alone of all the nations in his incarnation, they would not receive him, recognize him or perceive him, and would not even understand.

The prophetic Spirit testified that the first words were spoken by the Son in his own person. In the words that follow, however, it is no longer the Lord but the Spirit itself that reproaches those whom the Lord has just accused, saying: "Woe, sinful nation."

For these reasons the Holy Spirit convicts the nation of the Jews and pronounces them wretched, as worse than all the nations. They gained nothing from their adoption as sons, or from the honor God counted them worthy of when he exalted them and gave them a great many special gifts. They gained nothing even from the many times they were struck, beaten and chastised for their impieties out of the abundance of God's love. For "the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives."

It must be noted that the people called Israel prided themselves on tracing their descent from Abraham and on being born, according to the flesh, from the seed of men dear to God. Yet the Holy Spirit calls them a sinful nation, a people full of sins, an evil seed and lawless sons. It teaches that those who pride themselves on their race and forefathers are puffed up for nothing.

Here he calls the Son "Lord." And it would suit the Son of God, since he is the Word, to say of human nature and of the rational souls in human beings: "I have begotten sons and raised them up." He adds: "You have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger." Whom did they forsake, if not Christ? It was because they provoked and forsook him that they suffered what is described next. It must be noted that this passage accuses the whole nation of the Jews, rulers and ruled alike, of nothing other than forsaking the Lord. It does not reproach them for idolatry. It reproaches them for forsaking the Lord, whom the ox and the donkey recognized but Israel did not understand. So it rightly pronounces Israel wretched, since it has proved much worse than creatures that are irrational by nature.

He reproaches them with an incurable disease that cannot be treated: every head is in pain, he says, and every heart in grief; from the feet to the head there is no soundness in him. Then the word gives up hope of their cure, saying: "There is no poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandages." If these words are taken of the times after the Savior's coming, they fit, since that is when the wrath came upon them to the full. If they are taken of earlier times, they would not be true, because in every period and every generation, even during the captivity in Babylon itself, there were men among them dear to God. So it is reasonable for us to take these words of their final fall. At that time, because they did not understand God's Christ who had come to them, they were besieged by the Romans and never lifted their head again. They were turned back and estranged. Every head among them, that is, every ruling authority, was humbled and came to pain, and every heart to grief, so that from the feet to the head, that is, from the least to the greatest, there was no soundness in them, and no saving remedy could be devised for them. How could they possibly find another remedy that would bring health and salvation? They had denied the Lord, and they neither recognized nor understood the physician of souls who had come to them. He alone is able to heal every disease and every infirmity of souls and bodies alike. In place of "there is no soundness in him, neither wound nor bruise" and what follows, Symmachus translated it this way: "There is nothing healthy in him, only a wound and a bruise and the blow of a stroke, not bound up or bandaged or softened with oil."

The words "Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire," and what follows them, were in no way being fulfilled when they were spoken. The prophet foresaw them as things that would happen at some time long afterward. In place of "like a tent in a vineyard," Symmachus says "like a hut in a vineyard, and like a night watch-post in a cucumber field, and like a city sacked." The same prophet makes clear later on that the vineyard named here is the whole nation, when he says: "For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is a beloved young plant." Then he adds the cause of their desolation, saying: "I waited for it to do righteousness, but it did lawlessness; not righteousness, but an outcry."

Since they were the first to forsake the Lord and provoke the Holy One of Israel, it is fitting that they are said to be about to be forsaken. Being left "like a tent in a vineyard" signifies their complete fruitlessness. As long as a vineyard is full of good fruit, it has a guard, who pitches a tent up high, looks down from the height and watches over the vineyard. But if its fruit disappears, the guard leaves the tent deserted and withdraws from his watch, so as not to labor in vain. The divine Spirit prophesies that this very thing will happen to the temple. The whole nation was set up like a vineyard, and the temple in Jerusalem stood like a tent in the middle of it all, from which the guard watched over the vineyard as from a lookout. But since the vineyard produced thorns instead of grapes, the Spirit prophesies that the city and the temple will accordingly be forsaken. It says "like a tent in a vineyard," and also "like a fruit-watcher's hut in a cucumber field." The reason is that the nation not only failed to bear the grape, the more precious fruit, by which virtuous deeds are meant, but did not even bear what is called summer fruit. Such was the temporary and bodily worship under the law of Moses: beautiful to look at and flourishing, but temporary. That is why the place where the summer fruit was at its prime was called the fruit-watcher's hut, and it too is said to be about to be forsaken. Once the master and guard had left his tent and the fruit-watcher's hut, the whole city in turn was besieged, and both the place and the nation were left desolate.

The seed that came from them, the band of apostles, understood and recognized him, so it is rightly set apart from the multitude. The word speaks of them in the person of the prophets, saying: "And if the Lord of hosts had not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." For it would be absurd to think that the apostles are called the seed of the ungodly, of whom it was said above: "evil seed, lawless sons."

So the prophets, seeing these things by the divine Spirit, brought them consolation over the destruction of the whole nation, saying: "And if the Lord of hosts had not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah."

He compares them to the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah. This may be because of the catastrophe that was going to come upon them too, like the one that came upon the utterly ungodly men who lived in Sodom and Gomorrah. Or it may be because their way of life was similar, as the prophet himself shows further on when he says: "They have proclaimed and displayed their lawlessness like that of Sodom. Woe to their soul, for they have devised an evil plan against themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us." So it has been shown why he called them rulers of Sodom.

The children of the Jews prided themselves on the virtue of their fathers and thought highly of themselves as the seed of Abraham and the descendants of Israel. So the word rightly humbles their boasting and tears down their empty conceit. It names the rulers of renowned Israel "rulers of Sodom," and it calls the people known as the people of God "people of Gomorrah," since by practicing the same ways they had become like the ungodly of old.

The word introduces a new law of teaching, which sets aside the bodily worship of Moses. We refer these words to the rulers of the nation in the Savior's time, who dared to act against the Lord and then thought they could appease God with sacrifices, libations and the other bodily forms of worship under the law. It is to them that the word is directed when it says: "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?" and what follows. To this it adds: "You have become a surfeit to me," and what follows. After all this it reveals the reason for so great a threat, going on to say: "For your hands are full of blood." For they had filled up the measure of their fathers' wickedness. Notice that in all of this they are nowhere accused of idolatry. They are accused of not knowing the Lord and not understanding him, and so they forsook him and provoked the Holy One of Israel. On top of all this, their hands became full of blood through the murder of Christ, which they committed after countless murders of prophets. That is how their hands became full of blood. For this reason every feast and festival, and everything else by which they thought they obtained forgiveness of sins under the law of Moses, was taken away from them after their outrage against Christ. See what kind of threat is brought against them: "I will no longer forgive your sins." This too was fulfilled against them after the plot against our Savior, which is why the next words are: "For your hands are full of blood." Since their hands had become full of blood, it was fitting that these words were added: "I will no longer forgive your sins," and "Even if you multiply your prayer, I will not listen to you."

Quite consistently, the Lord who spoke the first words goes on to say these things as well to those he has identified as the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah. He calls them to good hopes, if they will turn from their wickedness, abandon the self-made worship of the bodily law, and obey his new covenant and his new law and word. So after setting aside the things of the old covenant, he introduces the mysteries of the new covenant and the new law. He himself also handed these down in the Gospels, saying: "Unless someone is born again of water and Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven." So the Lord, in his love for humankind, calls those held fast by such great evils and stained with the blood mentioned above to hurry to take up the new covenant. He holds out to them the promise of the forgiveness of sins that it secures even for those who have committed great impieties. That is why he says to them: "Wash yourselves, become clean." The saving word cleanses souls. It does not send them back to the ordinances of Moses but urges them to hurry to those of the Gospel. To "Wash yourselves, become clean" it adds: "Remove the wickedness from your souls," and "Do this before my eyes." Do not turn from your sins, he says, in the way people usually think of it, merely for show. Remove your wickedness from the very soul, which I see. So he adds: "Before my eyes, cease from your wickedness."

Then, once you have turned from wickedness, do not stop there. Take up the life of virtue, following the new teaching of the Gospel, for the good is something that must be learned. That is why he says: "Learn to do good and seek justice." Then, once you have achieved this, "rescue the one who is wronged, give judgment for the orphan, and defend the widow."

And when you have done all these things, take courage and come. Then let us argue our case as in a court of law, I and you. I will count up all I have suffered at your hands and all the kindnesses I have shown you. I will tell how, after so many offenses, I granted you amnesty for every evil and cleansed your hands, which were crimson with the blood mentioned above, making them brighter than snow through the washing of rebirth. As for you, if you have anything to say in answer to such great grace, bring it into the open.

To this is added: "And if you are willing and listen to me," by washing and doing the rest in the way described, "you shall eat the good things of the land." Here the word, since it is speaking to Jews, urges them on as if they were infants, by means of a bodily promise. In its true sense, however, the soul is understood as the land, as in the Savior's parable. There the land is said to receive the heavenly seed. Sometimes it chokes and destroys in various ways the word sown in it, and at other times it yields a flourishing crop, thirtyfold or sixtyfold or a hundredfold. So it follows that we should understand the good things of the soul. These are either its advances and perfection in virtue, or the things promised to them in the kingdom of heaven and in the heavenly land. The Savior himself taught about this land in the Gospels, saying: "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the land." It is in this heavenly land that the truly good things are found, "what eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the human heart." The heavenly Jerusalem is also understood to be there.

So the word promises these things to those who obey, but it threatens the disobedient, saying: "If you are not willing and do not listen to me, the sword will devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." In the literal sense, the outcome followed the words at once in actual events. Those who did not heed the saving grace, both the rulers and the people of the Jewish nation, were handed over to the enemy's sword immediately and before long, when the Romans came against them and subdued them all by the law of war. And if there is also a sword of the devil, they were given over to that too, because they disobeyed the call of Christ's grace.

Neither the Hebrew nor the other translators mention Zion here. The word teaches that long ago faithful men lived in the city, and so it was called a faithful city, as one might say "a city of the faithful." It was also full of judgment and righteousness, since it had become a home for virtuous souls at that time. That is why righteousness is said to have lodged in it, that is, to have dwelt and rested there. So long ago it was full of these things, probably around the time of David. He was the first to take the city from the hand of foreigners. He established the ark of God and the tabernacle in it and made it his own royal city, so that the place was called the city of David. At that time it was very likely faithful and full of judgment and righteousness. But now it has become a harlot because of those who played the harlot in it. These are the ones he points to next, saying: "But now, murderers."

These words too, in agreement with what was explained before, may be referred to the times of our Savior. After calling murderers those who prostituted themselves away from the Word, the bridegroom, the Holy Spirit turns to them, saying: "Your silver is counterfeit." Even after prostituting themselves and becoming murderers, they pretended to proclaim words of piety, to interpret the divine scriptures and to compose fabulous secondary traditions on the readings. Their silver was counterfeit, that is, the Jewish teaching, which is fabulous, fit for old wives and therefore to be rejected. Their teachers themselves peddled their teaching, and so they were fittingly called tavern-keepers who mix the wine with water. With their fabulous and nonsensical secondary tradition they water down the pure, sharp and astringent sense of the divinely inspired scriptures.

For when the Saviour called them they did not obey. Instead they became companions of thieves: they kept company with Judas the traitor, who was a thief, and shared with him in betraying their Teacher. These same men took bribes and sold the uprightness of the just for gifts. They also chased after recompense, in that they refused to accept the reproof that was given for their own good and chose to repay it with evil. That is why Symmachus says they "pursue rewards." On top of all this, although they had been entrusted with the oversight of the needy, they neither judged for orphans nor took up the cause of widows. All these charges are brought against the murderers mentioned earlier, but they can also be referred to their forefathers, by whom I mean those who long ago murdered the prophets of God.

The phrase "Lord Sabaoth" is translated "Lord of powers" or "Lord of armies." The words refer to our Saviour and Lord, the only-begotten Word of God. Here, because of the deeds of the murderers who have been accused, he utters the threats that follow, saying: "Woe to the mighty of Israel." Who these were the Gospel shows when it says: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites." Those words were spoken to the rulers and powerful men of the nation, as the ones responsible for corrupting those under them. And woe will be theirs, says the Master, the Lord Sabaoth, since his wrath will not cease, he says, nor relent until he has punished them. By "wrath" he means his power to avenge and punish.

But the Word loves humanity and does not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance. He therefore promises to apply a way of healing to those who do not need wrath. What was this but his hand? This hand saves and heals and is something other than his wrath. He says he will bring it upon them and will burn them with fire in order to purify them and separate the worthless from the good. That is why Symmachus renders it: "and I will smelt your dross until it is pure," and Theodotion: "and I will smelt your grape-husks until it is pure." People who purify bronze or iron by fire cast off the dross, and those who press grape clusters in the winepress throw away the husks and whatever is left over from the trodden clusters. "In the same way," he says, "I too will smelt your husks until it is pure." Aquila says much the same: "and I will smelt your pomace until it is pure." He makes it plainer what the dross was, and what the husks among them were, when he adds: "and I will remove all the lawless from you, and all the proud." "When I have brought my hand upon you and separated off your dross and your husks," he says, "then I will take those who are left after the ones I have mentioned, tested like gold in fire, and I will appoint them as judges and counsellors. They will be like those of ancient times, through whom the city was then faithful and full of judgment and righteousness." He promises that these will be the remnant found among them, chosen by grace. Here again he means the disciples of our Saviour, appointed for the new city that would be founded afterwards. He names this city "the city of righteousness" and "the faithful mother-city Zion," and with these names he refers to the community of the God-loving commonwealth. Long ago this commonwealth was established among the Jews and then fell into ruin. Now, through the church of Christ, it has been raised up throughout the whole world, founded upon the rock. The judges and counsellors who preside over this fair city began with the apostles and disciples of our Saviour. Through succession from them, even now they spring up as if from good seed and shine out as the appointed presidents of the church of God.

The prophecy goes on to show that these things are foretold about the few of the Jewish people who were left: "For her captivity shall be saved with judgment and with mercy," or, according to the other translators, "and with righteousness." If her captivity is said to be saved with judgment, then plainly only those judged worthy of salvation will obtain the promise. So the children of the Jews imagine in vain that their whole nation will return from the dispersion. The word clearly does not promise that all will return, only those who will be judged worthy. And we should understand the return from captivity as the turning of souls from error to the true knowledge of God. The Saviour also showed this in the synagogue. He took the book of Isaiah and read the passage spoken in his own person: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor." Then he closed the book and said: "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." He was teaching that he himself was the redeemer of human souls.

The word has already taught who those were who forsook the Lord, when it said earlier: "Woe, sinful nation, a people full of sins, an evil seed, lawless sons! You have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger." It is these, then, whom the word threatens with destruction, utter desolation and ruin. Then they will come to their senses and be ashamed of the things in which their fathers long ago committed impiety by worshipping idols. In their shame they will give up the same error, and so it adds: "of their idols, which they themselves desired, and at the gardens which they longed for."

The shame they would feel at shameful things, once they became aware of them, was going to turn them from their shameless and impudent way of life. And the prophecy can be seen fulfilled in fact. The Jewish nation no longer worships idols as their fathers did. They were truly put to shame when they saw others turned from their ancestral demons to the word of godliness through the teaching of Christ, and by these I mean the gentiles. So the prediction has been fulfilled that said: "For they will be ashamed of their idols, which they themselves desired, and they were put to shame at the gardens which they longed for." It was mostly in gardens that their fathers carried out their idolatry.

Israel was once the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, a shady olive tree and a vine rich in branches. Now he teaches that they will change so much for the worse that they will be compared to a terebinth. And it is not even a terebinth in bloom but one that has shed its leaves. This will be a sign that they have no moist sap at all and take in no life-giving power, and that they bear only a multitude of shrivelled souls. For that reason they are compared to the fruit of the terebinth, which is very hard and very dry. You can see that the present multitudes of the Jewish nation are like this, and that is why it is said: "like a terebinth that has shed its leaves," or, according to Symmachus, "like a terebinth whose leaves have fallen away." They have also become "like a garden that has no water." If you looked at their recitations of the divine scriptures, their readings from the Law and the Prophets, their books of history and verse, and their kinds of hymnody and psalmody, you would see a true garden, a meadow of every kind of good thing. But if you looked among them for the living, fruitful and life-giving Word, whose drinker will have a spring of water welling up to eternal life, you would not find it. That is why it is prophesied that they will be "like a garden that has no water."

He says their strength will be like a stalk, and not a stalk of wheat or of any other useful crop, but a stalk of tow. This is because there has been taken from them "the mighty man and the mighty woman, the strength of bread and the strength of water, the giant and the mighty man." So they cannot say, as the disciples of Christ do: "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me," and: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress?" and so on. Their strength has become so like a stalk of tow that they have not only lost the freedom they once prided themselves on, when they had self-rule and a kingdom of their own, but they are even slaves to any Roman soldier who comes along. Their works have also become like sparks, since their deeds turn into causes of fire. They build not with gold or silver or precious stones but only with wood, hay and straw. That is why he adds after all this: "and the lawless and the sinners shall be burned together, and there will be no one to quench the fire." You see how the word threatens them with burning and conflagration. This is the end of the present prophecy against them. It came true to the letter, at once and not long after their outrage against our Saviour. The mother-city was burned, and the ungodly in it, by their own sparks, stored up for themselves the unquenchable, eternal fire and the wrath of God on the day of wrath.

Next, after the accusation against the people of the circumcision and the sentence pronounced on them, the prophetic Spirit passes on to the calling of the gentiles and foretells that they will turn to God. After this it speaks of a new law and word, and of a new mountain and house of God. It says the foreign nations will one day come to these, leaving their ancestral gods behind and coming to know the God of the prophets, who among the prophets is called the God of Jacob. It also gives a very clear sign of the time when these things would be fulfilled. The sign is the good news that at that time there will be peace among all the nations. There will no longer be many local rulers. The nations will not be divided and in conflict with one another, and the cities within each nation will not wage war and fight among themselves. Instead there will be concord and peace everywhere, so that those who work the land will no longer have to provide swords and weapons of war as they did in former times, when they were driven to it by the constant attacks of their neighbours. These things too were plainly fulfilled after the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ. In the times before this you could not find such a settled and peaceful state of affairs as we see with our own eyes under Roman rule since the times of our Saviour. The nations now mix with one another, and there is peace everywhere, in country and city alike. As a result, the new law and the gospel word began from the land of the Jews and from Zion itself, travelled unhindered over the inhabited world and filled all the nations. It is fitting, then, that the prophetic Spirit marks a break after the first accusation and the sentence against the Jewish nation, as if beginning a new subject. Starting afresh, as it were with a gospel, it introduces the word of God that came to Isaiah. This was the Word that the Gospel also mentions when it says: "In the beginning was the Word." Since the calling of the gentiles was being foretold, God the Word had to be put first, announcing to the nations the good news set out here.

According to Symmachus, the prophecy is said to be "concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem." One could therefore reasonably say that, by the letter and the plain sense, the word concerns them, because it was in Judea and Jerusalem that the saving grace of the gospel began to be proclaimed. The Christ of God went about Judea and Galilee and came to Jerusalem again and again, preaching the kingdom of God. So much for the letter and the history. As for the deeper sense, the Judea and the Jerusalem should be understood as different from those accused earlier, if indeed, as Symmachus has it, the word came to the prophet "concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem."

If some kinder promise were being made to the Jewish nation, it would be right to think that their land is meant. But as it is, the calling of the gentiles comes next, then a long accusation of the Jewish people, and then a further threat against Judea and Jerusalem. The prophecy brings in a new law, as it were, beside that of Moses, and a different word beside the old one. It also speaks of a new mountain, hidden in the past but now made manifest, and of a house of God known to all the nations and not to the Jews as well. Should we not, then, understand a Judea and Jerusalem of the same kind, the very ones promised to the gentiles, about which the present word speaks? What would one say Judea means in the deeper sense, if not the Judea meant in the saying "God is known in Judea"? So the soul that has received the knowledge of God would truly be Judea, if indeed "God is known in Judea," and in that case the prophet is calling the gentiles' knowledge of God "Judea." The house of God built in it would be the church gathered from the gentiles. It is called the house of God and is founded on the saving and unbreakable rock. And if you said the mountain is God the Word, you would not miss the truth. Here you would be taught by the prophet Daniel, who saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands. By this the stone hinted at the Saviour's humanity and the mountain at God the Word. He foretells that these things will happen in the last days. You will understand the house of God on the tops of the mountains when you hear our Saviour say of his church: "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden." The mountain of God is understood in different ways. In a more bodily sense, as the Jews would take it, it is the mountain in the land of Palestine. In the deeper sense it is the lofty and heavenly gospel word of God. In a third sense, the divine Apostle teaches that there is a heavenly Zion and a Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all. This mountain was not manifest to people in ancient times, but the divine Spirit foretells that it will become manifest to all the nations in the last days, when Christ has appeared to put away sins. All the nations, Greek and barbarian alike, will therefore hasten. They will turn away from the error of many gods and from the physical mountains once thought to be consecrated to demons or gods, and they will hasten to the God proclaimed in this passage. So they call out to one another and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it." To these nations, then, the word promises that it will make the mountain and house of God in heaven manifest and known to all who become disciples.

This would be the gospel law of Christ. It set out from above, from the heavenly Zion, and also from this earthly Zion. There the Saviour was put to death by men and rose from the dead, and there the mysteries and precepts of the new covenant had their beginning before going out into the whole world. This same law, the new law of the gospel word, was proclaimed to all the nations. It instructed those who received it about the mountain of God and his house, and it taught the nations, saying: "Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob." The same law also judged between the nations: it set apart the worthy for itself and chose the called from those who were not such. In judging between the nations in this way, the gospel word rebuked many peoples. Either it convicted those who believed in it of their former error, or it convicted those who did not believe of perishing through their own fault. Those who received it were freed from every warlike disposition. From then on they live in peace and lead an untroubled life. The opposing powers no longer make war on them, and they are no longer subject to the demons who once ruled them. To them the Saviour himself gave his own peace, saying: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you." These things were also fulfilled to the letter after his divine appearing and after the gospel law was proclaimed to the nations, when the deepest peace took hold of the nations. The word indicated [?] this by saying that they would beat their swords into ploughs and their spears into sickles, and would no longer learn war. In former times these skills were necessary and were practised from childhood in country and city, out of fear of hostile neighbours.

Next, having described the calling of the gentiles and the peace poured out on all people, the prophet shows his love for his own kin by urging his people to receive the grace of Christ that has been given to all the nations. So he says: "And now, O house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord." See how, to rouse and encourage the people, he counts himself among them as he urges them to share in the light of the Lord. By "the light of the Lord" he means the law of the new covenant that went out from Zion, the saving gospel word. He summons not Jacob but his house to come to the light of the knowledge of the Lord, as people who are in darkness. He makes this clear by adding next: "For he has let go his people, the house of Jacob." That is: "Hurry, then, you who belong to the house that has been let go, and come with me, since I myself am ready to walk with you in the light of the Lord." He calls the Jewish people the house of Jacob because they are not Jacob and are not worthy to bear their forefather's name. They are only a house, empty and vacant. As if defending God, he sets out the reasons why God let them go, adding: "because their land was filled, as from the beginning, with divinations," and so on. By this he shows that it was not without reason that the light of the Lord, which shone on all the nations, let them go. This is according to the Septuagint translation, in which "he has let go his people" and what follows are joined to the preceding clause: "and let us walk in the light of the Lord."

The prophet urged the people, saying: "Come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord," and there he stops. What he says next he no longer addresses to the people but to the Lord himself. In place of "For he has let go his people," Aquila translated: "For you have left your people, the house of Jacob," and Symmachus: "You have cast off." Next he presents signs that the people have been let go. In ancient times certain foreigners, Amorites, Hivites and Jebusites, lived in the place and did every kind of terrible thing, and in their day the land was filled with omens, divinations and every sort of idolatry. In the same way, he says, the land of the house of Jacob will be filled with foreign inhabitants. Foreign children will be born to them, and the land once called God's land will be filled with soldiers, whom he hints at with the multitude of horses and chariots. He says further that their land will be filled with people busy with gold and silver. In addition, he says, it will be filled with abominations, the works of their hands. Whose hands, if not those of the foreign inhabitants, who also worshipped what their fingers had made? All these are signs of foreign, idol-worshipping nations who were going to live in Jerusalem itself and in the land of Judea. These things were fulfilled after the coming of our Saviour and after the gospel word that enlightened all the nations. The Jews did not obey the prophet who called them, saying: "Come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord," and so they were handed over to the power of the Romans. Grieving in his soul over this, the prophet cries out to the Lord himself: "You have let go your people, the house of Jacob."

Then he presents the proofs that the people, let go and forsaken by the Lord, had their land handed over to foreign nations. After listing the impieties of these nations, he again cries out to the Lord himself: "And do not forgive them." In place of "and I will not let them go," Aquila translated: "and do not bear with them," and Symmachus: "and do not forgive them." It would make no sense for this to be said about the Jews, for the prophet would not have prayed against his own people. It fits the interpretation given above. He added these things about the nations already mentioned, who made war on Jerusalem and filled it with soldiers and every kind of idolatry.

I think that the foregoing was also fulfilled in one sense at the Romans' attack on the Jewish nation. As the country was being ravaged, they fled from the face of the enemy into the rocks and hid in caves because of the wrath from God that lay upon them. Then the proud were humbled, and those who had formerly exulted in their wealth were then shown to be nothing, when the day of the Lord overtook them—I mean the day of Christ's vengeance. On that day the day of the Lord pursued not only proud and arrogant men but also the beauties of the country, as the enemy ravaged and destroyed everything, so that they threw down towers, demolished walls and cut down everything lofty. And if some engaged in trade by sea, the enemy seized their ships as well. So at that time they humbled and plundered the Jewish nation on every side, since they did not make themselves obedient to the prophet when he urged them and said, "Come, let us walk in the light of the Lord." The prophet foretells these things, solemnly warning of the wrath that would overtake them if they did not accept the light of the Lord. In the same way he prophesies that idolatry among men will be destroyed, and that the Lord alone will be exalted among all, while every height raised up against the knowledge of God is brought low.

I think that the prophet, in the preceding verses, was distressed at what he had prophesied about the foreigners who were going to inhabit the land of the Jewish nation and to occupy Jerusalem itself, and that he petitioned God as in prayer and said, "Do not spare them." Accordingly he was granted a sight of God's righteous judgment, the Lord showing him the day of vengeance that will pursue all the ungodly. Having foreseen it, he urges them even now to guard against the wrath that is going to come upon all the ungodly. Therefore, as if addressing those very people who would inhabit the land, he tells them to enter into the rocks and hide in the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his might, when he rises to shatter the earth. For the eyes of the Lord are lofty, but man is lowly; and the loftiness of men will be brought low, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day. I think these things are said about the day of judgment; so the passage prophesies them not about the Jews alone, but universally about all people of this kind. At any rate, he adds next: For the day of the Lord of hosts is upon everyone insolent and proud, and upon everyone lofty and high, and they will be brought low. Through these words he clearly introduces a universal judgment against all the ungodly. That is why neither the Hebrew reading nor the other translators have "and now," which is found in our reading, where it says, "And now enter into the rocks and hide"; for he did not prophesy these things about the present time, but about God's universal judgment.

Then, since in the preceding verses he mentioned those who possessed chariots and horses and had amassed wealth and treasures of gold and silver, he accordingly hints at the judgment through figurative allegory, naming the cedars of Lebanon, the oak trees, the high mountains and hills, the lofty towers, the walls and the ships. He prophesies that all of these will be destroyed on the expected day of the Lord, in this way covertly alluding to the rulers of this age, its heights and dignities, the principalities and powers, and the world-rulers of this life who have not known God. The Holy Spirit showed these things to the prophet after he had prayed and said, "Do not spare them," healing the grief of his soul over his own people.

Then, since he mentioned in the preceding verses how the land was filled with abominations, the works of their hands, and they worshipped what their fingers had made, and man bowed down and a man was brought low, he accordingly prophesies in the passage before us, saying: And they will hide the things made by hands, carrying them into the caves and into the clefts of the rocks and into the holes of the earth; and again: In that day a man will cast away his abominations of silver and gold, which they made in order to worship them. For at that time, when the day of God has come, they will hide away in their broken minds the opinions they formerly held in their souls about the error of many gods; and more than that, they will cast out and throw away from their thinking every false notion about their idols.

And they will do this from the face of the fear of the Lord. Yet these things also began to be fulfilled in part at the first coming of our Savior, after the word of the gospel was proclaimed to all the nations. Indeed, already in our own time the error concerning those whom the nations formerly regarded as gods has been exposed, since they cannot help even themselves. Therefore every idolater has been brought low, and the Lord of all alone has been exalted. Those who formerly prided themselves on idols as on gods, now that their error has been exposed and the costly material of their statues is being taken away, have been hiding the lifeless statues in caves, as the prophecy said, because of the costliness of the material, so that they might not be seized by the imperial officials. From these things too, I think, it is established beyond dispute that these things reached their fulfillment after the Savior's coming. When Jerusalem was practicing idolatry, or rather when all Judea had gone astray, the war of the Babylonians was in a sense being proclaimed to Judea. The Babylonians ravaged the whole country, killed those they captured, and carried off women and children to their own land. But because the attack had been foretold and was about to come, such terror came upon the Jews, and they fell into such anguish, that they hid in caves and in the clefts of the mountains and took refuge in inaccessible places, since every hand of theirs was too weak to resist the attackers.

The words "Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for in what has he been reckoned?" are transmitted as an addition. The passage seems to urge them not to heed those people, nor to put their hope in mortal men whose whole life is in their nostrils.

What was said before concerned the day of vengeance, but the present passage, making a fresh start, threatens that God's gifts among the former people will be removed. He says they will be taken away from them not for idolatry nor for any other deeds, but for one counsel, truly godless, impious and wicked: the counsel against the Lord. See, at any rate, how after all the threats against them he adds: And they have proclaimed and displayed their sin like Sodom's. Woe to their soul, for they have taken wicked counsel against themselves, saying, "Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us." For this was the cause of everything that was threatened. From these things too, I think, it is established beyond dispute that these things reached their fulfillment after the Savior's coming. Therefore, he says, the Lord will take away from Jerusalem and from Judea the strong man and the strong woman—or, as Aquila has it, "prop and propping," or as Symmachus has it, "support and supporting." By this you will understand the apostle's saying, which called those distinguished by a godly life "pillars and foundation." For surely among the former people too there were some who were like foundations and supports of their whole nation, and the passage threatens that these will be taken away from them; and then, not bread nor water, but the strength of bread and the strength of water. This too you will understand from another prophet, who said: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. There is, then, a bread of the soul, a nourishing word, and likewise a rational drink. Even if the Jews think they partake of these by pursuing the divine scriptures and by devoting themselves eagerly to learning and reciting them, you would still not find among them the strength of the nourishing words or the nourishment of the life-giving spring.

He also threatens that the giant, the strong man and the diviner will be taken away from them. Neither the Hebrew word nor the other translators say "giant"; instead Aquila rendered it "mighty one," Symmachus "brave man," and Theodotion "potentate." So he threatens that the potentate and the mighty one will be removed, and in addition the warrior and the magistrate (for which the others have "judge"), and above all the prophet and the diviner. From these things too, I think, it is established beyond dispute that these things reached their fulfillment after the Savior's coming. For if anyone should wish, by forcing the sense, to say that these things happened in the times of the prophet Isaiah or at the time of the Babylonian siege, he will be shown to hold a false opinion. For at that time there were very many prophets with them in Jerusalem itself, before the siege and during the siege, and in Babylonia itself, and after the return from there; and there were also judges among them who judged the people. In Babylon itself Daniel judged the elders; after the return Jeshua son of Jozadak and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel led the people; and later still Ezra and Nehemiah, as well as elders honored for their understanding and wisdom, adorned their nation. Later you will find distinguished warriors arising among them as well, in the times of the Maccabees, among whom there were surely also captains of fifty in the military ranks. It is likely, too, that they had wonderful counselors, men wise in speech, and master builders. They also had intelligent listeners, who weighed the words of the prophets and rejected those of the false prophets, doing this by a spirit of discernment. In ancient times, then, all these flourished in the Jewish nation; but they failed all at once and were taken away from Jerusalem and from Judea, as the prophecy said, all of them together, at no other time than when they plotted against our Savior.

Having lost all the things just mentioned, those whom the prophecy accuses were handed over to mockers as their lords and to youths as their rulers. The passage will again teach the cause of all this. It does not accuse them of idolatry, but says that they took wicked counsel against themselves, saying, "Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us," and that their tongues, together with lawlessness, were disobedient toward the Lord. For this Symmachus has: "Their tongues and their practices are directed against the Lord to provoke him," and Aquila: "For their tongue and their practices contend against the Lord." You see the cause for which the things mentioned were taken from them. For indeed they sharpened their tongues against the Lord when they let out impious cries, saying, "Away, away with him! His blood be on us and on our children!" Then truly their tongue and their practices were directed against the Lord to provoke him. Therefore, clarifying the sense, he adds next: And they have proclaimed and displayed their lawlessness like Sodom's. Woe to their soul, for they have taken wicked counsel against themselves, saying, "Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us." This, then, was the cause of the removal of God's gifts, which had shone so brightly of old.

And who, seeing those whom the Jews call patriarchs—truly youths, not only in bodily age but also immature in soul and lacking sense—and their other teachers, would not say that they are the mockers whom the prophecy indicated? Moreover, the people have collapsed, man against man and man against his neighbor; the child will strike against the elder, and the dishonored against the honored. Since there is no order among them and no word of God governing their life, he says he will drive them into such poverty and lack of sense that they will have plenty of neither clothing nor bread: clothing, that is, of decent and orderly speech to cover the shame of their soul; and bread, that is, of the word that nourishes the mind. Therefore he says: A man will take hold of his brother or of a member of his father's household, saying, "You have a cloak; be our leader, and let my food be under your charge." And in that day he will answer and say, "I will not be your leader, for there is neither bread nor clothing in my house."

Then he signifies the desolation of the land and the complete fall of Jerusalem, adding next: Jerusalem is abandoned, and Judea has fallen. The cause has already been stated: they have suffered these things because of their tongues, with which they provoked God, and because they took wicked counsel, which turned out to be against their own soul rather than against the one who had counseled [?]. Therefore they will eat the fruits of their works, and woe has come upon the lawless people, since what happens to them will match the works of their hands, which are evil; for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.

Your exactors glean you. Of those who go wrong in some way, some stumble knowingly, overcome by vice, yet stung and wounded in conscience over what they do; others, being ignorant, are carried along like cattle. A third group, worse than those already mentioned, consists of those who, besides ruining themselves, also lead others by deceit into similar wrongdoing. So the Word of God, seeing many among the Jews stumbling through error, sets them apart from those accused earlier and exhorts them through the present words. As Christ and lover of humankind, he calls them his people, encouragingly claiming them as his own and drawing them to the knowledge of himself. For every human being is his, even one who sins. So he draws them to himself, granting pardon to those who go wrong through ignorance; that is why he says, "My people." Then he reproves those who caused their unbelief in him, whom in the preceding verses he called mockers. Therefore he says: My people, your exactors glean you. For the rulers of the Jewish nation, wishing to collect the profits that came from God through firstfruits and tithes and the other offerings brought to them as rulers and teachers, did not allow the people to take up the knowledge of Christ. He shows this when he says: Your exactors glean you, and those who make demands will rule over you. And what were they demanding, if not the profits just mentioned? For their sake they did not even reprove sinners, but flattered everyone and called them blessed. Therefore he refutes these as well, saying: My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and confuse the path of your feet. For by turning them away from the straight road that leads to the saving word, they perverted the steps of their soul. And those who are deceived by being called blessed find the path of their feet thrown into confusion; for affliction summons one to humility, but being called blessed breeds conceit.

Accordingly, then, he next says to those who do such things: But now the Lord will stand up for judgment; and again: The Lord himself will come to judgment with the elders of the people and with its rulers. So we who are elders and rulers, and who do not cultivate the vineyard through sound teaching and the good example of our own lives, will be charged with these things. Then, as if standing beside the Lord's tribunal, he blames them and reproves them to their face, saying: But you, why have you set fire to my vineyard, and why is the plunder of the poor in your houses? Why do you wrong my people and put the faces of the poor to shame? This applies to us if we keep in our houses what is given for the relief of the needy, defrauding those in want. It is the custom of those who wrong and defraud others, when they are accused by those they have wronged, to shame them with insults and abuse, belittling them and threatening them with blows. So this is what he says: the shame that belongs to you because of your injustice, you turn back upon the poor by your tyranny. Here again he calls "his people" and "his vineyard set on fire" those who were deceived by the plundering and perversion of the teachers. Calling them back and turning them to himself, he turns them away from the perverse teaching of those just mentioned. And quite consistently, having prophesied the first coming of the Savior and the perversion of the rulers of the people, he then sets out what concerns his second coming, saying: The Lord himself will come to judgment with the elders of the people and with its rulers.

For "the tassels" Aquila translated "bands"; for "the crescents" Symmachus has "necklaces"; for "the pendant" Aquila has "woven hairnets" and Symmachus "the hanging ornaments"; and again for "the bracelets" Symmachus has "the aprons." Since the prophecy seemed to have said everything in the preceding verses about men, and the women would probably think that nothing had been said to them, it necessarily sets out the threat against them as well. It describes their former condition as one of luxury and wanton living in wealth: in their great abundance they gave no thought to God. Therefore he threatens to strip them of the things in which they took their pleasure.

In place of their former luxury he signifies their change for the worse, adding: Instead of a sweet smell there will be dust; instead of a girdle you will gird yourself with a rope; instead of the ornament of your head you will have baldness because of your works; and instead of the purple-striped tunic you will gird on sackcloth. These things can be said not only of women but also of slack and effeminate souls. It is likely that these things too were fulfilled upon the people of the circumcision after their opposition to our Savior and Lord. For those who still lived in Zion at that time were overflowing with wealth, and their daughters lived wantonly, insensible of the evils that surrounded them.

Fittingly, then, the prophecy also uttered threats against them, saying that they would be delivered to the sword of the enemy, and alluding to the Romans' attack when it says: And your most beautiful son, whom you love, will fall by the sword, and your strong ones will fall by the sword. Symmachus rendered this as follows: Instead of beauty, the fair ones of your number will fall by the sword, and your mighty ones in war, when the city will be emptied and will mourn. And to the city, according to the Seventy, it is said: And you will be left alone and be leveled to the ground.

Since these words signify the utter desolation of the place, he goes on, as though the men had failed and were no more because they had been slain by the sword, to say that seven women will take hold of one man. They will ask him to provide them with nothing more—for they would need nothing from him—except his name, and that he be seen as their protector, so that they would not be desolate and reproached for having no one to protect them. Therefore, as if they had found in him something rare when all others had perished, they say to him: Only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach. That is the sense of the text. Others, however, have said that the first man is the Savior and the seven women are the seven powers of the Holy Spirit, which came upon the first man because they found no one else able to contain them; and that these are the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and godliness, and above all the spirit of the fear of God.

In that day God will shine forth. He teaches that both the earlier things and the present ones will take place at one and the same time; but those were gloomy, while these are kinder. How, then, was it possible for the kind promise also to be fulfilled for the same people at the same time? For "in that day" signifies the time of the same Christ, in which the foregoing will also take place: God will shine forth in counsel with glory upon the earth. For this Symmachus has: The Lord will be a dawning, for the power and glory of the land, and for preeminence. If he had gone on to apply the kind promises to the whole people, the passage would have seemed to contain contradictions. As it is, however, the promise is made not to the whole nation but only to the remnant left from it: God will shine forth in counsel with glory upon the earth, to exalt and glorify what is left in Jerusalem, and it shall be that those left behind in Jerusalem will be called holy. These were the very ones indicated in the earlier prophecy by the seed that was left, of which it was said: Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah. By this he signified those of the Jews who believed in Christ, among whom were the apostles, who sowed the rational and heavenly seeds among all the nations. It is about these, then, that the present prophecy foretells the things before us, saying: In that day—that is, at the time of the others' rejection—God will shine forth in counsel with glory upon the earth, to exalt and glorify the remnant of Israel, those called holy and enrolled for life in Jerusalem. And indeed one can see in actual fact how the first from Israel who believed in Christ, the apostles, disciples and evangelists of the Savior, were glorified and exalted, so that they became famous everywhere on earth and throughout the whole inhabited world; and even now both their name and their teaching are glorified among all nations, Greeks and barbarians alike. These alone will be called holy, who have been found worthy to be enrolled for the eternal life of the heavenly Jerusalem. Set beside these words our Savior's saying to the apostles: But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

He makes clear next how they will become worthy of these things, saying: “The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion and will cleanse the blood from their midst by a spirit of judgment.” Here he clearly means the washing of regeneration. He had pointed to it earlier when he said, “Wash yourselves, become clean,” and now he promises it. “By a spirit of burning” would differ in no way from “with the Holy Spirit and fire.” By “filth” he means the filth of souls, which became soiled when they were defiled by the blood. The word also mentioned this blood earlier, saying, “For your hands are full of blood,” and here it calls it the blood of Jerusalem, saying: “The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion and will cleanse the blood.” Which daughters of Zion does he mean? Surely those who were just accused in the preceding passage, where it is said, “Because the daughters of Zion were haughty and walked with outstretched necks,” and what follows. He says these things about those who took part in the murder of the Savior but a little later changed their minds and came to know his gospel. Paul was one of these. He once ravaged the church of God and approved of the killing of Stephen, and no doubt in some way approved of the Savior's blood as well. But later he changed and was baptized. It is “by a spirit of judgment” that all these who are washed as Paul was are said to be cleansed, for they were to be saved with judgment and with righteousness, and also by a spirit of burning. See whether the present passage does not agree closely with the testimony of the Gospel about our Savior, which taught, “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” For “by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” differs in no way from “with the Holy Spirit and fire.” The fiery words took hold of them and worked in them a cleansing of their sins. In the same way the Savior is said in the Gospel to baptize not with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire. John taught this when he said of himself, “I baptize you with water,” and of the Savior, “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”

To this he adds: “And he will come, and a cloud will overshadow by day every place in Zion and all that is around it.” Another prophet will show who it is that will come, saying, “The deliverer will come out of Zion,” as does the one who said, “In a very little while the one who is coming will come and will not delay.” When he comes he will fulfil what follows. Instead of “he will come,” the Hebrew and all the other translators read, “And the Lord will create every place of Mount Zion.” They are pointing to the new creation, the church of God, which has been founded in every place. And here the word of the gospel is called Mount Zion. The new creation was built on it, not by any human being but by the Lord himself, who also said, “On the rock I will build my church.” He says that a cloud will overshadow what is around it, “and as of fire, of a light burning by night; it will be covered with all the glory.” We will understand this if we go back to the history in Moses, where it is said that by day Christ went before them in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light. The present prophet foretells that it will be the same with the church of God. By day, he says, a cloud will overshadow it, so that it is not scorched by the heat, and by night there will be light and the glow of fire, so that it is not left in darkness. At the same time, he says, the glory of God will overshadow the whole of it, so that it is in no way harmed, either by the heat of the day or by the harshness of the day's rains. By these words the passage teaches that God's right hand will always overshadow his church, so that nothing harms it, whether in times of prosperity and peace or in seasons of persecution. It will remain forever unfallen and unshaken, overshadowed by the glory of God, so that it is neither scorched by day in the heat nor injured by harsh weather, rains and wintry winds. That is why it is said: “It will be covered with all the glory, and it will be a shade from the heat, and a shelter and hiding place from harshness and rain.”

The prophetic Spirit goes on to join further words to what was said before, and these too [?] are part of the vision that Isaiah son of Amoz saw concerning Judea and Jerusalem. It goes through the present passage in the person of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Let me sing to the loved one a song of my beloved.” Instead of “to my vineyard,” the Hebrew wording and the other translators have “to his vineyard.” He is saying: I will sing to the loved one a song that is not mine and was not made by me, but by the beloved himself, who sang to his vineyard a song full of lament and weeping. So Aquila translated it this way: “Let me sing to my dear one a song of my uncle to his vineyard.” Symmachus has: “Let me sing to my beloved a song of my beloved for his vineyard.” Theodotion has: “Let me sing to my beloved a song of my beloved to his vineyard.” The song, he says, is not mine but belongs to my beloved, who composed it over his vineyard, or for his vineyard, making it a song of lament. He was both the loved one and the beloved: loved by God his Father, and beloved of the Holy Spirit. The prophetic Spirit shows this when it says, “Let me sing to the loved one a song of my beloved to my vineyard.” In the song he lists his kindnesses to the vineyard, rebukes the vineyard's wickedness, and at the same time foretells what will happen to it. So this beloved of God, who had taken the first people, those of the circumcision, as his lot and portion, laments their destruction out of his surpassing love for humanity. For he says, “The loved one had a vineyard on a horn, in a fertile place.” Symmachus has “on a horn, in a place of olive groves,” and Aquila “on a horn, a son of oil.” They say this refers to the land of Judea because it is fertile and very rich. It is said to be “on a horn” because a royal capital, Jerusalem itself, was established in it, for Scripture usually calls kingdoms horns.

He put a hedge around the vineyard, that is, around the whole people, surely fencing it in with angels. He staked it, propping it up with prophets and holy men. He also planted it with a choice vine, a sorek. What was this vine, if not the divinely inspired Scripture and the word of godliness that was handed down to the whole nation? The vineyard of the Lord is said to be the house of Israel. In another sense the house of Israel is also called a vine, as in “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted its roots.” The people who came out under Moses is shown to be a vine. But the sorek vine planted within the people would be something different, and Symmachus translated it as “choice.” This was the Word of God himself, who taught about himself in the Gospels, saying, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” It was from him that the first people also received the planting of divine teachings. Besides this choice vine there was also a rational planting, which he grafted, as it were, onto the old Egyptian vine. He also builds a tower in the middle of the vineyard, namely the temple, and digs a winepress in it, the altar in front of the temple. Having done everything on his part, the lord of the vineyard then waits for fruit worthy of so much care. But instead of grapes it produced thorns: “rotten things,” according to Aquila, or “unripe things,” according to Symmachus.

After the Holy Spirit has said these things about the lord of the vineyard, the Lord takes up what follows and turns to those who are being judged, saying: “And now, you who live in Jerusalem, and you, man of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard.” He is saying: If there is anyone among you chosen ones, sprung from a royal race and from the tribe of Judah, then you yourselves, citizens of Jerusalem, about which my whole discourse is concerned, be judges of what I have said and of the vineyard's wickedness. Advise me also what ought to be done after so much care, or what ought to have been done that was not done. If you have nothing to say, then listen while I foretell what I am going to do. It is likely that you will profit from learning this and will act in such a way that you do not suffer what is threatened. First, then, I will take away the hedge I gave the vineyard, the wall of my oversight that surrounds it. Once this is done, it will be plundered and trampled by those who choose to plunder and trample it, and it will no longer receive the cultivation it once enjoyed. Thorns will come up in it as in waste ground. And I will command the clouds not to rain on it. By clouds he means the prophets, because their lives were pure and clear. It was through them that the heavenly word was supplied to the people, and the Lord threatens to take them away. He states the reason more plainly, saying: “Because I waited for it to do justice, but it did lawlessness; not righteousness, but a cry.” Every sin that leads to death raises a cry, since the deed itself cries aloud. So it is said, “The voice of your brother Abel's blood cries out to me.”

Some have thought that the present passage foretells what the people dared to do against the Savior. They put thorns around his head and raised a godless cry against him. For this reason complete destruction and utter desolation overtook them, the so-called “wrath to the end.” From that time until now they have been granted no visitation. The ruin of their tower, I mean the temple, remains unrepaired, and the whole nation is left without oversight and without cultivation. Nor do the clouds supply them with the rational rain. Yet in ancient times prophets were with them even in enemy land, as in Babylon and in Egypt, and after the return from there. So now the words “I will command the clouds not to rain on them” have been fulfilled against them in fact. Someone might say that the prophets had ceased even before the Savior came. Still, the temple stood and bodily worship was carried on until his coming. But the present prophecy was shown to have reached its fulfilment [?] only after the final siege, the one carried out by the Romans.

These words may be general precepts for those who suffer from greed toward one another. But they may also follow the sense of what came before. Since he is about to foretell the desolation of the land and the destruction of its men, he rightly pronounces woe on those who do not foresee what is coming. Instead they have given themselves over entirely to injustice and greed, seizing the houses of their neighbors and taking over the fields of those whose land borders theirs. The divine Spirit pronounces woe on them and teaches that they are truly pitiable and wretched, because they paid no attention to nature and so could never satisfy their greed. Then he threatens ruin not only to the houses but to the land itself. It will no longer receive God's blessing but will fall under a curse, so that it yields nothing worth the labor of the farmers who work it. “For where ten yoke of oxen work,” he says, “it will produce one jar, and whoever sows six artabas will produce three measures.” He had said of the vineyard that instead of grapes it would produce thorns, not righteousness but a cry, and instead of justice lawlessness. Very fittingly, then, he lists [?] what the thorns, the cry and the lawlessness are, teaching that they are the people's greed and injustice. The statement that ten yoke of oxen will produce no more than one jar fits closely with the song uttered against the vineyard. In short, the saying that a great deal of sowing and ten yoke of oxen will produce one jar hinted that only a few among them would be found worthy of salvation. A great deal was said about these few in the earlier passages too.

These too were part of the thorns that the vineyard is said to have produced instead of grapes. It seems likely that even after their outrage against our Savior, when they ought to have been mourning because of the wrath about to overtake them, they gave themselves up to carousing, drunkenness and other luxury. That is why the word pronounces woe on them: they did not perceive the evils that were about to overtake them. The meaning of the present passage is rather plain, so I am not free to linger over it, since I am hurrying on to examine the more obscure passages. Still, after rebuking those it has described for what they did, the word seems to threaten them with famine and death, war and captivity. All of these overtook the generation that lived in the time of our Savior. In the literal sense, all these things overtook them under Vespasian and Hadrian, the Roman emperors. In the spiritual sense, they were deprived of the rational bread of life, and even now their souls starve for lack of heavenly food. As the Scripture says about them, “They will return at evening and go hungry like a dog and go around the city.” Having denied the author of life, they have fallen into the death of the soul. Moreover, they turned away from the redeemer of souls held captive, who came to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind. So they were handed over to their spiritual enemies, and they remained in the captivity of souls. Instead of “And those who have been plundered will be fed like bulls,” Symmachus has: “And lambs will graze as they are led away, and sojourners will eat the waste places of the lawless.” This was fulfilled even word for word. The rulers of the people, who led them like a herd of bulls, were carried away into exile and plundered in a foreign land. Then certain sojourners came in, and certain settlers took over their deserted lands and occupied them. This was also shown earlier, where it was said, “Your land: strangers devour it before your eyes, and it is desolate, overthrown by foreign peoples.”

These words also follow from what was said before. They heard many teaching words from the Savior and from his apostles after him, yet they reaped no benefit from them. Instead they persisted in unbelief and in their outrages and kept adding to their sins. They committed a second offence on top of the first and a third on top of the second, and wove still others into these. Therefore Symmachus renders it: “Woe to those who drag their lawless deeds along as with a cord of vanity, and their sin as with the strap of a wagon.” When these same people heard the threats against them from the ancient prophets and from the Savior himself, they did not believe. That is why they said: “Let what he will do come near quickly, so that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel come, so that we may know it.” Here too “the Holy One of Israel” means the only-begotten Word of God.

These words also fit those who were accused first. The same people perverted the sound word and blasphemed the light of the saving gospel. They thought the sweet and nourishing words of our Savior were bitter, and on the other hand they accepted wicked and evil thoughts as good. They put the darkness of error that gripped their souls in the place of light, and they pursued the bitterness and poisonous nature of vice as if it were a sweet pleasure. Even now you can see the children of the Jews behaving this way, turning away from the truth of the gospel and pursuing old wives' tales and the darkness of ignorance. It was by this choice that they denied the Christ of God and asked for Barabbas, placing their lot with robbers and criminals. Moreover, they keep company with godless and impious nations. They welcome the idolaters, but they turn away from the sober and reverent people of Christ and persecute them.

These words would also suit the same people. They contain a general threat against all who think themselves wise, but they also convict those who are accused throughout the whole prophecy. They did not heed the Savior's words, and so they became their own bad teachers, wise in their own eyes and learned in their own sight. Then, as though they were strong and powerful among the people, they wrapped their own souls in drunkenness, stupefied by the darkness of ignorance.
