They also mixed an adulterated drink for others, the so-called sikera, which the other translators have called “intoxicating drink.” They did this by peddling the word of God. That is why it was said to the same people earlier, “Your dealers mix the wine with water.” These same people took bribes and declared the ungodly righteous and the righteous unrighteous. Therefore the word threatens them with what follows, saying:

The word deliberately announces what will happen before it happens, because it intends to check wickedness through fear of the threat. It was likely that the hearers would be brought to their senses by learning in advance what was coming. So he says “therefore” to those who persist in sin. It is not by chance, nor by natural necessity, nor by fate, but because of the outrages already described, that these things will come upon you. For you, the vineyard of the Lord, gathered no grapes or good fruit, but wood, hay and straw, and you multiplied your thorns. For this reason he rightly says: “As stubble is burned by a coal of fire and consumed by an unchecked flame,” so the root of your wickedness will be like fine dust and like what fire has devoured. Your flower too will be scattered like dust very soon: the beauty of the body, that is, and the glory of wealth and the splendor of the whole nation. He says these things will happen to them because, besides what was mentioned before, they refused to accept the law of the Lord of hosts and even provoked the word of the Holy One of Israel. Notice that here too he does not accuse them of idolatry, but of not wanting the law of the Lord of hosts. What law does he mean, if not the one of which it was said above, “For out of Zion will go forth a law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem”? They did not want the law of the new covenant, and they even provoked the living Word of God. Aquila has: “because they cast away the law of the Lord of armies and mocked the saying of the Holy One of Israel.” Symmachus has: “because they rejected the law of the Lord of powers and provoked the word of the Holy One of Israel.” For this reason he adds: “And the Lord of hosts was enraged with anger against his people.” He himself intended them to be his own people and to be called so, but they were unwilling. “And he laid his hand on them and struck them.” All this happened for the reasons already given. He adds to this, saying: “And the mountains were provoked, and their corpses became like dung in the middle of the road. And for all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still raised high.” By these words too he means an attack by enemies and a multitude of the slain, so that even the mountains are filled with dead bodies and the whole land becomes full of their corpses. God's anger against them was persistent and did not turn away even after showing them so much. The hand of God was still raised high against them because of their persistent unbelief. Notice how “his hand is still raised high” is put: it is said as though the wrath of God remains against them even now. The Apostle shows this too when he says, “But the wrath has come upon them to the end.” Next he shows by these words why the mountains and the land were to be filled with their corpses.

He describes a battle line and an attack by nations against the people that did not accept the new law and the word of the Lord of hosts. He shows why the mountains were provoked, or rather, as Aquila has it, “were shaken,” and as Symmachus has it, “were troubled.” He also teaches why their corpses became like dung in the middle of the road: all these things happened to them through the enemies' attack. The enemies did not undertake this attack on their own. God led them, all but dragging and hauling them, to besiege those who had been accused.

This is what the passage means when it says: “Therefore he will raise a signal among the nations that are far off, and will whistle for them from the end of the earth.” By these words it signifies the Roman army, which set out from the western regions against Jerusalem. Whenever it wants to speak of Babylonians or Assyrians, it usually mentions them by name, or else calls them “those from the north,” because they lived in regions further north than the land of the Jews. Here, however, as if writing a history, it calls the multitude of the Roman battle line “nations” that stand far off and dwell at the ends of the earth. Then it describes the fury of warlike men, and vividly sets before us the array of spears and swords and other weapons of war, and of horses and chariots besides. To this it adds, concerning the besiegers: “They rush like lions and stand ready like a lion’s whelps; and he will seize his prey, and will roar like the sound of a surging sea.” Here we should note that it likens the multitude of the enemy to the sound of a surging sea, so that whenever we come upon such things said as though about the sea, we may take from this passage the evidence for interpreting them. These things, then, are said about the besiegers. About those who were to be besieged it says: “And they will look to the earth, and behold, harsh darkness in their distress.” This is the end of the prophecy given in the time of King Uzziah. It began with “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken,” and continued as far as the present passage, which threatens them with the final war, and with the darkness that came upon those who provoked the oracle of the Lord and refused to accept the law of his new covenant. What follows is seen to come after the death of King Uzziah, in the times of Jotham, for he is recorded as having succeeded to Uzziah’s kingdom.

The prophet himself sees with his own eyes the Lord of Sabaoth at his temple, the Lord whom he had so often proclaimed. He recounts what follows in his own person, as he makes clear by adding next: “And I said, ‘Woe is me, for I am stricken to the heart! For being a man and having unclean lips, I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my eyes.’” These words clearly show the man himself narrating what he had seen, and that he had beheld with his own eyes the Lord of Sabaoth, of whom so much had been said in the preceding chapters. He also records the time of the vision, saying: “And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting on a throne, high and lifted up.” I think these words show clearly who the Lord, the Lord of Sabaoth, made known throughout the whole prophecy, really was. The name is interpreted “Lord of armies” or “Lord of the powers.” The prophet presents God as seen. Yet concerning the unbegotten Godhead it is said: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.” And the Savior himself teaches: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” Therefore the Lord of Sabaoth whom the prophet now beheld was other than the unbegotten, invisible and incomprehensible Godhead. And who was this but the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father? He came down below his own greatness and diminished himself from it, and so made himself visible and comprehensible to human beings. In this way he also appeared to Abraham, when he said to him, “To your offspring I will give this land.”

So Scripture adds: “And he built an altar there to the Lord who had appeared to him.” And again: “Abraham was ninety years old, and the Lord appeared to him.” And again: “The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre.” Concerning Isaac it is said: “And he went up to the Well of the Oath, and the Lord appeared to him that night.” And again, to Jacob it is said: “I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God.” Moreover, when he came to Bethel, he and all the people with him, “he built an altar there and called the name ‘House of Bethel,’ for there God had appeared to him.” And again it is said: “God appeared to Jacob once more in Luz.” On another occasion, appearing to him in the form of a man, he said to him: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have prevailed with God, and you are mighty with men.” Then Jacob called the name of the place “Form of God,” saying: “For I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved.” Moses, too, implored the God who was speaking to him, saying: “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me, so that I may see you clearly.” And he answered him: “This word that you have spoken I will also do for you, for you have found favor before me.” Ezekiel also saw the one seated on the cherubim, like the appearance of a man: from his loins downward fire, and from his loins upward like the appearance of amber. From all these passages we learn that the visions granted to those just mentioned were not alike but different. To Moses it had been said: “You cannot see my face, for no one shall see my face and live.” For the face of God the Word, the Godhead of the only-begotten Son of God, could not be comprehended by mortal nature. To Ezekiel the glory of the Word was shown in enigmas. To Abraham he appeared having taken on human form, so that he even came under the oak, had his feet washed, and shared a meal. Likewise in the case of Jacob a man is introduced wrestling with him. Scripture calls him a man, but the one speaking himself says: “Your name shall not be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have prevailed with God.” That is why Jacob said: “For I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved.” The present prophet, too, is attested to have seen his glory. It was therefore the glory of our Savior Jesus Christ that he saw in the passage before us.

So it was with Moses, so too with Ezekiel; he did not grant the visions to them in the same way. The prophet saw the glory of our Savior not, of course, with the eyes of the flesh, but with the eyes of the mind enlightened by the Holy Spirit. For just as the eyes of the body are helped to see things perceptible to the senses by the rays of light supplied from outside, in the same way the eyes of a purified soul, illumined by spiritual light, are able to behold divine things. This is why the Savior taught, saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Isaiah was one of these, and he saw the Lord at the time of King Uzziah’s death. But why did he not see this vision while Uzziah was still alive, but in the year in which he died? Because King Uzziah had dared his unholy deed, the glory of God, which had long overshadowed the house, had withdrawn for the whole remaining time of his life, during which he lived in Jerusalem as a leper. For a leprous king was living in the place. But when he died, Jotham his son succeeded to the kingdom, of whom it is written: “He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the Lord.” Fittingly, then, in that very year in which the leper departed this life and the one pleasing to God received the kingdom, the glory of God returned once more to the house, that is, to the temple. This is what the prophet records, saying: “And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and the house was full of his glory.” The house was filled with glory, but the prophet did not see the Lord inside the house; rather, he saw him sitting on a throne, high and lifted up. This was the one whom holy Scripture presented when it said: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his throne is in heaven.” And the Lord himself made this plain when he said: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet; what kind of house will you build for me? says the Lord.” So the prophet saw with the eyes of the mind the Lord enthroned over the heavenly kingdom, and he says that the house on earth was full of glory, lit up, as it were, by rays of light from heaven above, the flashing brilliance of the divine Word.

Certain incorporeal, divine and supramundane powers, which Daniel also indicated when he said: “A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.” Others have supposed that there are two seraphim. But I, paying close attention to the sense of Scripture, which says that the seraphim stood around him, believe that there are a great many of them. Like a crown, they guard him on every side as the bodyguard of a great king, and they surround the throne itself because they are illumined and given life by him. Because of these seraphim encircling him he was called Lord of Sabaoth, which is interpreted “Lord of the powers” or “Lord of the armies.” Six wings are said to belong to each one, because each is adorned, as if with wings, with innate virtues and powers that soar on high. By these they are borne flying through heaven and the upper air, exercising certain spiritual activities that accomplish things beyond our power to tell. Among human beings the saints of God shared in higher gifts, so as to prophesy what was to come, heal diseases, raise the dead, speak in tongues and words of wisdom, and partake of knowledge. Or again, in the body we make use of natural senses, five in number: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. In some such way, perhaps, it is likely that the nature of angels possesses certain divine powers, which work wonders and are unknown to us; and these the passage has called wings. For of the winds too it is said: “He who walks on the wings of the winds,” and we certainly do not lapse into imagining bodily shapes, as though the winds flapped their wings like birds.

Of the wings around the seraphim, that is, of their powers that accomplish wonderful works, two covered the face—not the Lord’s face, but their own—so that they did not dare to gaze intently at what they beheld. Hence no one has known the Son except the Father alone who begot him. They also covered their own feet, veiling the end of their own course and, as one might say, the steps and deeds of their life, so that they might not stand before their King with uncovered feet. So, covering themselves and as it were hiding the course of their own life, they allowed only their middle state to be seen. And in the only-begotten himself they marveled exceedingly at the wisdom of his intermediate providence and governance, daring to gaze neither on the face of his Godhead nor likewise on his feet, because of the boundless greatness of his endless and incomprehensible nature, but overwhelmed with awe at the ineffable Godhead of the one they beheld.

Symmachus rendered it this way: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and what was at his feet filled the temple. Seraphim were standing above; each had six wings.” He says that what was at his feet filled the temple, since the shrine on earth stood within God’s footstool: “For heaven is his throne, and the earth the footstool of his feet.” So what filled the house on earth was fittingly said to be at the feet of the one who was seen. And the seraphim stood above—above what, but the house? Certainly not above the Lord. The prophet calls himself wretched because he kept silent and did not cry out with the seraphim, nor join them in proclaiming the hymn that declares the holiness of the Lord. He says that the cause of his silence was that he had unclean lips from his dealings with the ungodly people.

“One called to another and cried out, saying: Holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.” They did not utter a single cry, nor did they all send it up together at once; rather, one to another, each displayed his own wonder and amazement at what he beheld. What astonished them most of all was the descent of the glory of God the Word from the higher realms to the lowly. This was what gave them the greatest wonder: that not only was heaven full of his glory, but it already reached as far as the earth, so that the whole earth was filled with his glory. For this is the height of the love for humanity of the one who sits on the loftiest throne yet fills the things on earth as well, among which, in ancient times, the temple in Jerusalem was then being filled at the time of this vision. That is why it was said above, “And the house was full of his glory.” The seraphim cried out in praise, but [?] that the whole earth too was going to be full of his glory; for they marveled exceedingly in foreknowledge of what was to come. And this was in fact fulfilled, in keeping with the prophecies, after our Savior’s coming among human beings. From that time he truly became known to all the nations, and not only the knowledge but also the glory of the teaching about his divinity was proclaimed to the whole earth. For since they saw that his glory was going to shine forth on earth without suffering any loss from the earthly and perishable substance, they fittingly cried out, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth,” proclaiming his holiness not once but many times—indeed, being overwhelmed with awe without number, without limit and forever. Hence one cried to another, each displaying his own wonder to his neighbor.

“And the lintel was raised.” At this cry the lintel of the temple was raised, and the house was filled with smoke. Here the passage hints in a hidden way that, as the whole earth was being filled with his glory, the shrine in that place was going to be stripped bare: with its lintel taken away, it would be left desolate and, given over to fire, would be full of smoke, for smoke is a sign of fire. By these words, then, the passage hinted at the burning that finally overtook the place, after which the whole earth was filled with the glory of the Lord himself—no longer a single house, but countless houses established throughout the whole inhabited world, far better than that one. When the prophet beheld these things following the cry of the seraphim, he fell into anguish, lest he too should perish together with the mass of the people. For he perceived that, while above the house was said to be full of the glory of God, after the cry had been raised it was full no longer of glory but of smoke.

Fittingly, having discerned the change of the house for the worse, he is troubled and anguished lest he be taken away together with those on whose account the place was suffering these things. Moreover, comparing the surpassing glory of the Lord he beheld with mortal nature, he makes confession, and on account of that nature calls himself wretched, saying: “Woe is me, for I am stricken to the heart! For being a man and having unclean lips, I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my eyes.” He confesses that he is unclean, not in his soul, nor even in his whole body, since he was conscious of no unclean deed of his own. He says only that he had unclean lips, as though the rest of his body and his soul were pure, in accordance with the saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” And he had unclean lips from no other source than his dealings with the unclean. For, as is likely, in speaking with unclean men he was compelled to say things suited to their wickedness, and by these he defiled his lips. So exacting was the prophet’s life that he was stricken to the heart even over the smallest thing. At the same time he disparages mortal nature as full of corruption and dishonor. That is why he says, “being a man”; for it was enough to his discredit simply to be a man clothed in perishable flesh.

When the prophet Jeremiah said, “O you who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am too young,” the Lord stretched out his hand and touched his mouth and said to him, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.” Since Jeremiah’s lips did not need cleansing, it was fitting that the Lord’s hand touched his mouth and filled him with prophetic grace. But here Isaiah, who needed cleansing, is approached not by the Lord but by one of the seraphim, sent by the Lord and carrying a coal, and it purifies his lips with the coal. Hence, fittingly, the seraphim, when their name is translated into Greek, mean “those who set on fire” or “burners.” And they seem to me to be purifiers of those who need cleansing. That is why the seraphim brought the purifying coal to the prophet’s lips, one of them having been commanded to do this. This coal was from the altar, perhaps because the Lord, in his love for humanity, fills his altar with such saving and purifying coals. That is why it is said somewhere, “Coals were kindled from him.” And God himself is called a consuming fire by Moses, and the Savior is testified in the Gospels to baptize the worthy with the Holy Spirit and fire. Through all these the passage teaches us that no one can obtain cleansing from sins in any other way than through the divine fire. For “the fire itself will test what sort of work each one has done,” and, it says, “the one who is to be saved will be saved in this way, as through fire.”

Fittingly, then, so great a prophet has his lips cleansed by a coal of fire, and so it is said to him: "Behold, this has touched your lips; it will take away your iniquities and purge your sins." And what iniquities and sins are meant, if not those with which he confesses his lips were filled?

After their cleansing he is accordingly counted worthy to hear a voice from the one seated on the throne, saying: "Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?" This voice, spoken without addressing anyone in particular, was testing the prophet's eagerness, so that he might win the reward of his good choice. That is why it did not order him to go by way of command, but asked in general who was ready to do this. And he, answering with great boldness, since his lips had now been cleansed, said: "Here I am; send me."

And the voice said to him: "Go and say to this people: You will hear with your hearing and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive." What they will see, and whose voice they will hear, he did not make clear to us, leaving us to work it out from the sequence of the passage, whose sense is this: The Lord whom you have beheld and whom you saw with your own eyes, O prophet, this people too will one day see; and the voice which you yourself have now heard, they too will hear at a certain time; yet they will not understand, nor know, nor be willing to accept his grace. By these words the speaker clearly indicated his own coming among human beings.

How it was that seeing they did not see, he explains next, saying: "They have shut their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes." For the Savior, being the light of all, enlightened their souls, so as even to grant sight to the blind; but they shut their eyes so as not to see, and thus seeing they did not see. For when someone has gazed intently and observed carefully, and yet disregards and despises what he sees, or shuts his eyes pretending not to have seen, then though seeing he has not seen. Their seeing, then, came from the grace of the one who appeared to them; their not seeing resulted from their having shut their own eyes and pretended not to see. In the same way a person hears with his hearing and yet does not hear, when he does not understand what is said, or when he pays no heed and despises what is said. This happens when someone makes his ears heavy, as though stopping them up and deafening them. These things, then, the voice of the Lord foretold would befall the Jewish people, and it was fulfilled in deed at the Savior's sojourn among us, when they saw him present with their eyes and did not see, and did not understand when he taught the mysteries of the kingdom. And even now, seeing the glory of the Lord filling all the earth through his churches, they are not pierced to the heart, because of the unbelief they have brought upon themselves. That is why he adds the cause, saying, "and they have shut their eyes": "lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them."

On hearing this the prophet asks: "How long, O Lord?" That is, what end will there be to such blindness of theirs? And he answers: "Until cities are laid waste for lack of inhabitants." By this he signifies the first siege brought upon the region by the Romans after what the Jews had dared to do against the Savior, during which very many cities of the Jews were ravaged under the emperor Vespasian and utterly obliterated, so that neither memory nor name of them remained. In place of "and after these things God will remove men far away," Symmachus rendered more clearly: "and the Lord will make men far off." The passage signifies the captivity which the bulk of the Jewish nation suffered at that same time, and the dispersion in which they were scattered as they fled the calamities pressing upon them. When those, he says, have been removed far away, then those who are left on the land will be multiplied, these being different from the former. Yet they will be such that, compared with the first, they will be reckoned a tiny fraction of that multitude; for, he says, "there will yet be a tenth in it." Then he shows what end awaits even these who are left, adding next: "And again it will be for plunder, like a terebinth and like an acorn when it falls from its husk"; or, as Symmachus has it: "And again it will be for grazing, like an oak and like an acorn which, stripped, stands alone," the passage thus foretelling utter desolation. This too was fulfilled in the times of Hadrian, when the Jews, having endured a second siege, were brought to such a pitch of misery that by laws and imperial decrees they were not permitted even to look upon the desolation of their own mother city from afar.

The passage uses very apt comparisons when it says of the Jewish people that they will be like a terebinth, or like an oak, or an acorn when it falls from its husk. For no longer, it says, will they be the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, nor like the garden of God, nor like a beautiful olive tree, nor like the palm to which the righteous is likened, nor like any other cultivated and useful plant, but like an acorn, and that not intact but fallen from its husk, and like a terebinth, or, according to the other translators, like an oak. Divine Scripture is accustomed to speak of the oak, the acorn, the thicket, and the barren and wildest of uncultivated trees whenever it wishes to signify the foreign nations; and it says that the Jewish people too will be like them, differing in nothing from the foreign nations either in way of life or in manners, and even finding themselves in a worse condition: for those occupy their own lands and bear their natural fruits, while these have been cast out of their own land and do not even produce as those do. For this reason they are compared to the oak, a wild tree, and to the acorn, a fruit that feeds irrational animals, and one fallen from its husk at that.

After this, with the addition of asterisks, he speaks of the holy seed that comes from them, of which it was also said earlier: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." The words "the holy seed is its pillar" are not found in our copies, and so they might seem superfluous. However, Theodotion rendered: "the holy seed is its pillar," Aquila: "a sanctified seed is its propping up," and Symmachus: "a holy seed is its prop." What, then, would he say is the prop or support of that fallen people, if not the holy seed from among them, which did not fall nor suffer a fall like the rest? These would be those who received the saving grace, who heard with their hearing and saw with their eyes, whom the Savior called blessed when he said: "But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear."

The first parts of the prophecy were spoken under King Uzziah. When Jotham succeeded him, at the beginning of his reign the prophet saw the vision set forth above, through which he presented the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God; and having prophesied what has been said up to this point, he stopped, since the time did not call for many words, owing to the pious disposition of the king, whom the people were likely to follow. After the vision, when an interval of sixteen years had passed (for that is how long Jotham reigned), Ahaz became king, the most impious of men, if ever there was one. In his time the present passage is prophesied, containing a prophecy of the birth of the Son of God according to the flesh. And the passage follows a very consistent order, prophesying, after his divinity, the things concerning his birth as a man. The occasion of the prophetic discourse is the uprising of two kings against Ahaz. One of them ruled Syria, Rezin by name, who had Damascus as his royal city; the other ruled the mass of the Jews in the city called Samaria, and this was Pekah son of Remaliah. These two, in alliance, march against Ahaz, who reigned in Jerusalem at the head of the tribes of the Jewish nation. And God delivers Ahaz, because of his very many impieties, together with the people under him, into the hands of these kings, so that they slew a hundred and twenty thousand of their men and led away captive no fewer than two hundred thousand. After such a rout in the first encounter, not long afterward the aforesaid kings, of Damascus, I mean, and of Samaria, again take up arms against Ahaz, intending to take Jerusalem by siege, to kill Ahaz and to set up another king in his place, the one called the son of Tabeel.

This did not escape Ahaz, nor the people under him, who were called the house of David; for that was the name given to those of David's lineage and to all who, in succession from him, ruled and were ruled. When, then, they learned that the aforesaid kings were about to attack them again, their soul was astonished, that is, troubled, or, according to Symmachus, shaken, or, according to Aquila, tossed. Not only the royal family but the whole people was gripped in soul by no small turmoil, at the memory of the former evils they had experienced not long before; and one could liken their soul, shaken and quaking at the news, to the trees of a forest tossed by a most violent wind. But the good Lord, taking pity on them, shows his love for humanity and sends his prophet to exhort Ahaz to keep himself fearless and untroubled; for he would find God his helper now at least, if not before, since the first time it was because God had handed them over to their enemies for their outrageous impieties that they had suffered what was described. And he commands the prophet to meet Ahaz at a certain place that seemed suitable to him, ordering him to take with him the son who was left to him, so that both of them, the prophet himself and his son, who alone out of the whole people seems to have been left over in soul, might approach the king and say what was commanded.

For the prophet's son, too, who had not perished along with the multitude but had survived, had to be trained from then on as his father's disciple in his father's teaching, by being with him as he boldly approached the king and carried out what was commanded. The prophet was to meet Ahaz and say what God commands: "Take care to be quiet"; according to Aquila, "Take care and be quiet"; according to Theodotion, "Pay heed and keep quiet." Trust in the word of God, he says; be unshaken and do not fear, and do not let your soul grow faint because of the two pieces of wood, which have no light at all but are like a firebrand that has gone out and is only smoking; for such are the two kings who keep you in fear and anguish. For even though my disciplinary power, which the oracles are accustomed to call wrath, did previously come upon you to expose those you took for gods, in whom you trusted but who were shown to be nothing when the enemy made you their captives, nevertheless, since my wrath does not last—for I am a good God and struck you the first time for your benefit—now again I will heal all that is sick in you, if you turn from your former error and learn to be truly pious.

These two kings, then, of Syria and of Samaria (Aram being what is now Syria, and Samaria the city now called Sebaste), though they made great threats in forming the plan described, will not carry out their intent. For I myself, the Lord of hosts, as Lord of the divine powers and of the angelic armies in heaven, will not allow their plan to be brought to completion, since I have decided to save you, so that you may have a most vivid perception of my beneficent and saving power. For it is enough for Syria to have Damascus as its head and Rezin as its king, and for Samaria to have Ephraim. (This was the name given to the mass of the nine and a half tribes of Israel, because of the king from Ephraim who reigned over them.) So let it be enough for these also to have Samaria, and for the son of Remaliah to rule it. Learn this too, Ahaz: very soon the kingdom of Samaria will be destroyed, and the people ruled in it will be taken captive together with their kings and deported to the Assyrians because of their exceedingly lawless deeds. And if you wish to know the time as well, know that within sixty-five years the king of the Assyrians will come upon them, take them all, carry them off captive, and resettle them in his own land.

These things God commanded the prophet to say to Ahaz himself and to the people under him, urging them to turn back to him, and to believe and not disbelieve what was said. Therefore he adds to all of it: "And if you do not believe, neither will you understand." Now the word of God was fulfilled before long: for when the foretold time was completed, both Damascus and Samaria, together with their rulers, were captured by the king of the Assyrians. In some such way, then, these events confirmed the prophecy through their outcome. As for the sixty-five years, the Hebrews say that they are exactly completed if one begins to count the time from the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah's reign. For Amos the prophet prophesied at the same time as Isaiah, and Amos was the first to foretell the captivity of Israel that was to come, saying: "And Israel shall be led captive from his land." The same prophet prophesies against Samaria in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, two years before the earthquake. They say that this earthquake is the one that occurred under Uzziah, when he entered the sanctuary to sacrifice and was struck with leprosy, and the fat of the altar was poured out as the earthquake struck. Since, then, Amos prophesied against Samaria and against Jerusalem two years before the earthquake, they say one ought to begin reckoning the sixty-five years from that point. The remaining years of Uzziah come to twenty-seven, since he is recorded to have reigned fifty-two years in all, and it was in the twenty-fifth of them that Amos first prophesied concerning the captivity of Israel; then come Jotham's sixteen years, and likewise Ahaz's sixteen. If the six years of Hezekiah's reign are added, the whole comes to sixty-five years; and indeed it was in the sixth year of Hezekiah that Israel underwent its final captivity. In keeping with these prophecies, God promises to give Ahaz a sign through which he would be saved; but he, being hard of heart and steeped in demonic error, refuses and declines God's sign, showing in this too his unbelief and insubordination. It should be noted that Origen's eighth volume of commentary on the prophet extended up to this point.

In place of "into the depth or into the height," Symmachus says: "Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God; go deep down to Hades or up to the height above"; Aquila: "Inquire for yourself a sign from the Lord your God; go deep down to Hades or rise up above"; and Theodotion: "Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God; go deep down to Hades or go high above." We shall understand the sign "into the depth or into the height" from the writings of Moses. For of the signs performed in Egypt through Moses, of which it is said, "He sent signs and wonders into your midst, O Egypt," some came from the earth, like the frogs, the locusts, the gnats and the dog-fly, and others from heaven, like the hail, the fire and the three days of darkness. One might also say that the sign given under Hezekiah came from heaven, when the sun turned back and the shadow went backward the ten steps. The sign that occurred under Saul was also from the depth, when Samuel, after his death, foretold what was to come. Likewise Jonah was a sign from the depth, coming out of the belly of the sea monster and preaching to the Ninevites, men of a foreign race. Ahaz, then, is told to ask for a sign by which he and the people with him would be saved. And God gives him the freedom to choose the sign: whether he would ask for it to be given him from the depth, and that from no other depth than Hades, or from the height, from the very heights above. But on hearing this he refuses, since he was impious and would not obey God's command, nor did he wish to make trial of God's wonder-working power. That is why he says: "I will not ask, nor will I put the Lord to the test."

Then the prophet, indignant at the man's folly, adds what follows in his own person, saying: "Hear now, house of David: is it a small thing for you to give men trouble? And how do you give trouble to the Lord?" Earlier, too, he called those who traced their descent from the line of David the "house of David," where he said: "And it was reported to the house of David that Aram had come to an agreement with Ephraim." So it is to this same house of David that he speaks the present words, no longer thinking Ahaz worthy of being addressed. And what is his answer to the house of David? "Is it a small thing," he says, "to give men trouble? And how do you give trouble to the Lord?" Aquila translated this as follows: "Hear now, house of David: is it a little thing to weary men, that you weary even my God?" Symmachus: "Hear now, house of David: is it not enough for you to tire men out, that you tire out my God as well?" Theodotion: "And he said: Hear now, house of David: is it a small thing on your part to give men trouble, that you give trouble even to my God?" The sense of the passage is this: Will you never stop causing toil and labour and struggle to God's men—I mean God's prophets—who labour for your salvation? Now you weary even my God himself, whom you do not know, causing him vexation and struggle by refusing to believe his promises. For he, being God, in the overflowing of his love for humankind, commands you to ask him for a saving sign, through which you will be saved and set free from your anguish over the two kings who have marched against you. But you, persisting in your own wickedness, cause him struggle and toil, treating him just as you treat his prophets, against whom in your unbelief you have often devised plots.

Yet even if you are like this, he, being God, is again true to himself and does not let you perish; he will provide the saving sign even though you do not want it. And what is it? A marvellous wonder will one day take place among men, a sign never heard of in all the ages: a virgin will conceive without union with a man, and will give birth to God, the Saviour of the human race. This very God, then, who is to have such a birth, God already gives you now as a saving sign. And this sign will reach both into the depth and into the height: into the depth through the descent he will make as far as Hades, and into the height through his return to heaven.

You, therefore, house of David, from this moment on, at the time of your clash with the enemies now at hand, call upon him, naming him Emmanuel—a name whose interpretation shows the force of the word, for it means "God with us." Believe the sign, then, and take courage. No longer call upon the gods of Damascus, nor enlist helpers for yourself who do not exist; call instead upon Emmanuel, as God who will one day be with men, taking courage in perfect confidence and trusting in the power of the name. Having come to this point, we should notice how precisely the prophecy commands the house of David to call the one who is to be born of the virgin Emmanuel, saying: "And you shall call his name Emmanuel." For you yourself, house of David, who are now present with the prophet and listening to these words, will call the one foretold Emmanuel—as if he were saying more plainly: Call upon him as your helper, continually and often, naming him Emmanuel and invoking him as God who is with you. For although the virgin will conceive and bear him only long ages afterwards—when the prophecy will also be fulfilled, when he will appear as the Saviour of the whole human race, and when he will also bear another name, one that signifies salvation—nevertheless from this moment on, you, house of David, having received a good token from the Lord, call upon him, naming him Emmanuel; for such an invocation will procure salvation for you, if you believe and obey what is said.

Now if it had said, "And they shall call his name Emmanuel," it would have seemed to postpone the whole prophecy to the future, and in that case the passage would have been open to dispute, since the name given to our Saviour, born of the holy virgin, was not Emmanuel but Jesus, according to the oracle of the angel, who said to Joseph: "Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." If, then, our Saviour and Lord, born of the virgin according to the prophecy, received the name Jesus and not Emmanuel, how could the oracle have proved true if it had said, "And they shall call his name Emmanuel"? That is why it was not said that way—for he was not going to be called by this title by all people—but the prophetic word says precisely "and you shall call." For you, house of David, for whose sake these things are prophesied, having received a token of salvation, at the time of your clash with the enemies, call upon Emmanuel, and credit him with your deliverance from the enemies: he will one day be born of a virgin, but he is already God and is with us, and from this moment on he will bestow great gifts on you for your salvation, if, believing the divine command, you continually invoke him as your helper, naming him Emmanuel. For you need something like a charm, so that you do not turn to demons as helpers, but call upon Emmanuel alone and are saved through him. This was he himself who gave these oracles through the prophet. Some, not understanding this, have written "and they shall call" instead of "and you shall call" in the Gospel according to Matthew, although the prophetic text does not read so; for the Hebrew has "and you shall call," and all the translators, in agreement with it, have rendered it so. And instead of "the virgin," the other translators use the term "young woman." But nothing prevents the virgin from also being called a young woman; for it is likely that the holy virgin who conceived the Saviour was not an immature child but a young woman in age, a fully grown maiden. This wonder, then, he foretells will happen in its own time; but to the house of David, which needed a saviour and helper, it was necessarily said: "And you shall call his name Emmanuel." Call upon him, then, he says, not as one who stands far off, but as one who is always present and with those who call upon him.

If you marvel at hearing that God is born, believe also that he will take an infant's food. For he will not appear to men as some kind of phantom, nor will what happens be mere appearance; he will truly undergo such a birth as to share in an infant's food—butter, I mean, and honey—like other babies. This, then, is the human side; but what demonstrates his divinity would be this: that before he knows or prefers evil things, he will choose the good; "for before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness, to choose the good." The passage indicates that even at his very birth Emmanuel was discerning and a doer of good, possessing the power of judgment from then on, shaking off evil and accepting only the good; for such, it says, will be his nature, from his very birth. Or we may say that the text describes the universal judgment that our Saviour is to carry out, in which he will reject every wicked man and accept only the good man as worthy of his grace; and this he will do from that very state of infancy and from his very birth.

Therefore you yourself, Ahaz, or you, house of David, and all of you of the royal line, must expect that a time will come when God will bring upon you, upon the people subject to you, and upon the house of your father—that is, David—days such as you have never yet experienced. This will be especially so from the time when the inhabitants of Samaria drew the Assyrian invasion upon themselves, diverting it and turning it away from its attack on you and drawing it upon themselves; for since they surpassed the inhabitants of Jerusalem in impiety, they were the first to feel the enemy, having turned them away from their attack on the house of David. But it will come at the appointed time, in the days that are to be brought upon you. What these days will be he goes on to teach, saying: "And it shall be in that day that he will whistle," and so on.

By these words the passage signifies an invasion of Egyptians, whom it likens to flies because they delight in the filth and blood of their unclean idolatry. It says they will come against the land of the Jews not without God, but at the bidding of the Lord himself, who rouses them and, as if with a whistle, urges them to come from Egypt—and not from the whole of it, but from a part of it. And the Lord is said to whistle not only for these Egyptian flies already described, but also for the bee that dwells in the land of the Assyrians—that is, a military power, which the passage compared to a bee because it used a warlike sting and at that time ruled over the other nations. These bees too, it says, permitted—or rather urged on—by the Lord's whistle, will come from the land of the Assyrians, and having come they will settle in the ravines of the Jewish nation, in the holes of the rocks, in the caves, in every cleft and on every tree, and so will take all their cities. It is for these lands of yours, then, that you ought to be anxious—you to whom my present words are addressed—and it is the coming of these Egyptians and Assyrians that you must expect and fear, not these two kings, I mean the king of Samaria and the king of Damascus; for they are smouldering firebrands with no fire in them, since their power has been quenched.

This prophecy was fulfilled literally and historically in the time of the first siege of Jerusalem, carried out by the Babylonians, when the Egyptians, those called flies, came—when their king, Pharaoh Necho, invaded the land of the Jews and killed Josiah, king of Jerusalem, a man dear to God. Then, not long afterwards, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, came with a great army, razed their city to its foundations and burned the temple, and having enslaved the whole nation and ravaged the remaining cities, he settled Assyrians as inhabitants of the land of the Jews. It was then, accordingly, that the oracles before us were fulfilled, when the warlike bees, transplanted from the land of the Assyrians into the land of the Jews, which had been reduced to utter desolation, settled there, occupying glens, ravines and caves, because the cities had been laid waste. Next is added:

The passage has foretold what would befall the land of the Jews: how their whole nation, in the prophesied days which it said would be brought upon them, would be handed over at one time to the Egyptian flies, so that the most pious Josiah fell into the hands of the king of the Egyptians, and at another time to the Assyrian bees, which, having mastered the whole land of the Jews, would occupy its deserts, its ravines, its caves and every tree, and would rest there at leisure, without fear and wholly free from care. Accordingly, after foretelling these things, it prophesies in the words before us the overthrow of the empire of the Assyrians and Chaldeans. For the Assyrians held sway over Asia, over all Egypt and Libya, and over most parts of the whole world for some thirteen hundred years in all. Their dominion was great and invincible, and it did not come to an end and was not overthrown until they had besieged Jerusalem, burned the temple of God, carried off the holy vessels and all the votive offerings in the temple to Babylon, and dedicated them to their own idols. For not long after these things were done, the Medes overthrew the Assyrian empire, and Cyrus became the first king of the Persians—he who granted freedom to the Jewish captives and allowed those of them who wished to return to the land of the Jews and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, and who also restored the votive offerings and the priestly vessels taken long before and ordered them to be dedicated in the temple that was being built.

But although these things were accomplished in this way in later times, the prophetic Spirit, through Isaiah, anticipating with foreknowledge what was to come, prophesies in the words before us what will befall the Assyrian empire after the invasion that the bees already mentioned would make from their own land into the land of the Jews. So he says: "In that day the Lord will shave with the great, hired razor of the king of the Assyrians"—not only the head, which once wore long hair when the Assyrians ruled the world, but also "the hair of the feet," that is, their manly appearance, and "the beard," that is, the adornment that by nature befits men. By the razor hired by the Lord the prophetic word meant a hardy race of enemies, through which, it said, God would shave the king of the Assyrians—that is, their whole kingdom and dominion—so that it would be shown to be humbled, unmanned, unadorned and disgraced. This too came to pass by God's will and judgment, when the Medes came and overthrew the Assyrian empire, and the Persians took over dominion over all Asia.

By these words the passage hints at extreme poverty and want, and also at a scarcity and lack of food from grain. For a man to own not herds of cattle but a single heifer, and to keep not flocks of sheep but only two sheep, would be a sign of utter destitution; and further, that everyone left in the land feeds on butter and honey points to a famine of bread. The passage shows this more clearly in what it adds next: "And it shall be in that day that every place where there are a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels shall become waste ground and thorns"; and again: "for all the land shall be waste ground and thorns." Because the land is waste and full of thorns, then, it will have no grain; the survivor will not be fed with the food natural to men, nor will he have wine, but only milk, butter and honey—and these gathered not from a large herd of cattle or from flocks of sheep, but from paltry and pitiful animals: one man will get them from a single heifer, another from two sheep. By these words it seems to foretell, once again, the events of the Babylonian captivity; for history shows that at that time, when the whole nation was deported, few were left in the place, saying: "And the captain of the guard left some of the poor of the land as vinedressers and in the land of Benjamin." And shortly afterwards: "And the people left in Judea, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left—and he set Gedaliah over them." And it adds: "And Gedaliah swore to the men who were with him and said to them: Do not fear the coming of the Chaldeans. Stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you." Some hold that the present passage, by foreknowledge, refers to these very people, hinting at their poverty and want when it says: "Everyone left in the land will eat butter and honey." For those left in the land were the people with Gedaliah, who, it foretells, for lack of food from grain would be fed on milk and butter from a very few animals, the whole country having been turned to waste ground and thorns for lack of men.

After the captivity in Babylon and the return from there, the Jews fell into extreme poverty in respect of God. The prophets failed them from then on, and nothing worthy of record arose among them after the writing of Ezra; moreover, their kingdom itself was dissolved, no one of the house of David ruled among them any longer, and no one rich in God shone forth among them. But even if, it says, there should arise among them a rational man worthy of the name of man, even he would scarcely find among them one heifer or two sheep, because the whole country of his soul had been laid waste; and this man would get from these animals nothing more than an infant's food—milk, butter and honey—so that this is all the man left among them would reap. And again, who among them would be the one left? Only some rare individual, rescued from the ruin of the many and preserving the character of a rational being, who, if ever he made disciples through the Jewish teaching, might gain one or two pupils in it, like a heifer of the herd and two sheep—gentle and clean animals. Yet even these he will find only rarely, because all the rest will turn into wolves or dogs or wild beasts or venomous reptiles. So this man left among them, having with difficulty found perhaps one heifer or two sheep, will rear them, and the fruit he receives from them will not be solid or suitable as food for mature men, but milky and fit for infants, since they cannot provide anything better than this because of the infancy of their minds. And even this man rarely reared the heifer and the two sheep, because of the desolation that had taken hold of the souls of their multitude, which the passage presented when it said, "for all the land shall be waste ground and thorns," and again, "where there are a thousand vines, they shall become waste ground and thorns." This they have suffered because of the invisible enemies that have besieged their soul, about whom it is said next: "With arrow and bow they shall enter there, for all the land shall be waste ground and thorns." And not only will all their land be waste ground and thorns, but also every mountain that was once ploughed, where there was no fear to be expected because of the height and elevation of the ground. It too will become waste ground, so that the waste and thorns bring forth no fruit that people need for food, but only useless growth, fit for sheep to graze and cattle to trample.

Having finished describing what will happen in the days enumerated—of which it was said, "But God will bring upon you and upon your people and upon the house of your father days that have not yet come"—the passage takes up again the thought about the birth of Emmanuel, concerning whom the house of David was urged to call upon the name of Emmanuel in place of a charm, taking courage and believing that through him they would be saved from the two kings pressing upon them. And it takes this up again of necessity. For since it had taught that Emmanuel would have a strange birth, foreign to mortal nature—that he would be born not of man and woman, but of an undefiled young woman, a virgin who had known no marriage—it is altogether fitting that here the Lord himself reveals, no longer to Ahaz nor to the house of Judah but to the prophet alone, the mystery of Emmanuel's ineffable birth, and how the virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son. Making this plain, the Lord himself says: "And I went in to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son." And so that these things should not reach the ears of everyone then living, but be kept in a secret writing, he commands the prophet to take a new and large volume—or a "roll," a "skin," or a "scroll," according to the other translators—and to write in it "with a man's pen," that is, in the script customary and known to men. For there is another writing of God, not written with a man's pen, but by the power of the Word of God, who enrols the worthy in the book of the living. But now he commands the prophet to write in it with a man's pen, "to make a swift plundering of spoils." He himself, indeed, was the one who long ago bound the strong one, the devil, and plundered his spoils.

…through the power of Emmanuel. For the time is already drawing near and is at hand when the two kings mentioned before, the king of Damascus and the king of Samaria, will be despoiled, as the king of the Assyrians attacks them through the secret title of Emmanuel. He commands the prophet to write the things about to be spoken on the new and large scroll, and to do this before two men as witnesses, one a priest and the other a prophet. The history mentions the priest Uriah as serving God as priest in the time of Isaiah the prophet, and it also mentions Zechariah, who lived under King Hezekiah. The book of Chronicles says: “And Hezekiah sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the fear of the Lord.” “Make these two men witnesses for me,” he says, “when you take the new scroll and are about to write in it with a man’s pen, with the witnesses present who bear witness in me. Then write these words in that scroll: ‘And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.’” It is the Lord who gives the oracle who says these things. We must pay careful attention to the wording of the whole passage, which joins “And the Lord said to me” directly to the words spoken in his own person: “And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.” This is what the one who gives the oracle ordered the prophet to write in the new scroll. Since it had been said above, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” and what follows, he now necessarily makes clear in the present passage how this would come about, when the Lord himself says, “And I went to the prophetess,” in place of “I myself will go to the prophetess.” He calls the virgin a prophetess because she shared in the Holy Spirit, as the one who spoke to her said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” This power of the Most High, then, saying through the prophecy, “And I went to the prophetess,” describes future things as though they had already happened, according to a certain prophetic custom.

“I myself will go to the prophetess, O prophet, and so she will conceive and bear a son. And you, O prophet, name him from now on: Quickly despoil, swiftly plunder. For even before his birth in the flesh he will bring complete destruction on these two kingdoms that now press upon the house of David. He will take the power of Damascus and carry off the spoils of Samaria. And he will do this through the king of the Assyrians. Speak these things only before the witnesses named, and hand them down in writing, so that they may be preserved for later times too, since the new covenant is going to contain the fulfillment of what is prophesied.”

These further things too are prophesied on the same subject, which is why it says, “And the Lord spoke to me yet again.” For in addition to what was said before, he says these things also to the prophet, but not to the whole people, teaching that the people did not do what they had been commanded. They had been ordered not to fear the two smoking firebrands, nor to dread the two kings already mentioned, but only to call upon Emmanuel, trusting in God’s command. This they were unwilling to do; they preferred to be slaves to those kings, enemies though they were, rather than to trust in God and call upon Emmanuel. That is why it was said to the prophet: “Because this people does not want the water of Siloam that flows gently.” And what was this water of Siloam but the Emmanuel promised to them, who is a spring of living water welling up to eternal life, a spring of water that flows gently? For at that time he still went along with the people hiddenly and quietly, wishing to water their souls and watch over them, and was not yet proclaimed to all the nations. That is why he is fittingly called the water that flows gently and the spring of Siloam, which means “Sent.” But the people accused here by the Lord, who would not believe the command and call upon Emmanuel, who was the water of Siloam that flows gently, are left bereft of him.

Since, then, being faithless, they preferred to submit themselves to the king of Damascus and the king of Samaria, enemies though they were, rather than to do what they had been commanded, the word therefore threatens that they will be subject not to those kings but to the king of the Assyrians. He calls him the water of the river, strong and abundant: in contrast to the water of Siloam that flows gently he has set the strong and abundant water of the river, and this was the king of the Assyrians. That is why he says that he will come up into Judea too and walk over all their walls, and take away from Judea any man who could lift up his head or was able to accomplish anything, so that they would no longer have a head from then on, that is, rulers and kings. He foretells that so great a multitude of enemies will come as to fill the whole breadth of the land of Judea. This came to pass in deed, according to the history, in the times of Jeremiah the prophet, when Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, came and brought what had been foretold to its fulfillment.

These things too depend on the subject of Emmanuel. Indeed, the passage begins with Emmanuel, which is “God with us”: the Hebrew text has “Emmanuel” where we have “God with us.” And again toward the end, where it says, “And whatever word you speak will not stand among you, for God is with us,” “Emmanuel” is said once more. So the prophet, having convicted those mentioned of being unwilling to call upon Emmanuel and so prevail over their enemies, himself calls upon Emmanuel, setting himself apart from those previously accused, whom he had threatened with the invasion of the Assyrians. He threatened the faithless with the things described above, but the prophet himself invokes Emmanuel, speaking in his own person and that of those like him: “God is with us.”

Then he turns his thought to the calling of the nations and urges them to recognize Emmanuel, saying, “Know, you nations.” Know what, you nations? Emmanuel himself. For the people of the circumcision neither knew him nor understood, nor were they willing to believe the prophecy; they did not even yield or submit to the command. “But you, the nations, take hold of the knowledge of the one who is prophesied, and once you understand him, do not dare to resist, but let yourselves be overcome and yield. Listen to the command, all you who dwell to the end of the earth; and you who are strong and mighty among you, give way to the word, overcome and yielding. Do this willingly, knowing that even if you are unwilling, you will be defeated against your will. But if, resisting God’s call, you devise schemes and plots against the word that calls you, you will be shown to labor in vain. For the Lord will scatter every counsel you take, and whatever word you speak, threatening to do something against Emmanuel, will not stand for you. And we say this because Emmanuel is with us.” These things, then, are said to the nations in the person of the prophets; but the word turns again and says the following about those who had not yet been willing to call upon Emmanuel.

Having called on the nations to recognize Emmanuel, the word passes on to the Jewish people, convicting them of disobeying the strong hand. For when they were called by it, they ought to have obeyed, but they disobeyed and spoke against it. That is why he says: “Thus says the Lord to those who disobey the strong hand, and who walk not in the straight royal road that is dear to God, but in the course of the way of this people: Do not say,” he says, “that the word is hard which says you must depart from the course of this people.” This people thinks it hard, but you who have departed from the course of this people, do not say that it is hard. “And if those of the faithless people plot against you as deserters, do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled when you are driven out and persecuted by them; only sanctify the Lord of hosts and take him as your fear.” For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and through it every fear of men is driven away.

Symmachus rendered it this way: “Thus,” he says, “the Lord spoke to me as with strength of hand, and he turned me aside from walking in the way of this people, saying: You shall not say ‘Conspiracy’ about everything this people calls conspiracy.” What he means is this: the Lord, taking hold of his own prophet—me—with his own hand, turned him aside and set him apart, so that I would not walk the same road as this faithless people that would not call upon Emmanuel. And he turned me aside saying, “You shall not say ‘Conspiracy.’” For these people, who refused to call upon Emmanuel, regard your withdrawal from them as a conspiracy, but you will not say so.

If you have him alone as your fear and trust in him, take courage, knowing well that he will be a sanctuary for you, so that you will no longer need the bodily sanctuary. Among the Hebrews the temple that once stood among them, and its innermost parts, was called the sanctuary. So for you, who are driven out by those people but trust in the Lord, the sanctuary will not be the bodily temple; it will be the Lord himself, sanctifying you, if you trust in him. Therefore fear nothing from this people; withdraw from them, but believe in the one who is your fear and take courage in him. For you will have him as a sanctuary, and you will not stumble against him as against a stone of stumbling, nor meet him as a rock that makes one fall. That is what he will be to the house of Jacob because of their faithlessness. For those in Jerusalem, dwelling as in a snare and in a pit, because they disobeyed the strong hand of the Lord, had him as a stone of stumbling and a rock of falling, though he is not such by nature; to those who believe in him he is a sanctuary. You see how he calls the Lord himself a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. He says that he will be such to those who dwell in Jerusalem and to the two houses of Israel, but he teaches that to those who have believed in him he will be a sanctuary. How, then, did Emmanuel become a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to the people mentioned, if not through his conception from a virgin? That is why the divine Apostle, teaching this, said: “To Jews a stumbling block, and to Gentiles foolishness.” There were two houses of Israel: one of those who ruled among them, the other of those who were ruled. To these two houses, that is, to the whole nation together, rulers and ruled, he says that the Lord himself will be a snare and a stumbling block.

In place of “Then those who seal the law so as not to learn it will be made manifest,” Symmachus translated it thus: “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my teachings”; Theodotion: “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my taught ones”; and Aquila likewise: “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my taught ones.” The Lord says this after what was said before about the two houses of Israel and about the inhabitants of Jerusalem: when what was foretold has happened to them, he says, then bind up the testimony, seal the law among my taught ones. For there will no longer be any need of the law of Moses or of the testimonies in it, because from then on he hands on a new teaching through the new covenant to those taught by him, that is, to all those from the nations who have been called to his teaching. They will then be made manifest as sealing the law so as not to learn it. For those who have received the gospel and have been taught to live according to the new covenant, as though setting seals upon the law, lay it aside as no longer useful, because what is better has been set beside it. These same people, waiting for the grace that comes through Jesus Christ, will say: “I will wait for God, who has turned his face away from the house of Jacob, and I will trust in him.” That is why he becomes their sanctuary, in keeping with the promise he made when he said, “And if you trust in him, he will be a sanctuary for you.” According to Symmachus: “And they will say, I will look for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will wait for him.” Who will say these things, he teaches when he adds: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.” Now the children of the Jews were bodily, born of man and woman; but the children of the Lord himself who gives this oracle were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh but of God, since the Father has given him such children, who no longer attend to the law given through Moses but wait for the Lord and trust in him. And not only have these children been given to me wondrously by God, he says, but also a great many other signs and wonders, which will take place in the house of Israel in the times prophesied. According to the other translators it says: “Behold, I and my children, whom the Lord has given me for signs and for wonders in Israel.” For these are the children, he says, whom God has given me so that through them signs and wonders may be done in Israel. This too was fulfilled when the Savior gave his children, that is, his disciples and apostles, authority to heal every disease and every sickness, and charged them to go to the lost sheep of the house of Jacob, doing signs and wonders. That is why he added: “Heal the sick, cleanse lepers.” All these things were done by the Lord of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. Who this was, and what his dwelling place on the heavenly mountain is like, has been shown in what preceded; of it the Apostle says: “You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.”

Having spoken first about the children of Christ—I mean his apostles and disciples—and about the signs and wonders accomplished through them, by which the calling of the nations also came about, the word fittingly teaches what follows to the young and new people formed through Christ from the nations, as though saying to them: “Hear this, you who are taught by me, who have turned away from the polytheistic error of the nations. If any of those long known and familiar to you, fathers or relatives, urge you to go back to your former error and to admire the divinations, oracles and the like performed among them by demons, do not be persuaded by their counsel. Do not admire demons that speak from people’s bellies, the so-called pythons, nor those believed to rise up from the earth through certain arts of sorcery; but honor your own Lord alone. For if each nation, though in error, still clings to its own god, what should those do who have received the knowledge that is free from error, but seek their own God, and not busy themselves with the dead, nor ask those deprived of all life about the affairs of the living?” For that is foolish and stupid indeed.

Since, then, you have the word of God and the law of the gospel given to you as a help, learn from it whatever you wish to know and walk by it, since it can never be turned aside from the truth by gifts. For the law of God is not of a nature to be perverted by money, as tends to happen in the divinations of the superstitious, where many of their sorcerers practice their arts and often sell the oracles they invent to deceive those who consult them. The law of God is not like that; being true, it will itself teach you the truth about all things.

But if you do not attend to the law of God, a harsh famine will come upon you; and when you are hungry, you will grieve and speak evil of the ruler and of the ancestral customs; and they will look up to heaven above and look down to the earth below, and behold, dire perplexity, affliction and distress and darkness, so that they cannot see; and the one in distress will not be at a loss until the appointed time. These things are said to those who are unwilling to search out the law of God, walk by it and honor it alone. For he says: you have heard once and for all that he has given a law as a help, a law impartial and incorruptible; those who walk by it must turn away from every error worked by demons and not be deceived by oracles or divinations, for the law of God suffices you in place of everything. But if anyone falls away from it, he will be handed over to famine—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. For if someone becomes a transgressor of the divine law and an apostate from it, led astray by those who hold out oracles and demonic divinations, a famine of rational nourishment will overtake him, along with bewilderment and exasperation, so that he falls into blasphemous thoughts, cursing the one who was formerly his king, whom he also used to call his God. According to the Seventy, those handed over to this famine, since their souls are not fed with the life-giving nourishment of the law, will grieve and speak evil of the ruler and of the ancestral customs, as though the ancestral customs—that is, the ordinances of the Church handed down to us from our fathers—contained nothing venerable. They will speak evil of these and blaspheme the ruler who leads the divinely inspired readings, the Word, Christ of God himself, the ruler of the law of the gospel. That is why their souls will be wrapped in darkness, since they have become apostates from the divine law and have given themselves over to deceptions from outside. They will also be gripped by affliction and perplexity, so that all of them, looking up to heaven and gazing down at the earth, will no longer see light, but only affliction and distress. The words “and the one in distress will not be at a loss until the appointed time” Symmachus rendered thus: “faintness and distress and darkness and banishment; for there is no faintness for one who has no affliction.” He says these things will befall those who have abandoned the divine law, who have slipped away after receiving the first grace and been dragged back again into the error of the polytheistic nations.

We will say that this section of the prophecy depends on the words about Emmanuel. In the earlier passages what was said concerned those who disbelieved him, but in the passage now in hand, quite consistently, what is set out is said about those who received him. Who were the first to receive the Christ of God may be learned from the Gospel, where this is said: “Now when Jesus heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, light has dawned.’ From that time Jesus began to preach and to say, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’” So the holy Gospel records the outcome of the [?], while the prophecy foretells what was going to happen. It is to those in Galilee, then, that the good news is first proclaimed; for it was necessary not to pass over in silence the region where Emmanuel, once he had appeared to men, was going to spend his time. The region was Galilee, to which the oracle proclaims a saving drink, saying: “Drink this first, act quickly, region of Zebulun and land of Naphtali.” These are two tribes, Zebulun and Naphtali, which received Galilee as their lot in the division of the land made under Joshua son of Nun. But since it happened that Greeks also lived in this region among the two tribes—for not only Jews but by then foreigners too inhabited the land—the word necessarily mentions them as well, saying: “and the rest who dwell along the coast and beyond the Jordan.” And very precisely, since there is also another Galilee, he adds: “those who dwell along the coast and beyond the Jordan.” By “the coast” he means the whole region around Lake Gennesaret, which the Gospel refers to as a sea; it says: “As Jesus passed along by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers.” It was from there that the disciples of our Savior came. Capernaum and Bethsaida and Chorazin and the other villages around the lake of Tiberias that the Gospel mentions are pointed out even now. But this Galilee, in which the Christ of God spent most of his time, also lies beyond the Jordan; that is why the saving drink and the great light are proclaimed first to those who live in it. The Savior gave a visible image of this life-giving drink when, at a wedding being held in Cana of Galilee, he worked his first miracle, the changing of water into wine. That is why the Evangelist remarked: “This, the first of his signs, Jesus did in Cana of Galilee.” It is precisely this that the prophecy signifies when it says: “Drink this first, act quickly.”

For he wants those who have been counted worthy of the great light of the saving appearance of God to yield, through their works, the fruit of the spiritual drink. That is why he says: “O people who sit in darkness, behold a great light; you who dwell in the land of the shadow of death, light will shine upon you.” And who were those in darkness and the shadow of death, if not those who were formerly held fast in ignorance of God and enslaved to the death of the soul? Those who, before Christ shone forth, were ignorant of the true light were in darkness. Those who committed sins leading to death were in the shadow of death, according to the saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die.” But as long as someone who sins unto death remains in the present life, he has not been so completely swallowed up by death that he cannot change and be saved. Yet he has not been entirely freed from it either, and that is why he is said to be in the shadow of death. To these, however, the one foretold in the preceding words shone first, and he gave them the grace of the great light.

In this region he first won a very large people, so much so that he chose the apostolic band from among them. That is why the next words are: “The greater part of the people, whom you brought down in your gladness.” In place of “whom you brought down,” the other translators rendered “you magnified.” If everyone who lived in Galilee had believed in the Christ of God, the present passage would have mentioned them all. As it is, a great many believed, but even more remained in unbelief. So it is fitting that it speaks of “the greater part of the people” as having shared in the saving gladness.

In its plain sense, this refers to our Savior's deed recorded in the Gospel. On one occasion he fed a crowd of about five thousand men from five loaves in the region in question, and on another he fed four thousand men, not counting children and women, from seven.
