That is why Symmachus renders it: “They will rejoice with gladness before you, as with gladness at harvest.” For people who are fed at harvest usually feast together, gathered in one place. In the spiritual sense, our Savior's apostles and their successors, and those who preside over his churches to this day, shared in a divine gladness before their Savior as they labored like reapers. They were workers in the harvest of the nations, as he himself showed when he said: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few; ask the Lord of the harvest, then, to send out workers into his harvest.” For truly, our Savior's disciples and apostles were few, and so were those who lead his churches in like manner, compared with the great and abundant harvest of the nations. These same men divided among themselves the spoils of polytheistic and demonic error, which the Savior himself gave them as plunder. That is why the earlier name was given: “Quickly despoil, swiftly plunder.” For at that time he overthrew the error of idolatry, set free the souls of men that he had formerly taken as spoil, and distributed them to his disciples and apostles and to their successors, to care for and tend them. Those who received them rejoiced like people who rejoice at harvest and like people who rejoice as they divide spoils. They were filled with gladness at the size of the crop in each church.

They rejoiced because the yoke that once lay upon the spoils had been taken away, along with the rod upon the necks of those same spoils. For a heavy yoke lay upon the souls enslaved to the devil, and a deadly rod bent their necks and made them bow down. With these removed, it was natural for those who divided these spoils to rejoice. He makes clear in the next words how the yoke and the rod lying on their necks were lifted from them: “For he has scattered the rod of the exactors.” In place of “of the exactors,” Aquila rendered it this way: “the yoke of his burden and the rod of his shoulder, the scepter of the one who exacts.” Symmachus has: “the yoke of his burden and the rod of his shoulder, the rod of the exactor has been defeated.” Theodotion likewise rendered “of the exactor.” They use the singular to indicate the one who demands and exacts, namely the devil. He was continually exacting the souls of men, demanding as a kind of tribute the sins that were supplied to him. But the one who stripped him bare scattered both this rod of the exactor and the heavy yoke. It is also likely that many others worked with the devil, and these too were among those who made demands on his behalf, for many were exacting from the human race. He took away the yoke and the rod and did these things against them “as on the day of Midian.” The story is found in Judges. It tells how, in Gideon's time, the enemy was defeated not by weapons but by an invisible and divine power. So, just as the enemy was defeated by a hidden hand at Midian, he says that now too the rod has been scattered — the rod of the exacting devil and of those with him who exact the souls of men.

“And they too, being defeated, will repay every garment gathered by deceit, and clothing with exchange.” The devil had plundered the soul's adornment and its robe, the tunic of virtue that it wore, when he held it in his power and left it naked and disgraced. The hostile powers with him also took it as their due, using deceit against it. So the prophetic Spirit fittingly says that they will all repay: “For they will repay every garment gathered by deceit, and clothing with exchange.” And these same beings who once exacted the souls of men, when they are about to repay everything at the time indicated, “will wish that they had been burned with fire” rather than see the Savior of all dwelling among men.

Who this is, he shows in the next words: “For a child has been born to us, a son also has been given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel.” This was the same one who was called son and child and Emmanuel. This is now the third time in the same prophecy that he is designated both son and child. The first time: “Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel,” to which he added: “For before the child knows good or evil.” The second: “And I went in to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son,” to which he added: “For before the child knows how to call father or mother.” The third comes in the passage before us: “For a child has been born to us.” This child, then, and this son, given by God as a gift to us who have believed in him, bears many names in the present passage. He is called Angel of Great Counsel. And yet this would be a modest name, even though it rises above not only every mortal nature but also the angelic. For he did not simply call him an angel, but the Angel of Great Counsel. And what would this great counsel be, and whose, if not the counsel of the great God concerning the calling and salvation of all the nations? Our Savior came as its angel, to serve the Father's loving counsel. For in the Hebrew scripture he is honored with titles greater than that of an angel. And he is said to bear the rule upon his shoulder. The rule of the prophesied child, that is, his glory and honor and kingdom, and his rule over all, is upon his shoulder. This is to be understood as the arm of the divinity within him. Because of this divinity he has been named Angel of Great Counsel, since he alone knows the secrets of the Father's counsel and has become its messenger to those who are worthy. We said that in the Hebrew reading he has been granted a title greater than that of an angel. Symmachus translated it this way: “And his name will be called Wonder, Counselor, and Mighty, Powerful, Father of the age, Ruler of peace.” Aquila has: “And his name is called,” he says, “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty, Powerful, Father still, Ruler of peace.” And according to Theodotion: “And he called his name Wonderful, Counseling, Mighty, Potentate, Father of the age, Ruler of peace.”

Where we have “Mighty,” the Hebrew word contains El, which signifies God. In many places in scripture El is used of God, and it has been used in the same way in the passage before us, so that by this word the child born to us is also proclaimed God. If, then, in the present prophecy about the child born to us and the son given to us, he is also named El in the Hebrew, along with the other names, it is clear that the prophecy reveals him to be God as well, since in the Hebrew language the phrase is El gibbor. Aquila rendered it “mighty, powerful,” as did Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered it “mighty, potentate, guardian.” In these renderings they presumably [hesitated?] to place the name of God on a child being born [?]. But we would not be wrong to translate it “mighty God,” since we have been shown that El translates as “God.” So we boldly call him this. The Hebrew El gibbor was rendered “mighty, powerful.” And Emmanuel, who includes El in his own title, has received the addition “with us”: “God with us.” Such titles of the child presented here show that his nature is greater than that of a man. That is why, I think, the Seventy, wary of the extraordinary and surpassing greatness of such titles, passed over them in silence and summed them up in their own sense and in a different way: “And his name is called Angel of Great Counsel.” We will understand how he is called Father of the age to come if we compare Adam, who became the father of the present age and of the mortal human race. But “as in Adam we all die,” according to the Apostle, “so in Christ we shall all be made alive.” Since, then, Christ is the firstfruits of the new age, “then those who belong to Christ at his coming, then the end,” for this reason he could be called Father of the age to come. He could also be called Ruler of peace, for “he himself is our peace,” having made peace among the things on earth and the things in the heavens, and having reconciled the world to his own Father. After these words comes: “For I will bring peace upon the rulers, and health to them.” Which rulers, if not those appointed to rule his church with him? I mean his disciples and apostles, and those who succeeded them throughout the whole world. He gave them health of soul and peace with one another when he said to them: “My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.”

And he adds: “Great is his rule.” In place of this, Symmachus rendered: “For his instruction has been made full.” Then: “And of his peace there is no boundary,” or “there is no end” according to Aquila, or “there is no limit” according to Theodotion. You will understand what his great rule is when you look at his church throughout the whole world. You will understand it even more if you consider the testimony of the holy Apostle about him, where he says: “according to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every rule and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named.” So great, then, is the rule of our Savior. And again: “Of his peace there is no end,” for it is endless, ageless and unbounded. That is why it is said: “In his days righteousness will rise, and an abundance of peace.” Having said so much about the child who was born, he adds this about him as well: “Upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, to set it right.” Observe carefully that it does not say he will sit on the throne of David. It says simply “upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, to set it right,” and we supply the thought that he will come to set right the throne of David and the fallen tent of David. The kingdom of David had been overthrown and destroyed from the time of the people's captivity in Babylon, yet there were prophecies declaring that the throne of David would shine like the light of the sun over the whole inhabited world. He came and fulfilled this very promise. He was born according to the flesh from the seed of David, and he illuminated the souls of men and strengthened his kingdom among all the nations of the whole world. For it was among these that he restored the throne of David, not with weapons and spears, but in judgment and in righteousness. And he did this “from now and forever.” “From now” signifies a definite beginning in time, which indicated the moment of his coming among men. “Forever” shows that his kingdom is infinite and enduring.

It should be noted that the first prediction about the one prophesied showed that he would be born of a virgin. The second, as if someone had asked how this would come about, brought in the Lord saying: “And I went in to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.” The third no longer mentions the virgin's pregnancy or the manner of the miraculous conception that came from God. Since we have already learned these things, it goes through what concerns his Child, teaching us the hidden truths of the theology concerning him. Those of the circumcision who refuse to accept our Savior claim that all these things are said of some ordinary child, but I do not know how they could make that case. His works bear witness to him, and the outcome of events sets its seal on the words. “The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do these things.” What zeal, if not the good zeal, fitting for him, with which he was zealous to save all who had been oppressed by the devil and dragged down into godlessness?

Now that the subject of Emmanuel has been brought to a close, the discourse returns to the prophecy about Israel, which was the reason Emmanuel was mentioned in the first place. The people ruled from Samaria, called Israel, were advancing with the king of the Syrians as their ally to besiege Jerusalem, and Ahaz was in anguish over the attack of the two kings. The prophet is commanded to declare the things recorded, among which were the things about Emmanuel. Having spoken at length about him, he now takes up again the prophecy about Israel, by which I mean the people ruled from Samaria. In it he says, in effect: the Lord sent death, or a word declaring wrath, not upon Israel but upon Jacob, the less perfect part of his people. He had not sent it primarily upon Israel, but upon Jacob, as the inferior and more bodily part. But the death, or word declaring wrath, that was sent upon Jacob also overtook those reputed to be the better among them, I mean those called Israel, as deserving wrath and death too, and it came upon them. You can learn the difference between Jacob and Israel from the first patriarch. By his birth in the flesh he was called Jacob, but when he advanced in godly progress and was counted worthy of converse with God, he was given the name Israel by the one who spoke to him and said: “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel will be your name, for you have prevailed with God.” Fittingly, then, in this passage he names the more irrational and bodily part of the Jewish nation Jacob, and calls those reputed to be more rational among them Israel. So the passage accuses even those reputed to be better, as having also become deserving of death. That is why it says: “The Lord sent death upon Jacob, and it came upon Israel.”

Who Israel was, he shows in the next words: “And all the people of Ephraim will know, and those who dwell in Samaria, who say in insolence and with a lofty heart: ‘The bricks have fallen, but come, let us hew stones and cut down mulberry trees and cedars, and build ourselves a tower.’” These were the inhabitants of Samaria. They bore the name Israel and were called the people of Ephraim because they were ruled by kings from the tribe of Ephraim. They mocked and belittled Jerusalem, saying that it was built of bricks and had roofs of mulberry wood, or of sycamore-fig according to the other translators. Then, as if they themselves were building a better city, they promised to build with hewn stones and cedars, and to raise up a tower for themselves in Samaria in place of the temple in Jerusalem.

Since they had dared to act so arrogantly, the passage goes on to threaten them: “And God will dash down those who rise up against Mount Zion, against him, and will scatter his enemies.” Because they behaved so insolently against Mount Zion and against the God who was honored there, he threatens to humble them and dash them down, as if from the great height of their pride. For those who rose up against Mount Zion were in fact committing impiety against God himself. He says that he will humble them and dash them down, and not them alone: he will scatter all his enemies. By this he means those in Damascus who were allied with Israel, as explained earlier. He also promises to scatter all those from the other nations who rise up against Mount Zion and the God honored there. Some of these were from the east, others from the setting of the sun, and the Greeks lay between them. For all of these devoured the Israel already mentioned with their whole mouth and dragged it down into the error of their idolatry, and they promised to help and fight alongside those who rose up against Mount Zion. You would not be wrong to say that those who fall away into apostasy through the wisdom of this age, the deceit of the Greeks, are devoured by the whole mouth of the Greeks and the foreigners. Such was the Israel accused in this passage. That is why the anger of God was roused against them and his high hand was made ready for wrath against them. But even then they did not turn back or seek the Lord of hosts. Instead, by their hardness and impenitent heart, they stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath. This does not mean that God is angry as one swayed by passion. Rather, the punishment against them is called wrath, according to the usage of scripture.

In place of “And the Lord took away from Israel,” Aquila has “and the Lord will destroy,” Symmachus “and the Lord will utterly destroy,” and Theodotion “and he will take away.” They used the future tense, since God was going to do these things. He foretold them before they happened in order to turn his hearers to repentance, so that they might not suffer what was threatened. He says that he will do all the things already mentioned, which are clear, “in one day,” that is, at one and the same time. By saying “head and tail” he alluded to an irrational animal, since having a tail is proper not to a human being but to irrational animals, and he compared the people to them. Or “head and tail” means the rational and the irrational, or the ruler and the lowest of those ruled. He made this clear when he said “great and small.” In place of “and those who admire persons,” Symmachus rendered “and the venerable.” So this venerable person and the elder can be the head, and the tail is the prophet who teaches lawless things, being, as it were, the last member of an irrational animal. The passage threatens that these will be taken away and destroyed at one time. Those who speak otherwise and call the people blessed are false prophets. He says they are deceivers who lead the people astray in order to swallow them up, carrying off gains from them for themselves.

That is why he lays such threats upon them: “Therefore the Lord will take no pleasure in their young men, and will have no mercy on their orphans and their widows,” and so on. God threatens to do these things as a good farmer of souls, so that the lawlessness in them may be wiped out like a rank, overgrown weed consumed by fire. He indicates this when he says: “And lawlessness will burn like fire, and will be devoured by fire like dry grass; and it will burn as in the thickets of the forest, and will devour everything around the hills.” According to these images, he says, the wrath of God will come upon the people already mentioned and cause great confusion among them. Brother will rise against brother, no one will spare his neighbor, and all will treat one another as enemies and foes. The strife and civil war blazing among them will go so far that even the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh will rise against each other and devour each other's arms. Yet they were born of one father, Joseph, they lived under the same kingdom, and they inhabited one and the same city, Samaria. They will no longer have time for the war against Judah or the siege of Jerusalem, but will sharpen their swords against themselves and destroy one another. These things will happen to them through the wrath of God, which will not stop even there but will bring still other things upon them. In the case of the serpent and the woman, God threatened to put enmity between her and him, but that enmity was to bring good and benefit. In the same way, God now promises to break up the harmony in evil of those whom the prophecy accuses. Similarly, the Savior is recorded in the Gospels as saying: “Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth; I did not come to bring peace on earth, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”

Besides its earlier charges, the present passage also accuses the people called Israel, by which I mean the people of the Jews who were ruled by kings in Samaria. It says that, out of rivalry and contentiousness toward those who wrote down God's true prophecies, they composed false prophecies. So there were very many false prophets, all those in Israel who spoke and wrote things contrary to God's true prophets. These same men also drew up writings that were lawless and full of every kind of wickedness. [?] to attend to the divine scripture of the law and to judge by it; but they, as if they were drawing up laws opposed to it, oppressed the wretched poor, and used violence to defraud orphans and widows who were utterly helpless. You could say the same of those who, even now, use their vile writings to pervert the souls of the simpler sort. The prophetic word threatens them, saying: "And what will they do on the day of visitation?" On that day affliction and the wrath against them will come from afar. For it was far off, because it is driven away by me, God. "But you", O you to whom these words are addressed, "as though by force you draw it down upon yourselves. When it comes, to whom will you flee for help?"

Then he adds, as usual: "For all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still raised high." For since those accused in this passage persisted in the same wrongdoing, it followed that the wrath against them would also persist. And here he brings his charges against the people to a close. After this, just as the prophecy had threatened, the Assyrians came from afar not long afterward, besieged Samaria, laid waste their whole country, and carried off nine entire tribes of the Jewish nation as captives to the land of the Assyrians. They did this in the time of Hezekiah, king of Jerusalem, when the kingdom of Israel established in Samaria was utterly destroyed. Once it had ended, only two and a half tribes of the nation were left, ruled by the successors of David in Jerusalem. So the passage brings its prophecy about Israel to a close at this point, and then goes on to the Assyrians themselves, foretelling in the verses that follow what was going to happen to them as well.

After the captivity of the people called Israel, the passage fittingly moves on to those who took them captive. These were the Assyrians, whom the verses before us threaten. That the people had been carried off by the Assyrians and Samaria besieged when these words were spoken is clear from what is said in them in the person of the king of the Assyrians: "And I took Arabia and Damascus and Samaria; as I took these, so I will take all the kingdoms"; and again: "For as I did to Samaria and her handiworks, so I will do also to Jerusalem." History, too, teaches that in the days of Ahaz the king of the Assyrians went up against Samaria and besieged it. At first he took only part of the people captive, but in the time of Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz, he deported the whole people to Assyria. Since the Assyrians had done such things, the present passage sets out the verses before us as if addressed to them. It says: The people who were not brought to their senses by the words of the prophets had to experience a rod that disciplines and turns them back. Therefore I roused the Assyrians against them as my rod, handing them over into the hands of the Assyrians, so that through them the anger and wrath they had drawn upon themselves might overtake them. So I sent my own anger through the Assyrians against the lawless nation, which was supposed to be my people, and I allowed them to make war on it, to plunder and despoil it, and to tear down all its cities, razing them to the ground and reducing them to dust.

But the Assyrian, once he received authority from me, did not think of it in this way. Instead he grew proud in his reasoning, as if he had overcome my people by his own power. Then, not content with besieging them, he threatens to go after countless other nations, as though he had conquered the stronger nation, the one consecrated to God. So when those who had become his subjects marveled at him and said, "You alone are ruler," he answers them, saying: Do not call me ruler or lord yet, since I have not yet taken all the lands everywhere. I have not yet subdued the country beyond Babylon, or Calneh, where the tower was built at the time when the languages were scattered. Those I have overcome so far are small and very slight: so far I have conquered Arabia and Damascus and Samaria. Yet as I took these, so I will take all the kingdoms. Since the Assyrians boasted in this way, the prophetic word rightly directs the present words at them and at their ruler, saying: Woe to the Assyrians, because they did not understand that it was my anger against the offenders that gave them authority over so great a dominion. Not reckoning this, they supposed they had conquered the nations by their own power. So much for them. In the verses that follow, God himself threatens Jerusalem, saying: "Wail, you carved images in Jerusalem! For as I did to Samaria and her handiworks, so I will do to Jerusalem and her idols." The book of Kings teaches how, in the reign of Ahaz and in the times after it, those of the people called Judah practiced idolatry in Jerusalem itself. So the passage threatens that Jerusalem will suffer the same as Samaria. It foretells this to call its hearers to conversion and repentance, and to bring them to their senses through fear of the example. For, he says, it was not the Assyrian who did these things to Samaria, but I, God, because of the impieties of its inhabitants. Therefore, by the rule of justice, it is likely that those in Jerusalem too will be handed over to the same siege, since they practice the same things as those who suffered what was described before. It should be noted that Origen's eleventh volume of commentary on the prophet extended this far.

The passage has already taught about the capture of Samaria by the Assyrians and the threats against the Assyrians, and it has foretold that Jerusalem will suffer the same because of similar idolatries. Following on from this, in the verses before us it teaches that the Assyrians and their ruler, though for the time being they have arrogantly boasted in the way described, having made Samaria and Damascus their subjects, will nevertheless be granted a respite of time until a certain point. After that their rule will no longer stand, since their long kingdom of many years will be utterly destroyed. He makes clear what this point will be, saying: "And it will come to pass, when the Lord has finished doing everything on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem." That is, when the Lord has finished and brought to completion everything he determined to do. And what he determined is what is set out in the prophecies and written in the sacred scriptures about the events that befell those places. Then, he says, he will bring [punishment] upon the great mind; or, as Symmachus has it: "I will visit," he says, "the fruit of the gladness of the heart of the king of the Assyrians, and the boast of the haughtiness of his eyes."

For he too gave no glory to God, nor did he reckon that it was the God of the universe himself who had handed over to him both Israel and Judah and all who deserved punishment. Instead he grew arrogant, thinking and saying to himself, as Symmachus renders it: "By the strength of my hand I have done it, for I am wise. I have moved the boundaries of peoples and confounded their kings, and like a mighty one I have brought down the inhabitants. My hand has found the whole power of the peoples like a nest, and as abandoned eggs are gathered, so I have gathered the whole earth." Against this proud reasoning, then, whether it belonged to some opposing power, like the prince of the kingdom of the Persians, the prince of the kingdom of the Medes, and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks (for in the same way one might say that there was also a prince of the kingdom of the Assyrians, the one who boasted and uttered the words before us),

whether, then, against him, or against the king of the Babylonians who besieged Jerusalem and burned the temple, seized all the sacred vessels and offerings in it, and dedicated them to his own idols in Babylon itself, the prophetic word replies to one who dared to say such terrible and reckless things. It says: You most foolish of all, do you not see that an axe would never move itself to cut wood unless someone else worked it, nor would a saw cut through what it is sawing if no one drew it, nor would a rod strike anyone, nor a club hit anyone, of its own accord? You should have reckoned, then, that you too, being a servant of God's wrath, would not have had such power as to overpower countless nations, to hew down some, cut up others, strike yet others, enslave whole cities and lay low countless multitudes, though you are worse than any saw or axe or rod, unless it was the Lord who handed over to your hand those who deserved this. But as it is, you reckoned none of these things, and you exalted yourself so far as to suppose that you were the great mind. For you did not set before your eyes the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding. Instead you thought yourself the highest mind, the greatest of all, and, lifting yourself up against God with haughty eyes, you planned to confound the boundaries of the nations on earth, which God had marked out and well ordered: "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God." But you thought that by your own wisdom and misguided understanding you could move the boundaries God had well ordered and bring the inhabited world under your power. For you thought that no one was watching or would intervene, and that God did not care about people on earth. That is why you supposed you would get hold of the nations of the inhabited world as if they were abandoned nestlings or deserted eggs.

So one must consider with right reasoning that even those you conquered you did not overcome without God's consent. For where would you have got such great authority if God had not permitted it and used you as an instrument for the punishment and chastisement of those who needed to be turned back? But since you did not reckon in this way, and did not recognize the one who was the cause of your having such great authority, know for this reason that the Lord of hosts himself, the master of every power and of the angelic army, will send dishonor upon your honor, and upon your glory a burning fire will be kindled. And the light of Israel, the God who of old enlightened his own people and sanctified them, will become fire to you, the proud one. In place of "and he will sanctify him in burning fire," Symmachus has: "and his Holy One for a flame." For to you, he says, the Assyrian, who dared to think impious and overweening thoughts, the Holy One of Israel, who of old was his light, will become a flame and a fire. He aptly compares to hills and mountains and forests both the multitude of the Assyrians itself and its leaders, who tower over the rest like hills or mountains. But these will be quenched; that is, those who were once fierce and hot will grow cold against their will. For death will devour them, consuming, as it were, both soul and body. That souls are not destroyed together with bodies is clear to everyone; but by these words he hints at the strength of the soul. In place of "and it will devour the wood like grass," Symmachus said: "And it will devour his stores and his treasures in a single day, and the glory of his forest and of his Carmel will be consumed from soul to flesh, and he will be like one melted away in flight. The rest of the trees of his forest will be few enough to count, and a child will write them down." By "forest" he means the multitudes with him, and by "his Carmel" his wealth and luxury. All these, he says, will be consumed by the punishing power of the fire mentioned earlier. When this happens to him, he will take to flight, and all those with him will do the same. And if a few are left anywhere, they will be so few that any child could take their number and put it in writing, since the rest of the multitude will have perished. These things are said both according to the letter and according to the sense. According to the letter they refer to Nebuchadnezzar, who burned the temple and the city; according to the sense they refer to the opposing power over the Assyrian nation, which led it in the past when their kingdom was flourishing and at its height. When that power suffered what the prophecy said, the dominion of the Assyrians was at once overthrown, and the Medes and Persians succeeded to the rule.

At that time, he says, when everything foretold against the ruler of the Assyrians described above comes to pass in deed, those who remain of the captive people of the Jews, set free from the enemy's land and returned to their own, will no longer attend to the wicked demons they once attended to, who wronged their souls and became the cause of all their evils. From then on they will attend to God alone, since he has become their redeemer and savior. These things were fulfilled according to the letter under Cyrus, king of the Persians, who released all the Jews in captivity. At that time Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, and their companions, and those who returned from Babylon with Ezra and Nehemiah, raised up the temple and recovered the city itself. But others are indicated by the words before us: "the remnant of Israel and those of Jacob who are saved." These, he says, will no longer trust in those who wronged them, as they did in the time of King Ahaz. For it is written in Kings: "And Ahaz sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians, saying: I am your servant; come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are rising up against me. And Ahaz took the silver and the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and of the king's house, and sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians. And the king of the Assyrians listened to him, went to Damascus, took it, deported its people, and removed Rezin." But, he says, once they have returned they will no longer be like this; instead they will trust in God, the Holy One of Israel, in truth, and the remnant of Jacob will hope in the mighty God. Note here that for "in the mighty God" the Hebrew wording has el gibbor, which appeared among the names of the child born to us, of whom it was said: "And his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel." For there too the Hebrew had el gibbor among his names, and here again it mentions him in connection with the remnant of the people.

And he adds: "And though the people of Israel become like the sand of the sea, their remnant will be saved. For he is completing and cutting short a word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word in the whole inhabited world." The first statement, then, referred to the remnant who returned from captivity. But the second, where the passage adds, without defining it and after a pause, "And though the people of Israel become like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved," presents a different meaning. For the sand of the sea is countless in number, but otherwise useless for farming. So when, he says, the people of Israel has spread out into a countless multitude, but has become useless in bearing fruit for God, then their multitude will perish and only their remnant will be saved. Here the passage signifies the useless multitude of the nation who lived in the land after the return from Babylon until Roman times. For these were the ones who were like the sand of the sea, of whom only the remnant was saved: those of them who believed in the Christ of God, his disciples, apostles and evangelists.

This will happen, he says, when the Lord makes a shortened word in the whole inhabited world. By these words he clearly hinted at the gospel of the new covenant, proclaimed throughout the whole inhabited world. And the word of the gospel was shortened in that it did not contain the commandments given through Moses. The Apostle also recalls the words before us, speaking in this way: "And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved; for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short. And as Isaiah foretold: If the Lord of hosts had not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." It should be noted that Origen's twelfth volume of commentary on the prophet extended this far.

The passage has completed its prophecy about Judah and Jerusalem, in which it showed that they too would suffer things like Samaria and Israel when handed over to the ruler of the Assyrians, and what [?] their besieger, the Assyrian. It has also spoken beforehand about those who would afterward live godly lives. Having foretold all these things about what would happen after long periods of time, [?] the present time, when the prophet Isaiah was known to those living in Jerusalem under King Hezekiah, who were anxious about an attack and in distress lest they too should suffer the same as those living in Samaria. He urges them not to fear the Assyrians. For their king, he says, will come and march against Jerusalem, so that those living in it will feel a brief blow, as if struck with a rod; but he will return having achieved nothing, put to flight. This too was fulfilled under Hezekiah son of Ahaz, who reigned in Jerusalem, a man unlike his father, but righteous and in every way dear to God. That is why the Lord says to those described: "Do not be afraid, my people who dwell in Zion, [?] of the Assyrians." For even though, with my permission, their king will come against you, he will strike you with a rod that turns you back; he will not attack you with swords or spears, conquering you by the law of war. And even this blow of the rod against you will not be unjust [?], for "yet a little while and the anger will cease." Do not be ignorant of why the Assyrian was permitted to deal you a restrained blow. It is because you gave yourself over again to the way of Egypt, devoting yourself to idolatry in the time of Ahaz. For this reason I have handed you over to the rod of the Assyrian, to bring you to your senses and turn you back. But very soon my wrath will cease, when you change for the better and come to know God, together with your king Hezekiah. So my indignation against you will cease, and as I shield your salvation, the Assyrian will flee in disgrace through your land and through your cities, escaping from one place to another. In place of "for he brings a blow upon you, so that you may see the way of Egypt," Symmachus says: "He will strike you with a rod and lift up his staff against you because of the way of Egypt."

"For the Assyrian will do these things to you on account of the way of Egypt, which you traveled; but God," it says, "will rouse up a scourge against him, like the blow on Midian in the place of affliction." In place of this Symmachus translated as follows: "And the Lord of hosts will rouse up a scourge against him, like the blow on Midian at Sur Oreb." The story is told by Moses in Numbers, when the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, "Avenge the children of Israel on the Midianites"; and next Moses said to the people, "Arm men from among you and draw up in battle before the Lord against Midian to carry out vengeance, a thousand from each tribe." Then he killed every male, and the kings of Midian, among whom was Balaam son of Beor. These things took place at Sur Oreb. The desert was called Sur, as Scripture teaches when it says, "Moses led the children of Israel away from the Red Sea and brought them into the desert of Sur"; and the mountain was called Horeb, for it is written: "And the Lord said to Moses, Go on ahead of the people; take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river, and go. And behold, I stand there before you on the rock in Horeb." So, he says, just as I brought the blow on Midian then, so I will do to the Assyrians too; and those struck by my scourge will turn back by the way along the sea. "And the yoke of the Assyrian will be taken from your shoulder, and the fear of him from you."

You will be free and released from all fear, while he, in flight, will first come to the city of Angai. Then from there he will pass on to another place, and there, worn out, he will lay down his baggage. After that he will cross from there to somewhere else, and from there to the city called Saul, then to another place; and so he will vanish in disgrace.

But you will be encouraged and will find consolation, no longer subject to the Assyrian yoke. That is why those who are able to encourage you and to be encouraged are commanded to do this from now on. "Encourage," it says, "today, on the way, to remain; encourage with the hand the mountain, the daughter of Zion, and you hills that are in Jerusalem." That is, encourage the daughter of Zion, meaning the inhabitants of Jerusalem, not to flee but to remain and to endure the chastisement that will come upon them for a little while. Notice how "today" is added. The things said before these about the ruler of the Assyrians pointed to the distant times of Nebuchadnezzar, but the present words were addressed to those living "today," in the time of the prophet Isaiah himself. That is why he says, "Encourage today, on the way, to remain": encourage the people not to flee from the attack of the Assyrian that is happening now and today, under King Hezekiah, so that they remain and do not flee once they have learned what the Assyrian now upon them will suffer. Whom he commands to do the encouraging he says next: "the hills that are in Jerusalem." He bids those who have climbed higher, and who are lifted up in soul and mind in a godly way, to encourage the people. For it is likely that when the blow from God struck the Assyrians, so that a hundred and eighty-five thousand of them fell in a single night, those who were left, together with the king himself, fled through the cities, villages and places named in the prophecy. History has shown how the Assyrian, in his flight, passed by the way along the sea onto the road toward Egypt, for it tells us that the Ethiopians rose up against him. The prophecy spoken about the Assyrian ends here; what follows makes a fresh beginning and foretells things concerning God.

The text has mentioned the Assyrians many times, and has shown that the rule of those who ruled among them and grew arrogant would be overthrown. In the present passage it goes on to treat the many rulers of the various nations. For at that time there were local governors, ethnarchs and petty kings, such as those of Egypt, Arabia, Tyre, Sidon and the other nations, who were also idolaters and insulted God, exalting and lifting themselves up and thinking overweening thoughts. Consistently, then, after what was said about the overthrow of the Assyrians, he prophesies about these too, and indicates their complete destruction when he says: "Behold, the Sovereign, the Lord Sabaoth, will throw the glorious into confusion with might, and those lofty in insolence will be crushed, and those lofty in insolence will be humbled," and what follows. Then, setting out the time when these things will happen, he very fittingly adds the coming of Christ among men. For since in the earlier passages he had already taught about his birth from a virgin and the manner of that birth, and the titles named after the powers conceived in him, he now consistently foretells from what race and what tribe he will come forth, and what his coming among men will accomplish. At the same time he indicates the overthrow of the many rulers described: of the other rulers who formerly held power in every nation through local governments and divided rule, of those who led among the Jews themselves, and, in a word, of all the rulers of the nations, and also of the invisible powers, the evil spirits and demons, who for a long age had strengthened the error of many gods among all the nations. The text threatens that all these will be overthrown at the divine appearing of the Savior, saying: "Behold, the Sovereign, the Lord Sabaoth, throws the glorious into confusion with might, and those lofty in insolence will be humbled, and the lofty will fall by the sword, and Lebanon will fall with its lofty ones." You see how many lofty ones he has named, and how often; and he likens their whole company to Lebanon and the very lofty cedars on it. That is why it is said elsewhere, "I saw the ungodly exalted like the cedars of Lebanon," and again in another place, "The voice of the Lord breaking cedars; and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and beat them small like a calf, Lebanon and all." This, then, is the first thing the text announces that the Lord Sabaoth will do: I mean, crush all the ethnarchies and divided rules among men. But since in many places of the divine Scriptures Jerusalem is called Lebanon, as we have often shown, he fittingly indicates her fall too, and the fall of the rulers of the Jewish nation who held great power in her of old, when he says, "And Lebanon will fall with its lofty ones."

How all these will be crushed and fall he sets out next, prophesying that a rod will come forth from the root of Jesse, which will crush and humble all the lofty ones mentioned before. That is why there is added: "And a rod will come forth from the root of Jesse." Instead of "from the root," the other translators agree in rendering "from the stump." And indeed the tribe and family from which the Savior came forth was like a stump that no longer had branches, because the kings of David's line had died out after the captivity in Babylon. So it seems to me that the fleshly line of David, whose father was Jesse, is called a stump. And so that no one should suppose that the one prophesied would be a king like David, he did not say "from the root of David" but "of Jesse," because of the likeness of his life and its plainness; for Jesse was poor and held no worldly office. Fittingly, then, a shoot is said to come forth from his root, or as from some old stump, according to Aquila, who rendered it "shoot," and so presented the modest and lowly state of our Savior according to the flesh. "Branch" and "sprout" are likewise used for the same reason. For instead of "and a flower will rise up from the root," Aquila said, "and a branch will grow from his roots," and Symmachus, "and a sprout will grow from his roots."

The shoot, then, or branch, or sprout, was the human being of our Savior, conceived according to the flesh; while God the Word, who dwelt in him, is made known by what comes next, where it is said: "And the Spirit of God will rest upon him, a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength, a spirit of knowledge and godliness; and a spirit of the fear of God will fill him." These words signify the fullness of the divinity of the only-begotten of God, of which the Evangelists say, "From his fullness we have all received," and the Apostle, "For in him it pleased all the fullness of the Godhead to dwell bodily." Each of the other prophets had received some particular gift, and each of the apostles likewise had received some part of the fullness; but he had the very fullness of the Godhead, which no human being ever contained except the one alone who was prophesied to come forth from the root of Jesse, in whom the Spirit of God dwelt—the Spirit of whom the Apostle says, "Now the Lord is the Spirit." It is a spirit of wisdom and understanding; and wisdom was the preexistent Word of God, through whom all things came to be. For "he made all things in wisdom," and "God founded the earth by wisdom," and, according to the Apostle, "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God." This spirit of wisdom, then, did not come upon the one prophesied for an hour, or a day, or some brief time, but rested upon him as in its own temple; and the same was the spirit of counsel and strength. That is why earlier he was called "Angel of Great Counsel," and it is said, "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God." The spirit of knowledge and godliness and the spirit of the fear of God are likewise said to be the same. We must not think of these as many separate spirits. Rather, just as we understand him to be the Word of God and light and life and resurrection and countless other things, according to the different aspects conceived in him, so too he is the spirit of wisdom and understanding and counsel and strength and knowledge and godliness and the fear of God. And all these must be understood as one and the same preexistent Word of God, who rested upon the one born from the root of Jesse and from the seed of David according to the flesh.

So in this way the union of the only-begotten Son of God with the son of man whom he took up has been shown, more or less. Next he sketches the life he lived while dwelling among men, saying: "He will not judge by appearance, nor convict by speech, but he will give judgment for the lowly and convict the lowly of the earth." Symmachus translated this more clearly, saying: "And he will not judge by what his eyes see, nor convict by what his ears hear, but he will judge the needy in righteousness and convict the poor of the earth in uprightness." You will find in the Gospels how our Savior and Lord did not judge by appearance. Showing partiality to no one, he rebuked with great boldness sometimes the scribes and Pharisees, sometimes the chief priests within the temple itself, to whom he also said, "The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits." Nor did he convict by speech. For they came to him saying, "Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you defer to no one, for you do not regard the person of men." But he did not convict according to their speech; knowing their wickedness, he answered, "Why are you testing me, you hypocrites?" He also gave judgment for the lowly, and convicted the lowly of the earth, or "the poor in uprightness," according to Symmachus—by the poor we understand those whom he called blessed when he said, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of God." Such were his apostles and disciples, whom he also rebuked, sometimes saying to them, "Are you also still without understanding?" and again, "Do you not yet perceive or understand?" and sometimes to Peter, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" And he is shown to have reproved and rebuked them on a great many other occasions; and this too the prophecy foresaw and foretold.

Then he adds next: "And he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with the spirit through his lips he will destroy the ungodly." You will understand this too when you hear him say, "Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth; I did not come to bring peace but a sword." The sword was the word of his mouth, with which he destroyed the earth and the earthly thoughts of those who had believed in him. And with the spirit he will destroy the ungodly, rebuking the godless and ungodly demons and driving them far away by the word that came forth through his lips, so that they cried out and said, "What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us? We know who you are, the Holy One of God."

Moreover, it says, "he will have his loins girded with righteousness and his sides wrapped with truth"; and according to Symmachus, "And righteousness will be the belt of his loins, and faith the belt of his flanks." Just as a king is girded with a belt of gold and precious stones, in the same way he assigns to the one prophesied a belt of righteousness and truth; and here too the divinity of the Word is to be understood. For he himself was righteousness, as the Apostle teaches when he says, "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." And the Savior himself is recorded in the Gospels as saying, "I am the light and the truth and the life." This truth, then, and this righteousness bound the sides and loins of the one from the root of Jesse, in royal and military fashion. With so many details the text displays his readiness for battle against hidden and invisible enemies, as though painting a portrait of the one prophesied.

Next he describes his achievements, teaching that through his grace and divine power the wolves among men, the rapacious and greedy, will turn from their wickedness so as to be gathered into one church, as one flock, with lambs gentle and meek of soul. Other men, utterly savage and brutal and no different from leopards, will lay aside the fierceness of the beast and lie down together with kids, that is, with the simpler and more innocent. And others, whose ways are like a lion's, will change their savage, flesh-eating character and feed together with the newborn of the church like calves and bulls, sharing the same food from the divine oracles. And if you ever see men of royal standing, honored with ranks and distinctions in this life, gathering in the church of God with the poor and humble, do not hesitate to say that in this way too the Scripture is fulfilled which said that lions will feed with calves. But all of these together—the wolves and lambs and leopards, the kids and lions and calves and bulls described—"a little child," it says, "will lead." "Will lead" is said instead of "will gather together." This too one can see in actual fact, observing in the church of Christ that most of those who preside are no different from infants in simplicity of soul and guilelessness, and yet they lead those who are gathered together from every race.

"And the ox and the bear," it says, "will feed together, and their young will be together." Here too he describes the fellowship, in one place, of men who are gentle and suited to the cultivation of the soul with others who are savage in their ways. When you see the children of rich and poor, of wicked and good, assembled together in the church, you will bear witness to the prophecy which said, "And their young will be together." The lion, a meat-eater by nature, feeding on straw like a grazing animal, would again be a beastly and harsh man who delights in the bare letter of divine Scripture. Its hidden sense would itself be the word that nourishes souls, while the wording that wraps around it is the straw.

Further, a little child, such as the one mentioned a little earlier, is said to put its hand on the hole of asps and to suffer no harm. The holes and lairs of asps and their offspring would be the bodies of those troubled by demons, in which the creeping and venomous spirits lurk and make their bed, using the senses of the body as their holes. A child of Christ—a simple man, an infant in wickedness—drives these out by the Savior's power and lays his hand on them, and they can do no harm because of the one who came forth from the root of Jesse, who gave his children authority to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. All these things, he announces, will take place on his holy mountain, the one also shown in the earlier passages, which is not foreign to the heavenly word of the gospel, on which the house of God and his church are built. So that no one may think that the holy mountain spoken of here is the one the Jews suppose, in a corner of Palestine, he makes his meaning clear by adding next: "For the whole earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas." In this way he signifies the church of God established throughout the whole inhabited world, and the godly knowledge preached in it, which, like a mighty flood, washes away all the brine of wickedness in human life and cleanses away all the filth of the soul.

"And there will be in that day," it says—clearly, at the prophesied time—this very one who will rise up from the root of Jesse, "the one who rises up"—clearly, after the resurrection from the dead—as ruler and leader of the nations, "and in him the nations will hope." For he will not be king of the Jews, nor, like David himself and his successors, will he hold some small corner; he will rule over people everywhere on earth. "And in him the nations will hope": thus that prophecy too is fulfilled which was spoken through Moses: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up, and he will be the expectation of the nations." He brings the whole passage to its end: "And his rest will be honor," or, according to Aquila and Symmachus, "And his rest will be glory." This follows very consistently. Having taught the first beginning of his birth among men and gone through everything in between, he sets out what kind of end he will have, saying, "And his rest will be honor and glory." Nowhere does he describe his death; he calls it rest, and glory, and honor. For this was the end of our Savior's saving work among men. Our Savior himself showed this when he said in his prayer to the Father, "Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed."

That the one who will come forth from the root of Jesse is none other than Christ, even the children of the Jews themselves admit, saying that the Anointed One they expect is clearly indicated by this prophecy. Yet although a thousand years [?] have already passed from the times of the prophet Isaiah down to our own, and the one prophesied, as they hold, has not yet come, they accept the prophecy but keep postponing it forever, stretching out their expectation without limit. So they slander the prophecy as though it did not foretell the truth, and deprive themselves of the hope of what was prophesied. Then they try to interpret the sense of the prophetic sayings, though, as the Apostle says, they understand neither what they are saying nor the things about which they make confident assertions. Come, then, let us now take up the passage before us. Since he foretold that the one who rises up from the root of Jesse would rule the nations, and added, "In him the nations will hope," he necessarily mentions the Jewish part as well in the present passage, so that no one should suppose that the one prophesied would benefit none of the people of the circumcision.

He teaches, then, that in that day, that is, at the time when the one foretold appears, the Lord will once more show his hand, to make the remnant of the people that is left an object of envy. In place of this Aquila says: "The Lord will add his hand a second time to acquire the remnant of his people"; and Symmachus: "The Lord will add his hand a second time to make the remnant of his people an object of envy." Once, long ago in Egypt, he freed the Jewish people from their oppression when they were worn down, putting forward through Moses his wonder-working hand, by which he worked those extraordinary miracles in the land of the Egyptians. In the same way he will add his hand again, moving it a second time, as it were, through extraordinary works, in order to acquire what is left of the people and make it an object of envy. Here again the remnant and the residue of the people mean what was named in the earlier passages, where it was said: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." This seed was the apostles, disciples and evangelists of the one foretold. They became a remnant chosen by grace out of the whole Jewish people scattered among all the nations, for some of the Jewish nation were scattered in the land of the Assyrians, or in Egypt, or in Babylon, or in Ethiopia, or in the land of the Elamites, or in the rest of the inhabited world. It is said that he will glorify and make objects of envy those among them who believed in the Christ of God and so became a remnant chosen by grace. This was fulfilled in deed through his own disciples and apostles. Through them and through the other Jews who received the word of Christ, the church of God was founded and the calling of all the nations was accomplished. First there were the twelve apostles of our Savior, and then the seventy disciples. Paul also mentions brothers to whom the Savior appeared all at once after the resurrection, and many other apostles.

Paul belonged to this same company, and so did Barnabas and Timothy and all the others whom Paul called his fellow workers and fellow soldiers, along with those whose memory the Acts of the Apostles has recorded. With these we should also include those who were gathered together with one accord on the day of Pentecost and filled with the Holy Spirit, who spoke in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. Scripture bears witness about them, saying: "Now there were Jews living in Jerusalem, devout men from every nation under heaven. When this sound came, the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. They were amazed and astonished, saying, 'Look, are not all these men Galileans? How is it that each of us hears them in our own native language? Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia, Syria and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs: we hear them speaking the mighty works of God in our own tongues.'" Then, when Peter had spoken to them about saving grace, the people just mentioned accepted the word and were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day. At another time more of the Jews believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. Scripture also relates that James and those with him said to Paul: "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews, and all of them are zealous for the law." Among the other nations, too, the apostles and the first evangelists of the word preached first to the Jews, and in every nation there were countless Jews proclaiming the Christ of God. Through all of them the gospel was spread to all the nations, while God bore witness with them by signs and wonders, by various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit. God made them objects of envy and glorious in the eyes of all who accepted the word they proclaimed.

And this remnant chosen by grace, he says, will raise a sign among the nations, and before all else will gather the lost of Israel and the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth. They had received the command to go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and so they did this. They first preached the gospel while healing the sick, cleansing lepers and casting out demons, doing these things freely as they had been commanded. Since they preached first to those of the circumcision, they gathered those of them who believed, who had long been perishing, into the church of Christ, just as the Savior taught when he said: "Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." They did these things in the four corners of the earth, travelling east and west, north and south. So they first shared the word of the gospel with those people and then preached to the other nations. That is why it was said: "And he will gather the lost of Israel and the scattered of Judah." And who will gather the lost of Israel, if not the company of the apostles, or rather the one from the root of Jesse whom they preached, and God the Word who dwelt in him? At that time they gathered them into a single church, no longer standing apart or separated from one another as before.

Before, the tribe of Ephraim and the peoples under it, ruled as a kingdom from Samaria, stood on their own, and the members of the tribe of Judah, living under the ruler [?] in Jerusalem, stood on their own. That is why he says that the jealousy between them will be taken away, so that Ephraim will no longer envy Judah, nor Judah Ephraim. That jealousy existed in the times of the prophecy, as the text showed in the earlier passages.

Next he says: "And they will fly in the ships of foreigners; together they will plunder the sea." As they went around the nations, they certainly had to travel by sea as well. So they covered even the sea route as swiftly as if they were flying, and in a short time they preached the gospel to a great many nations. Sometimes they travelled on foot, sometimes by sea, and their pilots were not Jews but the very people who had received the word of Christ. In the same way they also plundered the sea. By the sea the text means the islands: as they passed through them on their way, they brought the inhabitants into subjection to the saving teaching. You can see how the saying was fulfilled from a single example. The apostle Paul, one of those foretold, made his journey up to Rome by sea. He put in at an island called Malta and there showed the inhabitants an extraordinary wonder. He healed people who were sick in body and so astonished those who saw it that he took many of them as plunder and captured them for the saving teaching. That is why it is said: "And they will fly in the ships of foreigners; together they will plunder the sea, and those from the rising of the sun." So, he says, the disciples of Christ will plunder even those from the rising of the sun. In fact, some of them are recorded as having travelled as far as the land of the Persians and the Indians.

In the prophet's time the Idumeans, Ammonites and Moabites, the Arabian nations around Judea, were thought to be hostile to the God honored by the Jews and to be his enemies, because of their outlandish idolatry. So the text fittingly mentioned these very nations by name, since they too would accept the religion the apostles were going to preach. That is why he says: "And they will lay their hands on Idumea and on Moab," and he prophesies that the sons of Ammon will obey the preaching. These are nations among the inhabitants of Arabia that were once extremely superstitious but have now received the word of Christ. So he foretells as something extraordinary that those who were once enemies and opponents of the Jews' religion would submit to the heralds of the gospel. In Symmachus he says: "Edom and Moab, the stretching out of their hand." This too was fulfilled in deed when the disciples of our Savior stretched out their hand, and the works accomplished through them, to the inhabitants of Arabia as well, and filled their cities with churches of God. Our text says this as: "And on Moab they will first lay their hands," and again: "The sons of Ammon will be the first to obey." It should be known that neither the Hebrew nor the wording of the other translators contains the addition that they would be the first to obey. They say only that the grace of Christ proclaimed through the apostles would reach these nations too.

The three translators agreed in rendering it thus: "And the Lord will put under a curse the tongue of the sea of Egypt." Scripture usually calls "sea" the multitude of ungodly men, or the flood of wickedness, which is full of salt water, as it were. The Lord is said to put it under a curse so that they will no longer use the Egyptian tongue to strengthen their superstitious error, but will learn to speak the oracles of God and to swear by the name of the Lord. It is worth noting that in the passages before us, according to the Hebrew, the text also mentions our Savior Jesus, in the words: "Behold, God my Savior; I will trust in him." Where we have "my Savior," the Hebrew word reads "esouathi"; and again in "from the springs of salvation," the word for "salvation" is "esoua." In the earlier passages the text did not name Idumea and Moab and the sons of Ammon idly. It named them because these were extremely superstitious nations, hostile and opposed to the God of the prophets, and so it foretells as something extraordinary that these very nations would accept the teaching of Christ. In the same way it has fittingly brought in a mention of the idolatry of the Egyptians, since that too would be abolished in the times it describes. The present passage is not about Egypt. The prophecy about Egypt stands apart, set out under its own subject, with the heading "Vision of Egypt." This passage is about the remnant chosen by grace. It foretells these things too, teaching how, after the coming among men of the one who was to come forth from the root of Jesse, those who received him, the chosen remnant of Israel, would fill even the land of the Egyptians with the teaching of Christ, together with the other nations, and no one would stand in their way.

We have already observed that some parts of prophetic speech are given literally and need no figurative allegory, while others compel us, even against our will, to proceed by the allegorical method. The text compelled us to interpret figuratively the rod from the root of Jesse, and the flower and the stem, yet it was not right to allegorize Jesse as well. Again, what was said as though about wild beasts had to be transferred to the corresponding kinds of men, but the nations over whom he was said to rule were not to be taken figuratively. In the same way, in the passage at hand we must acknowledge that Egypt is the physical land of the Egyptians, but take its sea and river allegorically. He says these will be made desolate in the prophesied times, when the Lord is said to add to show his hand. By saying "add" he shows that other events of the same kind will follow those that had happened before. Long ago, through Moses, the hand of the Lord brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt, led them through the Red Sea, and brought them into the land of promise, which had belonged to foreigners before. Now the same hand of the Lord, adding further blessings through the one from the root of Jesse, made the apostles of the Savior and the heralds of the saving gospel glorious and objects of envy throughout the whole world. These men were Jews and set out from among the Jews, and their glory reached not least to Egypt itself, where they came without hindrance and no one stood in their way. They went down there to tear down Egyptian idolatry. In Moses' time the people went out fleeing Pharaoh and the Egyptians, but the disciples of Christ went into Egypt of their own accord as heralds of the saving word. For the people of Moses' time the sea was physically divided, and the water of the Egyptian river was turned into blood. But the addition of blessings in the times described threatens the Egyptian sea with desolation and their river with total failure. Then the heralds of the saving gospel could go all around the lands of the Egyptians without any hindrance, overthrow their superstitious worship of many gods, and hand on the knowledge of the God over all and of his Christ, who came forth from the root of Jesse. We should observe that the Lord is said to make desolate not the land of Egypt but its sea, which is how the multitude of idolatry is indicated.

If, then, the multitudes of wickedness in life are compared to a sea, consider whether it is not reasonable [?] the tongue of godless and ungodly men who in the past did not know God, as Pharaoh showed when he said: "I do not know the Lord, and I will not send Israel away." As the text goes on, it foretells that this will come about. The tongue of the Egyptian sea has been put under a curse in such a way that the oracles and prophecies of the wicked demons, which once loudly issued from it, have fallen silent, and the evil arts of sorcerers have also come to nothing. All of this was fulfilled in deed after the gospel was preached to the Egyptians themselves. From that time down to our own day, all the power of the gods worshipped by the Egyptians has been extinguished. The godless and impious men all over the world who follow Egyptian ways in the same kind of idolatry formed a sea that once overflowed and surged, and that sea has suffered utter desolation. The Lord is said to make the sea of Egypt desolate, that is, the multitude of idolatry. And he will not only make the sea desolate, but will also lay his hand on its river. This is how the text indicates the kingdom that had stood among the Egyptians from ancient times, and the "violent wind" is understood as the Roman ruler who first destroyed the kingdom of the Egyptians. At any rate the river itself was struck and broken up, or brought low, as it were, into deep valleys and changed into seven ravines. You will understand this too if you pay attention. Formerly the mighty stream of a single river, which signified the Egyptian kingdom, ruled over all the nations there. But once it had been struck and broken up, rulers over parts of the country governed them in turn. Some administered the regions of Libya, others separately those of the Thebaid, and others Egypt proper and Alexandria. Of these, some have been honored with governorships and entrusted with the care of civil and political affairs, while others separately command the military units, and all of them are appointed to these offices by the higher authority. Since they afterward return to private life, they are fittingly compared to ravines, by contrast with the river that once overflowed among them, I mean the kingdom. That kingdom flooded the whole of Egypt and the nations around it with a single stream, as one royal power held sway over everything. In this way, then, the Egyptian river was also struck, and separate ravines arose in its place, so that from then on Egypt was passable for those preaching the gospel of Christ. No one stood in their way or prevented them from entering.

Since the kingdom of the Egyptians no longer existed and the demonic power among them had been extinguished, the preaching of the gospel was proclaimed to them at leisure, in keeping with the oracle that said: "And there will be a passage for my people left in Egypt." And, he says, "it will be for Israel as on the day when they came out of the land of Egypt." The people of Moses crossed the Red Sea on foot as if on dry land, and after the crossing they sang the song that says, "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified." In the same way the prophesied evangelists of our Savior, who were themselves those left over from the whole Jewish nation, made their journey unhindered and travelled through the whole land of the Egyptians. They preached the gospel to the Jews in their synagogues and established churches of Christ from among the gentiles who turned to God. And they taught those whom they had helped to sing a new song, like the people in Moses' time.

This is what the prophetic text foretold when it said: "And you will say in that day: I will bless you, O Lord, because you were angry with me, and you turned your wrath away from me and had mercy on me. Behold, my God is my Savior; I will trust in him and be saved. I will not be afraid, for the Lord is my glory and my praise, and he has become my salvation." Those who proclaim the Christ of God in the land of the Egyptians, or else the Egyptians themselves who have received the Christ of God, are taught to say these things, since the river mentioned earlier no longer exists among them, nor the sea that once surged. That is why they say: "Behold, my God the Savior; I will trust in him and will not be afraid." They say this because there is no longer anyone to terrify them or to prevent them from worshipping God according to the word of Christ. "For my glory and my praise," he says, "is the Lord, and he has become my salvation." The words "you were angry with me" express a confession of former sins, which made the Egyptians deserving of God's wrath before the call to salvation. The words "you turned away your wrath and had mercy on me" signify the forgiveness of sins given to them after their call. For the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ granted release from bonds and pardon of sins both to the Egyptians themselves and to all who have received the Son of God.

Next he adds: "And you will draw water with gladness from the springs of salvation." Here again the water and the springs of salvation must be taken allegorically. You will understand them when you hear the Savior himself say: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water." So the springs of salvation were the words of the gospel, poured out like rain from the Holy Spirit, just as the prophetic words were called the springs of Israel by the Scripture that says: "In the assemblies bless God, the Lord, from the springs of Israel." It is from the springs of the saving word that the Egyptians are prophesied to drink, and so are those who served them the saving drink.

After what was said before, he also commands that these words be spoken: "And you will say in that day: Sing hymns to the Lord, call out his name." He addresses "you will say" to the company of our Savior's evangelists. "In that day," he says, meaning clearly in the prophesied time, "you, the herald of the saving gospel, will say to the Egyptians who have received the preaching: 'Sing hymns to the Lord, call out his name, declare his glorious deeds among the nations, remember that his name has been exalted.'" You, the company of the apostles, will say these things as you teach those who become your disciples. You will charge them not to keep silent, but to proclaim to everyone and cry aloud, for all to hear, the grace of the saving kindness.
Then again he calls on the same people to teach and to say: "Sing hymns to the name of the Lord, for he has done lofty things; declare all these things in all the earth."

After all this he adds: "Exult and rejoice, you who dwell in Zion, for the Holy One of Israel has been exalted in her midst." Zion has already been explained in many places as the word of the gospel, on which the church of God has been built. Since, then, the Holy One of Israel has been exalted in the midst of his church, he rightly says, "Exult and rejoice, you who dwell in her," because they have the Holy One of Israel himself in their midst. This fulfils the promise he himself made when he said: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst." Yet the prophetic Spirit once again uses the name Zion and bids those in Zion exult and rejoice. With these words it cheers those of the circumcision, because they suppose that these things are said about them, and so they hold the book in high regard, as though it foretold the finest things about them.

Having completed the prophecy about the one who was to come forth from the root of Jesse, and having foretold everything that would happen at the coming of Christ, the text begins another subject, the oracle against Babylon. It then places a second, the one about the Philistines, which is what Scripture usually calls the Palestinians. Third after these comes the word against Moab, then the word against Damascus, and after these the vision of Egypt. Sixth is the vision of the desert, then the vision of Idumea, then the burden in Arabia, which is followed by the vision of the valley of Zion, and last of all the word concerning Tyre. These are ten connected prophecies about the foreign nations. Among them he has also included the valley of Zion, counting the Jewish people too among the foreigners. To them he announces the good news of knowledge through Christ and promises of good things. He proclaims to all alike the message about God's judgment, urging all people to live godly lives and to remember God's tribunal. It was necessary for him to deliver the prophecies about these very nations to the Jews. Seeing things to come foretold, and seeing them turn out as predicted, the Jews would be persuaded that the one who spoke to them through the prophets is truly God, who exercises providence over them and counsels them in what is for their good.

So he puts the vision against Babylon first, having already set out at the beginning of the whole book the vision against Judea and against Jerusalem.
