For since God shows no partiality, he began with his own people, and he will bring the discourse back round to them again. Among the foreign nations he gives Babylon first place. This was the royal city of the Assyrians, very great and very powerful. The Assyrians are said to have been the first to rule the inhabited world, for a full thirteen hundred years, down to the time of those who besieged Jerusalem and led the Jewish people captive into their own land. For soon after this deed of the Assyrians, not long afterward, their power was overthrown. While they still endured, he had earlier foretold how the Assyrians would take Israel and Samaria. Since Jerusalem too was about to undergo a siege like Samaria's, he prophesied its end as well, and he also described what the Assyrians themselves and their rulers would suffer. Now he teaches about the city that had been their royal city from of old. He does not do this so that the Babylonians themselves might learn what was going to happen to them, for how could they, since they were not present? Rather, it was so that those who receive the primacy [?] here [?] might also know the righteous judgment of God that will come upon all people, and might have consolation for what would befall them, as one who is to be avenged [?]. Because the word is about to make a particular threat against Babylon, it first sets out a prophecy teaching about the universal judgment of God: what those who ruled over the whole world impiously and arrogantly will suffer before God's tribunal. After this universal teaching it passes on to the particular threat concerning Babylon.

"On a mountain of the plain raise a signal, lift up your voice to them, summon them with the hand. Open, you rulers! I am giving the orders, and I am leading them. Giants are coming to fulfil my wrath, rejoicing and at the same time acting with insolence." The divine Spirit in the prophet utters these words in the person of God the Word. It is he, then, who commands the angels around him to open the closed doors and to order those inside to come out, to arrive and hasten to punish the ungodly. I think these words show that there is a region set apart for the opposing powers, in which they are shut up as though in a prison. Perhaps this is what is called the abyss, which, as the passage that says "dragons and all the deeps" teaches, is full of dragons. That is why the demons begged the Saviour not to send them into the abyss, when they said, "You have come before the time to torment us." They knew well that a time would come for them to be shut up in the abyss. These opposing powers may be the souls of the giants, or else of the angels who came down from heaven and fathered the giants. The writing of Moses mentions these angels when it says, "When the angels of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all of them, whomever they chose." Then it goes on to say that those born of them were the giants who were renowned from of old. So whether they are the souls of these giants, or the spirits of those who fathered them, or some other rebellious powers cast out of their heavenly station, it is likely that they have been handed over to darkness and chains until the time of judgment. But when God's tribunal is set up and the universal judgment arrives, in which the Christ of God will judge the whole human race, seated on the throne of his glory, then, as he taught, "he will send out his angels, and with a great trumpet they will gather all the nations from one end of heaven to the other." He will bring about the resurrection of the dead, and the bringing of all the nations before God's judgment seat, through his angels who move about his throne. For he says, "He will send out his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other." But he will inflict the punishments on those who are to be punished through the opposing powers, as though through executioners. In the passage before us, then, he commands his own angels to raise a signal on a mountain of the plain. Here he calls the region on earth, the whole dwelling place of mankind, a "mountain of the plain." There he commands them to display the signal of the judgment of God that is about to arrive, and also to lift up their voice and summon to the judgment seat those who are to be judged.

Next he says, "Summon with the hand. Open, you rulers!" In place of this Symmachus says, "Move the hand, and let them come out of the doors." For he commands the powers mentioned above to come out of the outer darkness in which they had been shut up. That is why he adds, "Open the doors," doors that would never be opened in any other way except by my command as judge and by your service as my angels. "When you have opened the doors at my nod, lift up your voice to them and urge those who are called to hurry. For it is I who give them orders and lead them." Who these are he goes on to make clear, saying, "Giants are coming to fulfil my wrath, rejoicing and at the same time acting with insolence." Theodotion translated in agreement with the Seventy, saying, "Indeed, I have called my giants," while Aquila and Symmachus translated "mighty ones" in place of "giants." This is what he calls the avenging powers through which the wrath against the ungodly is carried out. These so-called giants are creatures who delight in evil, as if they were doing exactly what they wished. They rejoice in abusing and punishing the ungodly, since they have no heart of compassion, no kindness and no love for humanity, but are savage and inhuman. When they ought to groan over those who are perishing, they rejoiced even as they abused them.

So much for these. In what follows he speaks of the nations that are to be judged: "A sound of many nations on the mountains, like that of many nations; a sound of kings and of nations gathered together." For those who are about to be handed over to punishment will do nothing but cry out as they confess their own evils. All the nations and their kings together will raise one and the same cry, lamenting their own disasters. Then he teaches the reason for the cry of the nations and the kings, saying, "The Lord Sabaoth" (or "the Lord of the powers," or "the Lord of hosts") "has commanded a nation of armed warriors to come from a far country, from the farthest foundation of heaven: the Lord and his warriors, to destroy the whole inhabited world." Here he calls "warriors" those who were named "giants" above. They have long been far off, shut up, as it were, in the foundations of heaven. When the time calls for it, the Judge of all commands them to come and destroy the whole world of the wicked, after the righteous have been set apart. For in the Gospels too, the Son of Man, seated on the throne of his glory, first calls those on his right hand to the kingdom prepared for them before the foundation of the world. Once they have been received and brought into the promise, the threat of fire is pronounced against the remaining nations, those who will be found on his left.

Having taught what will happen on the day of judgment, the word calls to repentance those who have not yet reached that day but are still in this life. It urges them to turn back while there is still time, and to weep and wail over their own evils. That is why it says, "Wail, you carved images! For the day of the Lord is near, and destruction will come from God." What has been threatened, he means, has not yet arrived, but it is very soon to come. "So act first, and atone for your evils with weeping and lament and wailing. For the day of God's wrath spoken of before is about to arrive, in which every hand will grow weak, and every human soul will be afraid. The ambassadors will be thrown into turmoil, and pangs will seize them like a woman in labour. They will lament to one another, they will be dumbfounded, and their faces will change like a flame." By "ambassadors" he here means those who champion the doctrines of godlessness and act as ambassadors for idolatrous error, the teachers of godless and impious doctrines, upon whom all the things listed will fall. It is characteristic of people who are dismayed and have met with unexpected horrors that the colour of their faces changes.

To this he adds, "For behold, the day of the Lord is coming, a day of rage, fury and wrath, to make the whole inhabited world a desert and to destroy the sinners from it." At that time, he says, "the stars of heaven and Orion and all the array of heaven will not give their light, and they will be darkened when the sun rises." For at the time of the consummation neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars will give their light to the ungodly who are to be handed over to chastisement and punishment. The luminaries too will be changed, and will pass from their own service to another, better station, as though they were to obtain a kind of rebirth. They will no longer be in bondage to the futility of bodies, but will be set free from the bondage of corruption, as the apostle says.

So they will attain a rest above the heavens and beyond the world, and the highest glory. When the luminaries have withdrawn, the ungodly will be handed over to darkness and will suffer what is prophesied, as the next words say: "And I will command evils for the whole inhabited world, and for the ungodly their sins." All these things, then, have been said in general terms about the judgment that will come upon the ungodly at the consummation of the world. That is why throughout all these verses the word mentions the inhabited world and not Babylon. Our observation is therefore accurate when we divided the sense of the prophecy into a general discourse about the universal judgment and a specific one about Babylon. That is why the earlier verses mentioned the inhabited world in different ways. At one point it said, "The Lord and his warriors, to destroy the whole inhabited world"; at another, "For behold, the day of the Lord is coming, a day of incurable fury and wrath, to make the inhabited world a desert"; and again, "And I will command evils for the whole inhabited world." In none of these did the prophecy mention Babylon even once. Instead it gives a general teaching about God's righteous judgment, and on this subject it continues with the following words: "And I will destroy the insolence of the lawless, and humble the insolence of the arrogant." Why then does it mention only the Babylonians, as if harshly singling them out, and not other nations too, such as the Gauls [?] or the Spaniards? Because, he says, at that time no others troubled the Jewish nation except those listed, who constantly rose up against them, at one time sacking Jerusalem and at another laying waste their land. So the word had good reason to teach those under siege what would happen to those besieging them.

Having gone through what was said earlier about God's universal judgment, the word adds these things as well. It teaches what will happen to the ungodly throughout the whole world, and what will come upon those who ruled the nations godlessly and tyrannically. These were the arrogant and puffed-up men who held power over the earth at various times and seasons, of whom he says, "And I will destroy the insolence of the lawless, and humble the insolence of the arrogant." In place of "And those who are left will be held in honour," Symmachus says, "I will make a man more precious than gold, and a human being more precious than the stone from Ophir." For he means that among them anyone worthy of the name of man will be rare.

Indeed, no one will be found among them who preserves the rational humanity that belongs to our nature. For these people were bestial and savage in their ways, so that even heaven was stirred against them. By heaven I mean the heavenly powers, or else God's creation itself, which shares God's indignation, as it were, at the madness, boastfulness and godlessness of the people in question. That is why it is written, "For heaven will be enraged, and the earth will be shaken from its foundations, because of the fury of the Lord's wrath." I think that by saying the earth will be shaken from its foundations he signifies the consummation.

And if any among them try to secure their safety by flight, he says, they too will be easily caught. They will not be like full-grown gazelles leaping away and running lightly and swiftly, but like a young fawn; that is why, according to the other translators, it is called a "fawn." They will also be like a sheep that strays and is neither sought nor gathered in by anyone. Those who flee will pray to find someone kind and to discover a refuge with one of their acquaintances, but they will not find one, "for there will be no one to gather them." So some of them will be overcome, or, according to the other translators, "will be run through." Others, gathered together and forming themselves into a band, as it were, will fall by the sword of God's wrath.

The avenging angels who come upon them will deal in this way not only with the arrogant who have been mentioned, but "they will also dash their children to pieces before their eyes, plunder their houses and take their wives." Just like the men who are punished, their wives, who have themselves become godless and ungodly, will be subjected to equal punishments, and so will their ungodly children, the souls akin to them, made like them and grown close to them through the wickedness of their ways. These are the things, then, that he threatens all the ungodly, the lawless and the arrogant will suffer at the time of God's universal judgment. Next, from this point on, he proclaims beforehand what will befall Babylon, the Babylonians and the king of the Chaldeans in particular, making his prophecy specific and particular. That is why he also addresses the word directly to the Babylonians. It should be noted that Origen's fifteenth volume of exegetical commentaries on the prophet extended up to this point.

The words "Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against you" are confirmed by the course of history, which is recorded by the Greek writers who composed histories of the Chaldeans and Assyrians and by those who wrote histories of the Medes. We ourselves have collected a great many testimonies from them in the chronological works we laboured over. It is clear, then, that the Medes overthrew the empire of the Assyrians, and that Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, subdued the Medes. It was he who released the Jews from captivity and gave those of them who wished leave to return to their own land and rebuild the temple of God. That is why the prophecy mentions them by name: here it says, "Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against you," and in what follows it also makes mention of Cyrus by name.

The prophecy goes on to say about Babylon, "And Babylon, which is called glorious, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. It will not be inhabited for all time." This too must be noted, since it is proved true by events: Babylon is still seen to be uninhabited and completely deserted even now, as those who come to us from those regions testify. "Nor will Arabs pass through it," he says. By this, I think, he means those we call Saracens, who in ancient times used to pitch their tents even at Babylon itself while carrying on their trade. But it is so shunned both by its neighbours and by those who roam around it as from a distant nation that not even the shepherds from among the Arabs graze any of their flocks in it, because it has become utterly desolate. It should be noted that he calls "Arabs" the Saracen tribes that reach as far as Assyria itself and inhabit the innermost desert, for they live next to the land of the Arabs. That is why Symmachus says, "Nor will an Arab pitch his tent there." There is also another country, called Arabia Felix, which lies next to the land of the Persians, so the oracle could also refer to people from there. And since shepherds graze many desert places and make folds for their flocks in them, the word foretells that Babylon will not be of use even for this, saying, "Nor will shepherds rest in it."

He prophesies, then, that Babylon will be left utterly empty of tame and rational creatures, and that none of them will live there. But he says that there will be in it certain wild beasts, obscure and unknown to us, and certain harsh and savage demons and spirits. That is why, in place of "wild beasts," the other translators have rendered "siim"; in place of "sirens" they have said "ostriches"; and in place of "onocentaurs" they wrote "iim," using the Hebrew word itself because the meaning is obscure. Likewise, in place of "hedgehogs," the three translators rendered "sirens," perhaps because of the deceitfulness of such demons, since among the Greeks the sirens are recorded to have been sweet-voiced and deceitful creatures. "All these things," he says, "are coming swiftly and will not delay." For even what people consider the longest span of time is reckoned as very short by God the Judge. It is said, indeed, that a thousand years in his sight are like yesterday, and like a watch in the night. Moreover, what the prophecy foretold was fulfilled not long afterward, when Babylon suffered what had been predicted under the rule of the Medes.

After what was foretold against Babylon, he goes on, fittingly, to point to the return of the Jewish people from enemy territory to Jerusalem that took place under Cyrus. He teaches that once they have returned they will rest in their own land, and that "the sojourner will be joined to them." In place of "the sojourner will be joined to them," the other translators rendered "the proselyte." For he says that they will prosper so much in their own land that even foreigners will lay claim to their religion, become their proselytes and be joined to the house of Jacob. These were not descended from them, but by becoming proselytes they were made so much their own that they differed in nothing from the native-born, though they were foreigners.

He says that when they return from Babylonia to the land of Judea, nations will take them and bring them into their own place. This too was fulfilled, according to the history contained in the book of Ezra. Ezra relates that King Cyrus issued a proclamation giving any of the Jews who wished leave to return to their own land and to raise up the temple in Jerusalem. To this the scripture adds: "And the heads of the families of Judah and Benjamin rose up, and all those around them strengthened their hands with vessels of silver, with gold and goods, with cattle and with gifts." They were led by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, and the prophets Haggai and Zechariah were with them. After Cyrus, Xerxes king of the Persians sent Ezra, the scribe of the law, with letters ordering all the rulers of the nations between Persia and Judea to help Ezra. This was the second going-up, made by those who came with Ezra. After this, when Nehemiah went up, the king of the Persians again gave him letters to the governors beyond the River, and the king himself sent army officers with him to serve both as guides and as guards. These are the things the prophecy announces in advance when it says: "And nations will take them and bring them into their own place." The words "And those who took them captive will be captives, and those who ruled over them will be ruled" were fulfilled when the Persians and Medes brought the whole empire of the Assyrians, and the Babylonians themselves, under their hand and made them subject to their own power.

From this point on, the prophetic Spirit gives instruction to those who would read the prophetic scripture in later times. It teaches them how they ought to glorify and bless God for the benefits he has given them, and how they ought to lament over the king of Babylon. That is why it says: "And you will say on that day: How the exactor has come to rest!" Note that Origen's sixteenth volume of commentaries on the prophet went as far as this point.

"You will say, then, on that day," it says, "How the exactor has come to rest, and the taskmaster has come to rest!" For this Symmachus translated "How the tribute has been bound!" and went on: "The Lord has broken the staff of the ungodly, the staff of those in power." Again, where we read "All the earth has rested in confidence," Symmachus says, "All the earth has rested and been at peace." And he adds: "Be cheerful, exult; yes, all the pines rejoiced over you, the cedar of Lebanon." Here again the pine and the cedar of Lebanon allegorically stand for certain tyrants and proud men who had been besieged by the Babylonian and cut off from their own lands. They would naturally rejoice at the fall of the one spoken of.

"And they were filled with joy," it says, "at your destruction, saying: Since you have lain down, no one has come up to cut us down." Those on earth will say this. But those who have left human life and been left behind in the regions of Hades as if in chains will also rejoice at his destruction, and they will speak the words that follow. Hades, ahead of all those there, and the power set over the souls of the dead, will rise up against you with fury and anger from the dark recesses below, like the jailer of a prison. When this one, as ruler and master of those there, has been roused from his throne, all the rest of the giants rise up with him, or, as the other translators have it, the Rephaim. He explains who these were: "those who ruled the earth, who roused from their thrones all the kings of the nations." They had done the same things as the accused king of Babylon. Seeing the soul of the man who once reigned over Babylon naked and stripped of its body, they will say to it: "Has death proved stronger even than you, and shown that you are just like us? Then life on earth, with its wealth and glory and such great power, was nothing, if earth and ashes, worms and rotting flesh, are what come at the end of it all. We did not think you were mortal. We were deceived by the glory around you, and we compared you to the brightest light in heaven, the morning star that calls up the sun. And you thought even greater things of yourself. You exulted and boasted in your madness, so that you compared yourself to God Most High and imagined you would set your throne above the vaults of heaven. That is what we thought of you, deceived by mortal reasoning, and that is what you thought of yourself in your derangement. But in the end the time of your capture exposed the truth about your end as well. You did not even die as other men do. They paid their debt quietly and gently, in peace at their own hearths. But you were robbed of life by the sword of your enemies, and you will be thrown out as an unburied corpse, left exposed as food for beasts and birds." Note that Origen's seventeenth volume of commentaries on the prophet went as far as this point.

Symmachus rendered the sense of these words as follows: "You too were wounded as we were, and you have been counted among us. Your pride has been brought down to Hades, your mouth has been put to death; beneath you creeping things will be spread, and the worm will be your covering. How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, you who rose at dawn! You were cut down to the earth, you who wounded nations. You said in your heart: I will go up into heaven; I will raise my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; I will go up on a high cloud; I will be like the Most High. But you will be brought down to Hades, into the depths of the pit. Those who see you will stoop down to look; they will consider you: Is this the man who troubled the earth and shook kingdoms, who made the world like the desert and pulled down his cities, who did not release his prisoners to go home? All the kings of the nations have lain down in honor, each in his own house. But you will be cast out of your tomb like a loathsome miscarriage, clothed with the slain, those weighed down by the sword, who go down to the foundations of the pit."

In the Septuagint these words come next: "As a garment soaked in blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and killed my people," and so on. Symmachus rendered this roughly as follows: "Like a stinking body you will not share burial with them, because you have ruined your land and killed your people; an evildoing seed will never be named. He prepared his sons for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers, so that they might not rise and inherit the earth and fill the face of the world with cities." That is Symmachus's version. The versions of Aquila and Theodotion agree with it and suggest a deeper meaning, for they say that the king of Babylon ruined his own land. So it says, "because you have ruined your land," and it teaches that he killed his own people, and even that he prepared his own sons for slaughter. And earlier, in Symmachus, it was said: "who made the world like the desert and pulled down his cities, who did not release his prisoners." When did the Babylonian pull down his own cities? Which prisoners of his did he not release? How did he ruin his own land, kill his own people and prepare his own sons for slaughter? These questions deserve examination. If the text read as in the Septuagint, "because you have destroyed my land and killed my people," there would be nothing to ask, for clearly the Babylonian invaded and besieged the land of Israel and subdued the people that was once called God's people. But according to the other translators, and according to the Hebrew wording itself, he is said to have ruined his own land, killed his own people and brought slaughter on his own children. Consider, then, whether these words may be hinting at the hidden and invisible power set over the nation of the Babylonians. The prophet Daniel too teaches that angels of this kind are set over the nations. Gabriel, the angel who spoke with him, appears in his book saying: "And behold, the prince of the kingdom of the Persians came against me, and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks, and the prince of the kingdom of the Medes, and there was no one with me except Michael your prince." It is likely, then, that certain princes preside over each nation. The scripture of Moses shows this as well when it says: "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God."

As long as Babylon stood, and those who ruled there had a kingdom and great power, the power set over them may well have helped them achieve great things. But once the nation's kingdom had been wiped out, the prince set over them, as though he had completed his allotted time, was taken into the place of those like him. There all those called the Rephaim, or the giants, came to meet him. These too were presumably powers that in their own times had led other nations wrongly. Could it be, then, that this very one, once the prince of Babylon, ruined his own land because he was regarded there as a god? And in the same way, could he have killed his own people and handed his own sons over to slaughter, becoming the cause of destruction for those under his rule because they had come to regard him as a god? If so, it is time to refer the whole prophecy set out earlier concerning the king of Babylon to that power. Because it gained the glory of a god among those it ruled and grew proud, it is rightly refuted by the words aimed at such boasters: "You said in your mind: I will go up into heaven; I will set my throne above the stars of heaven; I will be like the Most High." You can apply the rest yourself to the interpretation given here, while also applying what the prophecy reveals to the visible king who is understood at first sight.

Having prophesied these things, and the words that follow them, about the prince of Babylon, about the city itself and about the nation of the Assyrians, the prophet goes on: "Thus says the Lord of hosts: As I have said, so it will be: to destroy the Assyrians on my land and on my mountains." This teaches that the country of the Babylonians and the mountains in it were not foreign to him either, for "the earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it." The Assyrians, then, it says, will be trampled down, made subject to those who ruled them afterwards. Their yoke will also be taken away. When they were in power they fastened it on those they ruled, hanging a heavy and unbearable yoke over them. Their renown, that is, their glory, which once rested on their shoulders, will be taken away too. For as it is said of the Savior, "whose rule is upon his shoulder," so here the glory of the Assyrians is said to be on their shoulders, and the word threatens that it will be taken from them.

Having brought the account of Babylon to a close here, the prophecy goes back again to the beginning of the present theme and says: "This is the counsel that the Lord has determined for the whole world." Whatever judgment has been pronounced on Babylon and its inhabitants, the same kind of judgment will fall on all the godless and ungodly men who have held power in the world. By the rule of justice, those who have committed the same impieties will suffer the same things. That is why it adds: "And this is the hand raised high over all the nations." Here we should take "nations" to mean the nations of godless and ungodly men, for it is not right to apply these words indiscriminately to the godly and to those devoted to God. So he ended in the same way he began, by mentioning God's universal judgment upon all. He had to mention it, to keep everyone who reads the scripture from thinking that what is said about Babylon has nothing to do with them. It would indeed have nothing to do with us if these things had been said about the Babylonians alone. As it is, the word turns us around and brings us to anguish and fear of God's universal judgment, which awaits all people, and so it rightly mentioned that judgment both at the beginning of the prophecy and at its end.

With the vision against Babylon concluded, the word begins a new theme. It addresses the foreigners living in Palestine, whom the Hebrew text and the other translators called Philistines, while the Greeks altered the name and called them Palaestini. While Ahaz was alive, idolatry was practiced in Jerusalem itself and in the other cities of Judea, as the history shows. It was natural that the neighboring foreigners, and perhaps also the wicked demons they called gods, rejoiced at the error and ruin of Ahaz and of the people under him called Judah. For the people called Israel and the kings in Samaria had already been taken captive by the Assyrians. The book of Kings records that the Lord humbled Judea because of Ahaz king of Judah, since he had fallen away in apostasy from the Lord. And about the foreigners it is written that the Edomites also attacked, struck down Judah and carried off captives, and that the foreigners attacked the cities of Palestine and destroyed Beth-shemesh. Here too, in place of "and the foreigners attacked the cities," we find the Philistines, that is, the Palestinians, who fell upon Ahaz. "For you are no longer allowed to rejoice, now that the ungodly king over whom you once rejoiced is dead and a God-fearing man has succeeded to the throne." This is attested of Hezekiah in 2 Chronicles and in 2 Kings. Under the ungodly Ahaz it was natural for the foreigners to rejoice and be glad. So under Hezekiah, a righteous man, the prophecy fittingly turns to them and says: "Do not rejoice, you foreigners." In the past, while Ahaz was still alive and doing what was hateful to God, you naturally rejoiced, since the yoke of Ahaz had been broken. He could not subdue you or lay the yoke of his rule upon you, and so evils multiplied.

Since there was no one to strike them, the creeping and venomous power of the wicked spirits multiplied in those days. But now that a man who loves God has succeeded to the kingdom, stop rejoicing as you did before, for the one who strikes, beats and disciplines you now stands over you. These things too were fulfilled literally in Hezekiah, of whom it is said in 2 Kings: "He struck the foreigners as far as Gaza and its borders, from watchtower to fortified city."

The saying could have this meaning. "Do not rejoice, you foreigners," in your pride over those you consider gods, because the wickedness of the present time has left no one to crush you. Even if the yoke of the one who struck you has indeed been broken, this did not happen for your good but for your harm. With no one to strike you, humble you and turn you back, evils have greatly increased among you. The wicked demons, who long ago lurked like serpents in your souls and lay in wait in your shrines and temples as though they were gods, have brought forth a terrible brood and an evil seed. From them asps are born, the worst of all venomous creatures, and from these in turn other serpents arise that fly through the air. At the present time these things abound not only among you foreigners but now also among the very people called God's, so that it is filled in every way with serpents flying through the air and with the offspring of asps, that is, with wicked and destructive spirits. But when the destroyer of all these is revealed in due time, the serpents and the asps and their wicked offspring will be gone, and they will no longer work these things among human beings.

The one who is prophesied will destroy this creeping and venomous race by famine. He will no longer allow them their usual food, that is, the sacrifices offered to demonic error. But he will feed his own poor and give them rest in peace, no longer troubled by the reptiles already described. These things can, however, also be fulfilled in another way with reference to Hezekiah. Throughout the whole Jewish nation there were those who had long been poor in God's sight, and he revived them with spiritual food and teaching. He set them in the good pasture of the law of godliness, so that they fed on the divine lessons and were nourished by the sacred teachings. These things are shown to have been partly fulfilled, as a matter of history, in the time of Hezekiah.

It refers to the king of the Assyrians. In Hezekiah's time he came from the regions farther north and subdued the foreigners living in Palestine. He besieged their cities, took the people in them captive and burned the city gates. For them the greatest proof that God is the guardian of his city will be that it suffered nothing like the other cities.

Salvation will come to the people not through a battle line of armed men, nor through the king at the head of the nation, but through God himself. This was fulfilled literally in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah's reign. In that year the king of the Assyrians invaded Judea and subdued its other cities, but when he marched against Jerusalem he went home having achieved nothing.

The inhabitants of Moab took great pride in their own gods, and they laughed at and mocked the God of Israel. For this reason the prophetic word set out the prophecy concerning them. So at the beginning it called the ignorance of God that prevailed among them night and darkness, and it threatened that their destruction would come in that very night, saying: "By night Moab will be destroyed, for by night the wall of Moab will be destroyed." Then, concerning the place where their idolatry was established, it adds: "For Dibon too will be destroyed; where your altar is, there you will go up to weep." At the end of the prophecy it mentions the same altars again, saying: "Because Moab has wearied herself at the altars, and she will go into her handmade idols to pray, and they will not be able to deliver him." From these words, I think, the reason for the present theme is clear. It concerns the destruction of idolatry among the Moabites, and it also foretells other things that would happen to the city itself and to the lands, villages and cities around it. These things were indeed fulfilled in history, at the attack of the Assyrians and Babylonians, and under those who in later times controlled the country of the Arabs. In the prophecy God also threatens to bring the Arabs upon them, perhaps meaning the neighboring Arabs, or the Saracens who live farther inland, to whom the word says he will also hand over Moab. There is no need to inquire closely into what happened to the other cities around Moab, or to busy ourselves with the villages and districts mentioned in the prophecy. I mean Nebo, Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Dibon and Luhith; the road of the Arabs, on which lies the water of Nimrim; Eglaim, the well at Elim, the water of Dibon, Ariel and Adamah, and the place called Arnon. These places and villages are still known today around the territory of the city now called Areopolis. So it is pointless to busy ourselves with the threats made against them, which were fulfilled literally, once and for all, at the time of the siege against them.

I also think that a figurative reading of these things is forced. Rather, just as in the case of the Babylonians the word prophesied that the Medes would rise up against Babylon, so now too God says that he will bring the Arabs upon the Moabites: "For I will bring Arabs upon the ravine," and again: "And the water of Dibon will be filled with blood; for I will bring Arabs upon Dibon." People also say that Ariel, a very large village, can still be seen today in the territory of the people of Areopolis, as can Sior, Esebor and the rest, unless perhaps one of them has vanished entirely over the long course of time.

Why, then, should we busy ourselves with these details, when we ought instead to draw so great a benefit from the prophecy? For it proclaims in advance the destruction and desolation of their idolatry and foretells that they will come to know the God who is over all, so that churches would even be established among them once the gods they had long worshipped were driven out. Nothing could be more astonishing than that. The word foretells these things in the following words: "For Dibon too will perish, where your altar is," and again: "For your alliance has been taken away, and the ruler who trampled upon the land has perished." By these words it means the evil demon lying in wait over the nation, or the ruler of the nation, like the ruler of the kingdom of the Persians, the ruler of the kingdom of the Greeks, and the ruler of the Babylonians. It says, then, that this demon, enthroned over the city of the Moabites, through whom they thought they received help in their battles with their enemies, will perish, since he trampled their souls underfoot, making them bow down toward the earth so that they could neither lift their heads nor look upward. That is why it says: "For your alliance has been taken away, and the ruler who trampled has perished from the land."

After his destruction it goes on to say: "And a throne will be set right with mercy, and one will sit upon it with truth in the tent of David, judging and seeking judgment and hastening righteousness." Do you see the marvel contained in the conclusion of the prophecy? For at the very moment it foretells the obliteration of idolatry among the people it describes, it announces to them the good news of hopes of good things. It says that the tent of David and the throne of God will be established among them, and that this will come about no longer through any human effort but through the mercy and love of God for humankind. That is why Aquila renders it: "And a throne will be prepared in mercy"; Symmachus: "And a throne will be prepared in mercy"; and Theodotion: "And a throne will be prepared with mercy." For whom will it be prepared, if not surely for the Christ who was to be born of the seed of David? It says, then, that among the Moabites there will be a throne of Christ, on which one will sit with truth in the tent of David. This is how the prophetic Spirit usually refers to the church of Christ, since it is also customary to call Christ himself David, because he was born of the seed of David according to the flesh. So it calls the church the tent of David, and by the throne it means the one set over the church, its presiding bishop, who occupies the bodily throne as a deputy, so to speak, for Christ.

The book of the Acts of the Apostles will show that these words were spoken about the church drawn from the nations. There James, the first bishop of Jerusalem, is recorded as saying: "Brothers, listen to me. Simeon has related how God first visited the nations to take from among them a people for his name. And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: After this I will return and rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins and set it up again, so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, and all the nations upon whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who has made these things known from of old." Here, having clearly mentioned the calling of the nations, he cited the prophecy about the tent of David. The prophet says, then, that these things will come about not through types and symbols but with truth. For when the tent of David has been established among the Moabites, the most superstitious of peoples, and a throne has been set up in it, the one who presides over it will sit judging and seeking judgment and hastening righteousness; or, as Symmachus has it: "and he will sit upon it in truth in the tent of David, judging and seeking judgments and swift to righteousness." Who would not be astonished at the fulfilment of this word, seeing with his own eyes the churches of God established, and the throne of Christ within them, in Areopolis itself and the surrounding districts, and in the other cities of Arabia, while the demons who long ago worked the most terrible deeds among them are no longer remembered even by name?

Symmachus gave a clearer rendering of these verses, translating them as follows: "We have heard of the pride of Moab—he is exceedingly proud—according to his arrogance and according to his pride. And his anger—not so his arms. Therefore Moab will wail, and everyone will wail for Moab; wounds have been found for those who rejoice in the wall of earthenware. For the branches of Heshbon have been laid waste, the vine of Sibmah; the lords of nations have cut down its shoots; it reached as far as Jazer; they wandered into the desert; its envoys set out to cross the sea. Therefore I will weep with weeping for Jazer, the vine of Sibmah; I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh, for a trampling has fallen upon your fruit harvest and upon your harvest. Gladness and joy have been taken away from your Carmel, and in the vineyards they will not exult or drink wine; the treader will not tread in the winepresses; I have stopped the stir of those who tread. Therefore my belly will sound like a harp for Moab, and my inward parts for the wall of earthenware. And it shall be, when it is seen that Moab has wearied himself on the high places, that he will go into his sanctuary to pray, and will not be able. This is the word which the Lord spoke concerning Moab. And now he has spoken: Within three years, as for a hireling, the glory of Moab will be dishonoured together with all its great multitude, and there will be left a remnant, small and not many."

We have already shown earlier, by citing the words of the prophet Jeremiah, that the power of the Moabites was great in the times when these things were prophesied: how Moab set itself up as Jerusalem's rival, how the Moabites belittled Israel, laughing at it as beneath notice, and how they prided themselves on their idol. The present prophecy also shows this when it says: "We have heard of the insolence of Moab—he is exceedingly insolent; I have removed his pride"; and in Symmachus: "We have heard of the pride of Moab—he is exceedingly proud—according to his arrogance and according to his pride. And his anger"—"but not so," it says, "his arms too." For his deeds do not match his proud words. Or, as the Seventy have it: "Not so your divination, not so." Since they prided themselves on their god and his oracles, it says that things will not turn out as the demon among them divines, nor as he promises through his oracles to those whom he deceives and who think him a god; at any rate, the time to come will expose their falsehood. That is why, at the end of the prophecy, it adds: "And it shall be to your shame, that Moab has grown weary at the altars and will go into her handmade things to pray, and will by no means be able to deliver him."

The words in between signify that the former luxury of the Moabites will be overturned. So it foretells that those who delighted in it will mourn and wail, saying: "Moab will wail, for in the land of Moab all will wail," and again: "and the plains of Heshbon will mourn." It should be noted that Origen's nineteenth volume of commentary on the prophet extended as far as these words. Next come the words: "Vine of Sibmah: you who swallow up the nations, trample down its vines as far as Jazer," and what follows. In these words too he hinted at the change of their land into wasteland and utter desolation, over which he also foretold that they would weep.

Then the prophet, as though grieving deeply and distressed at the destruction of the souls led astray among them, laments over them. First he had urged them to wail and called them to repentance by weeping for themselves. But since they did not do so, he himself takes up the weeping on their behalf, saying: "Therefore I will weep with weeping, and I will drench you with my tears." He explains the cause of his weeping, saying: "for a trampling has fallen upon your fruit harvest and upon your harvest." By the fruit harvest and the harvest, and by the vine so often mentioned, he means the flourishing vigour, the luxury and the charm of the life of those he speaks of, a life in which they passed their days as if drunk, delighting and revelling in their godless impieties.

So he wept over their destruction, saying: "Therefore my belly will sound like a lyre for Moab, and my inward parts like a wall that you have renewed. And it shall be to your shame." For my tears, he says, and my weeping serve no other purpose than to put you to shame. Then he foretells to them the obliteration of the gods they worshipped, saying: "That Moab has grown weary at the altars and will go into her handmade things"—or, as the other translators have it, "into his sanctuary"—"to pray, and will by no means be able to deliver him."

And this is the end of the word of God which he spoke against Moab. To it you should join what was said earlier: for once the desolation of the altars and the destruction of their gods have come, "a throne will be set right with mercy, and one will sit upon it with truth in the tent of David, judging judgment and hastening righteousness." These words have been inserted in the middle of the prophecy as though in mysteries, the Holy Spirit reserving the knowledge of them for those alone who would understand and be found worthy to contemplate them. In place of "The Lord spoke against Moab, when he also spoke," the other translators rendered: "which the Lord spoke concerning Moab; from then and now he has spoken." Here scripture very aptly observed that he spoke from that time, and that now likewise the Lord speaks the same things through the reading of the prophets; and that whereas long ago these things were foretold in words, now they are also fulfilled in deeds.

In place of the wording of the Seventy, "In three years of a hireling the glory of Moab will be dishonoured," in the Hebrew text and in the other translators a break inserted in between has made the meaning clearer. Aquila has: "in three years of a hireling"; Symmachus: "From then and now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, as for a hireling"; Theodotion: "From then and now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling." Then, as a fresh beginning, the other translators and the Hebrew text have: "And the glory of Moab will be dishonoured together with all its great multitude." The conjunction placed in between introduced a different sense, starting from "And the glory of Moab will be dishonoured." The preceding words indicated that the Lord spoke all the things foretold about Moab through the prophet over a period of three years, as though he had hired him and engaged him in the service of prophesying about these matters. For the prophet did not deliver the whole word of the prophecy in one continuous stretch, the way we read through the entire passage all at once; rather, he delivered it piece by piece at different intervals of time, so that the whole took three years, during which the things recorded were spoken to him. The Lord, then, spoke these things through the prophet over three years, and the conclusion of God's words was: "And the glory of Moab will be dishonoured together with all its great multitude, and it will be left very few and without honour." This too has been fulfilled to the letter, as those who visit those places can easily see with their own eyes.

Just as fitting words were spoken to Babylon, and appropriate ones to the foreigners who inhabit Palestine, and likewise certain other words peculiar to Moab, in the same way the prophetic oracle against Damascus also threatens that an end of its own will come upon it. For it says that it will be removed from among the cities; Theodotion has it that it will be removed from being a city. It suffered this in the time of the Assyrians, as the present book showed earlier when it presented the king of the Assyrians saying: "And I took Arabia and Damascus and Samaria; as I took these, so I will take all the kingdoms too." History also bears witness to this statement. It is written in 2 Kings: "And the king of the Assyrians went up to Damascus and seized it and deported its people to Cyrene"—or, as Symmachus has it, "to Kirra"—"and he put Rezin to death." But these events had come to pass before the present prophecy, whereas the present word speaks of things still to come, which were probably fulfilled literally in the time of the prophet Jeremiah, when the king of Babylon, marching against Jerusalem, captured Damascus again as well and left it utterly razed to its foundations. Jeremiah shows this, speaking somewhat as follows: "Damascus has grown faint; she has turned to flight and been cast out; trembling has seized her, and pangs have gripped her like a woman in labour. How has she not abandoned my city? She loved a village"—or, as Symmachus has it, "a praiseworthy city, a metropolis of gladness." "Therefore young men will fall in your streets, and all the men of war will fall on that day, says the Lord of hosts. And I will kindle a fire on the wall of Damascus, and it will devour the streets of the son of Hadad."

So the prophecy now before us declares things like those said before, saying: "Behold, Damascus will be taken away from among cities and will be left in ruin." The words that follow, I mean "for ever," appear only in the Septuagint translation; they are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators. So there is no need to think that the fall of Damascus is called everlasting, since its fall was only for a time, during the Assyrian siege, when Jerusalem too was captured. The Jews later returned, rebuilt Jerusalem and filled the land with inhabitants again. In the same way Damascus, after suffering at that time what the prophecy foretold, was rebuilt in later times, so that a kingdom was set up in it once more. This kingdom lasted until the time of the apostles. Paul at any rate mentions a king of Damascus, writing: "In Damascus the ethnarch of Aretas, king of the Damascenes, was guarding the city to seize me, and I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands." We shall therefore refer the first parts of the prophecies to the times of the Assyrians, when Damascus was besieged a first and a second time. It is likely too that in Persian and Macedonian times it suffered similar things from those who rose against it and besieged it from time to time. In those sieges the oracle was fulfilled which said: "Behold, Damascus will be taken away from among cities and will be left in ruin, as a lair for flocks and a place of rest, and there will be no one to chase them away."

The words that come next, "And it will no longer be a stronghold for Ephraim to flee to, and there will no longer be a kingdom in Damascus," might be referred to Roman times. Then, after the coming of our Savior, every local principality was abolished, and the kingdom of Damascus was dissolved as well. The first parts of the prophecy did not point to the complete destruction of Damascus, only to a partial fall. This is clear from what is said afterward, "and it will not be a stronghold," and again, "no longer a kingdom in Damascus." These things are said of a city that would go on existing but would no longer be fortified as of old or ruled by a king. The passages can also be taken another way, as though the prophecy foretold humiliation and an ordinary private life for the inhabitants of Damascus. That is how we usually speak: we say a rich man has fallen when he is reduced to utter poverty, and a man of rank has fallen when he loses the dignity he held. Such too is the saying, "The house of Israel has fallen; it will rise no more." So when it says, "Behold, Damascus will be taken away from among cities and will be left in ruin for ever," it hints at the overthrow of the royal power that the city once held in its splendor. At that time it alone ruled the whole of Syria, since the famous Syrian cities of our own day had not yet been built. Antioch, Apamea, Laodicea and all the other cities that later became famous were founded after the death of Alexander of Macedon. Before them Damascus ruled the whole of Syria as a royal city of the Syrians. It was going to fall from its royal dignity and be left modest, humble and very small, so that from then on ordinary private people and the common folk, like a herd of flocks, would live in the city and its countryside, and no enemy would trouble them any longer. For this reason it is said, "Behold, Damascus will be taken away from among cities," meaning, clearly, from among royal cities, as the passage leads us to understand. "And it will be left," he says, "in ruin for ever, as a lair for flocks and a place of rest, and there will no longer be anyone to chase them away."

These things were indeed fulfilled under Roman rule. Under that rule Damascus survived in part; it is the ancient royal city that he says was utterly wiped out. The city we now see stands just as the prophecy foretold. It no longer holds royal dignity or rules the Syrian nation. It has fallen from the power it once had and been left all but a lair for flocks and a resting place for herds, which is how Scripture usually refers to the herd-like masses and the common people. Everyone knows that no one besieges the city of the Damascenes now that it is under Roman government. It is just as plain that, in such a condition, it can give the Jewish nation no help as it did before. That is why it was said: "And it will no longer be a stronghold for Ephraim to flee to, and there will no longer be a kingdom in Damascus and in the rest of the Syrians." "Do not think," he says, "that Damascus will lose its royal rank while some other Syrian city takes a share in it. There will no longer be a kingdom in Damascus, nor in the rest of the Syrian nation." Next he explains the reason, addressing the city directly: "For you are no better than the sons of Israel and their glory." In the times indicated, the people who of old bore the name of God's own would fall from their proper dignity and from the self-rule and kingship they had long enjoyed. If that is so, you, Damascus, should not resent suffering the same. "For you are no better than the sons of Israel and their glory," the glory that has been taken away.

He goes on to explain how their glory was taken away, saying: "Thus says the Lord of hosts: In that day the glory of Jacob will fail, and the fat things of his glory will be shaken." These things too were fulfilled after the coming of our Savior. On one day, so to speak, by which I mean at one and the same time, both the dignity of the people of the circumcision and the kingdom of Damascus came to an end. That is why it is said: "In that day the glory of Jacob will fail." And notice that this means the overthrow of the glory they once enjoyed, not the total destruction of the nation. Long ago the glory of the former people was the priesthood and the kingship, the sanctuary and the worship prescribed by the law, the grace of prophecy and the freedom of the nation, and everything else the Jewish nation possessed. The passage foretells that all of these will be shaken at once, will fall, and will fail completely.

"And when these things happen," he says, "it will be as when someone gathers in the standing grain at harvest." At harvest the ears are gathered and only bare stalks are left in the field. In the same way, he says, the Jewish people will have the ears that once grew among them cut away, and only the stalk will be left. And if anyone worth mentioning should be found among them, he will be like an ear of grain that grew not on the plain but in a parched, stony valley or ravine. By the ear I think he means the company of our Savior's disciples and evangelists. Of these it was also said earlier: "If the Lord of hosts had not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah."

But it was also necessary to make special mention of the chosen ones among them, so he uses another illustration for them as well, saying: "or as two or three olives are left at the top of the highest bough, or four or five on its branches." In the times the prophecy points to, he says, those from Israel who are saved will be so few that all of them together are compared to a single ear of grain. The outstanding ones among them will be as few as two or three olives at the top of the highest bough. Here the passage hints at the foremost of the apostles. The Savior sometimes called them in pairs and sometimes in threes, and the Gospel presents them as more chosen than the chosen: I mean Peter, James and John. He took them alone up the mountain to witness his transfiguration, and he took them with him when the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was raised to life. The others besides these three are the four and the five. Together they make up the number nine, and they too are described as being at the top of the highest bough of the olive tree. If one adds together the two, the three, the four and the five, the total will be fourteen. Of these, one might say, twelve are the first apostles. The other two are Paul, himself also a called apostle, and James the brother of the Lord, who is recorded to have been appointed by the Savior himself as the first bishop of the church in Jerusalem; neither was inferior to the twelve in virtue. All of these are found at the top of the olive tree, that is, of the Jewish line of descent, and the present passage mentions them. The divine Apostle too knows how to compare the Jewish line of descent to an olive tree and to call them a holy root, firstfruits and a cultivated olive.

These few olives, then, were the only ones found among them and saved. And the ear of grain just mentioned was itself something rare. That is why the prophetic word says: "And it will be as when someone gathers an ear of grain in a stony ravine, or as two or three olives at the top of the highest bough."

After mentioning the apostles, he very fittingly goes on to foretell that the nations, who once worshiped many gods, will turn to the God of the universe. So the next words are: "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: In that day people will trust in the one who made them, and their eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. They will no longer trust in the altars, nor in the works of their hands, which their fingers made, and they will not look to the trees or to their abominations." They will no longer pay heed to sacred groves or tall trees as they did before. Those who were once cut off from the knowledge of God and strangers to the covenants of promise will acknowledge the Holy One of Israel alone "in that day," that is, in the time indicated.

After showing the calling of the nations in these words, he next adds: "In that day," that is, in the same period, "your cities will be abandoned, just as the Amorites and the Hivites abandoned theirs before the sons of Israel, and they will be desolate, because you forsook God your Savior and did not remember the Lord your God." It is a very striking prophecy. He did not simply say that their cities would be abandoned, but that they would be abandoned as the Amorites and Hivites abandoned theirs. "When those peoples perished," he says, "others came in and took over their cities and lands. In the same way your cities will have other inhabitants, once you have been cast out and driven away." This can be seen with one's own eyes. Jerusalem itself is inhabited by Gentiles, and no Jew dares to set foot in the place, while foreigners hold many other cities of Israel. A great many more were besieged by the Romans, razed to their foundations and reduced to utter desolation, as the oracle foretold. He says they will suffer these things because they forsook their Savior. Here the Hebrew wording even mentions Jesus our Savior himself, for the name Jesus, translated into Greek, means "savior." This was the reason given for why all the things foretold would happen to them: they forsook God their Savior and did not remember the Lord who was always their helper.

He himself teaches in the Gospels how he was always their helper, saying: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing!" The prophecy gives another reason too why they would suffer the things foretold: they planted a faithless plant and a faithless seed. This too consists in their refusal to believe in the Christ of God, who shone upon them first. "So when you sow this faithless seed and this faithless plant in your own soul," he says, "then you will go astray." But suppose you turn to the morning of the gospel light that has dawned on the world and plant another seed in your mind. This is the seed of which the Gospels say, "The sower went out to sow," and, "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his own field." Then, once you are in the light of the morning rising of the Sun of righteousness, it will blossom in you for the harvest. So you will pass on a good inheritance to your own children as well, those who will be born according to God through the saving teaching. This much the prophecy has included along with its word about Damascus. It refers the fulfillment of what was said about Israel to the same time that was given for Damascus.

Having prophesied that the nations would turn to God and that the Jewish nation would not believe in Christ, the passage moves on to the multitudes of the nations, in Damascus itself and in the other lands, who remained in unbelief and were going to persecute and besiege the church of God. It shows that these will be tossed and troubled like a surging sea, alarmed at the gospel preaching, which overthrows the error of idolatry. So he says: "Woe to the multitude of many nations; like water it will roar." When the sea is stormy and stirred up by the winds, its arching backs rise high, making a tremendous roar and frightening those who sail on it. In the same way the multitudes of the nations, in Damascus itself and in the other lands, who remained in unbelief and idolatry, will be driven by invisible spirits. They will roar like the waves of the sea as they rise up against the church of God. That is why it is said: "Like water it will roar, and many nations like much water, like much water rushing along."

Notice how he uses many images to show the godless and impious mind of those he has described. First he compares their rage to a surging sea. Then he likens their schemes against the Church to roaring water. Third, he compares them to a great mass of water driven by force, and in this way he hints that their life is fluid and passing away. By saying "like a great mass of water driven by force," he shows that they make these attacks on the Church because they are worked on and driven by others. Even so, he then describes their end, saying next: "And he will drive him away and pursue him far off." Aquila has: "And he will rebuke him, and he will flee far away," and Symmachus: "And he will be angry with him, and he will flee far off." With whom will he be angry, or whom will he rebuke? Either the multitude of unbelieving nations mentioned before, or the devil who works in them. And who will rebuke them, if not the one of whom it is said, "May the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you"? When the Lord has rebuked him, what will happen? He goes on: "And he will pursue him far off, like chaff that people winnow against the wind, and like the dust of a wheel carried off by a storm," or, as Symmachus has it, "and like a wheel before a storm."

Then he adds: "Toward evening there will be mourning; before morning, and they will be no more." Those who rose up against the Church like a surging sea will have mourning at the setting of their life and at its very end. In the age to come they will no longer exist, when the dawn of a new light and a new morning shines on the righteous. This is what he means: "This is the portion, the full share, of those who plundered you." Who are the "you" here, if not plainly those who have taken refuge in the Church of God?

In the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul once came to Rome and spoke with the leaders of the Jews about faith in Christ, they are recorded as saying to him: "We have received no letters about you from Judea, and none of the brothers who came here has reported or said anything bad about you. But we would like to hear from you what you think, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against." By saying this they showed that before Paul came to Rome they had been instructed not to accept the preaching about Christ, and that they were not the only ones who had received this instruction, but the Jews all over the earth as well. That is why they said, "For with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against." How did it come about that the Jews everywhere all spoke against the message about Christ with one voice, as if by a single watchword? We have found the answer in the writings of the ancients. The priests, scribes and elders of the Jewish nation who lived in Jerusalem drew up letters and sent them out to all the nations, to the Jews everywhere, slandering the teaching of Christ as a foreign heresy alien to God, and in these letters they instructed them not to accept it.

This seems to be exactly what the prophecy before us means when it says: "Woe to the land of the wings of ships, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends hostages by sea." For "hostages" Symmachus said "apostles," reading "which sends apostles by sea," and Aquila rendered it "envoys," reading "which sends envoys by sea." You see how the text pronounces woe on the Jewish leaders just mentioned and on their land, whose wickedness reached even as far as the Ethiopians. So Symmachus has: "Woe to the land whose sound is winged, which lies beyond the rivers of Ethiopia." By this he means that the sound of the wickedness of those who lived in the land of the Jews went out beyond the country of the Ethiopians and to the ends of the earth, carried as if on flying ships. Their apostles, bearing letters of papyrus, sailed over the waters and voyaged across the sea, running over the whole earth and slandering the message about our Savior. Even now the Jews customarily call those who carry circular letters from their leaders "apostles." This, then, is what he hinted at concerning them. Next, in place of "For light messengers will go," all the other translators said, "Go, light messengers," so that it begins a command. To me this command seems to be addressed to the disciples of our Savior. Because they bring the good news of good things to all people, he called them "light messengers," in contrast to the Jewish "apostles" he had described. So he says to them: "You messengers of good things, you disciples of Christ, go!" just as the Savior himself commanded you when he said, "Go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and, "Go and make disciples of all nations in my name." And as you go, he says, be light and unencumbered, so that your journey may be easy. The Savior himself again urged the same people to do this, saying, "Take nothing for the journey," and, "Do not acquire gold or silver or copper for your belts, no bag for the road, and do not have two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff."

So he rightly called them "light messengers." And he bids them go "to a nation hanging aloft and strange, and to a harsh people." For they were not sent to people they knew, or to their own kin and brothers, but to estranged and unknown men of other races among all the nations. Those people truly hung aloft, standing on nothing firm, wandering and carried about by every wind of polytheistic error. They were also a harsh nation, hostile and at war with the message of true religion. Even so, he commands the light messengers to go to them and preach to them, and to cross over even to the ends of the earth. So he adds: "Who is beyond it?" or, as Symmachus has it, "after which there is nothing beyond." This estranged nation hanging aloft was also without hope, so that the Apostle says, "We were once without hope and without God in the world." And the prophet before us, further on, prophesies about those without hope, saying, "And those of mankind who have lost hope will be filled with gladness." So they are sent to a nation without hope, a nation trodden down by the devil and by all the activity of the demons.

Then he gives them courage, saying: "Now all the rivers will be like an inhabited land; their land will be inhabited." Now, at your going, the rivers of the earth and all their lands will be inhabited. By this he seems to me to hint that the rivers are the multitudes of peoples who will come to know God, and their lands are the churches. Earlier he compared the multitudes of the unbelieving nations to a wave of the sea and to troubled waters; so now he likens the peoples of Christ to sweet rivers that flow steadily, and he signifies the Church by their land. In the past these rivers were uninhabited and alien to God, and their land was empty of true religion. But now, he says, through your preaching these rivers and their land will become an inhabited world. The sign of Christ will bring this about for them. It will be as well known and as plain to everyone as if a sign were raised on a high mountain, or as the loud call of a trumpet. In the same way your preaching too will be clear, conspicuous and heard by all people.

He must also teach how the rivers and their land, mentioned above, will be able to be inhabited without disturbance, and so he says: "For thus the Lord said to me: There will be security in my city." The land mentioned above is my city, the Lord's city. That is why there will be security in it, since I guard it and make it secure on every side. So it is fitting that it should be said of it, "Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God," and, "The streams of the river gladden the city of God." Scripture usually gives this name to the way of life that accords with God. Having said that there will be security in it, he adds that there will also be light in this same city—no ordinary light, but such as one might compare to the full brightness of the sun at noon. Yet though such light, like the heat of noon, will be in my city, he says, there will be no harm or distress to those who are illumined by it. Why? [?] … and a cloud [?] will overshadow them, as in the days of harvest.

The light, then, is the Word of God himself, who continually enlightens his Church. The cloud of dew is the Holy Spirit, who overshadows the highest theology of the only-begotten Son of God for those who cannot receive it. In this way the abundant and undiluted theology concerning Christ is tempered, because the Holy Spirit comes beneath it like a cloud.

And he says that these things will happen "before the harvest." By this he means the fruitfulness in the churches of God, which flowers and multiplies like ears of grain. He spoke of these earlier too, saying, "And they will rejoice before you like those who rejoice at the harvest." The Savior said the same in these words: "Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest," and again, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest." So the light of the Word's divinity will be undiluted in his city, as at the height of noon. But because human beings cannot receive it, the cloud of the Holy Spirit, full of dew, will come between and overshadow that city, so that, as in the days before the harvest, the light may shine out and the cloud may overshadow the city. These things will happen around the city of God before the consummation and before the harvest. But after the harvest and the consummation of the present life, those who are found worthy of that end will share in the undiluted divinity of the Word itself. Then, when the consummation has come, the fruitfulness of the Church of God will be compared to another image, and by this image he shows the separation that will take place among those gathered in the Church of God. For, he says, it is like vineyards. When the clusters are still unripe grapes, the vinedresser comes and cuts off not only the superfluous and useless branches but also the clusters that will not ripen and are, as it were, dead. Since these are not needed and have no good hope of bringing fruit to maturity, he removes them with a farmer's skill, so that the superfluous and useless parts may not harm the healthy clusters.

So he removes these and gives them as food to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, but he guards with every care the clusters that keep their fruit whole. This, he says, is what will happen at the time of the harvest. The superfluous branches of the vine and the useless clusters on it will be removed and cut off and given as food to the punishing powers, while the good clusters, the fruitful souls, will obtain the good hope that is with God. In this connection the Savior himself said that he is the vine, and he called the disciples the branches. It follows that we should understand the clusters on the branches to be those taught as disciples under the apostles. He teaches that at the time of judgment the useless little clusters among them, which are as good as dead and deprived of living power, will be thrown away. Likewise the branches that bear no cluster at all, such as Judas the traitor was, will be cut off like the useless clusters.

In place of "And he will remove the small clusters" and what follows, Symmachus says, "And its worthless parts will be cut off," and Aquila, "And he will cut off its castoffs with pruning hooks, and he will leave them to the birds of the sky and to the beasts of the earth; and the birds of the sky will gather upon them, and all the beasts of the earth will come upon them"—that is, plainly, the opposing and punishing powers.

Such is the end of these. Next he mentions the fruitful branches and the healthy clusters, and adds: "And gifts will be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people afflicted and stripped." This would be the one who travels the narrow and afflicted way that leads to life. The same person is also stripped, since he has become a stranger to the common life of mankind, and he is great and mighty before God. That is why it says, "and from a great people." These gifts, he says, will be brought to the Lord of hosts "from now and for all time." For both in the present life and in the age to come the people described never cease to send up to God spiritual gifts and bloodless sacrifices. This people is the same as the nation mentioned earlier, trodden down and hoping. It is hoping because of its endurance, of which it is said, "Endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame." And it is trodden down because of those who persecuted it and often trampled it. So Aquila has: "a nation enduring and trampled." You see how he has called the stripped people "enduring." And he adds: "which is in a part of a river of his land." Whose land, if not God's?

For this nation was in a part of a river of God's land, inasmuch as it lived as a citizen in the Church of God, so that it says, "We know in part and we prophesy in part." The land described did not hold the whole river, by which I mean the Word of God. That is why the nation described is said to have been in a part of a river of God's land. According to the other translators it says, "whose land the rivers plundered." For the enemies and persecutors of this nation of God once plundered its land, when those who plotted against the city of God drove them out, oppressing and trampling them. Of these it is said, "The rivers came, the winds blew," and again, "Our soul passed through a torrent; then our soul passed through the irresistible water." But once freed from all these, the people that was formerly afflicted and stripped, the nation that was trodden down but hoped in God, will bring gifts to the Lord of hosts. And where is it said that they will bring them? "To the place where the name of the Lord of hosts is, on Mount Zion." For when the people who have suffered so much are found worthy of the heavenly city, they will bring their spiritual sacrifices, under the Son of God as high priest, to the place where the name of the Lord of hosts is, to Mount Zion, of which the Apostle says, "We have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem."

This is the end of the prophecy concerning Damascus. It began with the times described above and ends with the consummation of the age and the thrice-blessed end of those who contend for true religion.

We should pay attention to how it says, "The vision of Egypt." It does not speak as it did of Babylon, "The vision against Babylon," nor as of Judea and Jerusalem, "The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw, which he saw against Judea and against Jerusalem," nor as of Damascus and Moab. It does not speak this way of Egypt too: it does not say "The vision against Egypt," but "The vision of Egypt." This is either because Egypt itself was going to see and behold with discerning eyes the things being prophesied, or because the prophet saw the vision that announced beforehand the finest things for the Egyptians.
