For what could be finer, what more blessed for the Egyptians, than that the Lord should count them worthy of his coming, should grant them knowledge of himself, and should do all the other things that the prophecy holds out to the Egyptians?

One might say that this was fulfilled at the level of history when the Lord himself, God the Word, who was in the beginning with God, came to the land of the Egyptians—not without a body or invisibly, but with the so-called light cloud of the body which he took up, formed from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin. If the words "he will come seated on a light cloud" had not been added, one could have said that God the Word is present everywhere by his bodiless and divine power, since he fills all things: "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him." And he granted his presence to Egypt too, by extending his oversight and providence even to them. But in this sense one could say that he was no more in Egypt than in any other part of the universe. As it is, by saying specifically that he will come to Egypt riding on a light cloud, the text shows that his coming would be particular and bodily. Anyone who holds this interpretation would say that it was fulfilled at the coming among men of God born of the holy Virgin, whom the prophecy calls Emmanuel. For as a cloud gets its substance from nowhere else but air and vapor rising from the earth, so the body which he took up, which came into being from the Holy Spirit and earthly substance, is fittingly compared to a light cloud. Seated on it, the Christ of God came to Egypt in his infancy. And even this was enough for the Egyptians, who received the greatest benefits, by an ineffable power, from the Savior's coming among them.

In a deeper sense, Egypt was in special need of the Lord's coming, because its people had become the most superstitious of all mankind. They not only attributed the cause of everything to fate and to the stars in heaven, but even sank so low as to make gods of irrational animals, of untamed wild beasts, of birds and of reptiles. They regarded the universe as so completely without a master and without providence that their king even said brazenly, bareheaded as it were: "I do not know the Lord," and: "Who is he, that I should obey his voice?" "And the handmade things of Egypt shall be shaken before his face, and their heart shall be overcome within them." The handmade things would be the statues and lifeless wooden images. He says that the lifeless wooden images will be shaken, but that the heart, meaning the demons, will be overcome, or, according to the other translators, will melt away by a hidden and invisible power. These things began to be fulfilled from the very time when churches of God adorned all of Egypt, as the activity of the demons was gradually and quietly extinguished.

These things reached their fulfillment in actual deeds at the time when churches of God were established throughout all Egypt, and the Lord himself came to dwell among the Egyptians, watching over his churches, in accordance with the saying: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." So the churches shone brightly with his grace, while the error of the demons there was being overthrown.

"And Egyptians shall rise up against Egyptians, and a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his neighbor, city against city and nome against nome. And the spirit of the Egyptians shall be troubled within them, and I will scatter their counsel." In place of "and they shall rise up," Aquila says: "And I will set Egyptians in strife among Egyptians"; Symmachus: "And I will set Egyptians against Egyptians"; and Theodotion: "And I will throw Egyptians into confusion among Egyptians." These things too were fulfilled after the preaching of the gospel had spread through all Egypt. Then the lifeless wooden images were shaken from the position in which they had stood unmoved from time immemorial, so that because of the shaking that came upon them they no longer stood firm or kept a secure footing, while the wicked demons lurking in them were thereby exposed as nothing at all. For a kind of civil strife broke out throughout all Egypt, as the inhabitants of the country were set against one another, cut apart and divided house by house and city by city: some of them ran to the preaching of the gospel, forsaking the demonic error of Egypt, while those who remained in it stirred up a relentless war against them. In this way Egyptians rose up against Egyptians, and a man fought against his neighbor and a man against his brother; and city was at strife with city and nome with nome. Among the Egyptians the districts of their country are still called nomes even today, and these too were set at odds with one another for the same reason. The life of the godless was separated from the way of life that is according to God, and nome was roused against nome, as the law of the gospel overturned the customs of the Egyptians, and the law of idolatry in turn made war on the word of salvation. All this happened because the Lord, who had come to dwell among them, was confounding the Egyptians' agreement in evil and their concord in the error of many gods. That is why it is said, according to Aquila: "And I will set Egyptians in strife against Egyptians," and according to Symmachus: "And I will set Egyptians against Egyptians." Akin and closely related to this, or rather the very same thing in other words, is what our Lord himself taught in the Gospels when he said: "Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth; I did not come to bring peace but a sword," and so on.

When these things take place, the text says, the spirit of the Egyptians will be troubled; according to Symmachus: "And the spirit of Egypt shall be torn apart within her"; according to Theodotion: "And the spirit of Egypt shall be split within her"; and Aquila: "And the spirit of Egypt shall grow slack in her inward parts." When this spirit is torn and troubled at the progress of the church, and the Egyptians devise wicked plans, "I," says the Lord himself, "will scatter their counsel." At a loss what to do, they will turn, according to their old custom, to those they regard as gods, to obtain oracles and divinations about the matters that trouble them. That is why it is said: "And they shall consult their gods and their statues, and those who speak from the earth, and the ventriloquists." But since none of these will appear to them any longer as they used to, they will fall into utter perplexity.

These are the things that the inhabitants of the various districts will suffer; but the text says that all Egypt together will be handed over "into the hands of harsh lords, and harsh kings will rule over them." Here I think the time of the fulfillment of the prophecy is indicated, for it signifies that there would be a change in the kingdom of the Egyptians at the time of the Lord's arrival in Egypt. And who would not be astonished on comparing the time of the preaching of the word of salvation with the overthrow of the Egyptian monarchy at that same time, so that from then until now their former rulers, I mean the Ptolemies, no longer hold power, and the Romans have been made their lords? In place of "and harsh kings," Aquila said: "And a king made strong shall have authority over them"; Symmachus: "And a mighty king shall have authority over them"; and Theodotion: "And a mighty king shall rule over them." You might say this was the one who held sole rule over the Roman empire at the time of our Savior's birth. For it was then that Augustus, a truly strong and mighty king, first subjected Egypt to the Romans, putting an end to the long-ruling succession of the Ptolemies who had reigned there. And the Roman emperors after him, truly strong and mighty kings, or harsh ones as the Seventy put it, reduced the Egyptian nation to slavery, and the military governors of Egypt whom they sent out from time to time treated them rather harshly. That is why it is said of them: "And I will hand Egypt over into the hands of men, harsh lords," and according to the other translators too these, I mean the local governors, were called harsh lords.

Next it is said: "And the Egyptians shall drink the water that is by the sea." In its place Aquila says: "And waters shall be drunk up from the sea," and Symmachus: "And waters shall vanish from the sea." Here too the text figuratively hints at the turbulent multitude of the Egyptians by the word "sea." It is as though a strange drink were being offered to them [?]: for since the river would no longer exist, nor any other Egyptian water, and sea water is not fit for drinking, he says that they will drink a new and strange water. This was the water supplied to them by the Lord from the springs of salvation. The same thing was shown a little earlier in the words: "Woe to the multitude of many nations; like a surging sea, and the back of many nations shall roar like water. Many nations are like much water," where he compared the turbulence of the nations to waters and to a surging sea. And the words "and the river shall fail" would signify that their kingdom would no longer endure. That the saying that the river of the Egyptians would fail referred to their monarchy we have already shown earlier, in the prophecy about the one who would come forth from the root of Jesse, where it was said: "And the Lord will lay his hand on the river with a violent wind, and will strike it into seven ravines, so that one may cross it in sandals." Those words were like the ones now before us, where it is said: "But the river shall fail, and every gathering of water shall be dried up," and like the earlier ones where it was said: "A nation without hope and trodden down, whose land the rivers have plundered." The discussion there was not about physical rivers but about what we explained in those places. So here too, when the prophecy says that the river will fail and be dried up, and further, after the first, that other rivers and the canals and every gathering of water will fail, it seems to me to hint at the overthrow of the kingdom of the Egyptians and of the local rulers they formerly had. And since they also had certain military forces, it prophesies that their concentrations of troops would also cease, along with the kings, at the times indicated.

But once the kingdom of Egypt has been brought down, it foretells that the rivers will become gentle and calm, adding next: "And then their waters shall be still, and their rivers shall flow like oil." After this it says that everything that grew there of old will vanish: the reed around the river, and of course the papyrus, the green sedge, and the other plants that sprout along the river itself, many of which are seen by the river of the Egyptians. I think that by these words it signifies a complete drying up of the waters, so that not even a trace of moisture would appear, whether in the river, in the marsh, along the banks of the river, in its midst, in the canals, or in standing waters; all of them would fail at once, so that no water would remain anywhere in the land of the Egyptians. Now if the prophecy had gone on from this to speak of the destruction of human beings as well, there would be nothing left to inquire into, since it would follow that when so great a river and all water had failed, every living creature deprived of the river would perish.

But as it is, even after the failing of the waters it speaks of multitudes of men who will be in Egypt: that there will be an altar in Egypt, that the Egyptians will offer sacrifice to the Lord, that he will send them a man who will save them, and that the Lord will be known to the Egyptians. Who would not reasonably ask how these people will survive when all the water has failed, so that the land does not even have anything green? This passage compels even the unwilling to turn to a figurative interpretation, so that by the rivers and waters of Egypt one must necessarily understand either the multitudes of the Egyptian forces, or their kingdom, which once overflowed like rivers, or, by another interpretation, the philosophy that flourished among the Egyptians of old, about which it is said: "And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians." For this wisdom was great, and great was the river that flowed among them, namely the teaching of the wisdom they admired. It had many parts, broken up into many canals and many rivers, namely the teachings of each of their disciples, and from these grew not vines, nor olive trees, nor any fruitful and necessary trees, but papyrus, reed, and green sedge.

When the waters of Egypt fail, the fishers of fish, that is, of human souls, are said to mourn. You will understand the fishermen and net-casters spoken of in the prophecy by comparison with other fishermen and casters of nets, I mean the apostles and disciples of our Savior, to whom he said: "Come, and I will make you fishers of men." For if these, through their teaching, caught the souls of men, drawing them to salvation, why should you not say that the so-called fishermen and net-casters of the Egyptians were the ancient teachers of their philosophy, who by Egyptian sorcery ensnared those they caught, luring them as if with hooks? You will understand their dragnets from our Savior's parable, in which it is said: "The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet that was cast into the sea and gathered fish of every kind." Just as in the parable people are called fish and the gospel message about the kingdom of heaven is called a dragnet, so here too the intricate cleverness of the Egyptians' teaching would be the dragnet and likewise the casting nets. And the fish caught and netted by them would be those who were dragged down by deceitful sophistries into every kind of godless superstition. So the net-casters of Egypt are said to groan and mourn, since they no longer have work because of the Lord who came to dwell among them and destroyed all their wisdom, in accordance with the saying: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will set aside."

In the same way you will understand those who work flax, not the strong and untearable kind but the split flax, that is, a teaching that is torn apart and split, and likewise the fine linen, since these too had a share in the river of the Egyptians, being watered by it. That is why the text says that those who work them will groan, since they no longer had at hand the fabrics made from these to clothe and adorn their wisdom. For with flax, as it were, and fine linen they devised adornment and clothing for themselves, covering their falsehood with plausible and deceitful words. And not only these will groan, it says, but also all who make, not wine from the vine, but Egyptian beer, which was itself spurious and muddy, and which they used as their drink before the Lord came to dwell among them. When this too failed, the Egyptians who made it are naturally said to groan and to be grieved in their souls. These, then, are the things it threatens that the sophists of Egypt will suffer, being beer-makers, as it were, workers of split flax and fine linen, and fishers of fish, who tended the river of Egypt and the teaching of Egyptian wisdom. Turning people away from it, another prophet cried out: "What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon?"

What is said next is prophesied about invisible rulers who once presided especially over the greatest and most famous cities of Egypt, I mean Tanis and Memphis. It is said in these words: "And the rulers of Tanis shall be fools; the wise counselors of the king, their counsel shall be made foolish," and again: "The rulers of Tanis have failed, and the rulers of Memphis were exalted, and they led Egypt astray." According to Symmachus: "The rulers of Tanis have grown weary, the rulers of Memphis have grown numb, they who led Egypt astray." For they say that it was especially in these cities that all the trickery of demonic idolatry was formerly concentrated, and that those who reigned over Egypt in the time of Moses had their royal seat there. That is why it is said that the signs in Moses' time took place in the plain of Tanis, and so too in the present case. Therefore, when the Lord came to dwell in Egypt, it says that, along with the river of Egypt, the ruling demons it has indicated would also be made foolish, even though they professed wisdom while the Lord was not present among them. But he brought proof against them that they had no share in wisdom, and they were truly fools at the Lord's coming. The kings of Egypt used these very ruling demons as counselors, as it were, being led astray by divinations, oracles, and the other demonic deceptions. That is why it is said: "And they led Egypt astray."

Then the text addresses those Egyptian demons themselves, saying: "How will you say to the king, 'We are sons of the wise, sons of kings of old'?" For since you no longer have a king, how will you be able to pride yourselves on your understanding? And how do you claim to be sons of ancient kings, putting forward Horus, Isis, Osiris, and Typhon, and claiming that races of gods, heroes, and the dead ruled Egypt in ancient times, gods and kings whose sons and descendants you claim to be, you rulers of Tanis and Memphis indicated by the prophecy? And how could you be gods, or what wisdom could you have, when you were unable to foresee or foretell your own exposure and the overthrow of the kingdom of those whose counselors you were, and whom you were ruining by entangling them in every kind of error?

Next after these words he addresses Egypt itself, saying: "Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you and say what the Lord of hosts has planned against Egypt." Where are your wise gods, who promised to foretell the future through divinations and oracles? Let them come forward and say what the Lord of hosts has planned against Egypt. But there is no one to say it; for it was not given to wicked demons to know the counsel of God, and in fact the demons no longer exist at all. For the rulers of Tanis and Memphis, who were once exalted and who led Egypt astray by the Lord's permission, have failed. For the aforesaid would not have had the power to lead Egypt astray, since a universal providence oversees the whole and watches over each part, unless the Lord himself had permitted them to do this, mixing for them a spirit of error. That is why they led the Egyptians astray like drunkards. And so great was the drunkenness they produced in the Egyptians that the Egyptians were like a man who is drunk and vomiting at the same time from the excess of his overwhelming drunkenness.

The extent of this drunkenness can be judged from the fact that they did not practice idolatry in the same way as the rest of mankind, but even sank to the point of making idols of irrational animals. That is why it is said: "As one who is drunk and vomiting at the same time staggers," or, according to the other translators: "As a drunkard staggers as he vomits." The one who is drunk and vomiting at the same time can also be understood in another way: for "at the same time" joins both, so that he vomits and drinks, and drinking becomes drunk, and vomits again, and vomiting thirsts once more. With some such drunkenness the rulers of Tanis and Memphis indicated above led astray the souls of the Egyptians, those for whom the Lord himself had mixed a spirit of error. For being wicked demons and hostile powers, they were minded against God and tried to fight against him. That is why they were handed over to error, God judging it fitting, in view of their wickedness, to hand them over to error. And they poured out their own wickedness on the Egyptians like a deadly venom, and led Egypt astray, "as one who is drunk and vomiting at the same time staggers."

But it was for the sake of these very people that the Lord came to dwell in Egypt, so that he might make them sober up from their error and scatter far from them those who had led them astray. That is why he adds: "And there shall no longer be any work for the Egyptians that will make head and tail, beginning and end." For the things formerly performed among them will be ineffective and inoperative for them, so that no work among them will have either beginning or end, since the Lord, being good, has brought this about too. For in former times the works of polytheistic error among the Egyptians had a beginning and an end and what was regarded as a certain coherence. But at the times indicated, of the Lord's coming to them, it says that there will no longer be any such work among them that is full, complete, and perfect; and even if one were ever found, it will be headless and without beginning, unfinished and without conclusion. This can actually be seen in fact, since their idolatry has not entirely died out; but it is of such a kind that it has neither a head nor any rationale that reaches to an end.

It prophesies that at the times stated, of the Lord's arrival in Egypt, the Egyptians will no longer have a manly spirit, but will spend their lives in trembling and fear like women, because of the hand of God raised against them. What could be understood by the hand of the Lord, as distinct from what is called his right hand, other than the Roman power that subdued the Egyptians and brought them under its hand on account of the Lord's coming? For thus the devil too is once recorded as having said to God concerning Job: "But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has; surely he will bless you to your face." So the power that served the will of God in subduing the dominion of the Egyptians was this very one that has been called the hand, namely the Roman army. And how the Egyptians serve the Romans like women, with fear and anguish, there is no need to say.

And the land of the Jews has also become a terror to the Egyptians who have received the coming of the Lord. You would not be wrong to call the divine Scripture "the land of the Jews." Those who have come to know the Lord approach it with fear and trembling and reverence, out of the depth of their devotion and faith. They no longer blaspheme it as they once did, but honor and revere it because of the Lord who is proclaimed in it. So whoever mentions it to them fills them with the fear of God, and the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

At the same time at which these things are foretold to happen, the text says that five cities will be established in Egypt. They will not use the Egyptian tongue but the Canaanite, and they will swear not by the ancestral gods they once worshipped long ago, but in the name of the Lord Sabaoth, the God known among the Jews. He was the one who came to them on a light cloud. It is remarkable to hear Egyptians calling out in the Hebrew tongue, which the Egyptians themselves used to call the Canaanite language, whenever they recite Hebrew words in the church of God, such as "hallelujah," "amen," "Sabaoth" and the others found in the divine Scripture. And there is no need to say anything about how they also swear by the Lord, making his name their oath and preferring the Lord Sabaoth, who was known only among the Jews, to their ancestral gods, for the truth itself sets its seal on the prophetic word. Although five cities are named in the prophecy, we should not fail to see that the five are in fact one. That is why a single name is given to them all, "Asedek," which Symmachus translated "of the sun." What could this city be but the holy church of God? According to the Seventy it is called Asedek, which means "of righteousness"; according to Symmachus it is called "of the sun," the sun of which it is said: "But for you who fear me the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings"; and according to the exact Hebrew wording it is called Areopolis. That might be translated: "The one city shall be called city of the earth." For this alone, over the whole earth, is the city founded for God, so that it is said of her: "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God."

The five cities of God within the church would be its different ways of life, divided into five orders. If you count the first order, that of the presiding bishops, the second, that of the presbyters, the third, that of the deacons, the fourth, that of those who have been enlightened in Christ, and after these the order of those still under instruction, you will see that these five orders live as citizens in the church of God. That is why five cities are spoken of as one, speaking the language that the Egyptians once considered Canaanite and swearing by the name of the Lord Sabaoth. Anyone who pays attention will see what is wonderful in this passage. The Egyptians were once the most superstitious of peoples. They utterly hated the Jews and habitually blasphemed the God worshipped among them. Yet these same Egyptians now use the Jewish Scriptures and have taken up the fear of the Lord Sabaoth, whose name was proclaimed among the Jews, so that they make his name their oath. And he rightly called the church a city of the sun and of light, because of the Christ of God, who is the light that enlightens every person coming into the world. Hence Symmachus has: "The one city shall be called city of the sun."

Having prophesied that a city of God would be established in Egypt, with different orders within it, the text goes on to mention an altar that will be set up in the city of God, and says this will happen in a surprising way. The gods once worshipped by the Egyptians will have perished, their river will have failed, the princes of Tanis and Memphis will have been made fools, and everything listed earlier will have come to its end; then, it says, an altar will be established to the Lord worshipped among the Jews. The outcome of events shows this before our very eyes, so that we need no longer wait for some future time to see the word fulfilled. Just as there is said to be one faith, one baptism and one church, so the altars in the churches of God throughout all Egypt, of which the text speaks, are one altar. And one pillar, the gospel Scripture, has been set up together with the altar in the city described, marking off the unbelieving Egyptians and separating them from the faithful. That is why it says: "and a pillar at its border." So the land of the Jews, which was said above to be a terror to the Egyptians, pointed to the Jewish Scripture and the word of the old covenant, while the pillar joined to the altar of Christ would be the gospel of the new covenant, which marks off the Egyptians who have believed in Christ from the unbelievers.

Besides this, it says, the Lord will be a sign forever in the land of Egypt. The Egyptians who have received the Lord have therefore learned to seal themselves with this sign and use it as a safeguard. In their afflictions they rely on this sign for help as they cry out and call on the Lord because of those who oppress them. Who were these oppressors, if not the Egyptians who remained in unbelief? Of them it was said at the beginning of the prophecy: "And Egyptians will rise up against Egyptians, and each will fight against his brother, city against city and district against district." When these oppress and persecute those who take refuge in God, the oppressed will cry out to the Lord, and he will at once set his Christ before them as a Saviour. That is why the other translators have: "And he will send them a Saviour, and he will fight for them," which points most plainly to Jesus our Saviour, for the prophecy translates his name. Instead of "and he will save them; judging, he will save them," Symmachus said: "and he will fight for them and rescue them." Who will rescue them but the Saviour sent to help those who are oppressed for his sake? And he will save them by judging: if he finds them worthy of salvation, he will deal with their oppressors by an invisible hand and by his discerning judgment.

It is above all in this way that the Lord will become known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day, clearly meaning the time of their affliction. Then, having learned to be thankful, they will offer him sacrifices, since they now have an altar among them and have been counted worthy to serve God as priests. Hence Symmachus has: "and they will bring sacrifice and offering." Here we must pay close attention, because the passage presents the introduction of a new law and a new covenant. The law of Moses commanded that there be no altar outside Jerusalem, and that no tribe but that of Levi should serve God as priests. Yet the prophecy sets up an altar to God in Egypt and foretells that priests who are Egyptian by race will bring sacrifices and offerings to the Lord of the prophets. As the divine Apostle says somewhere: "When the priesthood is changed, there must also be a change of the law." Next he adds: "And they will vow vows to the Lord and pay them," meaning, clearly, the Egyptians. For when they make promises in their vows, they will not break the promises they owe to God. That is why they endure the struggles for true religion even to the point of death.

Then it goes on: "And the Lord will strike the Egyptians with a blow and heal them with healing, and they will turn back to the Lord." For the Lord disciplines the one he loves and scourges every son whom he receives, so it is fitting that he should also strike the Egyptians out of love, whenever they need correction and turning back. But this is not for long. Without delay he heals them with healing.

On that same day, that is, at the time described, it says, "there will be a highway for the Egyptians to the Assyrians, and the Assyrians will enter Egypt, and the Egyptians will go to the Assyrians, and the Egyptians will serve the Assyrians." I think that here Scripture calls "Assyrians" the people now called Syrians, for in ancient times those who lived in Syria and Mesopotamia were known as Assyrians. The Egyptians and Assyrians were enemies and remained at war with one another continually. But now this passage foretells fellowship and free contact between them, something that had never happened before. Before Roman rule the Egyptians and the Assyrians each had kings of their own: the Egyptians had the Ptolemies, and the Syrians the successors of Antiochus and Demetrius. Judea lay between them and was governed separately under its own rulers. Caught in the middle, the Jewish nation was attacked now by the Syrians, now by the Ptolemies. The Syrians were also enemies of the Egyptians, and the Egyptians fought the Syrians, so that there was no contact between them and the roads from one to the other could not be travelled. That is how things stood in ancient times. But after the Lord's coming into Egypt, this passage announces to them the deepest peace, along with fellowship and free contact, when it says: "There will be a highway for the Egyptians to the Assyrians, and the Assyrians will come into Egypt, and the Egyptians will go to the Assyrians, and the Egyptians will serve the Assyrians. And Israel will be third among the Egyptians and the Assyrians, blessed." So it brings together those who were once enemies and foes, the Syrians, the Egyptians and Israel, and says that they will receive one and the same blessing from God. Israel is therefore no longer to be proud or to exalt itself over the others as if it alone were blessed and it alone were the people of God. And yet the prophecy teaches that, even so, the Egyptians will serve the Assyrians, that is, the Syrians.

Who, then, could see with his own eyes Roman camps of Syrian soldiers posted over the heads of the Egyptians, and the Egyptians serving them, without being amazed at how the prophecy has been fulfilled? Who would not marvel to see Egyptians crossing without fear into the land of the Syrians, and Syrians coming freely into Egypt and holding the Egyptians in subjection by the power of their official authority? But the most astonishing thing of all was this: that at one and the same time there would be peoples belonging to God among the Syrians, among the Egyptians and in the land of Israel, and that all of them would be blessed. Israel would no longer differ from the Egyptian, nor would the Syrian stand any higher with God than Israel or the Egyptian, nor would the Egyptian count for less with God than Israel or the Syrian.

It says that at the coming of the Lord those who were once enemies and foes of one another will share in so great a fellowship of good things. The Lord's people established in Egypt itself, and likewise the one in the land of the Syrians, can be seen plainly in the great number of churches. The people from the race of Israel flourished in the time of the gospel preaching, when the disciples of our Saviour, the apostles and all the evangelists, and those of the circumcision who had come to know the Christ of God, worshipped God just as the Egyptians and the Syrians did. So all of them alike were counted worthy of one and the same blessing from God. That is why it says: "Blessed be my people who are in Egypt and among the Assyrians, and my inheritance Israel." The other translators have: "Blessed be my people Egypt, and Assyria," so that no one should think the Jews living in Egypt are meant, but the Egyptians themselves and the Syrians themselves. And when it says that Israel will be third among the Egyptians and the Assyrians, blessed in the land which the Lord Sabaoth has blessed, let us not suppose that this land is anything other than the church of God. "Israel" can also be understood as the whole company of holy and God-loving men of the Jewish nation who departed this life earlier. That is why it says: "and my inheritance Israel." For when the Most High divided the nations, his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance. But then Israel alone was his people; now the Egyptians too are called his people, and a blessed people, and so are the Assyrians. The words "in the land which the Lord Sabaoth has blessed" might also refer to the heavenly land, of which the Saviour says, "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth." There too are the heavenly Jerusalem and God's heavenly Mount Zion.

The present passage will seem to contradict what was just said. There the text showed that there would be peaceful contact between the Egyptians and the Assyrians; now it says that the king of the Assyrians will take the young men and the old men of the Egyptians captive, naked and barefoot. The difficulty can be resolved if we pay attention to how the prophetic Spirit works. When it turned its attention to Egypt, it saw what was about to happen to the Egyptians immediately, in the prophet's own time, but it also looked ahead to the good things that would come to the land of Egypt long afterward. So, having first foretold the good things in the earlier verses, it now passes to what was to happen at once. These things were grievous for the Egyptians, and they were fulfilled before long, in the very times in which the prophet was known. The divine Spirit had to do this: after foretelling the Lord's coming into Egypt and the good things that would come to the Egyptians there, it attached events that were about to be fulfilled immediately. In this way, from the fulfillment of present events, those who heard the prophetic words at that time would also believe what was to happen long afterward.

So the present passage did not contradict what was prophesied earlier. The one pointed ahead to times still to come; the other proclaimed what was about to happen very soon. In the time of the prophet Isaiah there was a king of the Assyrians who invaded the nation of the Philistines and captured Ashdod, then the greatest and most famous of the cities there. After it fell, the prophet, who [?] wore a single garment because of his extreme ascetic discipline, a garment woven not of wool but of goats' hair, was ordered to take off that very garment, so that he would be completely naked, since he had no second covering for his body. He was also to remove his sandals, or "shoes," as the other translators have it. When he had done this, God said that the Egyptians, when the Assyrians made war on them, would suffer something like the prophet's appearance. They would be led away naked and barefoot, and not they alone, but also the Ethiopians, whom they hoped would help them and fight alongside them. For the Egyptians, trusting in the great numbers of the Ethiopians and in their military strength, which at that time was very great, looked down on the Assyrians. But God reveals what is to come, saying: "Just as my servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years, so there will be signs and wonders for the Egyptians."

See them attacked by the Assyrians and led away naked and barefoot, in the very image the prophet endured for their sake. That is why he goes on: "So the king of the Assyrians will lead away the Egyptians and the Ethiopians as captives, naked and barefoot, with their shame uncovered." When the Ethiopians are captured, the Egyptians will be put to shame and will blush over those in whom they trusted and had placed their confidence. Then those who live in this island, meaning clearly the land of the Egyptians, will condemn and blame themselves. He called it an island because it is flowed around and encircled on every side by the river within it. They will say, it says, condemning themselves and repenting that they had hung their hopes on men and not on the God of the universe: "And how shall we ourselves be saved, when those we expected to help us have suffered these things?" The prophetic way of life is worth admiring. The Apostle described it when he said: "They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, mistreated." The present passage presents Isaiah wearing a single garment, sackcloth, clearly mourning and lamenting those who had fallen far from God through their own impiety. And that, when he was ordered to walk naked, he did not hesitate but did it at once before the eyes of those around him, would be proof of the greatest obedience and eagerness toward God, and of a lofty courage and spirit that counted all human esteem as nothing.

In trying to preserve the literal sense of the present passage, I think I take my cue from the words it contains, where it says: "Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all her images and the works of her hands have been shattered." For this is plainly said about Babylon. And further on the text says again: "The Elamites are against me, and envoys of the Persians are coming against me," where Symmachus translated: "Arise, Elam; lay siege, you Medes." The Hebrew text and the other translators also mention the Medes here. These are the ones who brought down the empire of the Babylonians, as the earlier prophecy about Babylon showed, where it was said: "Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against you." And not long afterward the Persians, succeeding the Medes, destroyed what was left of Babylon. So I think it reasonable that the present passage is spoken about Babylon. What does the text mean when it says "the vision of the desert"? Here it is already calling Babylon a desert, because of what had been foretold about its desolation. So "the vision of the desert sea" signifies the sea of Babylon laid waste. If someone should ask why a passage about Babylon is placed here out of season, when the prophecy about Babylon had already been fully set out earlier, we will say this. Since it had just been said that the king of the Assyrians would lead away the captives of Egypt and the captives of Ethiopia, young men and old, naked and barefoot, the text had to indicate what would very soon happen to the Assyrians themselves. For just as God punished the Egyptians with just judgment through the invasion of the Assyrians, so too he handed the Assyrians over to the Medes and brought down their arrogance; then he subjected the Medes in turn to the Persians, and these again he chastened through others. In this way the thread of the present passage would be preserved.

After the heading, which contains "the vision of the desolated sea," the text goes on: "As a storm would pass through the desert, coming from the desert, from the land, a fearful and harsh vision was announced to me." I think these words are spoken in the person of Babylon herself. It is as though she had received a report of the evils about to come upon her and prayed that the report would pass her by and that what she expected would not happen. That is why she says: "A fearful and harsh vision was announced to me, as a storm would pass through the desert." She means: may it pass through and go by me, like a storm coming from the desert. For if the mere report of the vision that has reached me is harsh and fearful, what will the thing itself be like if it falls on me like a storm coming from the desert? But may it pass through and run on by, and not come upon me and settle on me. For I learn that "the one who rejects rejects, and the lawless one acts lawlessly." I have also heard the names from those who brought me the news: the Elamites and the Medes are coming against me as forerunners of the Persians. So no one would be wrong to call them "the envoys of the Persians." What then am I to do, when their storm is about to break on me? It seems that I will now groan. I did not do this before, when I was proud and lifted myself above the other nations, so that I made others groan. But now I myself, Babylon, and the people within me, will groan, and through my groaning I will comfort myself.

The news of these things has seized me. Because of it my loins, once tightly girded and full of youthful vigour, have been filled with faintness, and pain and pangs have gripped me. I, Babylon, who was once fearful to others, am now no different from a woman in labour. This has happened to me because, as I confess, I did wrong when I listened to none of those who advised me and made it my business to see nothing rightly. So she says, "Now, confessing, I say: I did wrong in not hearing; I made haste not to see. My heart wanders, and my lawlessness overwhelms me; my heart is set toward fear." In place of this Symmachus rendered: "My soul went astray, my heart was troubled; the calm of my contentment threw me into turmoil; it brought me to bewilderment."

I think these things were said by the prophet speaking in the person of Babylon, as though the words had been uttered by her, or by the nation that lived in her. Then the prophetic spirit turns to the Medes and the Elamites and to the envoys of the Persians, rousing them and urging them on to the war against the Babylonians. That is why it says, as if addressing them: "Prepare the table; eat, drink; rise up, you rulers, make ready the shields." He means: "I, the prophet, say these things moved by the prophetic spirit, since the Lord said to me: Go, set a watchman for yourself, and report whatever you see." Or, according to the other translators: "Let him report whatever he sees"; that is, the watchman.

Then he says that the watchman was stationed according to the Lord's command and saw two mounted horsemen, or according to Symmachus, "and he saw a chariot, a pair of horses." This is what he saw first. After the pair of horses he sees two other riders, one riding on a donkey and the other on a camel. These were signs and symbols of the enemy's battle array. Some of them advanced riding in chariots, while others came on pack animals, bringing what was needed for their use. This is what the watchman saw, the one God had commanded the prophet to set. "Listen," he says, "listen with great attention, and call Uriah to the watchtower." He commands him to lend his ears to hear the word about to be spoken, and to call Uriah to the watchtower. Instead of "Uriah," Aquila rendered "lion," Symmachus "lioness," and Theodotion "Ariel." None of these named Uriah, because the Hebrew word does not mention Uriah either. When the text earlier mentioned Uriah the priest, it marked the man with other letters. Here the Hebrew word has a different sound and different letters and means the lion, or the lioness according to Symmachus. So the Lord commands the prophet to listen with great attention to what is about to be spoken, and then to call either the lioness or Ariel. In this way Ariel too would come and be seen by the watchman, while the prophet watched together with the watchman. He shows this when he says next: "I stood continually all day, and I stood at the camp all night." So the prophet too stood together with the watchman, eagerly waiting for the sight that was about to appear to them, of the lion or the lioness or Ariel.

After he had held out through the whole day and the whole night, he adds: "And behold, he comes." Who is this but Ariel, mounted on a pair? So he says: "And behold, he comes, riding a chariot with a pair." Who could this have been but some avenging angel, through whom the siege of Babylon was to be carried out? Perhaps he was called Ariel, or perhaps he was that very one who "prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour." When the prophet saw him, he understood that this avenging angel would bring about the destruction of Babylon. So he cries out: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all her images and the works of her hands are shattered to the ground." The prophet uttered this cry because Ariel had been commanded to do these things. Here, then, two watchmen are presented, and two sights are seen. The first watchman saw two mounted horsemen, a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel. The second, who was the prophet himself, no longer saw riders on camels or donkeys but the rider of a chariot with a pair, the lion or Ariel. At his appearing the prophet announced the fall of Babylon and the shattering of her so-called gods. That is why Symmachus has: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the images of her gods are shattered." So the first watchman, who ranked below the prophet, saw the multitude of enemy soldiers about to come against Babylon. The second, the prophet himself, beheld the more secret vision, which I think was angelic, and through which the fall of Babylon was accomplished. It was fitting, then, that the Lord told the prophet beforehand, "Listen with great attention," since the prophetic spirit was about to cry out, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the works of her hands are shattered." He meant this very message about Babylon and her images. I think these words signify the complete overthrow of the Assyrian kingdom, which came about by God's judgment. And it would not have appeared [?] that this angel was foolish [?], had he not been cast [?] by the prophet at God's command.

After these things had happened in this way, the prophet goes on to make known what he had heard and seen to those who were left and who grieved among the people. These were only a few. They mourned over what was happening to the people and were the only ones left over from the error of the many. The prophet calls out to them, saying: "Hear what I have heard from the Lord of hosts; the God of Israel has announced it to you." He means that what God revealed to him, God has also made known to them, with the prophet acting as interpreter. This is the end of the prophecy about Egypt, and after it the text passes on to another subject.

The text did not include the prophecy about these people for no reason. They too were enemies of Israel and attacked them continually. History testifies to this, and so does the Psalm that says: "For they have plotted together with one mind; against you they have made a covenant: the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek." You see how he places the Edomites before all the other enemies of the people. This was a very large nation around Petra in Arabia, tracing its descent from Esau. Esau was the brother of Jacob, also called Israel, from whom all the Jews come. So the Edomites and the Jews were the children of brothers. Esau was called Edom, and that is why those descended from him are called Idumeans. Since the Edomites kept rising up against Israel, it was fitting that the prophet should see a vision about them too and foretell what would happen to them as well. God seems to speak to his own people, saying: "He calls to me out of Seir." According to the other translators he means: "I call those fleeing from Seir to me." Seir was the name of Esau's mountain in Arabia, where his royal seat stood, and the local people still know it by this name today. To those who were anxious about the threat from the Edomites he says: "Hurry and come to me, and once you are with me, guard your ramparts."

"And I will guard you day and night; stay with me." So if any of you needs help, let him seek help from me, and if anyone cares about his salvation, let him live with me. I think these words were addressed to those who were terrified by the threat from the Edomites. God calls them back to himself and promises them his help if they stay with him.

In what follows the prophet takes up another subject and speaks as one seized by the Holy Spirit, which is why he called the message an oracle. This oracle was no longer about the Edomites alone but also about the rest of the people living in Arabia, who were likewise enemies and foes of Israel. To them he says: "If you have always been insolent [?], as you are accustomed to exalt yourselves over my people, then now at least learn what is about to overtake you, and stop your madness."

"The enemies who will cut you down are already upon you. Most of you will perish. But perhaps one or two, or a very few, will be saved, finding safety in flight. For these I command that bread and water be prepared, since they are fugitives already exhausted and faint from fleeing. They will no longer have a city to live in, and when evening overtakes them they will sleep in the forest and in desert places. So that they do not die of hunger, I command that bread and drink be brought to them, worn out and thirsty from their toil. I say this to you who live in the land called Teman. It is right for you to welcome the fugitives kindly and treat them humanely, for they can no longer live in a city and will camp on the roads and in the forests. So do not ignore these people who have escaped the enemy's sword and are dying so pitiably of hunger. Out of so great a multitude they have barely managed to escape, while the rest have perished or wandered off to other distant places."

After revealing these things, God decreed that they would come to pass before long. Not even a whole year will pass before the city of the sons of Kedar is wiped out, though it was once exalted, renowned and conspicuous to all. Their assembled youth, a military force full of mighty archers, will fail, so that they are reduced to a small number of men. These things have been determined and decreed by the God of Israel, so that those named may learn not to trample contemptuously on his people. The prophecy ends with these people being reduced to a few.

There is no partiality with God. For this reason the word about Zion has also been placed in the middle of the reproofs against the foreign nations. Through it God ranks even the inhabitants of Jerusalem among the foreigners and pronounces his sentence against them as well. In Amos too it is said, in the person of God, to the Jewish people: "Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me? says the Lord. Did I not bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt, and the foreigners from Cappadocia, and the Syrians out of the pit? Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon all the kingdoms of the earth." The present oracle, "of the valley of Zion," is spoken not about Zion itself but about the valley lying beside it. That is why, as the text proceeds, it says: "And your choice valleys shall be filled with chariots, and the horsemen shall block your gates." I think that by these words God wishes to signify the rejection of Israel and their final falling away, and so he ranks them in the order of the foreigners, placing them in the middle of what is written about the foreigners. But I also think the fall of Jerusalem is indicated by the name "valley of Zion."

In another sense too, God is reproaching those of the Jewish nation who fell from the height of a godly way of life and sank, as it were, into the hollows and valleys of the depth of wickedness. Zion is a high mountain, and God's temple was built on it. That is why it is said: "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion," and: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." It was also shown earlier that Mount Zion signifies the word of the gospel. Those who fell away from this hope have fallen into the valley that lies beside Zion. For vice lies next to every virtue, and whoever slips from virtue falls into it. In the same way those who fall short of faith are turned aside into unbelief. So the people of the circumcision fell from the height of the gospel, were estranged from the heavenly Zion, and were overturned into the precipice of unbelief. For this reason God counted them among the foreigners. And so the prophecy, hinting at their final rejection, wrote "the oracle of the valley of Zion." Then, since they are puffed up for no reason while lying in the depth of wickedness, it says to them: "What has happened to you, that you have all gone up to vain housetops?"

The prophet saw in the Spirit their outcries against the Saviour and their godless blasphemies against him, for which they were rejected, and so he adds: "The city was filled with people shouting." And since there is a sin that leads to death, according to which "the soul that sins shall die," he points to the death of their soul when he adds: "Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, and your dead did not die in war."

And he adds: "All your rulers have fled," or according to Symmachus, "have been driven out," and according to Theodotion, "have been removed." So they no longer have, as they did of old, a king, or leaders, or high priests, or prophets, or even Pharisees or Sadducees, or any of those who long ago were honoured with offices among them. All of these have been removed. And those who even now have been captured by the besieger of souls are bitterly bound, since each is held fast by the cords of his own sins. That is why it is said: "And those who were captured are bitterly bound."

The prophet perceived these things in the Spirit and mourned the fall of the Jewish people from so great a height into the utmost wickedness, as into a valley. He says: "Therefore I said, Leave me; I will weep bitterly. Do not try to comfort me over the ruin of the daughter of my race." Or according to Symmachus: "Do not console me over the misery of the daughter of my people." He means: "I know for certain, and I foresee in the Spirit, that because of everything said before, the city dedicated to God will also be captured, and everyone in it will be handed over into the hands of enemies. So I am already lamenting from this moment, and weeping as if over my own flesh and blood. For besides what has been said, a day of tumult and destruction and trampling and wandering from the Lord of hosts has come upon the valley of Zion." I think these words too are spoken about those who gathered together in the plot against our Saviour. About them he adds: "They wander on the mountains, from the least to the greatest," meaning the people together with their rulers.

Then he brings in the threat against them, saying: "And the Elamites took up quivers, horsemen and an army drawn up for battle." He means hostile, invisible powers, enemies and foes, to whom God handed them over. The name "Elamites" is interpreted as "those who look past," because they disregard the salvation of those who are perishing and spare no one. So it is fitting that the armies that besieged them should be called by this name. With horses and a very great force they drew up against the valley of Zion already mentioned and brought it to utter desolation.

That is why it says next: "And your choice valleys shall be filled with chariots, and the horsemen shall block the gates of Judah and shall enter." This will happen not now, nor at the present time, but "in that day," meaning the time foretold in the prophecy. They will enter "into the houses of the city," when, in the siege, they search every place and every corner of the city and uncover "the hidden things of the houses of the citadel of David." These were the secret symbols of the kingship, or the things stored in the sanctuary, which no one was allowed to look upon except the high priest alone. He says that these too will be handed over to the enemies. Instead of "and they saw that they are more," Symmachus has: "and you will see the breaches of the house of David, that they have multiplied." After this he reproaches those in the valley of Zion for turning aside the waters of the ancient pool that were in the city and devising another water for themselves between the two walls. The water of the old pool in the city was the word of the old, divinely inspired Scripture. They turned away from it and devised for themselves a foreign water, the traditions of the elders, teaching human commandments as doctrines. The Saviour too reproaches them for this, exposing their lawlessness when he says: "And you have made void the word of God for the sake of your tradition, you hypocrites." Jeremiah also hinted at this very thing when he said: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water." In this way they turned aside the water of the old pool that was in the city and devised for themselves a strange water between the two walls, by which I mean the Old and the New Testaments. These are the two walls of the city of God, that is, of the godly way of life. Between them the people being accused devised for themselves an alien and strange water, the traditions of the elders, in which those among them called deuterotai take great pride.

The people described have also dared to do something else that is very wicked. They tore down the houses of the city and used their stones to build a wall of their own. You can see them still doing this today, when they take the words of divine Scripture and use them to wall in their own fables, throwing them around their own myths like a fence, a safeguard and a wall. Just as they devised a strange drink for themselves, so they put up a wall of their own, using the words of the divine Scriptures as stones. "And you did these things," he says, "without looking to God, who made it from the beginning and formed it." By "it" I mean the old pool of the divinely inspired Scriptures, which pours forth from the springs of the divine Spirit.

Symmachus rendered this passage as follows: "And you drew the water of the lower pool, and you counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore down the houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the walls and the ancient pool, and you did not look to the one who made it, and the one who formed it long ago you did not see." And Theodotion rendered it this way: "And you gathered the water of the lower pool, and you counted the houses of Jerusalem and pulled down the houses to make fortifications for the wall. And you made a cistern between the two walls for the water of the ancient pool, and you did not look to the one who made it, and the one who formed it from afar you did not look upon."

Next it says: "And on that day the Lord of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for shaving the head and putting on sackcloth. But they made merry and rejoiced, slaughtering calves and sacrificing sheep so as to eat meat and drink wine, saying, Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Faced with such great outrages, God did not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance, and so he urged them to mourn and weep over their own destruction. But they, caught up in such evils, ran aground on madness as though they had given up hope of their own salvation. They gave themselves over to drunkenness and luxury, as if God's judgment would not be waiting for them after the end of this mortal life. That is why the divine Apostle, borrowing these very words of theirs, writes: "If the dead are not raised, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

"But none of this," he says, "escaped the ears of the Lord of hosts." So, with their sin bound fast as if by a bond from God, a sentence was pronounced against them, which said: "And this sin shall not be forgiven you until you die." Consider how great the threat in this sentence is. And notice that nowhere in this passage did he accuse the people of idolatry. He accused them of going up to vain housetops, of filling the city with shouting, and of devising strange water for themselves after turning away from the old pool. Besides this, they built a wall for themselves by tearing down the houses of the city, and while doing these things they had no sense of their own destruction. The prophet, however, did not feel that way. He mourned them and said: "Leave me; I will weep bitterly." And the cause of his bitter weeping was evidently what was decreed against them in the end, the sentence issued by God, which said: "And this sin shall not be forgiven you until you die."

Shebna and Eliakim, who are named in the passage before us, were contemporaries of King Hezekiah, as the historical scripture testifies. The prophet before us himself also teaches this in what follows, where, when the Assyrian came against the city and stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool on the road to the fuller's field, there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward, and Shebna the scribe. It is therefore fitting to apply the present passage to that history. Now the Hebrew used to say that Shebna had been high priest, a man given to luxury and of indecent life, so much so that he even betrayed the people and deserted to Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians. The prophet is ordered to go to him "into the pastophorion" [chamber], or, as Symmachus has it, "to the one who pitches a tent," or, as Aquila has it, "to the one who dwells in a tent" (for this is how they rendered "pastophorion"). He is to say to him: "In vain, you there, and to no purpose have you hewn yourself a tomb here in the high rock, carving letters in it as tokens of your memory. You do not know that a decree has gone out against you from the Lord of hosts, commanding that you be removed from the honor you now enjoy, stripped of the robe that is upon you, of your crown and the rest of your glory, and that you die very far from this land, in some foreign and distant country. In vain, then, did you take such pains amassing all that wealth, and the chariots, and the rest of the pomp with which you are still surrounded even now.

"For all these things will be trampled underfoot once you are deposed and cast out of the high priesthood, of which you have been shown to be unworthy. God, being a just judge who allots to each what is fitting according to his desert, will bring these things upon you. But the other man, Eliakim, whom he has approved as his servant and good slave, he will clothe with your robe and honor with the crown of the high priesthood, entrusting to him the stewardship with which you are entrusted for the present. For the man is worthy of these things. And since he has been advanced by God, he will not be like you, an arrogant and boastful man. He will hold the place of a father toward all who are to be governed by him. Therefore, as to one gentle and meek, God will give him the glory of David, the meekest and most just of kings, so that he will rule the people with great authority and no one will gainsay what he does. He will be rooted, set up like a pillar, and firmly established in his ministry, so that every man of distinction among the people will have no anxiety and no suspicion that envy or malice will ever come from him, but will trust in him as in a father. So all together, from the small to the great, will hang upon him, confident in his care for all."

These things will happen concerning Eliakim, but what was said before will happen to Shebna. This very man, who is now fixed in a sure place, will be moved and removed, since he did not administer rightly or faithfully the stewardship entrusted to him. Therefore he will be carried away and stripped of his honor, and his glory will fall from him. All this will befall him because God has judged that he should suffer it. Through these things the word also chastens and instructs us not to grow careless in prosperity or puffed up in office, so as to forget the judgment of God. Then again, one might connect the present passage with the prophecy before it, concerning the valley of Zion, and refer it too to the time of our Savior's passion. On this reading Shebna, who falls from the priesthood, is an image of those among the Jews who served as priests in a bodily way according to the law of Moses; the prophecy declares that after the saving passion they will suffer what is foretold and cease from the priesthood. Eliakim, whose name is interpreted "resurrection of God," is a symbol of the new and fresh priesthood which the resurrection of our Savior established in his church throughout the whole world.

If the prophecies concerning the foreign nations dealt only with events long past and fulfilled in fact long ago, it would be superfluous to busy ourselves with them, since they would contain nothing that concerns us. But as it is, besides telling what was to befall the nations named, each prophecy carries a distinctive word bearing on godliness. And this is truly marvelous: for each nation certain distinctive things are foretold separately, and within these, again, things tending toward the teaching of godliness are distinctively included. For example, the vision concerning Babylon raised a universal doctrine about God's expected righteous judgment, and declared that Babylon would come to utter desolation when the Assyrian empire was overthrown by the Medes; yet it is not said that there will be an altar in Babylon, or that its inhabitants will become godly. The vision of Egypt, on the other hand, foretold the desolation not of Egypt itself but of its idolatry, and says that there will be an abundance of godliness and knowledge of God among the Egyptians themselves. So too, having foretold certain distinctive things to Moab, it adds the destruction of their altars, and prophesies that a church of God will be established and the throne of Christ set up among them. Likewise, in the passage on Damascus a great many things are added about the conversion of those who formerly did not know God, together with all the other things we discussed as we examined the passages in their places; and so it is in the present case as well. The things said about Tyre, then, contain certain distinctive details about what was to come upon it, and these were fulfilled long ago in the times of the Assyrians, by whom it was besieged and suffered what the prophecy sets out. But the word at the end of the subject, which says, "And her trade and her wages will be holy to the Lord; it will not be gathered for them, but for those who dwell before the Lord," shows that the main point of the prophecy tends toward the theme of godliness.

The oracle concerning Tyre, then, first signifies the siege that came upon the city at the time when the Assyrian, coming with the other nations, captured both Tyre and Sidon, as is also recorded in the histories outside Scripture. Indeed, we have found in those who have handed down Assyrian history in writing that the king of the Babylonians, the very one who sacked Jerusalem, came and subdued not only Palestine but also Arabia and Damascus and the whole race of the Phoenicians. For when God judged that the people that bore his name, I mean Israel, should undergo a harsher discipline meant to turn them back through the attack of the Assyrians, he did not let the other nations go unpunished either, as many as had risen up against Israel at the time of its capture. And who were these? "The tents of the Idumeans and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre." You see how the Tyrians too are mentioned, as having joined the attack at the time of the people's siege. Fittingly, then, the prophecy signifies what would come upon Tyre, and says that the time of Tyre's desolation will be as long as the desolation of Jerusalem. It says: "And Tyre will be left seventy years, as the time of a king, as the time of one man."

At that time, then, when the city of the Tyrians endured so great a desolation, it was natural that they no longer carried on their customary trade, seafarers though they were and wholly devoted to business by sea. Hence it is said: "Wail, ships of Carthage, for it has perished, and they no longer come." Why does the prophecy mention Carthage here? Because there was an ancient bond of kinship between the Tyrians and the Carthaginians: the inhabitants of Africa once received the Tyrians, who in fact became the first founders of Carthage. So when Tyre was destroyed, there was no longer anyone carrying merchandise from it to Carthage, nor anyone sailing, as they used to, from Carthage to Tyre. Hence it is said: "Wail, ships of Carthage, for it has perished, and they no longer come from the land of the Citieans," or "from the land of Kittim," according to the other translators. Cyprus is said to be meant by this, and Citium is a city on it, past which those sailing from Tyre used to pass. The reason why the Tyrians' customary trade no longer took place he sets out next, saying: "She has been led away captive"—clearly meaning Tyre.

In place of "To whom have they become like?" Aquila said, "Be silent," and Symmachus, "Be quiet, you who inhabit the island." For there was a time when they boasted, snorting with pride, puffed up, and using arrogant words; but now that they have been humbled, the word bids them be silent. These same people were once the merchants of Phoenicia, heaping up great wealth, so that the abundance of their business is compared to a harvest. But now that they have been robbed of everything at once and deprived of what they counted as goods, it is fitting that shame be poured out not on them alone but also on their neighbors the Sidonians, while the sea itself all but cries aloud and laments them, because it no longer has young men and virgins to nourish. For of old, being as it were offspring of the sea, they were nourished by it while the affairs of the Tyrians flourished; but now that they are no more, the sea fittingly weeps for them, and its strength laments, mourning as over children that have perished. And Egypt too, it says, which lies next door, will be in anguish, anxious and fearful for itself, lest it should suffer something like Tyre. When these things have come to pass, it says, "If you can, you who are left in Tyre after those who perished, cross over in flight to your colonists who inhabit Carthage. And staying there, weep for your homeland, blaming no one else for what you have suffered, but only your own arrogance and the insolence with which you tried to overwhelm all mankind."

"Do not ascribe what has befallen you, O Tyrians, to the necessity of fate, but inquire among yourselves who planned these things, who decreed that your homeland should suffer them. If you inquire, you will find that these things befell it by the just judgment of God. For the Lord of hosts, who is acknowledged as God among the Hebrews alone, issued this decree, humbling the insolence and arrogance not of Tyre alone but also of the other godless and impious nations." That is why he threatened Babylon with similar things in the preceding passages, and Moab, and Damascus, and the others named earlier. For God is one who opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

"No longer exalt yourself, then, you who boast of the wealth the sea provided you. Humbled, busy yourself with your own land, tilling it and living on the fruits of the earth, for your profits from the sea have ceased. For when you enjoyed them, you could not bear your own prosperity, but grew insolent and provoked all the neighboring kings. But you will no longer be allowed to do this, either against others or against your neighbor Sidon, which you also tried to wrong."

"And even if you go away to Citium, the city of the Cyprians mentioned above, as to an acquaintance and an old and familiar friend, even there you will have no rest from the one who drives you from every side and hems you in. And if you should wish to desert to the land of the Chaldeans, know that their royal city, Babylon, will also be desolate because of the impious and arrogant men who lived in it. That is why its wall has fallen—I mean the royal power by which it was fortified of old."

"What other refuge, then, will you have, or where will you find yourself any hope of salvation?" Therefore it is reasonable that your colonists, I mean the Carthaginians, should lament you, Tyre, who were once their stronghold. And all that is prophesied against Tyre will be accomplished within a few years, as many as those in which Jerusalem, the city consecrated to God, lay desolate. For God determined to fix the span of one man's life, I mean seventy years, for the desolation that was to overtake Tyre, or else the reign of a single long-lived king.

"During these seventy years all the people who once knew you well will sing a song and an ode about your desolation, as over a woman fallen from her honor. And you yourself, go about for the time of your desolation, wandering and moving from place to place and playing the harlot with the other nations, as one forgotten by God. But if you can take up your lyre and use your instrument no longer like a harlot but with skill, play much and sing much in prayers and supplications to God. For in this way you will one day be remembered before God: if you use the members of your body and your very senses, well tuned like a lyre, with skill, living soberly and singing in a way pleasing to God. For in this way you will be remembered, since God will count you worthy of his remembrance. Indeed, as soon as the foretold time is completed, you will receive his visitation and be restored again to your former state, so that a market will once more be established in you, and people from everywhere will stream to you in haste, bringing their wares to you."

Having gone through these things, and what follows in the same sense, concerning the desolation that overtook Tyre and its renewal, which still stands even now, the word adds: "And her trade and her wages will be holy to the Lord." But in examining the exact reading, I paid attention to the translation of Aquila, which says: "And her merchandise and hire will be sanctified to the Lord." For the Hebrew expression has precisely "merchandise" and "hire" without articles—not, as in the Seventy, "the trade" and "the wages," which seems to signify all the trade and all the wages—but, as in Aquila, "her merchandise and hire sanctified to the Lord." For not all her merchandise nor all her hire, but some part of the merchandise and some part of the wages will be sanctified to the Lord. And this is indeed fulfilled in our own time. For since the church of God has been established in the city of the Tyrians, as also among the other nations, much of what is earned there and gained from business is sanctified to the Lord by being offered to his church. Those who bring these things offer them with reverence, not for themselves, nor so that they may use the gifts offered to God, but for those who dwell before the Lord, that is, for those who attend the altar. For so the Lord directed that those who proclaim the gospel should live by the gospel, and: "Those who serve at the altar share with the altar." So the people described, by offering their firstfruits to these very men, as priests of God who dwell before the Lord, fulfill in deed the prophecy that says: "And her merchandise and her hire will be sanctified to the Lord, and it will not be gathered for them, but for those who dwell before the Lord." The saying itself is marvelous, that the Tyrians, idolaters and always enemies of Israel, were going to offer gifts and the firstfruits of their trade to the God of Israel; but the outcome proves greater than the saying, being fulfilled in very deed in your own day.

After this it is said: "All her trade, to eat and drink and be filled to fullness, a memorial before the Lord." Symmachus rendered this more clearly, saying: "For her trade will belong to those who dwell before the Lord, to eat to fullness and to be clothed until it grows old." In keeping with this we shall also adapt the sense of the Seventy: For those who dwell before the Lord will have what comes from her trade, so as to eat and drink and be filled, as a contribution and as a memorial before the Lord. Now if the words "all her trade, to eat and drink" really stood there, as in the Seventy, the passage might be explained otherwise. But since neither the Hebrew reading nor the other translators say "all her trade," but show that some part of her trade and wages is offered by the faithful who live in Tyre to those who dwell before the Lord, the conclusion of the oracle is shown in fact to be fulfilled according to the explanation given. Who that reads these things will not marvel at the prediction made so long beforehand? It declares that idolaters, wildly infatuated with the error of many gods, and at all times enemies and foes of the Jews, would come to so great a change as to know the God honored among the Jews and to bring him gifts; and these things are shown to have been accomplished in deed through the grace of our Savior Jesus Christ. With these the prophecies concerning the foreign nations come to a close; what follows takes up another subject.

At the beginning the prophet saw the visions concerning Judea and Jerusalem. Then, going on, after much said in between about the foreign nations, he went through them one by one, making particular mention of the nations listed. Now, in the passage before us, he consequently sets out a universal prophecy, foretelling things concerning the whole world. For since "the earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it," it is fitting that, as one who cares for all people, he should declare to the world the judgment of God that will overtake all people, "on the day when God judges the secrets of men." That the passage before us gives universal teaching you would recognize if you observed that it speaks not of Judea or Samaria, nor of Tyre or Damascus or Babylon or any other nation, but clearly of the consummation of this life and the judgment that will follow it, so that all people may be taught what awaits the ungodly after the present life, and what good things are stored up for the godly.

He begins with the grimmer things, so as to end with the more hopeful ones. So he says: "Behold, the Lord is destroying the world and will make it desolate." For when those on the earth are judged and moved to certain other regions of the whole universe, it follows that the ancient dwelling place of humankind should be left desolate, since it will no longer have anyone living in it.
