And he says that he will uncover the face of the earth, that is, its surface, so that those covered in it may come out into the light; here the text points to the manner of the resurrection of the dead. "And he will disperse those who dwell in it" (or, in Aquila's and Theodotion's version, "he will scatter"), one here and another there, in proportion to each person's deeds. For there are many dwelling places with the Father, and God's universe is great and vast, able to receive all the souls that have lived on the earth since the beginning. The ungodly are allotted Hades and the dwellings beneath the earth, recesses that are dark and unseen, as it says: "They shall go into the lowest parts of the earth; they shall be handed over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for foxes." The godly, however, will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so they will be with the Lord forever.

Once the bodies hidden in the earth have been uncovered, those being judged will all stand alike before the judgment seat of the great Judge. Those who in mortal life once seemed to have more than their inferiors, whether in rank, birth or wealth, will then differ from them in nothing, for all will stand on equal terms before the judgment seat of Christ. The priest will be like the people, and the people like the priest, and all will be alike, since there is no partiality with God. This is why it is also said in Job: "Small and great are there, and the servant who does not fear his master." Again, slave and master will be alike, and the woman who was once a maidservant will stand on equal footing with the woman reckoned her mistress. Likewise the one who buys and sells because he has greater means, and the one who lends to the needy because he is wealthy, will be like the one who borrows because he is poor and buys because he is in want.

Next to what has been said comes this: "The earth shall be utterly ruined, and the earth shall be utterly plundered; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Since a declaration of God has been uttered through the prophet, these things will happen to those who have received the worse lot, whom he calls "earth" because of their earthly mind. Just as it was once said to Adam, "You are earth, and to earth you shall go," so too the punishment of ruin is threatened against those who at the time of God's judgment are found to be lovers of pleasure and lovers of the body, and therefore earthly and fleshly. Others too will take them in hand, like executioners exacting the penalty for what they dared to do when they handed themselves over to corruption and outraged the image of God within them.

Who are these, if not certain avenging and punishing demons, who will plunder them by carrying off their souls? Then the souls that have done things worthy of mourning will mourn for themselves. This is why it is said: "The earth mourned, and the world was ruined." He makes clear who the mourning earth and the ruined world are by adding: "The lofty ones of the earth mourned." For the wrath of God will pursue these above all, since he opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.

Instead of "And the earth acted lawlessly because of those who dwell in it," Symmachus says: "And the earth was murdered by those who dwell in it." For these lofty ones of the earth mentioned before murdered it by committing murders and filling it with blood. The earth suffered these things because of those who dwell in it, "because they transgressed the law and changed the ordinance; they broke an everlasting covenant." All the people who have inhabited the world from the beginning, Greeks and barbarians alike, received the natural law and had the ordinances of God written in their souls. They accepted the everlasting covenant in their common notions. Then they gave themselves over to sins against nature and so became transgressors of the natural law. Therefore they will rightly stand before the divine tribunal to be judged and to give an account of their transgression.

"And for this reason a curse will devour the earth, because those who dwell in it have sinned." At the beginning of the making of the world, before sin yet existed, God blessed man; so at the consummation of the age, he says, a curse will devour the earth. Symmachus has: "Because of this curse the earth mourned." For because of the curse that has come upon human beings, the earth, which once was like a mother to them and which bore and nurtured them, will take up mourning over them. Again, instead of "Therefore those who dwell on the earth shall be poor," Symmachus said: "Therefore they shall be worn away." While everyone on earth suffers these things, a few will be left: those who have preserved the image of the heavenly one in their souls.

Instead of "The wine shall mourn," Aquila rendered "The fruit harvest mourned." By the example of ripe fruit he shows how short-lived the bloom of the body is, and how brief and changeable human luxury is. Then too, he says, all those will groan who in this present life have walked the broad and spacious road and wasted their lives in drunkenness and debauchery. They will no longer enjoy their pleasures; rather, they will be convicted of the shameful and lawless deeds they did and will be covered with shame. This is why it is said somewhere: "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise, some to everlasting life, and others to reproach and everlasting shame." The wine that is sweet now, and what is called sikera, which the other translators named "strong drink," will be bitter to them at that time. Then too every city will shut its house so that no one may enter, for there will no longer be communities like those of today, in which the ungodly do whatever they please. Often, when the text mentions wine, it hints at human luxury, or at the drunkenness of vice and the stupor of the soul, which turns the mind away from right and natural reasoning. Those being punished then will sober up, as it were, from this drunkenness and will let out cries and wails of mourning. So it adds: "Wail over the wine everywhere; all gladness has ceased."

After what was said before, the prophecy adds: "All these things shall be in the land, in the midst of the nations." This clearly teaches that what has been said refers to the universal judgment. It adds: "As when someone gleans an olive tree, so they shall glean them." No one among the ungodly will be left behind; God's judgment will pursue them down to the last one. Instead of "And if the vintage ceases, these shall cry aloud," Symmachus used a break in the sense and so presented two thoughts in the same passage. He said: "like gleanings, when the vintage is finished." Then, ending the thought there, he adds from a fresh start: "These shall lift up their voice." The first part belongs with the sense of what came before. Those who gather the fruit of the olive usually beat and shake the tree with reeds down to the very last olive, wherever one may be left. After the vintage, some people go back and gather the few small grapes or clusters left behind. In the same way the ungodly will be gathered up to the last one, so that none escapes the judgment of God. But while those suffer these things, "these shall lift up their voice." Who are these, if not those of the better rank? They would be those counted worthy of blessedness with God. So Symmachus next adds: "But these shall lift up their voice; they shall exult when the Lord is glorified." In the translation of the Seventy, however, those to be handed over to punishment suffer a final vintage and are gathered up to the last one. They raise their voices and cry out as they are punished, while those who have become God's portion "will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord." For then the Lord himself will come in the glory of his Father, with power and great glory. So those who long ago set their hope on him will rejoice in this glory of their Lord. Instead of "The water of the sea shall be troubled," Theodotion translated "The waters of the sea roared." This shows how great the shout will be when they glorify their Lord, for their voice will be compared to the roar of the sea.

"And the glory of the Lord shall be in the islands": that is, in the churches. Formerly they were cut off among the unbelieving nations, as if in the middle of the sea, and then the glory of the Lord will shine upon them. At this the text praises and extols God, who has given his glory to the islands. So it says: "O Lord, God of Israel, from the wings of the earth we have heard wonders: hope for the godly." Symmachus and Theodotion have: "From the wings of the earth we have heard psalms," and Aquila has "melodies." For those who belong to God's portion marvel at his just judgment and rejoice together with the glory of the Lord, and in their joy they send up to him hymns and psalms of thanksgiving. The prophet marvels at this: that from the ends of the earth even the islands counted worthy of the Lord's glory sing hymns and psalms to him. It is entirely consistent that, having mentioned islands (I mean the churches and what is done in them), he fittingly went on to say: "we have heard psalms." If the reading is "we have heard wonders," he speaks as if of extraordinary prodigies. It was indeed a great and prodigious marvel that foreign, alien and barbarian nations reaching to the ends of the earth should turn away from their ancestral gods, sing psalms and praise the God of the prophets. Then he adds: "hope for the godly." He had gone through the threats against the ungodly. Then he spoke about God's portion: they will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord, and the glory of the Lord will be in the islands. Having thus set out the righteous judgment of God, he consistently added: "hope for the godly." For a good hope of salvation is laid up for every righteous and godly man, even if he seems to be a foreigner and a stranger to the seed of Abraham.

After this, according to Symmachus, it is said: "And he said: My secret is mine, my secret is mine." The prophets had glorified God for the extraordinary thing just mentioned and had spoken of the hope of the godly. But they had not said what the things hoped for were, or what they were like, and they longed to learn and know what God has prepared for those who love him. So God tells them to be silent, saying: "My secret is mine, my secret is mine." Now, he says, is not the time to reveal "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered the human heart, what I have prepared for those who love me." The prophet perceived these things by the Holy Spirit and weeps for the ungodly, because he foresees their destruction. Just as he glorified God for the hope of the godly, so out of his overflowing love for humankind he laments those who are perishing, adding next: "Woe to the treacherous: those who deal treacherously, and the treachery of those who deal treacherously with the law." Instead of "Woe to the treacherous," Aquila says: "Ah me! The treacherous have dealt treacherously," and Symmachus: "Alas for me! The treacherous have dealt treacherously." You see how the men of God, out of love for humankind, suffered with those who were perishing and grieved for them beyond measure. They even turned the lament on themselves and said "Ah me!" over the treachery of the transgressors.

Next he adds the threat against them, saying: "Fear and pit and snare are upon you who dwell on the earth. And it shall be that whoever flees the fear shall fall into the pit, and whoever climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare." And he adds: "For windows have been opened from heaven." Here he hints at God's oversight and at his watchful power, which observes all things and surveys everything as if through windows of heaven. These windows seem to be shut whenever God overlooks the sins of those on earth and does not proceed against the offenders; then he seems to have turned away and not even to see the sinners. But whenever he decides to proceed against those who have sinned, the windows of heaven are, as it were, thrown open. The heavenly gates are probably what is meant by the windows of heaven. Of these gates it is said: "Lift up the gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in." At that time, then, all the gates will be opened for the kingdom of the Lord, so that those under his rule may enter through them. But now, when the windows of heaven are opened, what happens? "The foundations of the earth shall be shaken," he says, "and the earth shall be utterly troubled, and the earth shall be utterly perplexed." The earth will suffer all these things; here "the earth" means those who once inhabited it. He says they will suffer such things that they will be like men drunk and reeling from the excess of their troubles. Besides all this, the earth meant here, which is clearly the soul of the ungodly, will be like a watchman's hut in an orchard. In an earlier passage too this image signified desolation, where it was said: "Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall be like a hut in an orchard."

These things will happen to the earth, I mean to those who once inhabited the earth, because lawlessness prevailed upon it. So at the end of the passage he says: "And it shall fall and shall not be able to rise." The earth, whether this means earthly flesh, or the body-loving soul, or those who once inhabited the earth, falls once at the end of mortal life. It will share in the general resurrection, so as to stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body according to what he did, whether good or evil. But when they have been judged, fallen from every good hope and been handed over to the threatened punishments, then, having fallen away from God, they will no longer be able to rise.

Having finished its account of the inhabitants of the earth, the prophecy next passes on to heaven and heavenly things, saying: "And on that day," meaning the time of God's judgment already spoken of, "God will bring his hand upon the array of heaven." By this he hints at the consummation of the universe, when heaven and earth will pass away. For then, according to the saving teaching, "the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars of heaven will fall, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken." Then too "the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory." Hinting at all these things, the prophetic word teaches: "And it shall be on that day that God will bring his hand upon the array of heaven." Moses often calls the sun, the moon and the stars "the array of heaven," as when he says: "Take care that you do not look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars and all the array of heaven, and be led astray and worship them."

So the present prophecy also shows, as it goes on, what the array of heaven was, where it says: "And the brick shall melt, and the wall shall fall." Symmachus rendered this as follows: "And the moon shall be abashed, and the sun shall be ashamed"; Aquila has: "And the moon shall be put to shame, and the sun shall be ashamed"; and Theodotion likewise: "The moon shall be abashed," he says, "and the sun shall be ashamed." You see that he brings his hand upon the array of heaven when he brings the visible world to its end. He says, "God will bring his hand upon the array of heaven," and then adds, "and upon the kings of the earth; and he will gather its gathering into a prison, and they will shut them up in a stronghold." It seems to me that by "the kings of the earth" he means the rulers of this age. This is how Gabriel, who brought revelations to Daniel, explained it when he said: "And the prince of the kingdom of the Persians came out to meet me, and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks, and the prince of the kingdom of the Medes." Here the text calls such invisible rulers of the nations "kings," and says that they will be gathered by the hand of God, thrown into prison and shut up in a stronghold. So Symmachus has: "against the kings who are on the earth; and they shall be gathered as prisoners are gathered into a pit, and shall be shut up in confinement." For when the kingdom of Christ was about to prevail in the new age, it was fitting that the principalities, the authorities, the world-rulers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness should be cast down into the pit that suits them, the pit they dug for themselves. For every ungodly man "has dug a pit and hollowed it out, and will fall into the hole that he made."

Moreover, those meant here will be shut up in a prison that suits them, so that they may not trouble those whom God rules. They will remain there for as long as the Judge of all decides that they should be held in the bonds of that place. So the Seventy have: "After many generations there will be a visitation of them"; Symmachus: "And after many days they shall be visited"; Aquila: "And after a multitude of days they shall be visited"; and Theodotion: "After many days they shall be visited." By whom is not said: "by God" is not added, and the matter has been passed over in silence as something not to be spoken. Then the sun itself will be ashamed when it sees those it once gave light to exposed by the judgment and subjected to punishment. Likewise the moon will be abashed, because it contributed nothing to the reform of those on earth who lived ungodly lives. Think of stewards appointed to oversee and manage a householder's house, who see, when the master arrives, those who had long been under their care being punished and subjected to various penalties. In the same way the sun and moon, who for a long age served the will of God, are said by the other translators to be abashed and ashamed when those who once lived ungodly lives under their rays pay the penalty. In the Seventy, however, there is no mention here of either sun or moon. Instead, "And the brick shall melt and the wall shall fall" is said very obscurely. The translators presumably concealed the meaning because they were publishing the scripture for Greeks, and because the wording seemed incongruous.

To all this is added: "For the Lord will reign in Zion and in Jerusalem, and he will be glorified before the elders." In the account of the consummation we also needed to learn about the heavenly kingdom of our Savior that has been proclaimed. It will come after the overthrow of the principalities and authorities. We have often shown from the testimony of the apostles that Zion and Jerusalem are heavenly. There the kingdom of Christ will be established, and then he will also be glorified before his elders. For those whom he honored in the present life with the dignities of the church, appointing them elders, he will count worthy of his own divinity. So Symmachus has: "and glory before his elders."

Having completed the prophecy of God's universal judgment, which ended with the kingdom of Christ and the glory of his elders, the text cries out in wonder: "O Lord my God, I will glorify you, I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, an ancient and true counsel." We will understand how this counsel was ancient if we pay attention to the words of the Savior to those who will stand at his right hand: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Starting from this, the Apostle also wrote: "just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him, having predestined us to adoption as sons in him." This counsel, then, was ancient. These were the truly wonderful things: they were foreordained before the foundation of the world, but they will be fulfilled at the consummation of the ages, when he puts all his enemies under his feet and abolishes every rule and every authority and power.

At that time, when all wickedness has been removed and the last enemy, death, has been abolished, God will be all in all. Our Savior and Lord, reigning over the new age, will be glorified before the elders, when all his saints will also reign in life, reigning together with their Savior. This was the ancient counsel, and these were the wonderful things that amazed the prophet and led him to glorify God. Then, praying that these things might come to pass, he adds: "So be it," as if he were eager and longed for the consummation of good things to arrive as quickly as possible. This counsel was ancient because of God's foreknowledge and predestination, and true because of the way the end turns out.

For those who will be counted worthy of blessedness he prayed, saying "So be it." Concerning those who have passed their mortal life, he adds: "For you have made cities a heap, fortified cities, so that their foundations fall; the city of the ungodly shall never be built." Because of this he says: "I will glorify you," because you have demolished the cities of the ungodly by wiping out their godless polities and their impious buildings. But those of them who were saved "will bless you," or, according to the other translators, "will glorify you." These are "the people" who became poor for your sake in the former age, and the "cities" of people who were wronged long ago, wronged by the persecutors of godliness. These will bless you in your church, having been tested in various ways of life, and they will rightly bless you, since you became "a helper to every lowly city and a shelter to those who lost heart through want." When they were lowly, disheartened, and lacking every comfort as they lived among the wicked, you were their helper and shelter. They were also thirsty at that time, so that they said: "My soul has thirsted for you," and: "My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty, the living one." You in turn were a spring, refreshing them and giving them drink with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and you [?] them out of their faintheartedness, strengthening them by the power of your only-begotten Word.

So that the children of the Jews would not suppose that these things were said about themselves, he necessarily introduces the grace of Christ poured out on all the nations, saying: "And the Lord of hosts will make for all the nations on this mountain..." What he will make is given next as "a drinking feast" by the other translators. According to the Seventy it is: "They will drink gladness, they will drink wine." So in these words he prophesies that the Lord will prepare a banquet not for Israel, nor for the Jewish people, but for all the nations. It will not be in hollows of the earth, nor in ravines, nor in plains, nor even on many mountains, nor on just any one mountain at random, but on that one he pointed to when he said: "on this mountain." Which mountain was this, if not the one he spoke of a little earlier: "For the Lord will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and will be glorified before his elders"? On the mountain of his kingdom, where he will also show his glory to his elders, he will prepare the banquet for the nations too and give them the drink of immortality. That is why it is said: "On this mountain they will drink gladness, they will drink wine, they will anoint themselves with ointment." The Apostle shows what this mountain is when he says: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven."

Once they are there, it is not Israel but those from all the nations who are counted worthy of the promises who will drink gladness. They will drink the wine from the true vine, of which the Savior said: "I will not drink it until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of heaven."

"And they will anoint themselves with ointment." They will no longer receive only the pledge of the Holy Spirit, but will share in the very fullness of the godhead of the Son of God. They will no longer know in part and prophesy in part, but will become partakers of Christ in full, so that they themselves are declared anointed ones [?], sons of God, heirs of God, and fellow heirs with Christ. The word of the Gospel has handed down to us images and symbols of these things in the mysteries of the new covenant, through the mystical chrism and the saving blood, so that once we have been tested in these we may also partake of the greater things. "Deliver these very things that have been spoken," he says, "to the nations"; for Israel is not worthy of them.

Just as someone hands over a deposit in secret, so he speaks of the mystical teaching about what has been said: "Deliver it to all the nations, for this counsel is for all the nations." That is why the prophet rightly glorified God, amazed at his grace, when he said: "For you have done wonderful things, an ancient and true counsel."

Next he makes clear how the nations will obtain these things, although from of old they were godless and without hope because they were devoted to idols and demons. He says: "Death prevailed and swallowed them up." Nevertheless, the merciful Savior of all rescued human souls from death, set them free from the error of many gods and of demons, and "took away every tear from every face"; "and he took away the reproach of his people from all the earth." The reproach of the people from the nations was the idolatry that had held them in its power. God took away this reproach, and also the tears shed over it by those who, out of love for humanity, mourned the ruin of so many souls. This is according to the translation of the Seventy. According to the others, the passage gives a different sense, which Symmachus rendered more clearly in this way: "And on this mountain he will drown the face of the ruler who rules over all the nations, and the anointing that is anointed upon all the nations will cause death to be swallowed up forever. And the Lord God will wipe away every tear from the face, and remove the reproach of his people from all the earth, for the Lord has spoken."

The renderings of the other translators mean the same, and their sense seems to me to be this. At the time indicated, the Lord will make the banquet for all the nations on the mountain described and count them worthy to share in the wine, the ointment, and his ineffable mysteries. Then he will cause the face of the ruler who ruled over all the nations to be swallowed up and to vanish, that is, death. The Lord who reigns on the mountain spoken of will drown it so completely that it no longer appears anywhere. I mean death, which the prophecy here calls a "ruler," while the Apostle did not hesitate to call it a king as well, saying: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses." Since, then, death is abolished as the last enemy, the passage here fittingly says that the face of the ruler will perish. In place of "the face of the ruler," Aquila and Theodotion rendered "the face of darkness." And what was this darkness, if not the lightless region of death, full of gloom? At that time, then, when the saints reign together with the Son of God, death itself, which of old swallowed up everyone, will be swallowed up.

The cause of this will be the anointing that is anointed upon all the nations. Once they are anointed with the chrism, they will no longer be subject to death. Sharing in immortality and eternal life, they will render death powerless, as if it were dead. Therefore it is said: "The anointing that is anointed upon all the nations will cause death to be swallowed up forever." And once death is out of the way, the Lord God is said to wipe away every tear from every face and to remove the reproach of his people. It was no small reproach for human beings, made in the image of God, to fall from eternal life and be made subject to death. But the reproach will be taken away when death has been abolished and the darkness has vanished. The people from all the nations will then enjoy the kingdom of Christ shining forth in eternal life, set free from their former evils and counted worthy of God's promises.

When death has been swallowed up at the time of the resurrection, the sons of the new age will on that day sing a song of thanksgiving as they see their Savior in glory. They will say: "Behold our God, in whom we hoped." For long ago we held him in hope, believing the divine teachings about him, but now we also see him with our eyes, and that is why we long endured the painful things that came upon us. They will say these things, and he will give them rest on the mountain of his kingdom spoken of before. These will enjoy the good things that were promised, but the land of Moab, called Moab in the Hebrew wording, will suffer punishment for its godlessness. It will be trampled like a threshing floor under wagons, so that its hands grow weak and slack from exhaustion. Hence Aquila says: "And Moab will be threshed beneath him as straw is threshed," and Symmachus: "And we will thresh Moab like threshed straw into mud." Next he shows who those are who trample and thresh it, adding: "And the feet of the meek and the steps of the poor will trample it." I think that "Moab" here refers to the wicked demon, the opposing power that was once honored as a god among the Moabites. It had great pride and exalted itself against the God of Israel. It also wore down the nation under its power, and even in the time of Moses it dared to lead the people into fornication and to have them initiated into the rites of Baal-peor, which was the idol of the Moabites. For this reason the foregoing things are prophesied about it, as about some terrible power that fights against God.

In the vision concerning Moab, too, these words were spoken about the same demon to Moab itself: "For your alliance has been taken away, and the ruler who trampled upon the earth has perished." Since this wicked demon was thought to be fearsome by the Jewish people, the present prophecy teaches what end awaits it at the time of God's universal judgment, when it says: "And Moab will be trampled, and he will let his hands drop." For just as he brought others low to destroy them, it says, so he too will suffer the same. Symmachus has: "And we will thresh Moab beneath it like threshed straw into mud. And he will spread out his hands as he is threshed and trampled, just as a bather spreads them out to swim, and his pride will be brought low together with the strokes of his hands. And the fortress of the height of your walls will bow down and cleave to the ground." His wall and fortress were the powers with which he had fortified himself, and the passage says that these too will be pulled down. Through the single wicked demon that once ruled the Moabites, it teaches what will happen [?] to the others who were reckoned as gods. From one example it leaves us to understand what will also come upon the rest of the opposing powers.

For we needed to learn beforehand what the end of death and of the other opposing powers will be at the time of judgment, so that we would not be ignorant of their destruction. After this destruction, when our Savior has received his kingdom on the heavenly mountain, those worthy of the promises will sing the heavenly song on that day, once they have come into the heavenly Jerusalem. In the present passage the text called this Judea, in keeping with the land of the earthly Jerusalem. In this way it offered the children of the Jewish people who were listening some delight and encouragement toward the hope of what was set before them. At the same time it presented the true Judea, indicating in some way here the land and great breadth of the heavenly Jerusalem. So the place is to be understood as Judea, and the godly commonwealth of divine and evangelical spirits within it as the city of God. When they have come there, on that day they will sing the song that follows. What song those indicated by the prophecy will sing, the Holy Spirit now hands down through the prophet, prophesying in their own person and saying: "Behold, a strong city is our salvation." The city below on earth was not strong, for it was often captured by enemies, but this one truly is the strong city of God, and this is our salvation. According to Symmachus, those who sing the song will say: "We have a strong city," and according to Aquila: "A city of strength is salvation for us." In place of "salvation" and "saving," the Hebrew word plainly contains the name Jesus, in the very letters in which the name of our Savior is written in Hebrew. He himself, then, our Savior, will be the city of the blessed; he himself will be their wall and their outer wall.

And he himself will be all things to them. If Jerusalem is understood as heavenly, it follows that its gates should be understood as the various entrances to the dwellings there. He wants these opened not to Jews, nor even to Israel, nor simply to anyone at all, but only to those who keep righteousness, truth, and peace. Hence he adds: "Open the gates; let a people enter who keep truth, who lay hold of truth and keep peace." Longing for these gates, a man who loved God said: "Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will enter through them and give thanks to the Lord." It is right, he says, to open the gates to those just mentioned, since "they hoped in you, O Lord God, who humbled and brought down those who dwell on high; you will cast down strong cities and bring them down to the ground." These words are like what was said earlier: "For you have made cities a heap, fortified cities, so that their foundations fall." So now, presenting God's righteous judgment, he takes up the same thought again, glorifying him and saying: "O God, great and eternal, who humbled and brought down those who dwell on high." You cast them down from their height and humbled them, and you destroyed their cities, either by bringing their mortal life to an end or by making their godless and impious polities vanish. But your meek ones, whom you called blessed when you said: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth"—these, who were formerly lowly, you have now exalted at the time of your righteous judgment, making them trample on the heads of those who were once proud. Then the path of the godly became straight. With nothing standing in the way any longer, their path has become unhindered, unobstructed, and straight, and the cause of this is the righteous judgment of God. Therefore he adds: "For the way of the Lord is judgment."

The prophet has described what end will overtake the ungodly and what hopes await the righteous. He has shown what the kingdom of Christ will be like, how the gates of God's city in heaven will be opened only to the worthy, and what song those who enjoy the promises will sing. Following this, he sends up to God the words before us, in his own person and in that of those like him, saying: "We have hoped in your name and in the remembrance that our soul desires." For as if he were present at the fulfillment of the words and saw the events themselves with the enlightened eyes of his soul, he looks up to God and praises the giver of such great good things, sending up a prayer and speaking these words. For the treasures stored up with you are worthy of hope, and I say these things to you, the desire of my soul. You, Lord, are my desire and the divine love of my soul. That is why my soul has desired you, for the very remembrance of your name carries our soul out of itself and rouses it to longing for you. So we cannot even sleep through the hours of the night, but we keep awake in spirit during them too and hold you, our desire, in our minds. In this way even the nights are lit up for us like days, since your commandments and your words were given as light to us who still spend our time on earth, by night as well as by day. Having cried out these things to God with surpassing affection, the prophet turns to us and urges us to walk the same road as he. Therefore he says: "Learn righteousness, you who dwell on the earth."

In place of "for the ungodly has ceased," Aquila and Theodotion translated "the ungodly has received mercy," and Symmachus "the ungodly has been granted favor." The passage urges those who were formerly found in ungodliness to hasten to repentance. Since God's judgment awaits all people, all of you must learn righteousness, confident that God, who loves humanity, will have mercy even on those who were previously caught in ungodliness, if they repent. But if anyone is not persuaded by the preaching, does not learn righteousness, and does not do the truth, he will be taken away from among the living and will not see the glory of the Lord.

Having said these things to us by way of exhortation, he looks up again. Seeing the divinity of the Savior lifted on high, he cries out: "Lord, your arm is high, and they did not know it." For the ungodly were lowly and stood far off from the knowledge of his divinity, and so they wallowed in the darkness of their ignorance. But when the universal judgment comes and they see the high arm, those who once blasphemed him as though he did not exist will cease from their folly, covered with shame. When they see the blessed enjoying life in heaven, they will be filled with jealousy. Jealousy will seize above all the people who in the present life refused to accept God's instruction. Hence: "Jealousy will seize an uninstructed people." By this he hints at those of the circumcision who have not accepted the grace of God through Christ. Then he adds next: "And now fire will devour the adversaries," since they will be subject to the sentence that says: "Depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels."

Having said these things about them, he turns to God again and sends up a supplication, saying: "O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us all things." For everything else that comes from you is good too, but the greatest gift is the peace that comes from you and peace with yourself, so that we may be free from strife toward you and our soul may be kept at peace with you always. This would come about if you would deign to make us your own possession. We know no other than you, and we have put our trust in your name alone. Since, then, we possess no one else in life but you, we rightly entreat you to count us worthy to become your portion and your inheritance.

"We, then," they say, "are yours, O Lord, and you are our possession. But those who have given themselves over to sins that lead to death, and so have become dead in their souls—for 'the soul that sins, it shall die'—will not see the eternal life promised to the saints. Nor will physicians, wherever they may come from at the time of judgment, be able to help them toward salvation or raise them up from their fall. For who among physicians can save those whom you, the great, fearful, and just judge, have handed over to destruction?" In place of "and you took away every male of theirs," Symmachus translated "all their memory," and Aquila and Theodotion "all their memorial." For all memory of their wickedness had to be taken away at the time of judgment indicated here. But if it is read "every male of theirs," the passage introduces great kindness. It means that the sinners themselves are not going to be annihilated or utterly destroyed, but that their offspring are being referred to in this way, namely the wicked thoughts their soul has begotten. It is these, it says, that will be done away with.

Again, in place of "add evils to the glorious of the earth," we did not find "evils" either in the other translators or in the Hebrew reading. According to all the translators it says: "You have added to the nation in which you were glorified." Since they all agree in translating it this way, we must understand what he added to the nation. We shall understand it from the Savior's saying: "To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance." So to those who possessed good things he added what was stored up with him, "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart." But to those who have stored up evils for themselves he will in turn add what corresponds to their works. Next he adds: "You have removed far off all the ends of the earth." For those who have put themselves far from God he likewise puts far off. That is why God's own people, so as not to suffer the same fate as the ungodly, had to say in their prayer: "O Lord our God, take possession of us."

The prophet beholds the scene of the universal judgment as if he were present at the judgment and standing beside the tribunal of God. So in response to what he sees, he sometimes confesses, sometimes supplicates, sometimes gives thanks, sometimes describes the rewards God will give to the worthy, and sometimes lists the punishments to be brought against the others. He hands all these things down to us as well through his writing, so that we may be instructed and learn everything that he himself came to know through the illumination of the divine Spirit. So now he says: There was a time, O Lord, when we walked the narrow and hard road and were contending for godliness. Yet even in that affliction we did not forget you. Strengthened by the very remembrance of you, we endured steadfastly, so that we could say: "Afflicted, but not crushed; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed." Through that very affliction we were being disciplined, knowing that "the Lord disciplines the one he loves." Every affliction seemed small to us because of our longing for you, so that we could say: "The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us."

So, enduring every pain, we were like a woman in labour who cries out just as she is about to bring into the light what she has conceived in her womb. For so we too became before your beloved. Holding your only-begotten Word within our own soul, together with the fear of reverence for you that you had sown in us, we nobly bore every pain and the afflictions brought upon us. We struggled anxiously lest we should somehow miscarry your beloved, conceived within us, and the divine fear he had sown in us. And having persevered, we were not disappointed in our hope, but we gave birth to a spirit of salvation; for the outcome of our conceiving your beloved and his fear was the salvation of our spirit. When we had brought it to birth, we made it known to all people who dwell on the earth, so that they too might learn of it and profit by striving to conceive from fear of you and to give birth to the same spirit. For those who have not received this fear, nor given birth to the spirit of salvation, but have instead become barren and fruitless, will fall away from the hope that comes from you. But those who belong to your portion, who have endured every affliction for your sake, will by no means fall away from the life that is with you, even if they should contend against sin to the point of death.

For “the dead shall rise,” or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, “your dead shall live,” or, according to Aquila, “those of yours who have died shall live.” And who would his dead be but his holy martyrs? They are different from the dead mentioned above, of whom it was said: “But the dead shall not see life, nor shall physicians raise them up.” Those were dead because they had committed sins leading to death, whereas the Lord's dead, who for his sake endured every affliction even to death, will rise again, even after burial in the tombs. In place of “shall be raised,” the other translators rendered “shall awake,” as of people who have fallen asleep, not died. For this reason the death of the saints is called sleep, and accordingly their resurrection may be called an awakening. So according to the other translators the first clause says that those in the tombs will awake. In the second clause, they will “exult,” according to Symmachus, or “praise,” according to Aquila, or “shout aloud,” according to Theodotion. And the cause of their resurrection will be the dew that comes from you. For just as the dew that falls quietly and gently on the earth nourishes the seeds lying in it and makes them grow, in the same way the dew from you will provide healing, life and salvation to your dead, whose bodies were sown in the earth in their season. And you would not be wrong to say that this dew is the only-begotten Word of God. He will let his life-giving drops fall upon his dead, and at once bring them healing of their sins, if in human fashion they had committed any offence, and grant them resurrection, salvation and eternal life. But the lot of the ungodly will not be like this, for “their land will fall.” So, as those who have fallen away from God, they will be handed over in body and soul alike to the punishment that awaits them.

After the teaching on the resurrection of the dead, the prophetic Spirit beholds the saints of God standing before it, gathered together after the resurrection. Then, perceiving on the other side the wrath about to come upon the ungodly, it calls on the company of the saints to withdraw for a little while and hide somewhere far away, so that they may not even witness the destruction of the ungodly. So it says: “Go, my people, enter your chambers.” The chambers of God's people are the many dwelling places with the Father, set apart for each rank of the saints according to God's just judgment. “Into these chambers prepared for you,” it says, “you, my people, enter, and shut your door. Do not concern yourself with what lies far beyond your chambers, but hide yourself for a very little while, until the wrath of the Lord has passed. When it has passed, throw open the doors of your chambers and go forth with great authority and boldness to behold the new age and the kingdom of God promised to you.”

Next it teaches what the wrath will do when it comes upon the ungodly, saying: “And the earth will uncover its blood,” so that none of those who long ago were slain on it in their souls by sins leading to death may escape notice. It is for this that God is said to bring on the wrath, and here “wrath” is the name given to the angels who carry out punishments. Of the Egyptians it was said: “He sent upon them wrath and fury and affliction, a sending by evil angels.” So now too the wrath of God, rushing against those who long ago inhabited the earth, “will uncover the blood” poured out upon it “and will no longer cover the slain.” By these words he points to the killing of God's saints and the blood of the martyrs, of which Moses also spoke when he wrote in the Great Song: “For the blood of his sons is avenged, and he will take vengeance and repay justice to his enemies, and he will repay those who hate him.” And every earthbound soul that loves the body will also uncover its blood, by which I mean the deadly sins it has committed, when it confesses them.

When these things have been accomplished, “the last enemy, death, is destroyed.” So at the very end of all things, after everyone else, the text adds: “On that day,” that is, at that point in time, “God will bring the holy and great and strong sword.” In place of “holy,” all the other translators wrote “hard.” This sword he has, as it were, stored up for a long time, unleashing it on no one else, and he will bring it upon this one alone, for whom it was kept in proportion to his wickedness. And who was this but the one who in the beginning, in the paradise of God, tripped up the first man and threw him down from his standing before God? This was the crooked serpent, fittingly named a dragon because he drags himself along the ground and crawls and lies in wait at people's feet, to see whether he can bite someone, inject his deadly venom, and throw him down from the straight road that leads to God. The rod of God is straight and serves for discipline, as it is written: “A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.” It is reserved for those whose sins can be healed, and is applied for their discipline, their improvement and the benefit of their souls. But the one who has nothing upright or straight about him, but is crooked and twisted through and through, who crawls on the ground on his breast and belly and lies in wait at everyone's feet to trip them and throw them down, will, after all the ungodly, be handed over to the hard and great and strong sword which the great Judge has stored up for him alone. And what was this sword, which the Seventy called holy and great and strong, but the living Word of God, active and sharper than any two-edged sword?

Here he calls the working of justice a sword, but he also calls it holy. In this way he softens the terror of the threat, and at the same time shows that those who are punished will not end in destruction, but that the sword will be a cause of holiness for them if they repent. For when God disciplines, he does not wish to destroy, but to cleanse and sanctify those who turn back. This sword comes against so great a dragon as against its own adversary, the opponent of all its good works, to slay him and blot his very existence out of being, so that he no longer exists or is even counted among the things that are. That is why he is not even judged worthy of the wrath of God. For that wrath was meant to discipline and to turn people back, as the one who said, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath,” teaches us, since anger has the power to rebuke and wrath the power to discipline. So wrath pursued those who had sinned less gravely, bringing rebukes upon them and disciplining them. But the dragon deserved neither rebuke nor discipline, only utter obliteration. For this reason the holy and great and strong sword of God comes against him first. When he sees it, he will take to flight, being senseless and foolish and unable to say, “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” Yet as he tries to flee, the holy and great and strong sword of God will overtake him and slay his crooked self, removing his whole existence from being. He fled and tried to hide, as in his own lairs, in what is called the sea, of which it is said: “This is the great and wide sea; there are creeping things without number, small creatures with great,” and, “This dragon, which you formed to make sport of him.” And in Job the Lord, speaking of him, taught: “Will you lead the dragon with a hook, and put a halter around his nose? Or will you fasten a ring in his nostril?”

To which he adds: “This is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by his angels,” and again: “He is king of all that are in the waters.” In these words the text also resolves a difficulty. It teaches that he has been allowed to live for this reason: to be mocked by the saints of God, who train themselves by wrestling against him, now casting hooks around him, now binding a halter about his nose, now putting a ring through him. That is why it is said: “made to be mocked by his angels.” As long as the contest against this beast was set before God's athletes, and they gave proof of their virtue by training against him and through him, the dragon himself went on being mocked. But when at last the contest was over, and God's righteous judgment was granting rewards to those who had contended, at the consummation of all things,

then, after the judgment upon the ungodly, God will bring his holy and great and strong sword “upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the crooked serpent.” According to Symmachus it reads: “against Leviathan the crooked serpent, and he will kill the dragon that is in the sea on that day.” Aquila has: “against Leviathan, a hardened, or coiled, serpent, and he will kill the sea monster that is in the sea on that day.” And Theodotion says: “against the dragon, the strong serpent, and against the dragon, the crooked serpent, and he will kill the dragon that is in the sea on that day.” This same serpent and dragon is called Leviathan, as though that were his proper name. He was also the great sea monster that the Lord is said to subdue, as in the words, “he who is about to subdue the great sea monster”; for there too he is named Leviathan. In the Psalm that says, “This dragon, which you formed to make sport of him,” he is named Leviathan in the Hebrew. Likewise in Job, “Will you lead the dragon with a hook?” again uses the name Leviathan. In this way the many-headed and many-named one is called dragon and serpent and devil and Satan and great sea monster and Leviathan, and elsewhere also lion and basilisk.

“On that day,” that is, at that time of the consummation, God, the Judge of all, will slay him with his sword. It is on that day that he will strike him with blows. At his first coming among human beings, the Christ of God did not use the sword against him, and so did not slay him, but only trod upon him and trampled his powers underfoot. That is why it was said in his person: “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon.” And he has trampled him now, and still tramples him even now, by giving his disciples authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. But at the time of the consummation spoken of here, after all the ungodly, the sword of God will overtake him as he flees, make an end of him, and slay him, removing him from being so that he exists no more. Here the discourse on the universal judgment of God comes to its close. It began with the words: “Behold, the Lord is laying waste the world and will make it desolate.” Now that it has ended, the prophecy takes up a distinct subject from a fresh beginning.

“A fair vineyard, a thing desired.” Now that the prophecy announcing the universal judgment of God has come to a close, the prophet begins another subject. It contains threats against Jerusalem and its inhabitants because of their unbelief toward the Lord. After this comes the apostolic preaching that was spread through the whole world. Then he recalls the women with Mary Magdalene who saw the saving resurrection, and he points to the turning to God of the nations that once worshipped idols. Then he prophesies about the council of the Sadducees and Pharisees and chief priests who gathered against the Saviour, and about them he goes on at length. He begins with Jerusalem, saying: “A fair vineyard, a thing desired.” This was the very vineyard of which he spoke earlier: “My beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a fertile place.” Explaining what it might be, he then added: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” So it was once fair and a thing desired, when “his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, and Israel the allotment of his inheritance.” If you cast your mind back to the times when it flourished, under the reign of, say, David or another of the kings attested for their righteousness, you will see how fair it was, so that it could even be called a thing desired. It was adorned with prophets and spiritual men, with priestly dignity and high-priestly honour, and besides these with appearances of angels and with the very visitation of the Lord.

Now the text teaches us to begin a lament over her too, with the city in the vineyard speaking of herself: “I am a fortified city, a city under siege.” And truly she was once a fortified city, when a hedge had been set around her and she had been fenced in so as to be secured on every side. She was so strong that she suffered no harm even when besieged. But though she was once like this, she has now become fruitless and has been abandoned, so that it was said of her: “I will take away its hedge, and it will be plundered; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled; and I will abandon my vineyard, and it will be neither dug nor pruned.” He explains the reason when he says: “For I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” And in the passage before us it is said for the same reason: “In vain shall I water her.” For all the abundant provision made for this city was in vain. Therefore she will be taken by night by those besieging her. Caught in darkness, because she had removed herself far from the light, she became easy prey for her enemies, so that she came to utter ruin, having no wall to fence her in and guard her. For it had been torn down by the one who said: “I will take away its hedge, and it will be plundered; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled.”

Nevertheless, even though she has suffered these things, the prophet, out of his affection for them, goes on to say: “Who will set me to guard stubble in a field?” For even though she bore thorns instead of grapes and became barren ground, so that she had nothing more than stubble, he still longed to guard her even in that state. Symmachus renders it: “Who will make me barren ground, abandoned in war?” The sense is the same in the other versions as well: “I wanted,” he says, “to be the guardian of the field just mentioned, or of the vineyard described, or of the once fortified city. But she became my enemy and made me reject her, so far that I even gave her over to fire after the siege.”

Fittingly, then, the prophecy adds: “‘I am burned up,’ those who dwell in her will cry out.” For the fire of God's judgment will force them to confess even against their will. They, having become enemies of God, met such an end. But let us, who belong to another company, learn wisdom from what they suffered and make peace with him. The prophetic word addresses this counsel and exhortation to those who are his own and belong to his portion: “Therefore let us make peace with him,” it says, “all you who are coming.” And who these are it shows in what follows: “children of Jacob. Israel will bud and blossom, and the world will be filled with his fruit.” Here it plainly hints at the company of the apostles. For the apostles were children of Jacob, since they came from the Jewish nation and sprang from Israel according to the flesh. And they blossomed with a good shoot and a fragrant flower, so as to fill the whole world with their fragrance.

Next it is said: “Shall he be struck as he struck? And as he slew, so shall he be slain?” The meaning of the words is this: Did those who preached peace to the nations repay them evil for evil? The nations persecuted them, beating them and inflicting blows on them, while the apostles proclaimed to them the best of tidings, peace. Did the apostles then do the same to those of the nations who wronged the heralds of peace? No: they were beaten, but they did not strike back; they were killed, but they did not kill in return. Fighting and reviling them, the nations persecuted them and drove them out, but the apostles did not abandon peace or cease to proclaim good things to them. So the text goes on, as though addressing the unbelievers among the nations: “Were you not the one who plotted with a harsh spirit to slay them with a spirit of fury?” For this is what the unbelievers among the nations plotted against the apostles of our Saviour. Gripped by a harsh spirit, they thought of nothing else but how to slay them with the spirit of fury that was in them. But those who sprouted from Jacob and blossomed from Israel suffered all this and bore it nobly for Christ's sake. For this reason he adds: “The iniquity of Jacob will be taken away, and this is his blessing, when they take away his sin.” For these things, he says, will be the cause of the forgiveness of Jacob's sins, and because of them blessing will come upon him as his sin is taken away. For if, as the Apostle says, she “will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith and love and holiness with self-control,” it follows that Jacob too, who sprouted such children and blossomed with such fruit, shares in their blessing through their virtue. The text indicates that through the grace of the apostles many of their kin according to the flesh will also be saved.

And this will happen above all, he says, when the children of Jacob already mentioned, the flower from Israel, have gone all around the world and filled it with their godly teaching, and by his power have overthrown the polytheistic error that had ruled the nations from ages past. Then they will make all the stones of the idolatrous altars like fine dust, crushed to pieces; they will cause the trees and groves in the temples to disappear; and they will lay them so utterly waste that they can be compared to a thicket.

These, then, are the achievements of those already described. But the flock that once dwelt in the land, the people of Israel, “will be left at large like an abandoned flock,” since they would not receive the good shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep. Therefore the land of their soul will be pasture for a long time, so that in them is fulfilled the saying: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has fed on it.” “And there,” it says, “they will lie down,” that is, those who graze on it and ravage it. And it will be turned into such a wilderness that nothing green will remain in it. So it is said: “And there will be nothing green in it.”

He calls on women, since no men worthy of salvation were found among them. So he urges the women to come and hasten to bear witness from the sight of the extraordinary and wonderful works, so that when they come they may enlighten the people sitting in darkness and their abandoned city. So according to Aquila it says: “Women coming enlighten her,” and according to Symmachus: “Women coming and making her known.” And who is “her” but the city mentioned above, of which it was said: “For the fortified city, alone and fair, has been forsaken and abandoned like a wilderness”? These words were fulfilled to the letter and in actual events at the time of our Saviour's resurrection. At that time, according to Matthew, “Many women were there, looking on from a distance, who had followed him from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.” And according to Luke: “The women who had come with him from Galilee followed,” and so on. Since, then, “the people that has no understanding” would not believe the preaching of the apostles, though the nations were receiving the word, the divine Spirit calls the women to bear witness to the word being preached, because it saw that the people were blind. That is why it says: “He who made them will not have compassion on them, nor will he who formed them show them mercy.”

"And it will be in that day," he says, that is, at the time indicated, "the Lord will fence in from the channel of the river." Instead of "will fence in," all the other translators have said "will strike," meaning that the Lord will strike those unbelievers and the people without understanding. Then he marks out the region, saying, "from the stream of the river to the torrent of Egypt," in Symmachus's version, which the others match in sense. I think these words point to the war that came upon the Jews throughout the nation of Palestine after their outrage against Christ. The passage certainly seems to name the very borders of Palestine when it says "from the river," probably meaning the Jordan, "to Rhinocorura." This is a city lying near the frontier between Egypt and Palestine. That is why the other translators have "to the torrent of Egypt": as I said, the passage hints at the war that would be waged against the Jews in the nation of Palestine.

Next he gives a command to the heralds of the word, saying: "But you, gather the children of Israel one by one." For even if the people does not wish to come all together to the saving preaching—since it is a people without understanding—still, gather at least a few of them one by one, the children of Israel. It is something to be glad of if even one at a time, or a second, or some few that can easily be counted, are saved from among them in each city or each nation. So gather these one by one; but for the rest of the nations a great trumpet will sound, as the word cries out so that all people can hear. That is why it says: "And it will be in that day: he will sound the great trumpet, and those who were lost of the people of the Assyrians and those who were lost in Egypt will come, and they will worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem." By the Egyptians he means the idolaters, and by the Assyrians the enemies of Israel, those who had besieged the land of the Jews. When the word has proclaimed to them through the gospel trumpet, which is truly great, the idolaters among the nations and those who were once foes and enemies of Israel's worship of God will change, turn back, and come to God. So those who had long been lost in the error of idolatry will be transformed, and will hasten to come to the knowledge of God's word and obtain the salvation that is through Christ.

He sees in the Spirit the godless assembly of those who gathered together against our Savior. Calling their league for evil and their agreement for evil a "crown of insolence," he cries out: "Woe to the crown of insolence!" He was hinting at the council of the Pharisees, the chief priests, and the other rulers of the Jewish people. Because they came together from different ranks into one body, he compares them to a crown—not a crown of any honor or glory, but of insolence and dishonor. That is why he says, "Woe to the crown of insolence," or, in the other translators, "to the crown of arrogance." They were arrogant men, boastful and reckless, and among them were also "the hired men of Ephraim." Judas the traitor was said to have come from the tribe of Ephraim. He calls him a hired man because he had been bought with money to betray his teacher. He was also "the flower that has fallen from glory": he had shared in the glory of the apostolic company, but by his slide toward the worse he became the flower fallen from glory. A little earlier the apostles of our Savior had been called a flower and a shoot, where it was said: "Children of Jacob—Israel will sprout and blossom, and the world will be filled with his fruit." But the traitor, who fell away from them, is called "the flower that has fallen from glory."

All those mentioned above gathered together "on the top of the fat mountain." This phrase signifies the offspring of those whose souls had grown fat, of whom it was said: "For the heart of this people has grown fat." So the rulers of the people that had grown fat were like the top of the fat mountain, since they were its head; and the flower fallen from glory joined itself to them, which is why it is pitied as wretched. Instead of "on the top of the fat mountain," Aquila translated "of the ravine of filth," Symmachus "of the ravine of fatness," and Theodotion "of the ravine of fat things"; and the Hebrew word contains "Gethsemane." I heard one of our dear friends explain this, saying that it is the place named Gethsemane in the Gospel, where the traitor came upon the Savior with the crown of insolence and carried out his betrayal.

These same men were "drunk without wine," and he goes on to threaten them, saying: "Behold, the wrath of the Lord is strong and harsh, like hail driven down; like a great mass of water sweeping over a country, it will make a resting place on the earth for hands and feet." For in this way, he says, the wrath of the Lord will come upon these very men who are drunk without wine, so that it is compared to hail crashing down on the heads of men who have no shelter. And just as a great flood of water sweeps along until it carves out a channel for itself across the land, so too, he says, will the wrath of God be brought upon those he has described.

Then he adds next: "And the crown of insolence, the hired men of Ephraim, will be trampled underfoot." Formerly they were a crown of insolence, drawn up in battle array to commit outrage, which is why they were also called a crown of arrogance; but in the end such a fate will overtake them that they will be trampled underfoot. And so they were trampled, both by the wrath of God that came upon them and by the enemies who enslaved them. These enemies also made their city a place for themselves to trample, after driving out its former inhabitants.

This, then, concerns the crown of insolence. Next he speaks particularly about the flower that fell from glory: "And the flower of the hope of glory on the summit of the high mountain will be like an early fig; whoever sees it will want to swallow it before he takes it in his hand." Judas was someone of this kind: he had been a flower, but he fell from the hope of God and from glory. Once he was indeed on the high mountain, though not in the same way as those on the top of the fat mountain. For he too was one of those on the high mountain, of whom this same prophet says: "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion." But he became such that he was like the unripened fruit of an early fig, lovely and fine to look at but otherwise useless, because fruit fit for food had not come to maturity in it. So when the one who envies all that is good saw that he had become an early fig, he hurried and snatched him first, so eager was he to swallow him before even taking him in hand. And so, having prevailed, he did swallow him.

So much, then, concerning the crown of insolence and the fallen flower. "But in that day," he says—clearly, at the same time—"the Lord of hosts will be the crown of hope, woven of glory, for the remnant of the people," that is, for those left over from the destruction of the people as a whole. These were the apostles and disciples of the Savior, to whom he promises that the Lord himself will be a crown of hope. Then, since they are said to sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, the Lord himself became for them "a spirit of judgment" as well; and besides this he himself was their strength for receiving at the gate of the church those who were to return from war.

This concerns the apostles. But then the passage turns again to those of the left-hand rank, and adds: "For these have been led astray by wine." Who these are he explains, saying, "priest and prophet." You see who the crown of insolence was: clearly the priests mentioned in the earlier passage and those called their prophets—people who were not prophets but still laid claim to the prophetic office. All these, he says, "went astray through wine, and through strong drink," through gall and bitterness and the rage of dragons. "They went astray through strong drink"—what the other translators called "intoxicant." So that no one would take the wine and intoxicant in the obvious sense, he guarded against this earlier by saying, "those who are drunk without wine." So this wine was something different, and the so-called strong drink or intoxicant by which they were led into error was something else. Then he adds: "This is an apparition." For it truly was an apparition and a phantasm that all of them together should suffer such things and should devise a dreadful and godless counsel—one that the curse from God would overtake. Judas betrayed the Savior for money and out of greed for it. The others, laying claim to the profits they drew from the people, and fearing for their rule lest the word of Christ should somehow overthrow them, contrived the plot against him. That is why it says: "For this counsel they devised for the sake of greed." By "counsel" he means a plot.

Having laid out the prophecy concerning the crown of insolence and what follows it, the passage turns again to the apostolic rank, for whom the Lord of hosts himself was said to be the crown of hope and diadem of glory. It teaches this rank—I mean the apostolic company—to prepare themselves and be ready for the afflictions that would be brought upon them because of the word of Christ. So, as if calling out to them, he says: "To whom have we announced evils, and to whom have we announced a message?" As if he were saying more plainly: "Who, then, is eager to accept the evils that are being announced?" By "evils" he means, in the common way of speaking, hardships and things thought painful—that is, the labors and afflictions endured for the sake of godliness. Who is it, then, to whom we announce these things? Let him hear that we announce to him not only evils—afflictions and labors and things thought painful—but in addition a good message about the prizes that will be awarded to those who have contended well. "Hear, you who have been weaned from milk": for the word is addressed to you, the apostles, and these are the things we announce concerning you. When you were infants, nourished with milk as if at the breast, nothing of this sort was laid on you, because your spiritual age was still immature. You were like that when you were being nursed under the tutor, the law of Moses, with the first elementary lessons of the teaching about the worship of God. But now that you have grown in age, you have been released from the tutor and have come to the perfect teacher, weaned from the milk of the law and drawn away, as from a mother, from the Jewish and bodily worship.

Since you are now partaking of the more perfect food, that of salvation and the gospel, prepare yourselves for afflictions. For those who contend for godliness must expect affliction, and not just this one, but a second one after the first. These words are spoken to the apostolic company and to all who are made disciples by the saving gospel. You must not lose heart at the afflictions, nor despair of your own salvation as though you were to be in affliction forever. For no sooner will the affliction have ceased than the prizes that follow it will succeed it for you, when you have been declared victors and are to be crowned with the crown of hope woven of glory. That is why he brings in hope upon hope, not after a long interval from the affliction, for the time between will be short. That is why he says: "Yet a little, yet a little." For affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope; and hope does not put us to shame.

Your affliction will come "through contempt of lips and through another tongue." Those who afflict you will go on holding you in contempt and mocking you, reviling and blaspheming, using a strange tongue; but you must despise this because of the hope that will succeed it for you in yet a little while. These words, then, are spoken in direct address to the apostles, disciples, and evangelists of our Savior. What follows, however, the passage uses prophetically to teach the Jewish people: the disciples of Christ, having learned these very things about affliction and about the hope that follows affliction, will speak to them to persuade them that herein lies the rest that God has stored up—I mean in being afflicted and enduring everything for the sake of godliness.

And what is thought to be this "rest" and this "ruin" turns to benefit for the one who thirsts and hungers for the worship of God. These men will speak these things to this people—the passage points to the unbelievers of the circumcision—but they will not be willing to hear. Therefore, he says, the oracle of the Lord will be to them, in another way, "affliction upon affliction." For since they were unwilling to be afflicted for Christ's sake, or to walk the narrow and constricted way, but went off along the broad and spacious one, "they will fall backward, and be crushed, and be in danger, and be taken." All these things will come upon them because they were unwilling to accept the oracle of the Lord spoken earlier, and so became the causes of their own fall and ruin.

And since they brought such things upon themselves by not believing the word spoken earlier, he declares to them what follows, saying: "Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you afflicted men and rulers of this people in Jerusalem," or, according to Symmachus, "you scoffing men, who hold authority over this people, who are in Jerusalem." For there were also other scoffers, among the Greeks, who ridiculed the word of Christ. So that no one would suppose these words were spoken about others, he added, precisely and necessarily, "who hold authority over this people." And since there were many leaders of the people outside Jerusalem too, throughout all Judea and Galilee, he indicates precisely to which rulers and authorities over the people these things were said.

These were the crown of insolence mentioned above, and so these words too are still addressed to them: "Because you said, We have made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death"; for "you said, We have made falsehood our hope, and by falsehood we shall be sheltered." Since, then, the scoffers mentioned before thought these things and spoke them to one another—mocking and ridiculing the word of Christ, which taught them that they ought to expect affliction upon affliction and, after it, hope upon hope—they chose instead to make a treaty of friendship with death and to take refuge in Hades. By doing this they expected that they would never experience affliction or fall into anything painful or unpleasant. And even if it should happen that a storm, flooding in from somewhere, from the opposing power, should come on, you supposed it would not reach you, because you were friends of the opposing power and of death itself.

Since, then, you have said these things among yourselves, hear for this reason what the Lord of all has commanded to be said to you: "You did not accept the grace that was proclaimed to you first; but I will set my own costly and precious stone at the head of the corner and make it lofty, conspicuous, and plain for all to see, so that everyone who believes in it may not fall from hope." According to the other translators: "whoever believes will not be in haste"—for the one who believes will be patient, waiting for the promise of the word. This stone would be the same as the rock of which the Savior said: "On this rock I will build my church."

He promises to lay this stone in the foundations of Zion. And he did this in deed when he said, and fulfilled, "On this rock I will build my church." For we have often taken Mount Zion to mean the preaching of the gospel and the church founded upon it. He promises to lay this stone, costly, chosen, and precious, in the foundations of the church. Hence it is called a corner stone and a chief cornerstone. This name would refer to the human body of our Savior, since in Daniel too a stone was seen cut out without hands: the stone being understood as the human body, and the mountain as the Godhead of the Savior.

"And on this stone," he says, "I will lay judgment for hope." For when this stone judges, it will offer good hopes to those being judged, since mercy is joined with it together with the most just weight and measure. That is why it says: "And my mercy will be for weights." These things are said about the stone. But to those who said above, "We have made falsehood our hope, and by falsehood we shall be sheltered," he adds what follows: "And you who trust in vain in falsehood: for the storm shall not pass you by—will it not also take away your covenant of death?" "Do not deceive yourselves," he says, "by saying: Since we have made friends with death, no storm will come upon us, nor shall we experience anything painful.
