From this, now, hear and learn, you who trust in falsehood and have said, 'We have made falsehood our hope, and by falsehood we shall be sheltered,' that the storm, as it passes, will not pass you by, but will take away your agreement with death, and your hope in Hades will not remain. For you entrusted yourselves to a rotten thing when you hung your hopes on death and Hades. Therefore, if the rushing storm comes upon you, you will be trampled down by it."

"And even if it is about to pass by and go away, it will drag you far off and carry you along with it. This will not be long in coming for you, but 'early in the morning'—that is, it will come upon you swiftly, as soon as God's visitation begins to look upon you. By day and by night it will come upon you, and this will be the end of the hope you sketched out for yourselves when you handed yourselves over to death and Hades."

"Even if you lend your ears unwillingly to such words, still, though you are hard-pressed, listen to what awaits you, and do not say, 'We cannot fight for the truth, and we ourselves are too weak for you to be gathered.' For if you were willing, you too would be gathered into God's portion, and you would not grow weak in contending for godliness. But since you have willingly allotted yourselves to death and Hades, know that the Lord himself will soon come upon you, bringing wrath against you for all the things spoken of above."

The wrath of God will press upon you like some very high and very heavy mountain against the ungodly. Symmachus says: "As on the mountain of breaches, so will the Lord stand"; and instead of "and he will be in the ravine of Gibeon," the same translator says, "in the valley at Gibeon." The story is told in the book of Joshua son of Nun, the successor of Moses, where Joshua, fighting against the foreigners, prayed, saying: "Let the sun stand still at Gibeon and the moon at the valley of Elom." Then the sun stood still at Gibeon and the moon at the valley of Elom; then the sun stood still for the space of a whole day, until all the foreigners had perished. So just as was once done against the ungodly on the mountain of breaches, in the valley of Gibeon, so now too the Lord will rise up against those accused here and will do his works with wrath—works of bitterness for those who needed them, as one needs a bitter antidote, because of the wickedness lying in their souls. The Lord's wrath will treat them as strangers, and his bitterness will be shown not according to his own sweetness, kindness, and goodness, but according to the punishment fitting for them. When bitterness, anger, wrath, and similar things are said of God, they customarily signify nothing other than the punishments of the ungodly that will come upon them from the divine court of judgment.

"Since, then," he says, "such things await you who refuse to accept the precious and costly stone, for this reason do not rejoice with an evil rejoicing, and do not let your bonds grow strong—the bonds with which you bound yourselves when you made a covenant with death and agreements with Hades. Rather, if you have any hope of salvation, break your bonds with death, withdraw from what you take to be rejoicing, and stop your passing pleasure, for you have learned what its end will be. Do not think that it is I, the prophet, who am saying these things. What I heard with the hearing of my soul, spoken by the Lord of hosts, I have passed on to you. For he willed that you should not be ignorant of the matters that he has judged, determined, and set in order. For even if the judgment that awaits human beings has not yet come upon them, it has already been determined and decided by him; and having heard these things, I have testified them to you as well."

The passage still addresses these words to the crown of insolence already identified, urging those who rejected the chosen and precious cornerstone first to give ear, and then to listen and obey what is being said. It teaches them that punishment will pursue them as they deserve, for "the mighty will be mightily tested." The weak and lowly man may obtain pardon, or will undergo a punishment suited to the measure of his lowliness; but the one who has had great power will, by the rule of justice, be mightily tested. So it teaches that the rulers of the people, the priests, and the leaders will themselves undergo punishment according to the greatness of the office entrusted to them.

Then he uses an illustration from nature. In farming the land, the time for plowing is one thing and the time for sowing is another, and the seeds sown must suit the soil beneath. In one field the farmer will sometimes put black cumin, in another cumin, in another wheat, in yet another barley and millet, and in others again spelt. Then, when the crop of all of these has ripened, at harvest time he gathers each kind separately and cleans it apart from the others, and he does not use the same method for cleaning them all. He does not use the cart, with its iron wheels made like saws, on cumin or black cumin as he does on wheat, barley and spelt. Nor, on the other hand, does he clean wheat by beating it with a rod, for it is not its nature to be cleaned in that way, as black cumin and cumin are. For the weaker seeds he takes the rod, and he cleans cumin and black cumin by beating them with it. But on wheat and barley and the grains like them he brings the cart's wheels, which are iron and sharp and strong enough to cut and strip away whatever is superfluous from the wheat. In the same way the farmer of souls, the Word of God, wishes at the fitting time to break up people's souls like fallow ground, by rational teaching that splits open and cuts through the thoughts hidden in the depths with the plow of the word. That is why he commands, saying: "Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns."

When the surface of the soul, so to speak, has been leveled, and all the wickedness that once grew in it like thorns has been cleared away, then the seeds are cast in, matched to the differences among those who receive the sowing. To some are given weaker and smaller seeds, comparable to black cumin and cumin; to others more valuable and necessary ones, likened to wheat and barley, millet and spelt, because of the great and varied power that is in these too. For there are varieties of gifts and varieties of workings; to one these things are given through the Spirit, to another other things, and to yet another what suits him. And when the time of harvest arrives (and the Savior taught that the harvest is the end of the age), then each will be required to render fruit in proportion to the seeds he has received. Those who received modest gifts but did not use them fittingly will undergo a milder discipline and punishment, like being beaten with a rod. But those who were counted worthy of greater seeds and more perfect gifts, yet rendered no fruit worthy of the power granted them, will be handed over to the greater fiery blasts of punishment.

So it is with you to whom this word is addressed. You were appointed rulers and leaders of the people; you were its teachers and priests; you received such glory and honor from God. Yet you have become a crown of pride and the hirelings of Ephraim, and you have dared such things as to pervert the people and to reject the precious, chosen cornerstone. Therefore those among you whose power was more modest will meet a more modest judgment, while on those who had great and abundant power the heavier penalty will be laid. The words "and his God will instruct him for judgment" (according to Symmachus), or according to the Seventy, "and you will be instructed by the judgment of God," teach that the farmer uses right judgment, following natural reasoning, from a kind of natural instruction provided by God, as it were, to all people. So he does not approach the cleaning of all seeds in the same way, but cleans some with a rod and others by harsh treatment, bringing the cart's wheel upon them. The one occupied with farming did not learn these things from human lessons but from God's instruction, since God instructed him and taught him to use this judgment.

"Bread will be finely crushed," according to Aquila, is said instead of "will be eaten with bread." In place of "will be eaten," Aquila said "will be finely crushed," and Symmachus and Theodotion "will be ground fine." "But he will not thresh it to the end," he says, "nor will the wheel of his cart disturb it, nor will he grind it fine with its hooves." For, he says, when the cart's wheel goes round over the wheat, it grinds fine the straw around it and threshes it with the wheels themselves, and the oxen's hooves reduce the straw to fine chaff, but it does not destroy the wheat as well. By this he shows that the substance of the soul is not obliterated or utterly destroyed in the punishments brought upon it. Understanding this, the Seventy rendered it in this way: "For I will not be angry with you forever, nor will the voice of my bitterness trample you." For I do not, he says, so punish the ungodly as to obliterate their substance and destroy their souls completely, since, according to the illustration, the cart's iron wheels do not destroy the wheat either, but strip away all the straw around it in order to preserve the wheat and make it clean.

All these things, he says, which seem like portents to those who do not understand, do not suppose a human being has spoken. For the decree has come forth from the Lord of hosts; take counsel concerning it, you ungodly, to whom these things are spoken. And if you are able, raise up for yourselves some vain comfort and consolation to set against it.

The children of the Jews themselves agree that the Ariel lamented in the present passage is Jerusalem. But they say that, properly speaking, it was the altar standing before the temple that was named Ariel, and that this is clear from Ezekiel, where near the end, in the description of the city, it is said: "And these are the measurements of the altar in cubits, a cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth: the hollow, a cubit deep." And next he adds: "And the Ariel was four cubits, and from the Ariel and up to the top of the horns a cubit. And the Ariel was twelve cubits long and twelve cubits wide, square on its four sides." They say that Ariel means "lion of God," and that it received this name because the altar belonged to God and devoured all the animal sacrifices offered on it.

They say that the words "the city that David fought against" do not appear in the Hebrew. Instead, Aquila has "the little town of David's encampment," and Symmachus "the city of David's encampment." For the city formerly belonged to foreigners, and David brought it under his control by driving the foreigners out of it; so we can apply the same sense to the Seventy as well. It would then mean, "the city that David fought against when it was under foreigners." It can also mean "the city on account of which" or "on behalf of which David fought." The present passage, then, cries out concerning Jerusalem, and fittingly so. After what was said earlier about its rulers, by which their crown of pride was exposed, the prophecy now turns to the city itself and to what it was going to suffer because of the lawless deeds of those just mentioned. So the passage says to its inhabitants: While there is still time, O you, gather produce for yourselves, since you have been granted a respite of one year, and let it be a second year as well; for very soon you will be deprived of rational food. So, while there is still time, use these years for the benefit of your souls. And I think that by these words he is hinting at the time of the saving proclamation, when the Christ of God came among them and proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense. Perhaps he can also be seen to have conversed with them for a second year, or even a third. It is that very time, when he was imparting to them the teachings about the kingdom of heaven, that he signifies when he says: "Gather produce year upon year; you will eat." For the words "for you will eat with Moab" are not contained in the Hebrew text at all; that is why they are not found in the other translators either, and in any case the context of the thought shows them to be superfluous. At any rate, he says, there is still time: "Gather produce year upon year; you will eat."

For after what is about to happen, he will no longer allow you to gather produce so as to feed yourselves in security and peace: "For I will afflict Ariel," that is, Jerusalem. In place of "and her strength and her wealth will be mine," Symmachus has, "and she will be in pain and anguish, and she will be to me like Ariel"; and Aquila similarly, "and Ariel will be grieved and grieving." But since in the prophecy concerning Moab a certain city of the Moabites was called Ariel, about which it was said, "And I will take away the seed of Moab and Ariel," it is fitting that he also says of Jerusalem that she will be to me like that Ariel of the foreigners.

Then it goes on: "And I will encircle you like David." For just as David once surrounded you, Jerusalem, with an encampment when you were a city of foreigners, so I too, the Lord who speaks these words, will now encircle you, as David did then, "and I will set up a palisade around you." For now too you have become a dwelling of foreigners, filled with wicked rulers and with the crown of pride. These things were fulfilled in consequence of what the inhabitants of Jerusalem dared to do against our Savior. To them the Savior himself, weeping once over Jerusalem, is recorded as saying: "If you, even you, had known the things that make for your peace! For days will come upon you when your enemies will set up a palisade against you and surround you, and you will be dashed to the ground."

To this he adds: "And the wealth of the ungodly in her will be like dust from a wheel and like chaff blown away, and all this will happen in an instant of time, and it will be like an instant, suddenly, from the Lord of hosts." For it will not come from human beings, he says, but from God himself; the visitation upon them will come "with thunder and earthquake and a great voice, a sweeping storm and a devouring flame of fire." By these words he hinted that the city would also be burned with fire, when thunder, earthquake and storm were brought against it from God above. So much concerning Jerusalem.

Having dealt with this, the passage next prophesies about those who besieged the city: "And the wealth of those who marched against Mount Zion will be like one who dreams in his sleep." By this he hinted at the enjoyment of luxury in this life by the Roman rulers, for they were the ones who brought the final siege upon Jerusalem. It was necessary for us to learn something about them too, and to be taught what their end would be. So he says that their wealth and luxury, which lasts only as long as the present life, is like people dreaming in their sleep, who only seem to possess what they imagine they have; for such, he says, is the illusion of present wealth. After the present life, both the dream and the end of the luxury they thought they were enjoying will prove empty for them.

In place of "Faint and be astonished," and what follows, Symmachus translated thus: "Be utterly amazed and marvel; be deceived and be drunk without wine; stagger without strong drink. For the Lord has mixed against you a spirit of torpor, and has held fast your eyes, and has covered your prophets and your rulers, the seers." Having completed the prophecy about the crown of pride and about the siege of Jerusalem in the preceding verses, the passage next prophesies about those who would afterward seem to lead the people of the circumcision. They will recite the prophetic writings, it says, but not understand them; they will be no different from writings sealed with seals, so that none of the Jewish people can make out what is written in them. So the prophetic words will be unknown to them, whether they recite them by heart or are wholly unacquainted with them. As he is about to prophesy this, the passage cries out to them: Even if what is about to be said causes you the utmost faintness and astonishment of soul, it will be said nonetheless; so faint and be astonished, if you wish. And if, deceiving yourselves in any case, you would also twist the meaning of what is said, then be deceived and deceive yourselves, if that is what you love. In place of "be drunken," all the other translators said "be drunk without wine, and stagger without strong drink." For there is also a drunkenness that comes from deception, worse than the drunkenness that comes from wine. So if you delight in deceiving yourselves and in being drunk, so as to see one thing in place of another in the divine oracles and to misinterpret them yourselves, you would know [?]. For the Lord himself has handed you over to a spirit of stupor, or of torpor according to Symmachus.

Then he adds: "And he will close their eyes, and those of their prophets and their rulers." For when the Lord was present among them in human form, though they heard him with their ears they did not understand, and though they looked at him with their eyes they did not see with the sight of the soul; instead they closed their eyes so as not to see, and made their ears heavy so as not to hear. Since, then, they were the first to close their own eyes, for this reason the Lord too will do the same to them, and to their prophets (that is, their teachers) and their rulers, who professed to behold hidden things and to be the only ones able to discern and interpret the secret sense concealed in the sacred writings.

He will so restrain their eyes from seeing that the words, not only of the other divine Scriptures but also of the very book in hand, the prophecy of Isaiah, will be like a sealed book that does not permit anyone to know what is written in it, whether he is literate or illiterate. The one skilled in reading will be unable to make out its contents because the book has been sealed, while the other, being wholly unlettered, would be unable to do so even if the book had not been sealed. Yet the prophetic meaning will be like this not for all people, but only for those to whom these things were prophesied.

Pay careful attention to how it is put: "And these words will be to you"—to you, he means, who are present and see and hear. The word was addressed to the Jews, to whom he says the meaning of the prophecy will be unknown; to whom it will be known he will teach further on, where he adds: "And on that day the deaf will hear the words of a book, and the eyes of the blind will see, and they will rejoice." By the preceding words, then, the passage prophesies that those of the Jewish people who [?] learned the laws accurately and carry the divine readings in their memory by mouth, and those who are not such, will alike be ignorant of the meaning of the prophetic oracles.

God says that these things will happen to them, and he adds the reason. They pretended to honor God as far as mouth and lips, but their minds belied their profession: they made a show of worshiping him, while preferring to his words certain teachings and traditions of men, which they cherish, taking pride in holding to the secondary traditions of certain elders. For this reason, he says, the understanding of the divine Scriptures will be shut off from them. And all their people, he says, will be removed from the honor they had with me, so that they will no longer be the Lord's portion, nor Israel the allotted measure of his inheritance. And since they put forward the wisdom of men, turning away from my wisdom and my word and holding to certain other traditions of their elders as though those elders were wise men, for this reason they will not understand my Scriptures. "And I myself will destroy the wisdom of their wise, and set aside the understanding of the understanding among them."

Then, since they professed piety with their lips while in secret they did the worst things, steeping themselves in sorceries and impurities and countless other lawless deeds, and undertook all these as though God were not watching, he rightly laments over them, saying next: "Woe to those who make counsel deeply, and not through the Lord." Symmachus translated this: "Woe to those who go deep to hide counsel from the Lord, whose works were done in darkness, and they said, Who sees us, and who knows us in our perversity?"

Then he adds: "Will you not be counted as the potter's clay?" For if all of us human beings are like the potter's clay because of our body of clay, how does it not follow that the maker cannot fail to know what kind of workmanship the thing he has made is? And who can say, or who will dare to say, that God did not form him? If the clay that lies under the potter's hand would never say such things about the potter, it is clear that all are foolish who devise deep counsel within their souls and imagine that God does not know the deeds they do in darkness.

Nevertheless, because of these things, he says, in a little while Lebanon too, which is foreign and lies in the land of the nations, will be transferred to the land of the Jews, where Mount Carmel is, which in Hebrew is called Chermel. Lebanon will undergo a change for the better, but Carmel itself will undergo a change for the worse: what was once full of cultivated plants and good fruits will be counted as a forest. For Carmel, called Chermel, will be like a forest of wild and fruitless trees, while the foreigners' Lebanon, once transferred, will become what Carmel was in ancient times. By these things the passage hints that Lebanon is the people from the nations and Carmel the Jewish nation: the latter will become like a forest of wild and fruitless trees, while Lebanon, the people from the nations, which was once like a forest, will become what the Jewish people once was, filled with good trees and every kind of plant and fruit.

Then, when this change takes place, "on that day"—that is, at the same time—those who were once deaf will hear the words of the book. Which book, if not this very book in hand, of which it was said above, "And these words will be to you like the words of the sealed book"? But to Carmel, once fruitful but changed into a forest, the words of the book of the prophecy will be sealed, whereas to those once blind and counted as the forest of Lebanon, now changed to a cultivated and fruitful state, the words of the divine writings will become audible. And those who were once in darkness and gloom, so that they could neither see nor understand nor perceive because their eyes were blind, will be granted a marvelous change and will become beholders of the mysteries stored up in the divine writings. That is why it is said: "The eyes of the blind will see." "And they will rejoice"—those who were once poor through lack of every good thing; for they will be filled with the gladness that is with the Lord, even those who previously had no hope of salvation. For who ever imagined that people who were idolaters from their fathers' time, godless and impious and estranged from the knowledge of God, would come to such a hope? Nevertheless, he says, even the despairing among humankind will be filled with gladness.

And all these will enjoy these things because the one who formerly held sway and tyrannized over them, a lawless and ungodly ruler—I mean the devil himself—has failed and perished, driven far away: the arrogant one who once enslaved them. Moreover, those who acted impiously under him in their wickedness have been utterly destroyed, namely the evil demons, who make people sin in word. That is why it is said somewhere: "They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and abhorred a holy word." These same people were vainly turning aside the righteous one; for they turned aside the righteous word and the Righteous One, the Christ of God, and shook him off, though they had no charge to bring against him, acting vainly and unjustly in doing so. For the prophets who reproved them to their faces and turned them back from their sins they ensnared, hunting for grounds against them so that they might destroy them.

It is the custom of Scripture often to use the future tense in place of the past, as in "They will pass through the river on foot," found in the sixty-fifth Psalm, in place of "they passed through." So here too, following "the lawless one has failed," it would have been consistent to say, with the verb understood in common, "and all who set a stumbling block for those who reprove in the gates have failed"; but by scriptural custom he used the future tense.

The prophetic word is still directed to the same people. And since you have become such, he says, therefore the Lord of all says this to you—I mean to you who are called the house of Jacob, which God himself separated and estranged from that blessed friend of God because they did not prove worthy of Abraham by their works. For the children of Abraham are recognized by their works, as the Savior taught when he said: "If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham." According to Symmachus: "Thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham"—but did not redeem these, to whom the word was directed. That is why he says this to them: It has been said about you that you will not understand the words of this book; and it has also been said about the nations, once blind and unbelieving, that they will understand the words of the sacred, divinely inspired Scriptures, will behold the meaning of the divine oracles with the eyes of the soul, will receive the knowledge of God, and, though once without hope, will share in the gladness that is with him. But now, when these things are being prophesied, you have no perception of what is said. That is why you are not ashamed now, nor do you take notice of the threats made against you, nor does your face change as you hear these things at present. But a time will come when you will be ashamed and confounded, and you will change your face from this shameless and brazen stance.

What would this time be, the time when my words are fulfilled, in which your children will see foreigners, people alien to your race, glorifying and sanctifying my name? For then your own children will be put to shame and confounded when they see the astonishing change of the nations: men of another race sanctifying the Holy One of Jacob and the God of Israel; those who had wandered astray for a long age taking up the fear of the God who is over all; those very people who were long ago found in error coming to understanding; and those who murmured against providence and accused it learning to obey and to heed my commands. And the stammering tongues, which could say nothing clear or true, will return to their natural state and speak most clearly, having learned to speak words of peace, as tongues freed from all war that have made peace with God.

In place of "Not now shall Jacob be ashamed, nor now shall he change his face" and what follows, Symmachus translated thus: "Not now shall Jacob be ashamed, nor now shall his face be confounded; but when he sees his children, the works of my hands, in his midst sanctifying my name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and hold the God of Israel mighty, and those who have strayed in spirit will know understanding, and murmurers will learn instruction." Here the end is marked of the prophecy that began against the crown of pride, after the threats against the dragon and the crooked serpent. What follows these earlier words must be read as starting from a new beginning.

Having completed the threats against the crown of pride and everything added after them, the text passes on to another subject. It prophesies, as the children of the Hebrews say, the events of the times of Jeremiah the prophet. At that time, after the Babylonians had taken Jerusalem and led the people away captive, those left behind in the land of Judea, among whom were the prophet Jeremiah, Baruch and some others, took flight for fear of the Babylonians, preferring to hand themselves over to the Egyptians rather than to serve the Babylonians. These things are recounted in the prophecy of Jeremiah. The prophet Isaiah anticipates them, having lived nearly a full hundred and fifty years before Jeremiah. At any rate, he writes about those very people who did not obey the voice of God, which through Jeremiah forbade them to enter Egypt, saying: "Woe, rebellious children" (or "transgressors," according to Symmachus), "says the Lord. You have made a plan, but not through me, and covenants, but not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sins, you who set out to go down to Egypt but did not ask me, in order to be helped by Pharaoh," and what is said after these words. Among these he also teaches this: "that there were in Tanis chieftains, evil angels." He clearly shows that there were demons among the Egyptians at that time, calling them evil angels, and that they were especially active in the Egyptian city called Tanis, where Pharaoh's palace was established at that time. All the native Egyptians who reigned over their country were called Pharaoh, though they also had their own personal names, so that one of them, for instance, was Necho, while also being called Pharaoh.

The Psalter mentions Tanis, since the wonders done through Moses in the land of Egypt took place in the plain of Tanis. And in the prophecy concerning Egypt this same prophet taught, saying: "Where now are your wise men? Let them declare to you and tell you what the Lord of hosts has planned against Egypt. The rulers of Tanis have failed." But there, since he was prophesying the coming of the Lord into Egypt, he accordingly announced the failing of the rulers of Tanis, which was fulfilled when our Savior appeared among men. In the present passage, however, the text, signifying the events of Jeremiah's times, does not say that the rulers of Tanis have failed, but that there were then in Tanis chieftains, evil angels, the same as the rulers of Tanis mentioned above. Yet even these chieftains in Tanis, he says, these evil angels, will be of no use in defending those who fled to them and called on them for help; and besides being of no use to them, they will become a shame and a reproach to them. This was fulfilled for them at the time when the king of the Babylonians, having subjected Egypt, enslaved by the law of war not only the Egyptians but also those of the Jews who had taken refuge with them. For then the Jews' hope in Pharaoh was turned into shame and reproach for them. It should be noted that Origen's thirtieth volume of commentary on the prophet extended as far as this point.

Next after these comes: "The vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert. In affliction and distress, the lion and the lion's cub from there, and asps and the offspring of flying asps." I think that by these the text alludes to the gods of the Egyptians, for among them nearly every kind of four-footed animal was regarded as a god. In place of "The vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert," Symmachus says "oracle of the beasts of the south," and all the other translators likewise rendered "of the beasts of the south." So the Seventy called the land of the Egyptians, which lies in the southern region, a desert when they said, "The vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert," because at that time it was entirely deserted by God and filled with the four-footed beasts deified among them and with the demons at work among them. That is why they were also said to be in affliction and distress: in great distress of soul and in extreme affliction they proclaimed as their gods those very wicked demons who afflicted and distressed their souls. Among these were lions and asps and their offspring, serpents, and countless other reptiles and beasts, whose images were the visible animals deified throughout all Egypt. For they have honored as gods actual lions, asps, serpents and countless others. Indeed, they have even named their cities after their supposed gods: Leonto after the lion, Cyno after the dog, and yet another city after yet another beast. This, then, is the vision of the four-footed beasts in the Egyptian wilderness which the prophet beheld; and it was to these that the Jewish refugees carried off their wealth, for they handed over the storehouses of their own souls to the Egyptian error. They are said to carry their wealth on donkeys and camels, which in some way indicates their irrationality and folly. And they went off to a nation that will not profit them, for neither the visible Egyptians nor their supposed gods were going to help the people of the Jews who had fled to them.

As for what the prophecy announces next, since it is clearer, I think it superfluous to try to interpret it at greater length, since [?] they contradicted him, saying that he was lying when, speaking in the person of God, he urged them not to go into Egypt. For this reason the present prophecy says: "who would not hear the law of God, saying to the prophets, 'Do not announce things to us,' and to those who see visions, 'Do not speak to us.'" According to Symmachus it reads: "and to the seers, 'Do not see right things for us; speak smooth things to us, see delusions for us; turn aside from the way, turn the path away from me, make the Holy One of Israel cease from before us.'" For those who did not believe the words of Isaiah said these things to him and to those who thought as he did.

Therefore he threatens them with what follows, and then exhorts them, saying: "When you turn back and groan, then you will be saved"; and according to Symmachus: "In repentance," he says, "and in rest you will be saved, and your strength will be in hope." For if, he says, you remain in the place of Jerusalem, having repented and given up your rush toward Egypt, then you will be saved, living in quiet and rest; and your strength, he says, will be in hope, for by believing and hoping in God you will be able to be saved. But they would not listen, he says, but said: "We will flee on horses." That is why he threatens them with what follows, saying: You will flee, yes, but you will not be able to escape the hand of the Babylonians, which will overtake you even in Egypt.

He says that they will flee so far that they will be left "like a mast on a mountain and like a signal on a hill," or according to Symmachus, "like a mast on a mountaintop and like sails on a hill." For just as, when a ship has been wrecked and lost at sea, a mast set up on a mountaintop is a sign that it is no longer needed, so the destruction of those he is speaking of will become conspicuous.

Yet he says that not all will perish entirely, but a few will be left, whom God, having mercy on them and taking pity on them, will save, being glorified and exalted by his mercy toward them. For he is a just judge in this way: he punishes those who deserve punishment, and counts worthy of his salvation those who are able to obtain mercy. Therefore "blessed are all who abide in him," or, according to Symmachus, "who wait for him." For it is good not to lose heart nor to despair of God's help in the misfortunes that overtake us.

Quite consistently, having spoken in the foregoing of what happened in the time of Jeremiah the prophet, the text prophesies the people's return from captivity: how, once they had returned, they would raise up the temple in Jerusalem and inhabit the city again, so that it was filled with inhabitants, and the whole land was farmed by Jews living in great and most profound peace. This was fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, under whom the temple was rebuilt while Haggai and Zechariah were prophesying; after them Ezra returned from Babylonia, and likewise Nehemiah after him, and they accomplished great things toward the completion of the city; and after them both the city and its temple remained free from siege for many years. These very things, then, the text foretells in the present words, saying: "And again God will wait to have compassion on you, and for this reason God will be exalted to have mercy on you." And it adds next: "for the Lord God is a judge." Being a just judge, he handed over to captivity those who deserved it, but saved those whom it was just to pity. Hence it is blessed to abide in him, or, according to Symmachus, to wait for him. As a just judge, then, and as one who is good, he will have compassion again, so that Zion and Jerusalem are built a second time and a people dwells in it once more. By "the glory of Israel" he means God, the Savior of all.

Since it is written, "for a holy people will dwell in Zion," one must be aware that neither the Hebrew wording nor the other translators include the word "holy"; rather, according to Symmachus, "a people," he says, "will dwell in Zion." This indeed happened, but the whole people that afterward inhabited Jerusalem was by no means holy. "With weeping," he says, "she did not weep, 'Have mercy on me'"; for this is what the Hebrew wording contains. That is why Symmachus renders: "In Jerusalem you will not weep with weeping," and likewise Theodotion: "In Jerusalem there will be no weeping with weeping." For there was no longer a time for weeping for those who, through the mercy of God, had recovered their ancestral soil and were rejoicing and glad over it, as it is said: "Coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves." And the cause of this for them was that they had obtained the mercy of God. In place of "When he saw the voice of your cry, he heard you," Symmachus says: "At the voice of your shout, as soon as it is heard, he will hear you." This is like the saying "Let it be done to you according to your faith," which the Savior used to say. For now, he says, she did not weep, but at another time she does so. Nevertheless the text exhorts her to cry out to God always, for at your voice, he says, God will answer you. According to the Seventy it reads: "And Jerusalem wept with weeping, 'Have mercy on me.'" For in a sense the very soil cried out to God over the wickedness of its inhabitants; and moreover the strong wept for the weak, and the better for the worse. That is why it goes on to say: "When he saw the voice of your cry, he heard you."

"For the present," he says, "the Lord will give you bread of affliction and scant water." But after this it goes on to say: "The bread of the produce of your land will be abundant and rich," and: "Then there will be rain for the seed of your land." By these words he teaches that at the beginning of the return those who came back from the enemy's land suffered much affliction, as the surrounding peoples oppressed them, so that the work of building the temple was even halted; this, indeed, is what the history in the book of Ezra teaches. That is why it is said that the Lord will give you bread of affliction and scant water. "And no longer," he says, "will those who lead you astray come near; for your eyes will see those who lead you astray." Therefore they will no longer lead you astray; for even if some should try to do this, your eyes will see them, and having seen them and understood, you will not be led astray. And again, if others should try with deceitful words to speak perversities to you, your ears will not accept their words either, even if they deceitfully say, "This is the way, let us walk in it, whether to the right or to the left"; for you will not be persuaded when they say this, but you will go by the royal road, walking the middle way and turning aside neither to the right nor to the left.

Therefore, as one no longer led astray, you will defile the idols; that is, you will regard them as defiled and unclean, turning away from them as from stinking dung and shameful filth. And when you do this, then the Lord will still [?] give you bread of affliction and scant water. Then there will be rain for the seed of your land, and the bread of your produce will be abundant and rich. Everything will be fulfilled for you as you spend your life in great prosperity and most profound peace, so that even your animals, especially those that work the land, will be filled with their natural food. And these things too were fulfilled after the restoration of Jerusalem in the times that followed, when both those who lived on the farms in the countryside and those who lived in the cities rested in peace.

These things, then, may be referred to the times we have indicated. But what follows, where it is said, "And on every high mountain and on every lofty hill there will be water running through," compels even the unwilling to hasten to a figurative interpretation. For what sense does the next passage have: "In that day, when many perish and when towers fall, the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, in the day when the Lord heals the brokenness of his people, and he will heal the pain of your wound"? What logical connection could these words keep with what was said before them? I say, then, that it is necessary to consider that these too were added consistently with what was said before. For since the text has made bodily promises, saying, "and the bread of your produce will be abundant and rich; and in that day your cattle will graze in a rich and spacious place; your bulls and the oxen that work the land will eat mixed chaff with winnowed barley," it fittingly adds to the bodily promises the more divine ones as well, for those worthy of them.

These are what is signified by: "And on every high mountain and on every lofty hill there will be water running through." And when this will be, he shows by indicating the time, adding: "in that day, when many perish and when towers fall," or according to Symmachus, "in the day of great slaughter, when the great fall." And when will the great slaughter be, and when will the great fall, if not at the time of the universal judgment that will take place after the consummation of this age? That is why the Seventy say: "when towers fall and when many perish"; for many will perish at that time, the time in which the promised rewards will also be given to the worthy. What, then, does he teach by saying that on every high mountain there will be water running through, and that the moonlight will be multiplied for them, and the sunlight likewise will then become sevenfold? Many great lights, then, and divisions of waters (for so Symmachus translated, saying, "and on every raised hill, divisions of channels of water") will be given to those worthy of the promises at that time when those who deserve slaughter will be handed over to slaughter, and those who in the present life are exalted and boastful fall from their own height. That is why Aquila renders: "in the day of much killing, when those who are magnified fall."

You see the coherence of the text: to those in the multitude who are more bodily it makes bodily promises, but to those who have risen higher in mind and are set apart in soul it pledges loftier promises. Just as we have often understood Zion as the heavenly mountain, so the many dwelling places with the Father are heavenly mountains, where those worthy of the kingdom of God will dwell. On each of these mountains or dwelling places, he says, there will be water running through, surely that which springs from the fountain of which it is said, "For with you is the fountain of life," from which the river of God also pours forth, of which it is said, "The streams of the river gladden the city of God," and, "The river of God is filled with water"—by which the only-begotten Word of God, life-giving and saving, is in some way indicated. So, then, on every high mountain and on every lofty hill the water that produces immortal and eternal life will run through and make immortal those who drink from it, at the time when creation itself, set free from the bondage of corruption, will receive the rewards of its labors. That is why the moon and the sun too will enjoy greater glory, since they have toiled in the present age and served the will of God. And these things, he says, will come about "when the Lord heals the brokenness of his people, and heals the pain of your wound."

Here he mentions neither Israel nor Jacob nor the Jews at all, but "his people," so that all who are worthy are called the people of God, the promise being extended to all. I think the holy Apostle drew on this when he said: "For the eager expectation of creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God, because creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God." You see that the Apostle speaks of the freedom of the children of God, which the prophet called the healing of his people. So creation too will be set free together with his people, for this happens at the same time, in that very day, that is, at that very season, when the Lord heals the brokenness of his people. Then the sun and the moon will surpass themselves, receiving manifold light and greater glory. That is why it is said: "because creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God." These children of God and his people had much brokenness and pain while they lived this mortal life; for they were in pain and broken, so that it is said, "A broken and humbled heart God will not despise," and, "A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit." These same people lamented their sojourn on earth and mourned those who did deeds worthy of mourning, as the Apostle teaches, saying, "We who are in this tent groan, being burdened," and, "I will mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented." God will heal the brokenness and pain of these very people, restoring them when he grants what was promised. And this is what the Savior also showed when he said: "Blessed are those who weep, and blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted."

In the time of Jeremiah the prophet some people fled to Egypt, against God's command. The word first threatened them with what would overtake them in Egypt itself. Then, in the prophecy addressed to the same people, it declared that they must not despair of Jerusalem's restoration. Those who had been driven out of the city would come back from the enemy's land and live in it again, and would farm the whole land of Judea in peace and without fear. Then to these promises, which were spoken in a more bodily sense, it added the heavenly promises, which will be given to the worthy after the end of the world. At that time the ungodly too will be handed over to destruction and ruin. After prophesying these things, the word adds the present passage, which concerns God's universal judgment. So it says: "Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time." Where this has "after a long time," the other translators said "from afar." Notice that it does not say the Lord himself comes, but "the name of the Lord." In this way it hints at the Christ of God, of whom it is said: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has appeared to us." When he comes and makes his second and glorious coming, punishing powers will follow him. Through them the punishments will be brought on the ungodly, and the present scripture calls these powers wrath and anger. For "burning wrath, with glory" and what follows, Symmachus translated as follows: "His wrath blazing and heavy to bear; his lips like a flooding torrent reaching up to the neck, to separate nations with a separation of vanity." According to the Seventy, a burning wrath, that is, an opposing power, will follow the glory of the Lord. Yet it will do nothing without the judge's command. That is why it adds: "the full sentence of the lips, the full measure of wrath." The works of wrath will be brought on those who are to be punished in accordance with the verdict of the oracle.

And his spirit, sent against the ungodly, will come sweeping like floodwater in a ravine, sweeping away those who undergo punishment up to the neck. This punishing spirit will be split into many divisions, because those who are punished differ so greatly from one another. So it will trouble the nations for the things in which they went astray in vain, and for which error pursued them in their former life.

Having said this, the word turns what follows against those who pretend to be godly but have wasted their lives in luxury and pleasure. It says: "You must not always be making merry and entering my holy places all the time as though keeping a feast, and going up with the flute as though rejoicing to the mountain of the Lord, to the God of Israel."

Having said this to those who pretend to be godly with hypocrisy, it goes on: "And the Lord will make his voice heard, and will show the wrath of his arm, with wrath and anger and a flame of fire." And it adds: "For by the voice of the Lord the Assyrians will be defeated, by the blow with which he strikes them." Here "Assyrians" does not simply mean the nation. It means those who ruled as tyrants as the Assyrians did, and who used their power over people with the same arrogance. The children of the Hebrews have also passed down this understanding in our discussions with them. They say that the meaning of the name "Assyrians" points to people who prosper and succeed. The present passage teaches that these people will be punished at the time of judgment by the blow that will be brought on them.

Then, it says, those who strike and beat them, the punishing demons, will surround them on every side and inflict the punishments. It makes clear who these are when it says: "From the very place where their hope of help lay, in which he himself had trusted, they will fight against him with drums and lyre." The ungodly hoped for help from their gods, that is, from the opposing powers and the evil spirits. They devoted themselves to these as gods and hoped that help would come to them from that source. They did not know that these very beings would be their punishers. The wrath and anger sent against the ungodly will be carried out through evil angels, who will fight them with drums and lyre, since they delight in evil. So it was also said earlier: "Giants are coming to fulfil my wrath, rejoicing and at the same time insolent." So the beings just mentioned will turn and fight against the ungodly. Instead of friends, they will become enemies.

At that time they will also be called to account and made to pay for everything they have done wrong. These things, it says, await you who were once given to luxury and arrogance. Or perhaps you are deceiving yourself and expect that a kingdom has been prepared for you too, as for those who walked the narrow and hard way, who became poor for God's sake and were persecuted for righteousness' sake? The kingdom has been prepared for all of those, but not for you, who have walked the broad and spacious road. So the deep ravine already described has been prepared for you. It is full of the sweeping water, of wood, and of fire kindled beneath, so that the whole ravine is filled with nothing but wrath and anger, kindling sulphur and fire to punish those who will be condemned there. Having said this much as an interlude, he resumes the prophecy to those who had fled to Egypt and adds the words that follow.

In the prophecy about those who fled to Egypt, the word has spoken of God's universal judgment as an interlude. In the present passage it resumes its threat against them and pronounces woe on those who go down to Egypt for help. God had ordered them to stay where they were. Yet, as though he could not rescue them from the hands of their enemies if they stayed there, they found [?] idolaters to be their saviours. They boasted of the God of Israel and called themselves by his name, yet they trusted in Egyptian chariots and horses. They did not remember how their God had once thrown Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea. So the word blames them because they did this instead of trusting in the Holy One of Israel. It threatens that evils they did not expect will overtake them in Egypt itself. That is why Symmachus has: "The Egyptians are men and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit. The Lord will stretch out his hand, and the helper will grow weak, and the one helped will fall, and all of them together will be brought to an end." He calls the Egyptians the helper and those who took refuge with them the ones helped.

Through this whole narrative the word teaches what to do in times of persecution, if God should ever decide to hand over his people, or his church, to those who attack godliness. One must not abandon the divine faith or give up trusting in God. One must not despair of being reconciled with God, or desert to the Egyptian way of life, by which I mean the life of the idolaters. For in such times many have fallen away from the teaching of godliness and have pinned their hopes on the help of idolaters.

After what was said before, it again turns to the return of those who would come back from captivity, with God protecting them. It says that a lion, the royal beast and the strongest of all, rouses itself to hunt for food and leaps on a flock of sheep. It pays no attention to the shouts of the shepherds or to the number of those trying to drive it off. In the same way the Lord himself will fall on the enemies and rescue his own people from them, and restore them to their own place in Jerusalem. He will shield them in the way we often see among birds, when mother birds fly around the nest and fight for their chicks. In that way he too will shield Jerusalem. Having promised to shield Jerusalem, God next addresses those who had gone into Egypt, saying: "Turn back, you who devise deep and lawless counsel." For even now they can still repent and return to their own land, once they have learned what God has promised about it.

Then it promises that at the time when the people return, idolatry will no longer take hold among them. So it says: "For on that day people will cast away the things made by hand." History confirms this as well. After they returned from Babylon and rebuilt the temple in Jerusalem a second time, they are no longer found using idols.

They had left their homes in Judea and fled to Egypt out of fear of the Assyrian. So it promises them the Assyrian's fall, saying: "And Assyria will fall by a sword not of man." This signifies the overthrow of the Assyrian kingdom and their fall, as of a power brought down from the height of its former royal dignity to a low place. And this, it says, will happen to them not through any human attack but through God's wrath against them. Men certainly did seem to be the agents of their overthrow. Yet it was God himself who overthrew them through those men. That is why the earlier prophecy about Babylon said: "Behold, I will stir up the Medes against you."

For "For they will be enclosed by rock as by a palisade and will be defeated, and the one who flees will be captured; thus says the Lord," Symmachus gave this version: "His rock" (clearly meaning the Assyrian's) "will pass away in terror, and his rulers will be defeated, says the Lord." By "rock" he means the Assyrians, that is, the firmness, stability and strength their kingdom once had. The word says this will pass away, hinting at the overthrow of Assyrian power. Then it says: "Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem." With these words too it urges those who had hurried off to Egypt not to leave the place where God's temple was. It even calls blessed those who will have seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem, because the city was going to be renewed and regain its own glory, or even a greater glory than it had before. That is why it was said elsewhere: "And the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former." It should be noted, however, that none of the other translators has "blessed." For "who has seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem," Symmachus says: "The Lord has fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem." Aquila and Theodotion said: "He has light in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem." The passage teaches that the God and Lord of the universe, who threatened the Assyrian with these words, has fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem. Whenever he wishes, he can use that fire and furnace to burn up and roast those who need burning. So it is not right to despise the city of God.

These things could fittingly be said of the church as well, since the church is the glorified city of God. Of her it is said: "Glorious things were spoken of you, O city of God," and "The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God." In her too there is fire and a furnace, to burn up and consume the wood, hay and straw in each soul. And if it is read as "He has light in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem," we will take "light" to refer to those gathered in her who are worthy of the light. We will take "a furnace in Jerusalem" to refer to those who need burning and cleansing.

The Septuagint version joins these words to the sense of the preceding passage. It first said, "Thus says the Lord: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem," and then went on: "For behold, a righteous king will reign, and rulers will rule with judgment." Since these things were to happen in Jerusalem, it fittingly calls blessed those who would enjoy them there. The other translators, however, joined "says the Lord" to the preceding sense, and so presented the present passage as a fresh start. So Symmachus has: "Behold, a king will reign for righteousness," Aquila has: "Behold, a king will reign for what is just," and Theodotion has the same. The children of the Jews will probably apply this to Zerubbabel. He was of the tribe of Judah and of David's line, and he led those who came back from captivity on their return from Babylon in the time of Cyrus, king of the Persians. They might also say that the rulers who will rule with judgment were those with Zerubbabel: Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, and whoever else was prominent alongside them.

But I do not think they can account for what follows, namely: "And he will appear in Zion like a rushing river, glorious in a thirsty land," together with the words attached to it. No one could show that these were fulfilled in the time of Zerubbabel. The prophecy about those who went down to Egypt in Jeremiah's time has, so to speak, been completed. So the word takes up another subject and makes a fresh start, prophesying the appearing of the Christ of God. For he alone has appeared among men as a righteous king. And his apostles led his church with the judgment of their king. The order makes sense. The prophet first outlined the prophecy about those who went down to Egypt in Jeremiah's time. Then he foretold the return from Babylon, the renewal of Jerusalem, and the resettlement of the people that was to take place in the land of Judea. It is fitting that the prophecy about Christ should come next, in sequence: Christ is the one being prophesied, together with the good things obtained through him for all people.

He foretold that people in the time of Jeremiah the prophet would go down into Egypt many years later, and that the return from captivity would follow. So there is nothing surprising in his prophesying things that would happen much later still, at the coming of Christ. According to the other translators, he calls Christ a righteous king who reigns for righteousness. For through his gospel the righteousness of God has been revealed, so that the knowledge of God is proclaimed not only to Jews but also to Greeks and to people throughout the whole world. So the Christ of God reigned for righteousness, and this kingdom was something new. He did not take up the kingdom with an eye to human rank, or to honour and glory among men, but for righteousness. In the same way his rulers did not rule because they had been promoted to worldly offices, but for judgment. That is why the other translators have: "And rulers will rule for judgment."

For "And the man will hide his words," Symmachus has: "And a man will be like a hiding place from the wind and a shelter from the storm." Who then will this man be, if not the one who was called righteous above? He himself will be a man. He is not a man by nature but something higher than human nature, yet he will be a man who conceals his divinity. That is why Symmachus has "like a hiding place from the wind and a shelter from the storm," and Aquila has "like one hiding the wind, and a hiding place from the tempest." You see how the word presents the economy of his humanity as something hidden. According to the Seventy, the passage refers to his speaking everything in parables. That is why it says: "hiding his words, and he will be hidden as from rushing water." The multitude of the Jewish people was rushing water that was running to waste. So he hid himself from them and veiled his words from them, but revealed them to his disciples. That is why it goes on to say that he will be manifest to his church: "And he will appear in Zion like a river." Who will appear, if not the righteous king himself? He will appear like a glorious rushing river. And who is this Zion, if not the one that would openly receive him who was hidden from the others? It teaches how great a river he is when it says: "like a glorious rushing river in a thirsty land." The land that was once desert and thirsty, the church from the gentiles, is this Zion. In her, it says, they will no longer put their trust in men. Here Symmachus translated: "And the eyes of those who see will not be dimmed." He means those in the church of God, who see and understand the river that has been made manifest to them, that is, the only-begotten Word of God. Of him it is said: "The river of God was filled with waters," and "The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God." That is why the Saviour himself taught: "Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly."

To this it adds next: "And their ears will give heed to hear. And the heart of the weak will attend to hearing." Here Symmachus says: "And the heart of the foolish will understand so as to know." You see how it promises those who were once foolish an understanding of the righteous king, who hid himself from others. "And stammering tongues," it says, "will quickly learn to speak peace." Symmachus has: "And the tongue of stammerers will be quick to speak clearly." So Zion, which is also the thirsty land that was once desert, would be the church. The heart of the weak and the stammering tongues belong to the nations who once did not know God and did not speak rightly, and to them it promises a change for the better.

To this it adds: "And they will no longer tell the fool to rule." That is what they did before, when they entrusted their souls to their truly foolish teachers. These were the wise of this age, whose wisdom God made foolish. Formerly they entrusted the rule over themselves to this teacher, whose folly made him godless and a worshipper of many gods. But now, the word says, they will no longer tell the fool to rule. For "And your servants will no longer say, Be silent," Symmachus has: "Nor will the deceitful man be called a saviour." For all the rulers of former times, being foolish, would not allow those who wanted to learn something to ask about the truth. That is why the Seventy have: "And your servants will no longer say, Be silent, for the fool will speak foolish things." Such, truly, was everyone who professed the wisdom of this age. "And his heart devised vain things, to accomplish lawless deeds and to speak error against the Lord, to lead hungry souls astray." The other translators have: "to cut off," or "to cut down, hungry souls, and to leave thirsty souls empty."

All these things the foolish rulers of mankind did in former times. Their counsel was wicked, and they plotted lawless things, to destroy the humble in soul with their words. Symmachus has: "to destroy the meek with lying speeches and to scatter the words of the lowly." If anywhere some modest and humble person put forward a true word about the truth, they would scatter it and make it disappear. That is how things were before. But this, it says, will no longer happen in the new Zion. They will not tell the fool to rule, nor will the deceitful man be called a saviour. Instead the godly, it says, have made wise plans, and this counsel will stand. In Symmachus, after the account of the foolish rulers, comes: "But a ruler will devise princely things, and a leader will arise." These words signify the apostles of our Saviour, to whom the righteous king has given the rule and leadership of his church. That is why it is said in his own person: "But you, man, my leader and my close friend."

It is worth noting that nowhere in these promises is Israel named. Judah is not named either, though it is named so often elsewhere, and neither is Jacob. This is because the prophecy concerns Christ and those in his church who turn back from the error of the [?]. So at the beginning of the passage the Seventy fittingly have the word call blessed those who have seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem. Clearly this means the new Zion, the new Jerusalem of Christ. In her the seed of the blessed men of old blossomed and bore fruit, so that the whole world was filled with the blessing that came from them. That is why the blessed prophets of God of old said, prophesying about them: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." Yet those who said this did not become seedless, childless and fruitless like Sodom and Gomorrah. So they are called blessed in the church of God, since they have gained such seed and such kinsfolk. That is why it says: "Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem." As you read further, you will find in many places of this prophecy that the church from the gentiles is spoken of in this way.

The word has foretold the appearing of Christ, and the oversight his apostles would exercise with right judgment, by saying: "Behold, a righteous king will reign, and rulers will rule with judgment." It then added the turning of the nations to God. Now, in the present passage, it addresses the people of the circumcision and urges them to weep, beat their breasts and lament, as a people that has fallen from the grace of God through its unbelief toward God. And to rebuke the unmanliness and effeminacy of their soul, it calls them women. It says that their synagogues are meant by the prophecy that runs: "Rich women, rise up," or, as the other translators have it, "women at ease." For in truth they were once rich and flourishing in the things of God. Or perhaps he calls them rich and at ease because they seemed to abound in bodily wealth and to live in luxury. So the word urges them not to attend to what is said carelessly or in passing, but wide awake and with composure. That is why it says: "Rise up and hear my voice." Or does it also command them to rise up as women who have fallen? In place of "daughters in hope," the other translators agree in saying "confident daughters"; for even then they still seemed, as women who were rich and at ease, to think highly of themselves and to trust in their wealth. You might say that the women mentioned first signify the assemblies of the Jews in ancient times and the crowds gathered in them, and the daughters the synagogues of the same people that would be set up in later times.

So the word commands both of these groups to listen intently and attentively to what follows. Through it, the word teaches that they ought to call to mind "a year of days," and to do so in pain, while also marking out a good hope for themselves. By "year" the prophetic word means the time of the gospel preaching, when our Savior and Lord lived among men and preached. This is clear from what is said next in the person of Christ: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." It is this year, then, that he wants these women to call to mind. They are to do so in pain, pierced with remorse for what they have dared to do, but also with good hope, because of the hope promised to those who repent of what they have done. Now when the house of Israel was the vineyard of the Lord, and the man of Judah a beloved young plant, the vintage among them was great. I mean the time when the temple and the altar still stood, and gifts and the sacrifices required by the law were brought from the whole nation as from a vineyard. But now, it says, "the vintage is used up and has ceased." At another time, during the captivity in Babylon, this vintage did cease and was taken up again when the place was restored. But now, learn that it will never come again, for it has been used up and has ceased once for all. In Symmachus' version: "The vintage," he says, "is finished; it has been proclaimed that it shall not come."

What, then, must you women just mentioned do about this? He goes on to say: "Be amazed, be grieved, you who are confident." Let godly grief take hold of you, he says, and turn away from your former unbelief by giving yourselves to repentance; for godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret. So show the fruits of repentance in your deeds. Strip off the garment of wealth, lay yourselves bare of luxury and ease, gird your loins like men, and beat your breasts over the desolation that has overtaken the vineyard you once delighted in. What the field has suffered, and the vine that bore so much fruit, he says next: "On the land of the people thorn and grass will come up." He made this plain earlier when he said: "And I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns." And he went on to explain what these meant: "I waited for it to do justice, but it did lawlessness, and not righteousness but an outcry." These, then, are the things he urged them to mourn over, and above all because of the threat that follows, where it is said: "Joy will be taken away from every house." And this once-rich city: its houses will be left desolate, when the wealth of the city and the sacred and precious things of the holy house are abandoned by God. "And it will become," he says (that is, the city once so proud and called God's own), "a dwelling for wild asses and a pasture for shepherds," or in Aquila's version, "a pasture for herds." Who, seeing Jerusalem inhabited by foreign settlers, idolaters gathered from various nations, would not rightly say that wild asses and herds of every kind graze upon it? That is why it says: "a joy for wild asses, a pasture for shepherds."

For these reasons, then, the word commanded you to make loud lamentation and to stay in mourning until a spirit from on high comes upon you, or in Symmachus' version, "refreshment from on high." There are different kinds of spirits, but nothing can restore you and give you rest from mourning and lamentation except the Spirit sent down from on high, if it comes upon you. This is the one the Savior spoke of: "Behold, I am going away, and I send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth," and again: "until you receive power from on high." Since, then, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted," and "Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh," it is fitting that he gives these women a good promise, the one that comes through the Holy Spirit, if they have shown their repentance by lament, weeping and mourning. Then he again explains what was said earlier, in a different way: "And Chermel will be a desert, and Chermel will be reckoned as a forest." In Symmachus: "And Carmel," he says, "will be a desert, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest." It was also said earlier: "Yet a little while, and Lebanon will be changed like Mount Chermel, and Chermel will be reckoned as a forest. And in that day the deaf will hear the words of a book, and the eyes of the blind, who are in darkness and in gloom, will see; and the poor will rejoice with gladness because of the Lord, and those among men who had lost hope will be filled with gladness." In Symmachus: "Yet a little while," he says, "and Lebanon will become Carmel, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest." In these words Lebanon, the mountain in Phoenicia, signified the nations, while Carmel, the mountain that once belonged to the Jews, signified the people of the circumcision. That is why Chermel, which is Carmel, is interpreted as "knowledge of circumcision." Lebanon, then, the foreign people of alien race from the nations, will be changed, he says, to become what the people of the circumcision once was when God honored it, while the people of the circumcision itself, called Chermel or Carmel, will be reckoned as a forest. This, then, is what the word means in the passage before us too. In Symmachus: "And the desert will become Carmel." As there Lebanon was said to be changed into Carmel, so here it is the desert; the desert and Lebanon are therefore the same thing, and both signify the church from the nations, which has been changed into Carmel. For just as in former times the Lord's portion was his people Jacob, and Israel the measured lot of his inheritance, and Carmel possessed the knowledge of this, so Lebanon and the land that was once a desert have been changed for the better and have become God's portion. Carmel, in turn, was reckoned as a forest, and a forest is a place full of wild and fruitless plants. That is why divine Scripture regularly calls the nations who do not know God a forest, as we have often shown.

Next, as to one already found worthy of great blessings, he promises the desert what follows: "And judgment will rest in the desert, and righteousness will dwell in Carmel." What Carmel, if not the desert itself, of which it was said: "And the desert will become Carmel"? He promises, then, that judgment and righteousness will rest and dwell in the land that was once a desert. That is why in the earlier prophecy too it was said: "Yet a little while, and Lebanon will be changed like Mount Chermel." And there followed the turning of the unbelieving nations to God: "And in that day the deaf will hear the words of a book, and the eyes of the blind who are in gloom will see," and so on. So here too he adds things like those, saying that in the land once a desert judgment and righteousness will rest, and works of righteousness will be done in it. But also, he says, there will be in this desert those who are confident forever, "and his people will dwell in a city of peace." For in place of that great and proud city which was destroyed, he foretells that another city will be founded for God: the catholic church, stretching from one end of the earth to the other, and the godly commonwealth within it. In Symmachus: "And my people," he says, "will be settled in a house of peace." Here Israel is no longer mentioned, nor Jacob, but God, who has made his dwelling in the new city of peace, in which he says his people will dwell in confidence and rest in wealth. The Apostle points to the wealth of the church when he says: "I thank my God through Jesus Christ that in every way you have been enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge."

Earlier he had shown that the wrath of God would come upon the ungodly at the time of judgment, saying: "With fury and wrath and a flame of devouring fire he will strike violently with thunderbolts, and like hail driven down with force." So it is fitting that here he adds, concerning those who are now pronounced blessed: "And if the hail comes down, it will not come upon you." And also, he says, "those who dwell in the forests will be as confident as those in the plain." You see how he holds out good hopes to the wild and fruitless plants of the forest: such souls will no longer be in forests, but in level, even and cultivated country, so that they can take courage and be confident in their own fruitfulness.

Having foretold these things, the word goes on, as follows naturally, to call blessed those who have cultivated this desert. So it says: "Blessed are those who sow by every water, where ox and ass tread." By these words it calls blessed the apostles of our Savior and the first heralds of the gospel, who preached to both Jews and Greeks and scattered their seed upon every man, the Jew first and also the Greek. For the people of the circumcision is called an ox, as a clean animal because of its fathers, while the idolatrous people is called an ass, as an animal unclean from its fathers. Since, then, the apostles of our Savior scattered the seed of the gospel first among Jews and then among Greeks, it is rightly said: "Blessed is he who sows by every water, where ox and ass tread." By water he is hinting here at the divinely inspired Scripture, which is trodden both by the Jews and by the people from the nations.

"But for my part," says the prophet, "I count you blessed. Yet I see others who count you wretched and call you miserable"—I mean your persecutors. "So of them I say: Woe to those who make you miserable." And truly woe to them, because no one makes you miserable; and whoever rejects you thinks he is rejecting men, but it is not you he rejects but the one who sent you. Akin to this are the words the Savior spoke to his disciples: "Whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me." For in times of persecution there are, one might say, two groups, those who inflict and those who suffer. Blessed would be the one who suffers and does not inflict, and wretched the one who inflicts and does not suffer. And woe will come upon them in another way too, since those who reject will be caught and handed over to the one who takes charge of those who have become castaways from God. Once he has received their souls, he destroys them in the way described next: "And like a moth on a garment, so they will be overcome."

The prophetic word has called blessed the apostles of our Savior, who sowed the heavenly seeds of the gospel among Jews and Greeks alike, and has pronounced woe on those who rejected them, as though laying them under a curse. Now, in the person of the apostles themselves, it offers up a prayer that says: "Lord, have mercy on us, for we have put our trust in you." For the seed of those who refused to obey the preaching of the gospel was handed over to destruction, but you yourself, O Lord, are our salvation, standing beside us in the time of affliction.

Then, concerning those who did not believe the preaching of the apostles, he adds: "At the sound of the fear of you peoples were driven out of their wits, and nations were scattered." Aquila has "at the sound of a crowd," and Theodotion "at the sound of a multitude peoples withdrew." It points to the siege of the Jewish nation: when a multitude of enemies came against them, they were driven out of their own land and scattered among the nations. In place of "from the fear of you," Symmachus said "at your being exalted they were dispersed," while Aquila and Theodotion have "at your exaltation they were scattered."
