Then, as if speaking to them after they had been scattered among the nations, he adds: "But now your spoils will be gathered, of small and great; as one gathers locusts, so they will mock you." Here he shows how easily the Jewish nation would be overpowered and captured, and he compares their great numbers to locusts. And "they will mock you," spoken to them, means that their enemies will treat them as playthings, not only plundering their spoils, small and great, but also mocking them.

Having said these things about them, he passes on to the company of the church of God, and for its sake he glorifies God, saying: "Holy is God who dwells on high; Zion has been filled with judgment and righteousness." You will understand which Zion this is from its being said to be filled with judgment and righteousness. Earlier it was said: "And judgment and righteousness will rest in the desert." So what was earlier called the desert he now calls Zion, and in this way he signifies the church of Christ. For this was the land once a desert, in which judgment and righteousness came to rest. That is why God is now blessed: because it has been filled with judgment and righteousness.

Then it says: "They will be delivered over in law." For those in this new Zion were delivered over to a new law, that is, the law of the gospel. But also, "our salvation is in treasures." What treasures, if not those laid up in heaven? In place of "they will be delivered over in law," Symmachus has: "And the faithfulness of your time will be a wealth of salvation, wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is his treasure." In its place the Seventy rendered: "Wisdom and knowledge and godliness come to God." For all these are brought up from men to God like a spiritual and acceptable sacrifice, and these very things—wisdom, knowledge and godliness in men—are treasures of righteousness. That is why it said: "Our salvation is in treasures."

After this, the apostles themselves are addressed: "Behold, in your fear they themselves will fear; those whom you feared will cry out because of you." For fear of you will fall upon the unbelievers, and those whom you once thought fearsome will cry out in defeat. In Symmachus: "Behold, I will be seen by them; they cried out earnestly." And who cried out earnestly he adds next: "Messengers of peace wept bitterly." In Aquila: "Behold," he says, "I will be seen by them; I will cry out earnestly; messengers of peace will weep bitterly." And in Theodotion: "Behold, I will be seen by them; they cried out earnestly; messengers of peace will weep bitterly." In all of them, then, "Behold, I will be seen by them" is clearly stated, the word showing that God will be seen by them. By whom, if not by those who have stored up for themselves the treasures of righteousness and wisdom? "To these," he says, "I will be seen." These were the apostles of our Savior, to whom, he says, "I appeared." And they, the messengers of peace, cried out earnestly, and so they also wept bitterly, crying out earnestly in prayer over the destruction of the former people. For the apostles of our Savior were messengers who wept bitterly and mourned, because those whom they called to the peace of Christ would neither obey nor believe them. That is why the Savior himself, weeping over Jerusalem, said: "If you, even you, had known the things that make for your peace!" In the same way, then, the messengers of peace wept bitterly, lamenting their destruction.

So he adds: "For their ways will be made desolate; the fear of the nations has ceased, and the covenant with them is taken away, and you will not count them men." Symmachus rendered this more clearly, saying: "The ways have vanished; the one who walks the path has ceased; he has scattered the covenant, rejected cities, taken no account of men." The words "the fear of the nations has ceased" are found neither in the Hebrew text nor in the other translators. The meaning is that the ways of the people of the circumcision have come to an end, that the covenant with them, the one given to them through Moses, is taken away, and that no one will any longer count them as men.

After this he adds: "The land has mourned"—fittingly, given what has been said about it—"Lebanon has been put to shame, Sharon has become marshes; Galilee and Chermel will be made manifest." In Symmachus: "The land wept, it grew weak; Lebanon was put to shame; Sharon became useless, as if impassable; and Bashan and Carmel stretched out." All these are parts of the land of Judea: I mean Carmel, the region called Bashan, Galilee and Sharon. Lebanon, which in this passage is placed among Sharon, Bashan, Carmel and Galilee, is to be understood here specifically of Jerusalem, because of the sacrifice offered up there, in which frankincense (libanos) was also offered under the law of Moses. So when he says that Lebanon has been put to shame, it is as if he were saying more plainly that the sacrifice and the altar have been, because the worship prescribed by the law of Moses has been abolished. In other places too Jerusalem has been called Lebanon, as it is said in Zechariah: "Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars." And Ezekiel says: "The great eagle with great wings, which has the purpose of entering Lebanon, and it plucked off the tender shoots of the cedar."

Then, explaining the meaning of the saying, he adds: "when Nebuchadnezzar comes to Jerusalem," making it perfectly clear that the eagle is the king of the Babylonians and Lebanon is Jerusalem. And the region called Sharon, or Assaron, became marshes, he says, or useless. By this he signifies that the richest lands of the Jewish nation—that is, those understood to lie in their souls—will vanish. The words "Galilee will be manifest" are said because of what was prophesied about it earlier, as in: "Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness, see a great light; on those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death a light has dawned." For these reasons Galilee will be manifest, and Chermel likewise, he says, will be manifest. Which Chermel is this, if not the one of which it was said earlier: "And the desert will be like Chermel"? This desert, then, having become like Chermel, will be manifest together with Galilee.

So God, who loves mankind, sent messengers of peace to the Jewish people, weeping bitterly and urging them to accept the peace announced to them in the gospel. But since they did not receive them, he goes on to say: "Now I will arise, says the Lord, now I will be glorified, now I will be exalted; now you will see, now you will perceive." Here he promises his second and glorious coming, when they will see him and come to perceive his divinity. Then he himself will be glorified and exalted. And then they will know that the strength of their spirit was vain after all, for fire will devour them. That is why it is said to them directly: "Vain is the strength of your spirit; fire will devour you." In place of "and nations will be burned up," the Hebrew wording and all the other translators have "and peoples will be set on fire," the word thus clearly singling out the peoples to whom it was addressed. For these, he says, will be like a thorn thrown away in a field and trampled underfoot.

Even though he foretells these things about those of the Jewish people who did not accept the grace announced to them in the gospel, you, though you hear these prophetic words with your ears, do not understand or recognize that these very things, spoken and written to you in the Hebrew tongue, and all the other wonders I performed for you—those who dwell far off, even to the ends of the earth, [?]; and what I spoke among you and did before your eyes, those at the ends of the world will know. And how will they know, except by drawing near to God, coming to him, and learning his strength?

These very people will know how the lawless in Zion have departed from me. For this reason, because of their apostasy, trembling will seize them. Then, as if speaking to those of the people of the circumcision who did not believe, he goes on to say: Who will declare to you that a fire is burning? He had spoken of this fire a little earlier: Fire will devour you. And again: Who will declare to you the everlasting place? He plainly means the place prepared for the devil and his angels. Who, then, will be the one who knows these things and warns in advance those who do not know them? Who, if not everyone who walks in righteousness and speaks the straight way, everyone who hates ungodliness and injustice, who turns away from bribes and stops his ears so as not to hear a judgment of blood, and who shuts his eyes so as not to look on an unjust deed? Such was each of the prophets of God, and every man dear to God, and the company of the apostles and disciples of our Saviour. Everyone of this kind, then, he says, will declare to you that a fire is burning, prepared for the ungodly. The same person will also show you the place of everlasting condemnation, warning you in advance to take care not to fall into it.

This very man, who has come to be far from the fire and from the everlasting place just mentioned, will dwell in a lofty cave and on a strong rock. In Symmachus it reads: He will make his dwelling on the heights; his height is like strongholds of rocks. By these words we are to understand the ascetic discipline of the blessed and their life at the summit of philosophy. Therefore he adds: Bread will be given him, and his water will be sure. Such a man, having disciplined his present life with bread and water, will have as the reward and fruit of his discipline the glorious sight of the King.

Therefore it is added: You will see a king with glory. What king, if not the one on whose account the present passage has listed all these things, beginning from the words: Behold, a righteous king will reign, and rulers will rule with judgment? It is he, then, whom people such as the passage has described will see in glory. They will attain these things. But as for you, to whom it was said, Who will declare to you that a fire is burning?, your soul will see from afar the heavenly land of promise. You will not be in it but will see it from a distance. For the meek will inherit that land, while those cast far away from it will fall into fear of their own condemnation.

Therefore it is said to them: Your soul will meditate on fear. Then the discourse turns again to the people of the circumcision and says: Where are the scribes? These are the men who championed the letter of the law and knew how to understand nothing but the promises of the literal wording, the men whom the Saviour lamented in the Gospels, saying: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! Where, then, he says, are the scribes, where are the counsellors? Where will they appear on the day of judgment, these men who rear their disciples on flattery? Therefore he says: He who counts those who are being reared, the small and great people, with whom they did not take counsel. Instead, by rearing them on flattery they perverted them. Symmachus has: He who counts, he says, those who have been reared, the shameless people. You will not see a people heavy of lips, so as not to hear the speech of a tongue. So he says: You pervert the shameless people, O scribe of the law, rearing them on flattery and deceit. But you do not see, and you will not see, my people who are heavy of lips. Nor will you hear, since you lack understanding, the speech of the tongue spoken of above: And the stammering tongues will quickly learn to speak peace. You will not hear these tongues, nor will you understand the deep-voiced people. And how could they possibly understand these things, lacking understanding as they did, so that it is said of them: A despised people, and the one who hears has no understanding?

Instead of Behold, Zion the city, Aquila has: Zion, the township, was seen in a vision. Symmachus and Theodotion have: See Zion, the city of our holy ones. Here the discourse addresses Zion and urges her to behold the city called our salvation, or to behold the city of our holy ones. And again it goes on: Your eyes will see Jerusalem. This is said as though Jerusalem were about to become known, and as though your eyes will see another city, the city of the festivals. By these words the discourse means by 'salvation' the Christ of God, and by 'the city of festivals' the church of God. The church is a rich city, and tents that will not be shaken. The pegs of its tent will never be moved, nor will its cords be broken. For the tents of the Jewish Jerusalem were often shaken, when it was besieged in various ways and razed to the ground by those who made war on it at different times. But the pegs of this new city, he says, will be immovable. For even if at times it seems to be harried and besieged in persecutions, yet it stands on the rock and remains unfallen for ever. He who said this did not lie: On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. And again: The rains came down, the rivers came, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded on the rock. That is why he says its cords will not be broken.

He adds the reason, saying: For the name of the Lord is great for us; it will be a place for us, rivers and canals broad and spacious. The very name of the Lord, he says, will be a place for this new city that cannot be shaken or fall. That is why it remains unshaken, built as it were upon the Lord, who is its place. In Symmachus it reads: There, he says, the Lord is mighty for us, a place of rivers, spacious canals, where no rowing boat will go, nor will the command of a mighty one cross it. In Aquila it reads: There, he says, the Lord is exceedingly great for us, a place of rivers, streams broad on both sides, in which no oared ship will go, and no huge trireme will cross it. Theodotion also rendered it in much the same way. Through these words the passage says that for the city just mentioned the Lord will be a place of rivers that have streams and broad canals. So one may say: The rushings of the river gladden the city of God; and again: The river of God was filled with waters. These rivers that gladden the city of God are so secure that no rowing boat and no huge trireme can travel through them, because the Lord himself is their place.

Hence enemies and foes cannot set foot in the rivers that encircle and wall in the city of God just mentioned, serving it in place of a rampart, so that they cannot be crossed by any stranger. For the Lord, who is its place, is great: he was the rock on which it was built. The same one, he says, is also our judge, he is also our ruler, he is also our king and saviour. Since the Lord is all these things for us, the city rightly cannot be taken by siege, and the rivers that encircle it cannot be crossed by any enemy. We shall understand the rivers that fence in this city by analogy with the first, great and perfect river whose rushings gladden the city of God, namely the Word. And his angels, who always behold the face of the Father in heaven, would be the rivers that guard his church. Having said this much about the city of God, however, the discourse changes course and turns to address, as it were, the old city.

And he says: Your cords have broken, because they had no strength; your mast has leaned so that the sails slacken; it will not raise a signal until I hand it over for plunder. By these words he means the fall of the bodily Jerusalem. Its cords were broken, and its mast, like that of a ship wrecked in storms and heavy seas, leaned over and fell when the cords holding it were torn apart. Symmachus has: Your cords, he says, were cast loose, so that they do not hold; so too their mast, so that it cannot spread a sail. Then he divided it up, down to much spoil. When a ship has broken up and been wrecked in a sea battle, the enemies who have won seize the spoils of the lost for themselves and plunder everything. In the same way, he says, when Jerusalem fell and was handed over to its enemies, all the precious and venerable things in it, and the priestly vessels, were distributed as plunder, because God had handed it over. For the enemies were not strong enough by their own power to master it. Indeed, those who carried off the plunder were in fact lame, limping and halting in the steps of the soul, so that they did not walk the way of godliness. They were idolaters, these men who took the shipwrecked city without toil or effort. Hence it is said: Now many lame will take plunder, and the people dwelling among them will not say, 'I am weary'; for their sin has been forgiven them. Sin was not counted against them for besieging the city, because they did this by the judgment of God.

In the preceding passages, wherever the discourse foretold the siege of Jerusalem, it then went on to bring in the judgment upon all the nations. As it is said elsewhere: Begin from my holy places. So here too, having foretold the plundering of Jerusalem and its fall, he joins to it the judgment upon all the nations. Surely the discourse did not threaten Jerusalem with these things without also threatening the remaining nations, who persisted in their own lawless and ungodly deeds. That is why the discourse summons the nations together with their rulers, and the peoples, and the whole earth and all who are in it, and then, separately, the inhabited world. The earth is to be understood as, one might say, the whole element of dry land, together with the wild and savage men who live on it in deserts and in places unknown to most people. The inhabited world is the world of our nations, who make their homes in cities and buildings. That is why he speaks of a people in the inhabited world.

Then a proclamation is made to all alike, bearing witness to the universal judgment of God that awaits everyone. He presents it in these words: For the wrath of the Lord is upon all the nations, and anger upon their number. Symmachus has: upon all their power, and Aquila: upon all their host. He goes on: to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter. To whom will he hand them over, if not to the powers that punish and take vengeance?

Of those who are punished, some will be wounded and others dead. The dead are clearly those who have sinned unto death, whose deeds done during their mortal life give off a stench at the time of judgment. Hence in Symmachus it reads: And their stench will rise up. Instead of The mountains will be drenched with their blood, Theodotion has: The mountains will melt away from their blood. What these mountains are he goes on to say. Aquila has: And all the host of the heavens will melt. Symmachus has: And all the power of the heavens will melt. Theodotion has: And all the powers of the heavens will melt. These, then, were the mountains of which it is said: And the mountains will melt from their blood. The powers of the heavens are to be understood as mountains, and they are said to melt because they were the cause of the destruction of the people just mentioned. They would be the powers of which the Apostle says: Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. These powers, which roam the region of the air, are called powers of the heavens, since Scripture also usually calls the birds that move through the air birds of heaven, saying: the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea.

The words And all the powers of the heavens will melt are not found in the translation of the Seventy, so they were added with asterisks from the translation of the others. Since we also needed to know when these things will happen, the prophetic discourse teaches this too, showing that what was foretold will come about after the consummation of this age. Therefore it adds: And the heaven will be rolled up like a scroll, and all the stars will fall like leaves from a vine, and as leaves fall from a fig tree. The Saviour too, when he handed down in the Gospels the teaching about the consummation, said: And the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. Instead of And all the stars will fall like leaves, Aquila has: And all their host will flow away, as a leaf flows away from a vine and as fruit drops from a fig tree. Symmachus has: And all their power will fall, as a leaf falls from a vine and as fruit drops from a fig tree. Theodotion has much the same: And all their power will fall, as leaves fall from a vine and as fruit falls from a fig tree. We have recorded these readings to show that what the Seventy called stars, the other translators named powers of heaven. What powers, if not those spoken of just now? Aquila has: And all the host of the heavens will melt. Symmachus has: And all the power of heaven will melt. Theodotion has: And all the powers of the heavens will melt. These, then, are the powers that we have explained to be the principalities and the authorities, the world-rulers of this darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. It is these that are said to fall like leaves from a vine at the time of judgment, when the heaven will be rolled up like a scroll.

Now that we have reached this point in the text, it is worth noting that the passage does not mean that heaven will be corrupted, destroyed or made to vanish. When a book is unrolled, what is written in it is made visible, yet the book is not destroyed. In the same way, when the writing in heaven that contains the deeds of the whole age is unrolled, the opposing powers flow away and fall from their abode in the air. Daniel too, teaching about the judgment, said: The court sat, and books were opened. What books? Surely those that contain, written in them, all the deeds of those who have lived in every age. You would not be wrong to say that these books are the heaven which is said here to be rolled up like a book, and in which the deeds of all are contained as in a writing. At that time the opposing powers, which of old deceived many by appearing like stars, will fall. For Satan himself, who disguises himself as an angel of light, has fallen like lightning from heaven.

These powers will fall because, he says, my sword has become drunk in heaven. By the sword we understand the punishing power, to which those that deserve such punishment will be handed over. Someone else might say that when the whole visible world comes to its consummation, the fluid substance of bodies will be dissolved. Heaven itself and the stars in it, by which I mean the invisible powers in it, will then put off the bodies that clothe them and be changed to a better life. This, he might say, is shown by the Apostle when he says: that creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. The sword of God just mentioned first visits the wicked and opposing powers in the region of the air, and then visits the souls of the ungodly on earth. Therefore he adds: It will come down upon Idumea and upon the people of destruction. Who will come down, if not the sword? Idumea is interpreted 'earthy'. The sword comes down upon it, is filled with blood, and grows fat, as it were, on the fat of the slaughtered.

Who are these lambs and goats and rams of which he speaks? The lambs (or 'young sheep', in the other translators) signify those who have led the ordinary life of private people. The goats and rams signify those who have wielded great power in offices and positions of authority. The sword of God will visit them, performing a kind of sacrifice by slaughtering and sacrificing the lambs and goats and rams just mentioned. It will do this in Bozrah, which is interpreted 'into the flesh'; here the passage signifies the resurrection of the flesh. So, teaching that the slaughter of those mentioned will take place in the flesh, he says: For there is a sacrifice to the Lord in Bozrah and a great slaughter in Idumea. For the sword will visit every earthy soul, since Edom is interpreted 'earthly' and Idumea 'earthy', as elsewhere too. Therefore the prophet himself, further on, speaking of the Saviour and of the judgment he will carry out, says: Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed red from Bozrah? In this way he pointed to the Saviour's coming in the flesh upon earth.

However, he says in the present passage that the mighty ones, the rams and the bulls will fall together, so that the earth will be drunk with the blood and the fat of those slaughtered by the sword of God. Symmachus has: And lofty unicorns will come down, he says, and calves with the mighty, and the earth will be drunk with blood, and their dust will be made fat with fat. I think the divine Spirit used such threatening language to set forth God's vengeance on the ungodly, and to frighten those who hear these words with their ordinary and rather dull hearing. Not everyone is able to understand in any other way the punishments that will be brought on the ungodly, nor can they conceive how the punishment will be carried out. That is why he used cruder words and more familiar expressions that inspire fear, so that those who hear them, frightened at least in this way, might turn back.

The passage hinted at the siege of Jerusalem by saying: Your cords have broken, because they had no strength; your mast has leaned, it will not slacken the sails; it will not raise a signal until it is handed over for plunder. Then it went on to speak about the nations that besieged the city, and about the universal judgment of God that will visit all the ungodly. Now it resumes its discourse about Zion and Jerusalem, teaching that a year of recompense and a day of judgment will come upon her. Above, too, it was said: Rich women, arise; remember the day of a year in pain, with hope. What, then, was this year for which he commands them to beat their breasts in pain? The present prophecy shows it in the words before us. Beside these words we must set the words that the same prophet speaks later in the person of Christ: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to call the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense to our God, to comfort all who mourn, that glory may be given to those who mourn for Zion. You see how here too a year of the Lord and a day of recompense are mentioned. These words are like the present ones: For it is the day of the Lord's judgment and the year of recompense of Zion's judgment. It is therefore one and the same year and one and the same day. On that day the poor receive good news, and those who mourn for Zion are comforted at the coming of Christ. The women who had become rich are called to lamentation, and what is said in the present passage was about to befall Zion. All these things were fulfilled at the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ. At his coming, those who believed in him and received the grace given through him enjoyed the better good tidings. But those who made themselves strangers to his grace fell away from every good hope and became subject to the threats of grimmer things.

Their own august and royal city itself suffered just what the present prophecy foretells when it says: “And its ravines shall be turned into pitch burning day and night, and it shall not be quenched for all time, and its smoke shall go up on high; for its generations it shall be made desolate, and for a long time.” According to Symmachus: “Its land,” he says, “shall become pitch blazing night and day; it shall not be quenched forever; its smoke shall go up; from its generation to generations it shall be made desolate for ever and ever.” By these words the passage plainly shows that utter desolation will overtake both the place and the nation. It goes on: “There shall be no one passing through it,” and, “There shall be no one going by in it.” In these words he prophesies that no Jew will pass through that place any longer. This was in fact fulfilled by Roman laws and decrees, which forbade Jews to set foot in the place.

Although none of them passes through it, he says that others will dwell there: birds and hedgehogs and ibises and ravens. By these he hints at unclean souls, such as the souls of the idolaters from foreign and alien nations who later settled the place. He says that not only these will inhabit the place instead of its former inhabitants, but also onocentaurs and sirens and ostriches. By these he hints at certain demons that made their lairs in the statues of those people's idolatry. That is why he adds next: “And demons shall meet with onocentaurs, and they shall cry out one to another.” Further, he says, “a measuring line of desert geometry shall be cast over the place.” Symmachus rendered this as: “And a measure of obliteration shall be stretched over it.” All these things, however, will happen once the former inhabitants have been driven out and handed over to destruction. That is why he adds: “Its rulers shall be no more; for its kings and its great men shall come to destruction.” And when you consider their synagogues outside Jerusalem, hear what he proclaims about them as well: “And thorny trees shall spring up in their cities.” By this he means their fruitless teachings. That is also why, in an earlier passage, he showed that their vineyard had produced thorns, saying: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” Since utter desolation has come upon their souls and their land has been filled with thorns, he fittingly foretells that the unclean spirits will rest among them: “There onocentaurs shall rest, for they have found rest for themselves. There the hedgehog has made its nest and kept its young safe.” Or, according to Symmachus: “kept them safe, and hatched them, and gathered them.”

For all these reasons, then, he says that their ravines will be turned into pitch and sulphur. By the ravines he means their souls, which lie somewhere down below in hollows and ravines. Their land, he says, will become pitch burning day and night, and it shall not be quenched for all time. Their eternal punishment will be unquenchable, and the smoke of their fire will go up on high. The sulphur of their punishment in the depths will be visible to those above because of the wickedness that underlies them, a wickedness likened to pitch for its darkness and blackness. Since so many evils will befall the desert of Zion in the year of its recompense, let us see what he says will come next: “There deer met and saw one another's faces.” Divine Scripture regards the deer as a clean animal and teaches many good things about deer, as when it says: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God”; and again: “The voice of the Lord prepares deer”; and again: “Let a loving deer and a graceful foal keep company with you”; and in Job: “You have watched the months of the deer; you will send forth their birth pangs.” Even the beloved of the bride in the Song of Songs is compared to a deer, as she herself teaches when she says: “My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.” Since, then, the bridegroom himself is compared to a deer, who would you say the many deer here are, if not his disciples and apostles? The deer is also a killer of snakes and is counted among the clean animals. So the present passage teaches that certain deer, the disciples of our Savior, came forth from the desolation of the Jewish nation. For “there deer met and saw one another's faces”: they recognized one another and knew the features of their souls, which were made in the image of God.

Yet they passed by that place and kept themselves apart from it. That is why it is said: “They passed by in number, and not one of them perished.” They did not stay in one city but ran off, one here and another there, fulfilling the gospel. For this reason it is said: “One did not seek the other; for the Lord commanded them, and his Spirit gathered them.” He who said to them, “Go and make disciples of all nations in my name,” himself commanded them not to spend their time in one place, but to travel everywhere and see to the founding of his churches.

“And he himself casts lots for them, and his hand has apportioned them pasture for all time.” So he gave them strength and help, and also allotments for generations of generations, so that they might rest in their own allotments, namely the nations allotted to them. Among those nations their memory is rekindled for generations of generations in the churches they founded.

You see what he prophesies for the deer. It is clear to everyone that these promises could not be fulfilled in the desert of Zion described earlier, for hedgehogs and onocentaurs and demons were said to dwell there. So the land of the deer must be a different one, in which the Lord himself cast lots for the deer and his hand gave them pasture for all time. What else, then, is this land assigned to the deer but the one presented by the passage in the Psalms that says: “The voice of the Lord prepares deer and will uncover forests”? So he distributed their allotments to them in the forests, that is, among the nations. It has often been shown that the forests are to be understood as the foreign nations. Since the deer we have identified received allotments and portions in another land by God's command, it followed that we should learn what land this was. In the Psalm, then, it is said, “The voice of the Lord prepares deer and uncovers forests.” The passage teaches that through the deer prepared by the Lord certain wild and wooded forests were laid bare, as the deer drove out the beasts and reptiles in them. The forests signified the foreign nations, which were alien to God.

This, then, is the desert to which the prophecy brings good news in the passage before us, after what it said about the deer: “Rejoice, thirsty desert.” Many other things are said about this desert later in the same prophecy, where it says: “Rejoice, barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate one are more than those of her who has a husband.” This desert, then, must be different from the Zion described earlier, in which hedgehogs and ibises and ravens, demons and onocentaurs were said to dwell, and whose ravines were to be filled with pitch and sulphur. Since those things were said about Zion and Jerusalem, it is time to understand that the present words refer to another desert. This desert was the forest of the deer and the land of the foreign nations, where the Lord distributed allotments to the deer we have identified. The passage brings it good news: “Rejoice, thirsty desert; let the desert exult and blossom like a lily.” This desert was once thirsty, deprived of heavenly streams. But because of what follows, the passage bids it rejoice and be glad, and blossom like a lily as well, so that it can say: “We are the fragrance of Christ to God in every place.”

“And it shall also blossom,” he says, with young shoots and lovely flowers, of which the Song of Songs says: “The flowers have appeared in the land”; “The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance.” He makes clear which desert he is describing when he says: “And the deserts of the Jordan shall exult.” Here he points to the gospel narrative. It was at the river Jordan that John first preached the kingdom of heaven. When the worship performed under the law of Moses was no longer in force in Jerusalem, this same prophet gave the baptism of repentance and the washing of regeneration at the river Jordan itself. Then our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, set his seal on John's preaching by being baptized by him in the Jordan, and himself confirmed the mystery of regeneration. And the once desert, waterless and fruitless one, I mean the church of God, carried on the work of the Jordan [?] through the cleansing of the washing of regeneration, baptizing and at the same time proclaiming the kingdom of God. This the church of God, once a desert, preserves throughout the whole world. That is why the passage bids it be glad and exult, and blossom like a fragrant lily. To it, too, the glory of Lebanon and the honor of Carmel have been given. In earlier passages Lebanon signified the altar and the temple, where the sacrifices with frankincense and the worship prescribed by the law were offered in the offerings. Carmel, as has often been shown, hints at the people of the circumcision. So the prophecy foretells that the honor of the old people and the glory of the temple in Jerusalem will be given to the former desert, I mean the church from the nations. Then he adds: “And my people”—no longer Israel, but “my people,” he says—“shall see the glory of the Lord.” The passage offers this promise to the new people because it would receive the Savior's first coming. That is why it will also see his second and glorious appearing and behold his majesty.

After this he brings good news to those who will be freed from the passions of the soul through the shining forth of the Savior, saying: “Be strong, you slack hands and paralyzed knees; take comfort, you who are faint-hearted in mind.” According to Symmachus: “Be strengthened, slack hands and weak knees; be firm; say to the senseless, Be strong, do not fear.” Aquila and Theodotion rendered it in much the same way. The passage bids the disciples and apostles of our Savior to strengthen the slackened souls among the nations and to make firm the knees of the weak. It also bids them call out to those who were formerly faint-hearted: “Be strong, do not fear.” For even if some persecute you with threats, try to frighten you, and inflict torments and tortures, yet you, he says, who were once faint-hearted, have received strength and power. So do not fear, since you have your God with you always. That is why, according to Symmachus: “Do not fear; behold your God; the vengeance of recompense will come; the Lord himself will come and save you.” Having been taught these things, then, you who were once faint-hearted, be strong, do not fear.

Having foretold these things and clearly announced the coming of God, the passage goes on to list signs and tokens of his mighty works: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of stammerers shall speak clearly.” These things were plainly fulfilled at the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ. At that coming each of the things mentioned was accomplished, as he healed every disease and every infirmity of the body by the power of his divine authority. Nor did he heal only bodies: by the word of his teaching he also cured the passions of souls. And so even now, throughout the whole world and among all the nations, people who once, through the maiming and blindness of the soul, gaped in awe at lifeless and motionless wooden images as if they were gods, have had the eye of the soul lit up by his light and have received their sight. Now they spit on the superstition handed down from their fathers and acknowledge the one and only true God. Those who were once deaf and could not hear divine words have now, by his grace, become skilled hearers of the divinely inspired oracles. Those whose soul's feet were paralyzed have leapt up like deer, made like their teachers, whom the prophecy a little earlier called deer. And the tongue of the stammerers, which Satan had bound so that they would not speak of the true God, has learned to utter clear and well-formed words. You would not be wrong to give the name of stammerers to those among the wise of this age who hardly ever dared to think or say anything right about God.

In addition to all this, at the foretold appearing of God, water, he says, broke forth in the former desert as a life-giving spring appeared in it; a ravine has been found [?], and, according to Symmachus, torrents and streams in a thirsty land. The water was that very water of the Jordan of which it was said a little earlier, “The deserts of the Jordan shall exult.” By it the prophet hinted at the washing of regeneration and the mystery of the new covenant. The streams signified the Savior's gospel words.

Moreover, in the desert just described there came to be “gladness of birds and a fold of flocks.” These are souls that are winged and soar on high, and others that are gentle and meek, governed by the good shepherd, so that they can say: “The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing.” Earlier, then, ibises and hedgehogs and ravens and onocentaurs and demons were said to dwell in the desert of Zion. To the desert now under discussion, however, the passage announces all these good things. The one was said to be filled with pitch and sulphur and fire, but this one with a spring of water, streams and torrents.

“And there shall also be,” he says, “a pure way here, and it shall be called a holy way.” This must be the way that leads to the thrice-blessed goal, the heavenly city of God. The Savior presented this way when he said: “I am the way.” The saving Word leads those who travel by him by the hand to the Father and establishes them in the kingdom of heaven. The prophecy foretells that he will be given to the desert in addition to its other blessings. And it is evident that no unclean person passes along this way. “But the scattered,” he says, “shall walk on it.” Who are these, if not those who were once scattered away from God and wandered far from the truth? These will turn back, find the straight way that leads no one astray, and walk in it.

“And there shall be no lion there,” he says, meaning on the way just described, “nor shall any of the evil beasts go up onto it or walk there.” For how could anything evil be found in the one who said, “I am the way”? Not even the ways of a serpent upon a rock could be found, as Solomon says. “But the redeemed shall walk in it,” he says. These are clearly the people he himself redeemed with his own precious blood. “And those gathered by the Lord”: not by a prophet, nor by any human effort. Those redeemed and gathered by the Lord himself will walk the way described, and by it they will come to the thrice-blessed goal, the heavenly Zion. Of this Zion the Apostle says: “We have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” That is why it is said: “And they shall come to Zion with gladness.” Zion here cannot be taken as the Zion of which it was said: “And a year of recompense of the judgment of Zion, and its ravines shall be turned into pitch,” and so on. We must therefore understand that the places called by the same name of Zion are different. The one is earthly and subject to the threats. The other is heavenly, and to it those redeemed and gathered by the Lord are said to come. Of them it was said: “And everlasting gladness shall be upon their head.” For those declared victors in the great contest will be crowned with a crown of gladness. The divine Apostle knew of this crown when he said: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness.” That is why it is said: “And everlasting gladness shall be upon their head,” and again: “For upon their head shall be praise and exultation, and gladness shall overtake them.” These are the people who have walked the saving way without swerving and have reached by it the thrice-blessed goal. There those honored with the crown will enjoy eternal life in the kingdom of heaven, where pain and grief and sighing have fled away.

The passage before us is a history, a wonderful account of events that took place in the time of Hezekiah. It is included with the other histories in Second Kings and Second Chronicles. Nevertheless it has also been placed in the present prophecy, or book, because near the end of the history it contains a prophecy and a great and extraordinary deed accomplished in the time of Hezekiah. We should also note this: in the sixth year of Hezekiah's reign the king of the Assyrians, this same Sennacherib, came against Samaria. He overthrew the kingdom of Israel there and carried the whole people called Israel away captive into the land of the Assyrians. Seven years later, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, he attacked the cities of Judea and took its most strongly fortified cities, and he was already making an attempt on Jerusalem itself. The book of Chronicles recounts a great many of Hezekiah's achievements that deserve to be remembered with honor. It tells how he did what was right before the Lord in all things, just as David his father had done. It tells how he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and repaired them after they had been ruined in the time of Ahaz his father. It tells how he cleansed [?] the temple and the priests who ministered in it. It tells how he celebrated the feast of Passover, so that scripture testifies that there had been no such feast in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel. It tells how he cut down the groves and pulled down the high places and the hills, and destroyed all the idolatry that had spread over the whole of Judea in earlier times. And it tells how he did what was good and true before the Lord God: in every work he undertook in the service of the house of the Lord, and in the law and in the commandments, he sought his God with his whole soul; he acted and he prospered. After bearing witness to these and countless similar things about him, scripture adds: “And after these words and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came into Judea and encamped against the walled cities, and he said he would seize them.”

Then it teaches that Hezekiah, although he trusted in God, still did not neglect the security of the country. So, like a good general, he stopped up the springs outside the city, so that the enemy would find no water when he reached those places. He also fortified the wall of Jerusalem itself all the way around, built another outer wall beyond it, and provided weapons and every kind of military equipment. Then it tells how, after all this effort, he called the people together and strengthened them with God-fearing words, telling them that they must fear no enemy, since, he says, "There are more with us than with him; for with the Assyrian are arms of flesh, but with us," he says, "is the Lord our God, to save us and to fight our battle." To this is added: "And the people took courage from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah." "And after this Sennacherib king of the Assyrians sends his servants from Lachish to Jerusalem, to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people in Jerusalem, saying" the words set out here. So, in addition to Hezekiah's other achievements, God gave him, through the preparations for war, an exercise in virtue and an occasion to show still greater piety. In this he shone out: he set everything in order for the war like a general, yet he entrusted the whole matter to God and gave the people under him God-fearing instruction. His father Ahaz was not such a man. At one time he made himself and all the people under him slaves to the Babylonian, and at another he was being taken captive by the Syrians who lived in Damascus. So by allowing the Assyrian to approach Jerusalem, God gave Hezekiah an opportunity to show his virtue. We should note that the prophet also mentioned earlier the men named here, I mean Eliakim and Shebna, in the oracle concerning the valley of Zion, where it is said: "Go into the chamber, to Shebna the steward," and so on, and "I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah."

We need to note this in order to fit the words of that prophecy to the present history. The Hebrews say that this Shebna deserted to the Assyrian, having later pledged him his hand along with others out of fear of him, and that this is why the things prophesied about him earlier were spoken.

How full of arrogance and madness the enemy's voice was is shown when it says: "Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians." It is as though some opposing power answered the prophetic word that says, "Thus says the Lord." This man too cried out, "Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians."

Then, since the enemy knew well that Hezekiah and those with him prevailed by prayers and God-fearing words, the Assyrian's general mocks these very things, speaking as though Hezekiah were present: "In whom do you trust? Is a battle fought with counsel and words of the lips?" Then he challenges him to meet him in arms. To him Hezekiah and those with him might answer: "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call on the name of the Lord our God." In Symmachus, instead of "In whom do you trust?" it reads like this: "What is this confidence in which you have trusted? I said: only a word of my lips for counsel, but strength for war."

Being a slanderer, the enemy tells lies about Hezekiah, saying: "Look, you trust in Egypt and in Pharaoh king of Egypt." Pharaoh proves worse than any enemy to those who lean on him and trust in him, because he does not know how to keep his agreements with those who flee to him for refuge. That is why he is compared to a staff of reed, which is both rotten by nature and harmful to those who lean on it. Having put the alliance with the Egyptians first, the Assyrian then mentions in passing the help from God, in which Hezekiah himself and all the people with him trusted. Moreover, since he did not know that the God of Israel is himself the God over all, he supposed that Hezekiah's overthrow of idolatrous error was an overthrow of what belonged to the God of the universe. That is why he says that they trust in vain in the God whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed. He was mistaken, and did not know that the things Hezekiah destroyed were alien to God.

After this, as though the Jews did not know how to ride, he said that he himself would give them two thousand horses, but that Hezekiah could not supply riders for them. Indeed, it was likely enough that the king, being God-fearing and obedient to the law, had for the law's sake taken no pains over cavalry. For the law of Moses says about the one who is to reign piously: "He shall not multiply horses for himself, and he shall not multiply wives for himself." But the Assyrian says: if you cannot supply riders for the horses we provide you, because you have no experience of fighting on horseback,

"How can you turn back the face of our governors?" Instead of "And how can you turn back to the face of the governors?" Symmachus has: "And how will you withstand the face of a single officer among the least of my lord's servants?" And if, he says, you trust in the horses and riders of the Egyptians because you have no cavalry of your own, know that the Egyptians themselves are our servants; so much more, then, are those who trust in them. But nothing he said was true. They neglected to provide themselves with horses not because they trusted in the Egyptians, but in order to keep the divine law.

Then, since the Assyrian's campaigns against Samaria and Damascus and very many other nations had succeeded, he reasons, as it seemed to him, saying: "Is it without God that I have taken all these? I would not have mastered so many if the one who holds authority over all had not delivered them into my hands. So it is in obedience to God's command that I have come up against your land too. For the Lord," he says, "said to me: Go up against this land and destroy it." And he says that clear proof that these things happened by God's command is that he captured Samaria and carried all Israel off into captivity: "Just as I took them, your brothers, only because God willed it, so in the same way, at his nod, I will take you as well." Whether he said this by inference, reasoning from his conquest of the people called God's people (I mean Israel), or whether he truly perceived that God had put it into his mind to attack the land of the Jews because of the transgressions they had committed, you yourself must consider.

Having said these things at the start, at the end of his speech Rabshakeh uses promises to urge the crowds standing on the very walls and towers of the city to hand it over on the terms he had offered. And since Hezekiah's piety had become known to all, he tries to discredit him before the people, saying: "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you by saying, God will deliver you." Earlier too he had said: "whose high places and altars he removed"; for he knew well that the people had delighted in these in the preceding period, during the reign of Ahaz. So he slandered Hezekiah to them as though they were still attached to these things, and by his very accusations he actually bore the strongest witness to his piety. For it is a fine thing to be slandered by enemies for things one might rightly take pride in before God. Then he adds: "Did the gods of the nations each deliver his own land?" And he adds: "Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? And where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim? Could they deliver Samaria from my hands?" By these words he showed why Samaria and Israel had been handed over to him: it was because they had given heed to many gods, contrary to their ancestral law. Then he reasons that, just as the gods of the nations, he says, could not rescue those who belonged to them, so neither will the God of Jerusalem be able to save those in it. He thought that the God honored in Jerusalem was no different from those whom the other nations mistakenly took for gods.

In response to such boasting and blasphemy from Rabshakeh, those who heard kept silent by royal order, answering nothing, because the king had commanded this. It was a sign of great wisdom and piety in Hezekiah to order that no answer be given to such insolence. For one who had uttered such things against God was no longer dealing with men, and it is not fitting for a devout person to argue with a blasphemer, lest he be provoked to fall into further blasphemies. That is why it is said somewhere: "Do not kindle the coals of a sinner." Indeed, it is not even holy to exchange words with such people, or to expect to do any good to those whose souls are incurably sick. Instead one should simply be fenced about, as if with armor, and secured on every side by silence, keeping the true words hidden within oneself and waiting for God to move against the blasphemers. When the king had given this order, the leaders of the people wisely did as they were commanded. We too should do the same in times of persecution, or in public debates with godless and blasphemous men.

Since the history is clear and needs no interpretation, we will say only this much about the passage. Those who had heard the blasphemies against God tore their garments, and so did King Hezekiah himself. They did so either because they had shared in impious words by hearing them, or because God had been blasphemed on their account. For they supposed that they themselves were to blame for this, since the enemy would not have been allowed to come right up to the gates of the city of God and speak so insolently unless they themselves were to blame. They did so, further, because they were anxious that they too might suffer the same things that Samaria and its people had suffered for their impieties.

Instead of his royal robes Hezekiah put on sackcloth, taking on the signs of mourning and affliction. Dressed this way, he went up through the middle of the city from the royal palace to the temple of God, and by showing himself humble before God in this guise he sought to obtain pity and mercy. The others, the priests of God, clothed in sackcloth instead of their priestly robes, he sent to the prophet Isaiah, instructing them to say: "Thus says Hezekiah", without adding "the king". For the occasion did not allow him to call himself that, humbled as he was by the present disaster. Then he says: since the present crisis is a day of rebuke, in that it exposes our sins, it is also a day of wrath; for when we are rebuked we are shown to have done things deserving wrath. To this we have now been handed over. We are like a woman in labor who is about to give birth but is too weak to endure the pains. For we cannot say: "Through fear of you, Lord, we conceived and were in labor and brought forth a spirit of salvation." For this reason we have sent to you, the man of God, begging that through you your God may come to our help in our hour of need. We do not even dare to call him our own God, but we know that he is truly your Lord and God. So we beseech him not to look upon our offenses or remember our sins, but to pay heed to the godless words of the enemy and to such overweening arrogance, and to do whatever pleases him, whether he wishes to pardon or to punish.

"But you, O prophet of God, remember that our whole people has already been taken captive by this same Assyrian, and do not hesitate to intercede with God for us who are left. For we believe and are convinced that your prayers on our behalf will do much to bring about our salvation." These were the words the king instructed them to say to the prophet.

But as soon as they arrived, Isaiah, anticipating what they had come to say, told them to report the prophecy that follows. In it God says that he will put a spirit into the Assyrian, and that, deceived by this spirit, he will return to his own land, where he will end his life by the sword. This is the first prophecy the text gives in the present history.

When the prophet had delivered this oracle, Rabshakeh, who had been so insolent, abruptly withdrew from the siege without having achieved anything and hurried off to meet the king of the Assyrians, God having unsettled his mind. The king of the Assyrians, who after Lachish was besieging Libnah, another city of Judea, was thrown into confusion by bad news, as God had said, and hurried off against the Ethiopians. Yet he did not drop his threat against the Jews. He sent messengers with a letter, ordering them first to tell Hezekiah by word of mouth what the letter contained, and then to hand over the letter itself. So, puffed up by so many successes, with these words and promises [?] deceiving, do not be ignorant [?]. Then once again the impious man let fly blasphemous words, boasting against God, and listed the nations that had fallen into his hands, their own gods having given them no help. The prophet had revealed this boasting of the Assyrian earlier, before the event took place, when he cried out and said: "Woe to the Assyrians: the rod of my anger and wrath is in their hands," and so on. "But he did not intend it so, nor did he reckon it so in his soul, but he said: As I did to Samaria and to the works of her hands, so I will do to Jerusalem and to her idols." After this he went on to pronounce the threat. These things had been spoken long before, but now they were being fulfilled in the present time.

Hezekiah, just as before, now again hurried to the house of God and showed the letter to God alone. Then he offered a supplication in prayer, saying that God alone is God and there is no other. Since he alone is the maker of heaven and earth and the whole world, and no one else shares this divine power with him, he alone would be the living God. The others are lifeless and dead, while he alone lives. He has a life that is without beginning and unbegotten, and he is acknowledged as the cause of everything that shares in life. Now, taking courage as one addressing a God who lives, who is present to all, and who hears his words, he asked him to show all the kingdoms of the world that he alone is God by saving those who have put their hope in him. This time, as the occasion allowed, the king set out such great and lofty theology in his prayer. Yet he had not prayed when he first went up to the house of God dressed in sackcloth, because of his overwhelming reverence; at that time he did not even dare to open his mouth before God. That is why he sent to the prophet and asked him to intercede for them in prayer to God. But now he had been granted an answer from God, and he believed the holy promises given through the prophet and the predictions against the enemy. So he boldly offered, in the words before us, this prayer, which contains pious teachings about God.

When the prophets of God foretold things that would happen long afterward, that was not how the people recognized them as prophets. For people did not consider them prophets on the basis of predictions whose outcome they did not know. Rather, it was from the proof they received when predictions were fulfilled at once that they came to trust their predictions about the future. Thus Samuel once foretold to Saul what would happen about the donkeys, another prophet foretold what would happen to a king who was sick, and yet another foretold the death of the king of Israel. This happened so that the people would not be drawn away, by a longing and craving to know the future, to the oracles and divinations of idolatrous error. Since their own God provided them with enough knowledge of the future, not through lifeless images but through his own prophets, they took no account of anything from outside. So in the present passage too, King Hezekiah, as one dear to God, went up to the house of God and offered the written supplication, and God answers him by sending his prophet Isaiah to him. Through him he gives Hezekiah this second oracle, showing that he had indeed heard the words of his prayer.

Then, as if speaking to the Assyrian, who had boasted greatly and threatened the people and the place, he makes a speech of this kind: “You there! Like a tyrant you threatened to do such things to the place I have guided. You thought your threats would frighten the city of God, which is incorruptible and for that reason likened to a virgin, and the people in it, who are called daughter Zion and daughter Jerusalem and are likened to a virgin because they are pure of all idolatry. But she, trusting in her own purity and in God her helper, despised and scorned your arrogant reasoning and those threats as worthless.” That is why Symmachus renders it: “The daughter of Zion has set you at nought and despised you; behind you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head.” For although she gave you no answer while you were uttering your blasphemous words, after you withdrew and went back, this daughter of Jerusalem, who is the same as the virgin daughter Zion, shook her head at you. And she did this no longer keeping silent but giving an answer; that is why she shook her head at you.

And the answer was this: “Whom have you reproached and provoked?” (in place of which the other translators rendered “have you blasphemed”) “or against whom have you raised your voice? You did not look up to heaven, or consider God the Most High, or reckon that he was in fact the Holy One of Israel, whom you reproached, disparaging and mocking him as one of the many gods that had fallen under your power. For you reckoned within yourself that by your own power and the multitude of your chariots you had gone up to the heights of the mountains and to the farthest parts of Lebanon, so as to cut down the beauty it displays in its many cedars and cypresses.” By these words he was hinting at the kingdoms among the other nations that were exalted and flourishing. For the great abundance of Lebanon in its very tall cedars and cypresses (or junipers, according to Symmachus, or firs, according to Aquila) he took as an image of the nations that were flourishing at that time. In place of “to the height of part of the forest,” Symmachus translated “to the height of its summit, to the forest of its Carmel.” Here too the text uses “forest” to hint at the unfruitful wood of the nations that do not know God. Having brought these under his hand, the Assyrian, thinking highly of himself, said: “I went up to the height of the mountains and to the farthest parts of Lebanon, and I cut down the height of its cedar and the beauty of its cypress, and I entered the height of part of the forest.”

He went further in his insolence, saying: “And I laid a bridge, and I dried up waters and every gathering of waters,” or, according to Symmachus: “I dug,” he says, “and drank water, and with the sole of my foot I dried up all the rivers that were confined.” You see how here too the text mentions waters and rivers being made to vanish by the Assyrian. By these, I think, it signifies the multitudes among the nations and their teachings about gods, by which they thought souls were nourished. He prided himself on having made desolation with the tread of his foot, boasting of nothing good, but of the desolation of the lands he had trodden and of the destruction of the beauty of Lebanon already described.

“But you said these things to yourself, reckoning in your own mind that it was by the multitude of your chariots that you had accomplished so much. I say to you: Do not deceive yourself; it is not by your own power that you have overcome all these. It was I who decreed these things against them, even if you did not know it, even if you did not hear my counsel from of old. For long ago, from ancient days, I myself determined that these things should be carried out through you against the godless and impious nations. And now I have shown my counsel in deeds, raising you up to destroy those who deserved punishment, and using you as a sign, to lay waste nations and to uproot those who dwelt in fortified cities, which formerly I guarded and preserved.

“But since they acted impiously and did not acknowledge their own Savior, I let go of them and handed them over to you for punishment, and at once they became desolate, deprived of my care. That is why they immediately withered and became like dry grass on the housetops and like couch grass. This, at any rate, was the cause of their destruction: they bore no good fruit of piety. That is why they were likened not to a vine or an olive or any fruitful plant, but to dry grass and couch grass, when they were most justly handed over into your hand. But you, ruler of the Assyrians, did not think in this way; your reasoning was godless and impious, and you supposed you would take the city dedicated to me, God, just like the others that do not know God. But since I know your thoughts, and the going out and coming in of your reasonings, I say this further to you: the rage you have used against the people that bears my name has not escaped me; your bitterness has come up to me” (or, according to Symmachus, “your arrogance has come up into my ears”). “Since, then, you have dared such things, hear now, you there, what awaits you: I will put such a muzzle on your mouth that it will grip your very nose and choke you, so that you no longer utter such things.” According to Symmachus: “And I will put,” he says, “a ring in your nostril and a bridle on your lips,” so that you may not go where you please, but be dragged back even against your will; “for you will have to turn back by the road on which you made your journey here.”

These things, then, were spoken as if to the ruler of the Assyrians; though he is not present in body, let them nevertheless be addressed to all. “But since I must also answer you, Hezekiah, concerning the prayers you have made, receive now the word addressed to you. You have heard what was said about the ruler of the Assyrians; and if you need a sign to confirm my words, know that this present year you will have for food what the earth puts forth of itself, because the land cannot be farmed as usual on account of the enemies’ invasion. So eat this year what you have sown.” In place of “what you have sown,” all the other translators rendered “what grows of itself.” “And in the coming year likewise eat what is left over from the previous year.” In place of “in the second year, the remainder,” Aquila rendered “and in the second year, what springs up of itself,” Symmachus “and in the second year, from the trees,” and Theodotion “and in the second year, what springs up of itself.” “For these two years you will be in straits because the land cannot be farmed as usual. In the third year you will be filled with every abundance: sow, then, and reap, and plant vineyards and eat their fruit. Know well that you who are left in Judea after the captivity of the multitude in Samaria will continue in peace, if, in keeping with my counsel, you put down a firm root of godliness in your souls and render to me the holy fruit of my cultivation, looking upward to me.” Thus, then, those left in Jerusalem will be saved, if they become fruitful before him and render the fruits that are worthy of them. For the Lord, being zealous for the city dedicated to him as his own and for the people that bears his name, will grant all these things.

“And neither the king of the Assyrians nor anyone else will set foot in the city, nor will anyone be permitted to make war against it. For I myself, as for my own city, will shield and save both it and its inhabitants, since this befits me, being God. So I will do these things for my own sake, and not because those who are helped are worthy. And if I must also honor a man, so as to say that I am protecting the city for his sake, I will guard the city for the sake of David my servant” (or, according to the other translators, “my slave”), the founder of the city and the first king of those who arose there, so that others too, learning how great an honor this God-loving man has received from me, may become his emulators and imitators of his godliness.

In this way, then, the words of God were announced through Isaiah the prophet to King Hezekiah. And not long after, immediately upon these utterances, a fearful and divine deed followed the words: by no human means, myriads of men were all at once found lying dead, struck down by the hand of a single angel. For he was mighty enough to serve the judgment of God and to slay such multitudes of the enemy, so that their king might learn by experience what kind of God he was blaspheming. It was for this reason that, while so many perished, he did not perish with them: so that, having witnessed what was done, he might muzzle his godless tongue. That is why it had been said in the words of God: “And I will put a muzzle in your nose and a bridle on your lips,” so that he would not dare to utter such things. Nevertheless, though he did not share the fate of the multitude for the reason stated (the same reason for which Pharaoh too was preserved as a witness while the rest of the Egyptians were punished), yet when he reached his own land he found his own sons to be his murderers.

God, who said, “I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal,” struck the enemies with just judgment through a single angel, and healed the God-loving king and made him alive, rescuing him from death by his own hand. Fittingly, then, the text noted: “At that time Hezekiah was sick unto death” (or, according to Aquila, “to dying,” or, according to the others, “to death”). For at the very time when the Assyrians suffered what was described above, the time of death came upon Hezekiah. But God, wishing to save him, did not leave hidden the end that his sickness was to bring. So, providing him with occasions of salvation, he made the outcome of the illness plain to him through the prophet, so that, learning it, he might pray, and having prayed might obtain an addition of life even beyond the death appointed for him. The text thus teaches us that there is no necessity of fate governing human life, and no unalterable time of death fixed for human beings. Rather, God himself, who rules all things, is the cause both of life and of death. For reasons that he alone knows, he brings each of those who enter life into it at this time or that, and gathers them in after so many or so many years and through this kind of death or that. And to him alone it is possible to call back even those who are, so to speak, at the very gates of death: as now he saved Hezekiah from a deadly illness and granted him an addition of life of fifteen whole years, and as he made others, as many as the divine Scripture presents, come back to life even after they had died. So the doctrines about fate are utterly refuted, since the God who is over all rules even necessity itself and every substance and nature.

Knowing these things, Hezekiah, when he was healthy in body, hastened to the temple of God and there called upon God to be the Savior of himself, of the people, and of the city. But since his illness at that time kept him from doing this, he sent up his prayer to God from his very bed, convinced that God is present everywhere and hears everyone who is godly. Then, having only mentioned with great boldness that he had lived in a way pleasing to him, he did not go on to beg to be spared death or ask for years of life. Knowing that God discerns the thoughts of his mind, he left the outcome of his prayer to God’s will, and added great weeping besides, a point worth attending to. Why ever did the godly man resort to this, when he ought to have pictured good hopes for himself after death, especially as he was calling God himself to witness, with a good conscience, that he had lived pleasingly to him in truth and with a true heart?

The cause of his weeping he himself will explain further on. Meanwhile the prophet, as soon as the king had prayed to God, was sent by God a second time and said: “Thus says the Lord, the God of David your father.” God called David his father, giving him the highest testimony, as one worthy to be enrolled under that God-loving father because of the likeness of their ways. That is why in the Histories too he is recorded as having done what was right in all things, as David had. So God says through the prophet: “I have heard your prayer and I have seen your tears.” For the words of his prayer, not wrapped up in many words, were worthy of God’s hearing, and his weeping, done reasonably and of necessity at the right moment, drew God’s watchful eyes toward him and moved his love for humankind. So he grants him an addition of life, showing in deed that death is fixed for human beings neither by an inflexible [?] nature nor by inexorable necessity.

And not only years of life, but, as God, abundantly beyond that, he promises him a good life in a stable and peaceful existence, undertaking to deliver both him and the people with him and the city from the hand of the enemy; and he gave him a sign to confirm what had been said, through another wonder. So he says: “And this shall be the sign to you from the Lord, that God will do this thing: Behold, I turn back the shadow of the steps which the sun has gone down, the ten steps of the house of your father; I will turn back the sun the ten steps.” According to Symmachus: “Behold,” he says, “I will make the shadow of the steps which the sun has gone down on the sundial of Ahaz your father run back ten steps backward.” How this was the house of Hezekiah’s father — I mean Ahaz, an idolater — the house still shown even now in Jerusalem near the enclosure of the temple, which people still call Hezekiah’s, I myself cannot say. So I necessarily turned my attention to Symmachus’s translation, and found the place named not the house of Ahaz but the sundial of Ahaz. Perhaps the flight of steps in that place had been made into a sundial by Ahaz, who used to mark the hours of the day by the sun’s rays falling on them. According to Aquila it is called “the ascents of Ahaz,” and according to Theodotion “on the steps of Ahaz.” None of the translators attests that the place was the house of Ahaz; it is either a sundial or an ascent, perhaps because Ahaz used it as his entrance into the enclosure. There the sun, having advanced in step with the revolution of the heavens, wondrously went backward from west to east and ran a second course through the same hours. The marvel was a sign that Hezekiah too would run back from the setting of the sun to a second life.

The length of that day was doubled in hours. And since the king had received God’s promise together with the miracle, he composes a word of thanksgiving. That is why, according to Aquila, it is written: “A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah when he was sick, and he lived after his sickness”; and according to Theodotion it is called “a writing of Hezekiah king of Judah”; but in none of them is it called a prayer.

So it is fitting to call the present writing a word of thanksgiving. In it he says: “I said: In the height of my days I shall go into the gates of Hades” (or “I said: In the fullness of my days,” according to Aquila; or “I said: When I was sick,” according to Theodotion; and according to Symmachus, “I said: When my days were silenced”). “For seeing myself already drawing near to the gates of death, I despaired and gave up hope of my life among men. So I said: I shall leave behind the remaining years. And this too I said within myself: that, deprived of life, I would not see the salvation of God in the land of the living.” According to Symmachus: “I shall not see,” he says, “the Lord in the land of the living.” “These things I said to myself,” he says, “considering whether I might perhaps be unworthy of the life with God after death and of the portion of those who live with him, where the salvation of God was.” For he was not ignorant of the oracle in the Psalms that says: “Return, O my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you… I will be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living,” and again: “I will be pleasing to the Lord in the light of the living.” He knew, then, of another land of the living besides the present life, and of the soul’s rest with God, and of a light, not that of the sun but that of those who live with God; and he was anxious lest he be deprived of these and fall away from the salvation of God, which was his Christ. Naturally, then, being in anguish over what follows departure from life, he reminds God of his own godliness and with weeping entreated him that he might not fall away from the land of the living. He was in the utmost anguish over this too: that after death he might not see a man of God, and might not rest with the blessed and God-loving souls.

Besides what has been said, this too grieved Hezekiah: that he had no successor from his own seed, since no child had yet been born to him at the time he said these things. Since, then, he was about to die childless, leaving no successor from whom the salvation of humankind was expected to come, he naturally lamented as if he were being deprived of the birth of Christ from the seed of David. “I was saying within myself,” he says, “that my spirit had gone out and departed like one who has pitched a tent and then takes the tent down.” He calls the body a tent, since the divine Apostle too named it a tent, saying: “We who are in this tent groan, being burdened”; and by the taking down of the tent he means the laying aside of the body, which the spirit brought about by dissolving and leaving the body. “And like the web of a weaver who is now cutting off the cloth, so the fabric of my life and of my whole existence was drawing to its end, being cut off.” For each of the saints weaves a robe and puts adornment on his own soul through his own deeds.
