That is why he likened himself to a weaver’s web, and added “nearing the cutting off,” because of the death that had come upon him, as he says: “I was handed over as if to a man-eating lion, which meanwhile, through the illness laid upon me, crushed all my bones all night and all day, and was all but about to swallow me whole. Yet even in these straits I did not lose heart or depart from my God; but, recovering myself with faith and good hope, I gave myself over to weeping and lamentation and prayer.”

“Then like a swallow I cried out, lamenting, and like a dove I moaned, weeping. And as I prayed persistently,” he says, “and pressed on in supplication to God, my eyes grew weary from looking to the height of heaven toward the Lord. But he did not delay; he rescued me and took away the anguish of my soul,” all but making good the very word he promised to his saints when he said: “While you are still speaking I will say: Behold, I am here.”

“So, then, he also rescued my soul from death. For it was about my soul that I made my plea and on its behalf that I entreated him in prayer; for I was most concerned for my soul, that it not be swallowed up by death. But you heard me, O Lord, and raised me up, and, having been comforted, I lived.” According to Symmachus: “You made me flourish again,” he says, “and gave me life, and changed my bitterness into peace, and you chose my soul,” snatching it away from the very gates of death, which it had already reached, so that it would not perish with the perdition of the soul. “And you did this not because I was worthy of these things — for I myself was full of many sins — but these things came about by your mercy and your love for humankind. So you cast my sins far behind you and counted me worthy of these things, rescuing me from the death of the soul, so that it would not perish, deprived of the land of the living that is with you, dragged down to the depth of Hades and numbered among the souls of the ungodly.

“For those in Hades will not praise you, nor will those in Hades hope for your mercy”; for this is the place of the ungodly. “So, my soul having been freed from it, I joyfully render thanksgiving to God. But the land of those who live with God will receive those who praise him; there I believe I too will be from now on, since your grace has granted me this.

“And even if succession had formerly failed in my family, yet now, taking courage in your mercy, I believe that from this day I shall beget children who will proclaim your righteousness. So I will not cease to bless you all the days of my life. And this I will do before the house of God, attending upon you continually and never parted from your sanctuary.” This is what Hezekiah’s writing contained. After it, when seven years had passed, a son, Manasseh, was born to him. This is clear from the fact that fifteen years were added to his life after the illness, and that when he died his son succeeded him at the age of eight, as the book of the Histories records.

After this, another affliction, I think, befell Hezekiah’s body — it was a localized sore. So that one should not ask everything, even the smallest things, of God, the prophet advises him to use a cake of figs and to plaster the sore with it, teaching that the remedies people devise for treating the body are by no means always to be rejected. There are times when one should use them too, since the prophet himself advised doing so. All the other translators also called what was healed by the fig cake a sore. But the first affliction was not a sore; it was an illness, a sickness unto death. So in that case weeping and prayers and God’s care were called upon, but for the localized sore, bodily treatment, which the prophet suggested. The king, however, does not want the fig cake to be the sign of his healing, but says: “This shall be the sign of my salvation: to go up to the house of God. For it is enough for me to be able to go up and worship my Savior, entering within his house. This will be better for me than any good thing, while the sore is of no concern to me, unless it should keep me from entering the house of God.”

As we were examining and investigating together the matters in the present passages, the teacher of the Jews said that Hezekiah fell ill because he had not sung a song of thanksgiving to God for the fall of the Assyrians, as Moses sang at the destruction of the Egyptians, Deborah at the destruction of Sisera, and Hannah at the birth of Samuel. Because Hezekiah had not done this, he fell into the illness. The Babylonian king learned of his recovery from the illness and sent men to him, and not idly: it happened that the day on which the sign of the sun's turning back took place lasted twice its usual number of hours. This did not escape the notice of the Babylonians, who were skilled in the observation of the stars. And since they made the sun a god and saw that it had been turned back by a greater power, they sought the cause of this. Then, when by diligent inquiry they learned that the God of the Hebrews was great, the creator of the whole world, and learned also of the illness of King Hezekiah, on account of which the miracle had happened, the king was understandably astounded at what had been done and wished to make friendship with Hezekiah as with a man beloved of God. So much for the Hebrew.

But I observe that all these things happened within one and the same year: I mean the Assyrian's invasion of Judea, the blow struck against the Assyrians through an angel of God, Sennacherib's flight, the uprising of his sons, and the destruction, passed over in silence, of the son who succeeded him. All these things, I think, put sober reflection into Merodach-baladan, who sprang from another line and was king of Babylon and of the nation of the Chaldeans. For it is likely that he profited from knowing these things, so as no longer to embrace enmity or war, but friendship with a king so beloved of God that the deliverance from his illness, granted by God, had come to him in a wondrous way. That these things happened at one and the same time you may learn by noting that the Assyrian's invasion took place in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah's reign; and he died having reigned twenty-nine years in all, of which fifteen were added to him after the illness. So he fell ill in the fourteenth year, and all the rest, which came before the illness, was accomplished in that same period. So it was the report of all these things together that drew the king of the Babylonians to friendship with Hezekiah, so that he even sent him gifts, envoys and letters.

At this Hezekiah, giving way to a human weakness, rejoices at their welcome and, seized by excessive vanity, uncovers to the envoys his treasuries and the house of nechotha, which Aquila and Symmachus rendered "the house of spices." Moreover, he shows them the silver and the gold, the spices and the fine ointment, and all the storehouses of his vessels; for so Symmachus translated.

Then, since he ought not to have uncovered the wealth there to foreign men so tastelessly and heedlessly, the prophet came to him and foretold that there would be a time when these very Babylonians would take everything and carry it off to their own land. He added also that from his sons, who did not yet exist but were to be born of him, they would make eunuchs by castration, and would make them stand in attendance on their own kings. Hearing this, Hezekiah answered with reverence and piety alike that every word God speaks is good, even if men think it grievous. But he asked that what had been threatened should not happen in his lifetime, but that there should be peace and righteousness, or according to the other translators peace and truth, in his days.

On this point again the Hebrew said that God did not approve of Hezekiah's choice; for to have made a request on his own behalf while taking no account of the people appeared blameworthy to God. That, he said, is why the prophet next adds: "Comfort, comfort my people, says God." For even if this man, he says, being self-loving, made his request out of concern for himself and made no mention of the people, yet God, caring for his own people, commands those who are able to do so to comfort it.

The words "Priests, comfort the people" we have found neither in the Hebrew nor among the other translators, and for this reason they are marked with an obelus in the Septuagint as well. In Symmachus, at any rate, it reads: "Console, console my people, says your God; encourage the heart of Jerusalem," and the others have words equivalent to this. It is worth considering who those are whom the word commands to comfort the people, what the heart of Jerusalem is, and what sort of Jerusalem we must understand, one that has a heart like some living creature; for the word that says "Speak to the heart of Jerusalem" clearly presents it as animate and rational. Now one could say that Jerusalem is the people dwelling in it, as we often name a city in place of its inhabitants; but here the word itself mentions the people, saying "Comfort my people," and then separately adds "Speak to the heart of Jerusalem." So it is time to determine who are those commanded to comfort, which is the people being comforted, and what the heart of Jerusalem is. Those who comfort would be those who have received the Spirit, the Comforter, namely the apostles and disciples of our Savior, the evangelists, and those like them, to whom the Savior said: "And I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Comforter, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth"; and again: "But when the Comforter comes, the Holy Spirit whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things"; and again: "When the Comforter comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me"; and again: "And it is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you." All, therefore, who have received the Spirit, the Comforter, are commanded to comfort the people of God, but not Israel, nor Jacob, nor Judah. What people of God there was besides the Jewish nation the prophet Zechariah will teach, when he says: "Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming and will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations will flee to the Lord on that day and will become a people to him, and they will dwell in your midst, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you." By these words many nations are clearly declared to be about to become God's people. And it is the Lord who says this, sent by another Lord, and foretelling his own coming among men. Just as the people of God has been identified, so the heart of Jerusalem will be understood as the higher rank of the people. For as in a body the heart is the most governing part of the whole, so also in the body of the church the most governing rank may fittingly be called the heart of the whole: that is, the rank of the more rational, who excel in understanding, intelligence and reasoning. If, then, it is said, "Speak to the heart of Jerusalem," the word must be taken as though it said more plainly: "Speak to the intelligent and more rational among the people of God." To these, then, the priests are commanded to speak, and to comfort the rest of the people as needing comfort and consolation.

Having thus brought to a close the subject of the history of Hezekiah, the prophecy begins the gospel message from a new starting point, crying out to those who have received the Spirit of Christ, the Comforter: "Comfort, comfort my people, says God." For it commands them to comfort all who are worthy to be called his people, chosen out of all the nations. This the apostles indeed did, as Paul teaches when he says: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. For as the sufferings of Christ abound to us, so through Christ our comfort also abounds. If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation, which is at work in the patient endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer; and our hope for you is firm, for we know that as you share in the sufferings, so you share also in the comfort." You see at what length he gave his account of comfort; and elsewhere, as though obeying the prophetic command, he cried out: "We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God"; and again: "I, the prisoner in Christ Jesus, appeal to you." In the same way the other disciples of Christ too, being comforters, comforted the people of God; and they also spoke to the heart of Jerusalem, that is, Jerusalem understood spiritually, I mean the higher rank of the body of the people, or, on another interpretation, to the more rational of those who lived in Jerusalem itself. For since the rest of the multitude was carnal and like a very gross body, those among them who excelled in understanding, intelligence and thought might fittingly be understood as the heart of Jerusalem. To them also he wishes those who have received the Spirit of comfort to speak, and to comfort them, since they are the heart of Jerusalem, by proclaiming to them too the good news of the forgiveness of sins, because of the prophecy about Christ's coming that follows next. So he wants those just described to speak in secret to the heart of Jerusalem and to persuade it that its humiliation has ended and its sin has been loosed; for indeed it has endured double punishment for the sins it committed. And it is fitting that from now on it should receive comfort and consolation because of the appearing of the common Savior of all men, which has shone upon our life. You might say that a double punishment came upon the heart of Jerusalem: in historical fact, the people meant here shared in the miseries of the multitude, being humbled under foreign nations, and in their minds they also punished themselves, mourning the rejection of the multitude and lamenting the fall and destruction of the many. Moreover, Jerusalem, besieged a second time so that the temple in it was razed to the ground, endured a double penalty for the impieties dared within it.

Nevertheless, the appearing of the Savior who is proclaimed next imparted comfort also to the understanding ones in it, whom he called the heart. What that comfort was he shows next, saying: "A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God." To this he adds: "and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God"; that is, the gospel proclamation. And this was the comfort: the oracle that the salvation of God would be made known to all men. Long ago Moses led the people of the Jews through the wilderness, but now he mentions another wilderness and a man crying in it, or according to Aquila, "a voice of one calling in the wilderness." Who was this man crying in the wilderness? What sort of wilderness was it? And to whom were the words "Prepare the way of the Lord and make straight his paths" spoken? It was natural for those who heard these things to inquire, to look for the fulfilment of the prophecy, and to pray that they might see the prophesied salvation of God. Hence, because those versed in the prophetic words expected these things to come to pass, those sent to John by the chief priests and teachers of the people asked him who he was and inquired whether he might be the Christ, or Elijah, or the Prophet. He said he was none of these; and when they asked him further, saying, "Tell us, then, who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?", he gave them this answer: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said." It was enough for them to hear "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness," since they knew the prophecy accurately and were expecting its fulfilment, which he taught was being fulfilled in himself. He presented himself as the one crying in the wilderness and showed that the wilderness in which he spent his time was a different one from that of Moses. And he signified that the salvation of God, which according to the prophecy was to be made known to all flesh, was already at the doors. When the prophecy says, "A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord," this is the gospel proclamation, or this new comfort, which seeks that the salvation of God should be made known to all men.

It showed clearly that the things foretold would happen not in Jerusalem but in the wilderness: I mean that the glory of the Lord would be seen and that the salvation of God would be made known to all flesh. These things were fulfilled historically and literally in John the Baptist, who proclaimed the saving manifestation of God in the wilderness of the Jordan, where the salvation of God was also seen. Christ himself and his glory became known to all when, at his baptism, the heavens were opened, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon him, and the Father's voice came bearing witness to the Son: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." All these were signs of the saving glory, accomplished in the wilderness of the Jordan and witnessed by John the Baptist. Yet in the spiritual sense the prophecy was also referred to the church from the nations, long a wilderness with respect to God, in which even to this day the same voice cries, proclaiming the salvation of God and preparing the ears of those who come forward to receive the glory of God the Word, who was in the beginning with God. He did not call the one crying in the wilderness [?] or "word," but for the present a "voice" that prepares for the perfect Word who was to appear. Preparing men's souls for him, the voice cries that they must prepare the way of the Lord and make straight the paths of our God; or according to Symmachus, "A voice in the wilderness said: Make ready the way of the Lord, level a road in the trackless place for our God." For this was said on the understanding that God was about to come and dwell in the wilderness, in the land that from of old had been untrodden by God. All the nations were a wilderness, empty of the knowledge of God, and untrodden by all God's righteous men and prophets. Therefore the voice commands that a road be made ready for the Word of God and that the trackless, rough place be made level, so that our God may come and set foot there; and it adds "our," for it says, "make straight the paths of our God." The one crying in the wilderness says this as though addressing others, for countless people, even from foreign nations, came to John's baptism; and the gospel word in the church likewise addresses these words to the nations throughout the whole world.

Then he rouses the souls brought low in the depths of wickedness, adding: "Every valley shall be filled"; and he teaches that the proud souls, exalted against the knowledge of God, will suffer the opposite, saying: "and every mountain and hill shall be brought low." Moreover, he says, "the crooked shall become straight," and he commands the rough soul to become smooth, so that it may be fit to receive God when he comes upon it. He necessarily commanded all these things to be done, because of the reason that follows, which he gives next, saying: "And the glory of the Lord shall be seen," or according to the other translators, "shall be revealed." To whom it will be revealed he makes clear by adding: "and all flesh shall see the salvation of God." Now "flesh" means all men who were merely fleshly and in no way partakers of the Holy Spirit. Moses also shows this, recording God as saying: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." That all flesh, then, was to come to know the salvation of God, the voice crying out in the wilderness taught through its first proclamation; for he who made the promise does not lie.

Yet the disobedience and unbelief of the Jewish people did not escape the prophetic Spirit. Therefore the same voice makes a second proclamation, crying out and saying: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass." Such, indeed, is the nature of all flesh, and of the man who bears the image of the earthly, I mean the one who loves the body and lives according to the flesh. Like the grass of the earth and its lovely flowers, he flourishes and is beautiful for a short time; then before long he withers away because of his fluid and unstable nature, as Scripture teaches, saying: "The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen." These things the prophecy taught in more general terms; but next the Hebrew text, making specific mention of the Jewish people, adds: "Surely the people is grass; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen." In place of "But the word of our God abides forever," Symmachus said: "But the word of our God will stand forever." These things the voice in the wilderness foretold about God the Word; I mean John, teaching about Christ that he alone will stand forever, and that he will keep those who stand with him and remain with him, those who have received his salvation.

These words too follow very closely the sense of what was said before, fittingly mentioning the evangelists and announcing God's coming to men, after what was said about the voice crying in the wilderness. For the prophecy about John the Baptist was followed by the word about the Savior's evangelists and the declaration of his manifestation as God. According to the other translators, instead of "he who brings good news" the text reads "she who brings good news." Symmachus, at any rate, says: "Go up for yourself onto a high mountain, Zion, you who bring good news; lift up your voice on high, Jerusalem, you who bring good news; lift it up, do not fear." Observe that here too the text regards Zion and Jerusalem as animate and living; for it commanded her to go up by herself onto a high mountain and to lift up her voice in announcing the good news of God's coming. Who, then, is this Zion who goes up onto a high mountain other than herself? For she too was a mountain, as Scripture shows when it says, "This Mount Zion, in which you have dwelt," and as the Apostle says, "You have come to Mount Zion." Surely she is the one earlier named the heart of Jerusalem. And is it not perhaps the apostolic choir, chosen out of the former people from the circumcision, that is signified here in this way? For this is the Zion and Jerusalem that has received the salvation of God, being itself lifted on high and likened to the mountain of God, his only-begotten Word; and she is commanded to go up onto a high mountain and proclaim the saving word as good news. Indeed, the gospel choir and the holy souls lifted on high in a virtuous disposition, which are called Zion and Jerusalem, are commanded to go up onto the high mountain of the divinity of God's Only-begotten, and from there, from on high, to proclaim the good news and preach to all men the coming on earth of the Christ of God.

Then, since many were likely to rise up against them, he necessarily adds: "Lift it up, do not fear." Then, in addition to what came before, he commands them to announce to the cities of Judah, I mean the Jewish synagogues, that the God long proclaimed through the prophets as one who would come and dwell among men had come: the Lord himself, whom they had long awaited.

They are also to announce that he will come again and make his second coming with great strength, and that his arm will come with lordship, as if he said more plainly, "with a master's and lord's authority." And he adds: "Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him." These words concern the second coming of Christ, in which he will come in glory to render to each according to his works. This he will do as Master and Lord, with strength and with what is called his arm.

But what is added next, "Like a shepherd he will tend his flock," was fulfilled at his first coming. Then he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and was found in fashion as a man; and, as a shepherd puts on a sheepskin, he put on the human body and tended his flock, or according to Symmachus, "fed his herd." For it says that he will tend his flock not as Lord with strength, nor as an arm with his own lordship and mastery, but as a shepherd. He himself bore witness to this in the Gospels, saying: "I am the good shepherd; I know my own and my own know me, and I lay down my life for the sheep." "And in his arm," it says, "he will gather lambs." His arm was the divinity dwelling in the visible body, through which he is said to gather lambs and to comfort those that are with young. By lambs he means the newborn, those reborn in Christ; by those with young he means the souls that had long been pregnant and in labor through the hope of his coming, whom he is said to comfort through his coming. That is why it says: "and he will comfort those that are with young." In another sense, too, the souls of his apostles, pregnant and in labor with those who were being reborn in Christ through them, had him as their comforter. You will understand this from a single one of them, who says: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." You see how Paul was in labor for those who were his disciples. In the same way, then, the other apostles too, like mothers carrying children in the womb, were in labor with those being reborn in Christ through them, in anguish lest anyone should become a miscarriage, slipping away and being aborted from formation and perfection in Christ. That is why the shepherd mentioned before is said to comfort them.

The wise of this age have attributed the universe to spontaneity, to some chance concurrence of nature, to the necessity of fate. The present passage shows that nothing that exists is by chance, but that all things have been constituted in measure and number by the Lord of whom it speaks. It shows that the watery substance, which most people consider a measureless sea, together with springs, rivers and torrents, has been measured by him. They are as many in quantity as he saw fit to establish for the sufficient need of the present order, so that they neither exceed what is necessary nor fall short of what is needed. Again, he himself measured the vast heaven, so immense a vault, with his own span, neither stretching it beyond what is proportionate to the compass of the universe nor shrinking and contracting it below what is fitting. He uses figuratively the measures familiar among us, so that from names known and familiar to us we may come to understand the teaching about the things signified. Then, since "from the greatness and beauty of created things the Creator is correspondingly perceived," he fittingly makes things that to us are exceedingly great seem small by comparing them with what is greater, and so summons us to a conception of him who constituted all things. He says, then, that the heaven, so great, which encompasses the whole world, is so small in God's sight that it seems to be measured by the span of a hand. Likewise the whole element of the earth is so very small in his sight that it seems to be held together in his handful. Instead of "Who measured the water with his hand," Aquila said, "Who measured out waters in his finger-span." He compares to the finger-span, the very smallest measure we take with our fingers, a small portion of God's power, by which things so great and of such a kind have been measured. Further, he says, if anyone has supposed that the mountains on earth, the hills and the valleys came to be without any reason, let him know that he is mistaken, since nothing among existing things exists at random and without reason. Indeed, the sizes and differences of the mountains over the whole earth, their heights, depths and lengths, received their constitution from the wisdom of God for the benefit of the universe. Likewise the elevations and masses of the hills have proportions fitting and corresponding to the proportion of the whole, so that their weights are balanced like the pans on a pair of scales, suitably to the proportion of the whole. Instead of "and the valleys in a balance," the other translators have rendered "and the hills."

To these words he adds: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, and who has been his counselor?" The passage gives this as the answer to the question that said: "Who measured the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth with a handful? Who set the mountains by weight and the valleys in a balance?" He had asked who it was that brought these things into being and who arranged them by measure and weight. Accordingly he answers that no one did, except the one Mind alone, which is incomprehensible to all. Therefore he adds: "Who has known the mind of the Lord," the mind that made all the things mentioned? It needed no counselor and took advice from no one. By its own wisdom and with ineffable power it brought things that in no way existed out of non-being into being.

Next, he teaches all those from the nations who have been called to the grace of the gospel, to whom the voice crying in the wilderness was also announcing the good news of God's salvation in the preceding words, that all the nations that do not know God are nothing. In heaven, in the air and beyond heaven there are rational spirits, divine powers and a countless multitude of God's ministers who surround the King of all. Compared with these, he says, the nations on earth that do not know God are like a tiny drop that has trickled off from the full company of divine rational beings. The same nations are like a scale tipped by the slightest inclination of weight, because they have been dragged down by the weight of wickedness into godless sin. Indeed, they differ in nothing from spittle that has been spat out and mixed with the dust of the earth. They have suffered the same fate as spittle: they are rational, but they have become mixed up with ignorance of God and with every kind of impiety.

Therefore he also teaches that all their worship by blood and sacrifices has nothing worthy of God. Not even if one were to offer all the four-footed beasts of the earth, nor if all Lebanon and the timber of everything that grows on it were taken for the whole burnt offering of the victims, would one have anything worthy of God. To this he adds next: "And all the nations are as nothing and have been reckoned as nothing." Which nations are these but those that do not know God and cling to the error of idolatry? These are the ones who were said to be reckoned as a drop from a bucket, as the tipping of a scale, and as spittle.

Next he rebukes these very people, saying: "To whom have you likened the Lord, and with what likeness have you likened him? Did a craftsman make an image, or did a goldsmith melt gold and overlay it with gold?" and so on. He added these words fittingly after setting forth the theology concerning Christ, in order to proclaim to the nations how great was he who measured the water with his hand, the heaven with a span and all the earth with a handful, and established the mountains by weight and the valleys in a balance. With these things he necessarily contrasts the error that had previously gripped the nations, turning them away from it and calling them to the knowledge of the one of whom he speaks. In this way the prophetic Spirit smooths the souls of the nations for the gospel proclamation, scouring them and, as it were, cleansing them of the superstition handed down from their fathers.

Then, having taught what sort of error it was among the nations to worship lifeless wooden images, he cries out to the ears of all, saying: "Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been told to you from the beginning?" Even if you were not taught by your fathers, yet now at least, having been brought to your senses, receive the benefit and learn who it is that holds the foundations of the earth. If you cannot raise your mind up to heaven, then at least, he says, consider the earth on which you spend your lives. Inquire on what it has been set, and who it is that keeps so great an element steady and unshaken. Speaking as a natural philosopher about the shape of the earth, he makes known that it is spherical. That is why he called it a circle, saying: "he who holds the circle of the earth." But he also urges us to know the Word of God who holds all things together, who, besides everything else, holds together so great an element as the earth, so that it neither falls apart nor moves from its proper seat. And who, he says, is it that scattered so many nations over the earth that they are compared to grasshoppers because of the smallness of their bodies? Then, rising again from the earth in his discourse, he urges everyone to marvel at the vault of heaven and at the hemisphere above the earth, suspended like a vaulted ceiling. He urges them to consider how great is the power of the one who established the heaven, and to reflect that he did not establish it idly. Like a tent it is spread out above over all things within heaven, while for those beyond heaven it has been laid beneath them as a divine dwelling. Just as, speaking as a natural philosopher, he called the element of the earth a circle, so he likened the hemisphere above the earth to the arch of a vault, comparing the expanse of heaven to a tent stretched out. And just as he made provision for the tent, so he also made provision for those who dwell within the tent.

Therefore, at various times and seasons, he sets rulers over the people living on the earth, providing rulers suited to those they rule. That is why he adds: "who gives rulers to rule for nothing." By "nothing" he means mortal life. Or else he teaches that the earth itself is as nothing, since he says next: "and he made the earth as nothing." Then he adds: "For they shall not plant, nor shall they sow, nor shall their root take root in the earth." All this is said about those who ruled and played the tyrant on earth in their own times, since they would come to such an end.

"Such are they," he says, "but to whom have you likened me, the God of the universe, that I should be exalted?" says the Holy One. "Lift up your eyes on high and see: who has displayed all these things?" It is not possible to count them or to describe them one by one. It is enough to see with one's eyes the magnitudes and beauties, the harmony and the motion of the universe, and from beholding these to marvel at the Creator of all. It is enough to know and recognize the one who, through times and generations, brings forth his own array in order and number, as if from storehouses and treasuries of his own, or, according to the other translators, "his host." That is why he is named Lord Sabaoth, which is translated "Lord of hosts." For angelic hosts, ranked as under a great king, administer his whole world. No one knows their names except him alone, who honored them with names that suit their natures. So too the particular titles of the divine spirits and archangels, and of the incorporeal powers beyond heaven that minister to God, whatever they may be, are incomprehensible and unknown to us. Therefore, when they are called by name by him alone, they obey. Because of his great glory and surpassing strength none of those called disobeys, but all serve at his nod.

After this account of God, the passage rebukes those who think that God does not watch over their actions, as many among the former people supposed. Therefore he addresses them directly, saying: Why do you reason this way within yourself and dare to say that your way has escaped God's notice, and that you are not subject to judgment because he does not know what you do? Have you not heard what was said about God a moment ago, that nothing escapes him? For it was just said: "By great glory and in the might of strength, nothing has escaped you." How then do you deceive yourself, saying: "My way has been hidden from God, and my God has taken away my judgment and departed"? Hear, then, in reply to this. If you did not hear before, or did not know or understand what has often been said to you, learn now at least that the eternal God, who encompasses all things, rules not only over the things in heaven but also over those on earth. He it is who fashioned the ends of the earth. Therefore you yourself will not be able to escape his notice either, when you reason so impiously and godlessly. Instead of "He will not hunger nor grow weary," Symmachus rendered "He did not grow faint nor hunger," and the others similarly. Just as there is nothing weak or human in him, so there is no searching out his understanding. The wisdom by which he governs all things is incomprehensible and beyond reach. And he cares so much for each individual thing in particular that, because he watches over human affairs and discerns them with divine reason, he gives each person a life of their own, apportioned to them. Thus to those who hunger for lack of food he often provides strength and natural vigor of body, while those who do not hunger but are awash in wealth meet with cares and griefs that chasten their luxury.

By the same reasoning he makes young men and youths weak, though they ought to be acting like men, surrounding them with afflictions and diseases, and he has caused countless people in the bloom of youth to be extinguished from life all the sooner. Yet [?] he has prolonged into deep old age those who had been driven to the extremes of poverty, so that they did not even have enough for their daily food. Others, in turn, who boasted of wealth and glory, he has suddenly removed from among men. In contrast to these, those who waited for God in times of persecution, though weak and pitiable in the present life, were counted worthy of a divine change. They not only obtained relief and freedom, but also grew wings like eagles, so as to fly up, be lifted high, travel through the heights and finally set out on the journey to heaven. For such is the nature of eagles: they fly up to heaven, and they alone are able to look directly [?] into the flashing rays of the sun's light. Like them, then, are those who waited for God and were afflicted in this mortal life for fear of him, who in times of persecution became homeless, without hearth, and, as far as human help went, without hope. After their surpassing afflictions they were counted worthy of God's visitation and finished their lives in peace, growing wings like eagles and lifted on high. And if those who contended for piety and conquered happened also to be perfected by martyrdom, then all the more would the promise fit them that says: "But those who wait for God shall exchange their strength." Exchanging mortal life and passing over into the angelic life, setting out on the heavenly journey, "they shall grow wings like eagles, they shall run and not grow weary, they shall walk and not hunger," or, according to the other translators, "not grow faint." If, then, he will grant such rewards to those who wait for him, while to those of the opposite kind he pays their due in part in the present life but most fully at the time of judgment, how do you who are called Jacob and Israel, you who have been schooled in the divine oracles, dare to say among yourselves that your way has been hidden from God and your judgment taken away and gone?

You, then, O Jacob, think such things. But the Savior of all, who does not treat the salvation of mankind as a secondary matter, has said to you what is fitting, and to the other nations he proclaims what suits them, calling all to hasten to the knowledge of him. Therefore he says: "Be renewed toward me, you islands, for the rulers shall exchange their strength." Instead of this Symmachus says: "Serve before me, you islands, and let the nations exchange their strength," and according to Aquila and Theodotion it says: "Be silent toward me." So he commands the islands to be silent and quiet, so that they may become hearers of divine discourse and of the saving proclamation. He constantly calls the churches from all the nations "islands," because they are surrounded by the briny wickedness of life as islands are by the sea. Then, having said above, "But those who wait for God shall exchange their strength," here he says, "for the rulers shall exchange their strength," or, according to Symmachus, "and let the nations exchange their strength." For what he promised above to those who wait for him, this very thing he now commands of the islands and the nations, saying, "and let the nations exchange their strength," that is, let them change their way of life and make the exchange from worse to better. Then next: "Let them draw near," he says, "and speak together." Clearly he means the nations: let them draw near to me, God, and let them speak my words together, gathered in one place, that is, in my church. And what those who are called ought to speak he teaches next, saying: "then let them declare judgment." For he wants the nations, once they have learned the word concerning judgment, to proclaim it to others as well.

He also commands the same people to learn this, namely to know: "Who raised up righteousness from the east?" For it was a work of righteousness that not only the Jews but also the rest of the nations should be called to the knowledge of God. Who, then, is it that raised up this righteousness from where the light rises, and called him to follow him? And who is it that set it before all the nations, so that the kings of the nations were astonished at the command? At first they were thrown into confusion, and they attempted to stir up persecutions and wars against the word of righteousness. But they were defeated by the God of righteousness, who fights for those who have received it. He destroyed the warlike forces of the enemies of righteousness like brushwood, and smoothed a road for himself, so that his feet might pass through in peace.

Who, then, accomplished all these things but the God who is over all? Therefore he adds next: "He called it," that is, righteousness, "he who calls it from the beginning of the generations; I, God, am first, and for the things to come I am." Instead of this Symmachus translated: "I, the Lord, am first, and with the last I am." For it was he who long ago and from the beginning was made known to the first people who became friends of God, and it was he in whom, after the former people, the church from the nations believed. Therefore he adds: "Nations saw and were afraid." The passage testifies to no ordinary benefit for the nations, if indeed they cast off their former blindness of polytheism and should see the one who said: "I, God, am first, and for the things to come I am." And when they saw him they were afraid, having arrived at the beginning of wisdom, for "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Moreover, "the ends of the earth were amazed." For this was the astonishing thing: that even the barbarian tribes, and those settled farthest from the land of the Jews, the only land in which God was thought in ancient times to be known, received the knowledge of godliness. So they were amazed at the righteousness of God, and hastened toward grace and came, in keeping with the proclamation that said: "Let them draw near and speak together." But there they were bidden to come and to speak, clearly meaning to glorify God, whereas here the passage says: "They drew near and came together, each one deciding to help his neighbor." For those who were called came not only to save themselves but also their neighbors, in keeping with the laws of love for mankind. Therefore, wishing to care for their neighbors, their own brothers and acquaintances who were still caught up in folly, they said the following to them:

"There was a time when a craftsman prevailed over us too, the one who produced idolatry, and a smith beating out his own gods with a hammer. But now we have recognized that they are nothing, and we have condemned the error of our fathers. You too ought to learn this and profit from it. A proof of the impotence of those we formerly took for gods is that they cannot even stand unless they are fastened with pegs and nails. And once they have been set up by others and stand, another proof of their lifelessness appears: they can no longer move. Since, then, they can neither stand by themselves nor move once they have been set in place by others, how could they be gods?" The passage prophesies that the nations would one day say these things to their neighbors. Above, the same nations had been commanded not only to draw near to God but also to speak, for it was said: "Let them draw near and speak together." So it is fitting that, once they had drawn near, the prophecy should declare in the words before us both that they came and what sort of things they said to their acquaintances.

In the earlier passage God was finding fault with Jacob and Israel for saying: "My way has been hidden from God, and God has taken away my judgment and departed." But in the passage now in hand he calls Israel his servant and says that Jacob is chosen. The passage clearly presents two orders within the people of the circumcision: one that is accused and rebuked, and another to which he has made the present promises. The first is made up of those who fell away from God because of their unbelief. The other is made up of those who obeyed in faith and were therefore counted worthy of saving grace. Such were the disciples and apostles of our Savior, and all the others from the people of the circumcision who believed in him, who were themselves also Israel and Jacob. So, consistently, the election of the apostles and disciples of our Savior is joined to the discourse about the nations. Therefore the prophecy speaks to them in person: "But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham, whom I have loved." He calls him first servant, then chosen, then beloved. He calls him servant as one who is at the beginning and still being trained under the fear of slavery. Such was the band of apostles, which had spent its earlier life under the law as its tutor. The same one he calls chosen, as one who has made progress and been counted worthy of the saving call and election. But "seed of Abraham" is an order distinct from that of the chosen. What could it be but the multitude of the Jews, to whom the Savior said in conversation: "I know that you are the seed of Abraham"? These were different from the children of Abraham, about whom he taught, saying: "If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham." Abraham, then, was beloved of God and his friend. That is why it says: "seed of Abraham, whom I loved," or, according to Symmachus, "seed of Abraham my friend," and, according to Aquila, "seed of Abraham my beloved." His seed, however, is no longer said to be loved as Abraham was. Yet he calls even the seed of Abraham through his chosen ones, saying to them: "Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."

And since this seed of Abraham was scattered over all the earth, he adds next: "whom I took hold of from the end of the earth, and from its watchtowers I called you," or, as Symmachus has it, "and from its corners I called you." By these words he means those of the Jewish people in the Dispersion, whom he first counted worthy of his call. The apostle Paul made this plain when he said to the Jews: "It was necessary that the word be proclaimed to you first; but since you turn away, we are going to the Gentiles." So it is to those among them who obeyed the call and received the word of the gospel that he says: "whom I took hold of from the ends of the earth, and from its watchtowers I called you." For in the apostolic age there were many from among the Jews who received the word of Christ, not only in the land of Judea but also among the other nations. Having spoken of the seed of Abraham up to this point, he goes back to the choosing of the apostolic band and says to them: "You are my child," or, as the other translators have it, "You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not forsaken you." So it was fitting that the divine Apostle confessed himself a servant, taking pride in the service of the Savior as a great honor. The text itself shows this as it goes on, where it says: "It is a great thing for you to be called my child." And here again it teaches that he first became a servant and was then chosen, when it says: "You are my child," or "You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not forsaken you," or, as Symmachus has it, "have not rejected you."

He gives courage to this chosen band, so that they may preach the gospel fearlessly to all the nations. The Savior himself made the same point in the Gospels when he said: "Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age." Then he adds: "Do not fear, for I am with you." And do not go astray, he says, "for I am your God, who strengthened you, and I helped you and made you secure with my righteous right hand." See to it, he says, that you never imagine it was by your own strength that you were able to serve so great a proclamation. You would have been nothing and could have done nothing if I had not been with you and travelled with you through all the nations. I strengthened you, giving you endurance, perseverance and power, and "made you secure with my righteous right hand," so that nothing would stand in your way as you preached the gospel to all.

And even if some who oppose the word you preach should try to stand in your way, take courage from this moment and despise them all. Know that "all who oppose you will be ashamed and disgraced; for they will be as nothing, and all your adversaries will perish. You will look for them and will not find the men who will act outrageously against you; for they will be as nothing, and those who make war on you will be no more." For though some seemed to be something for a little while, at the time when they were making war on you and persecuting you, you will remain and endure and will see their destruction. They will be no more, swiftly vanishing from life.

Therefore you must persevere and endure the afflictions they bring on you. Look to the end that awaits them, and take courage in my promise, for I am already telling you beforehand, and truthfully: "For I am the Lord your God, and I will hold your right hand, I who say to you, Do not fear, I have helped you." The words "I have helped you; do not fear, worm Jacob" are not found in the Seventy, but have been added from the other translators. The one who was called "chosen" above, in the words "Jacob, whom I have chosen," is now called "worm." This is because, like a worm, he slips into the cities of the unbelieving nations and destroys and wipes out all their polytheistic error and demonic activity from the very depths of human thought. It is also because the apostolic preaching was plain and unlearned. In the same way the Savior himself called himself a worm, saying: "But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people." Then, since our Savior's disciples were few in number, twelve apostles and the seventy after them, he adds: "Israel, few in number," or, as Symmachus has it, "the number of Israel," or, as Aquila has it, "you dead ones of Israel," and Theodotion too says "the dead of Israel." But after calling them worms and saying they were very few, he goes on: "Do not fear, I have helped you, says God who redeems you, the Holy One of Israel."

And he adds: "Behold, I have made you like the wheels of a threshing cart, new and toothed like a saw." This is how the power of the one who strengthened them was shown. They themselves were no different from a worm. They were also very few, and were the dead and departed of Israel. Yet even so, they cut through the demonic god-making of the foreign and godless nations as if it were straw, threshing it and sawing it down like the wheels of a cart. That is why he adds: "And you will thresh mountains and grind hills to powder." By mountains and hills he hints at the hostile powers that long ago raised themselves up against the knowledge of God. These powers, then, which are like lofty mountains, and the lesser evil spirits, which are like hills, you will grind to powder, he says, and thresh and winnow, "and the wind will carry them off, and the storm will scatter them," so that demonic error no longer holds sway among the nations. And when the mountains and hills just described have vanished, "you yourself," my chosen servant, through whom these things were accomplished, "will rejoice in the Lord, and in the Holy One of Israel you will be praised." In place of "they will exult in the holy ones of Israel," Aquila has "you will boast in the Holy One of Israel," and Symmachus has "you will be praised in the Holy One of Israel."

Having prophesied these things about the apostles, the text next makes a fresh start and speaks of the conversion of the nations: "The poor and the needy will seek water, and there will be none; their tongue has dried up with thirst." They had suffered this long ago, but now, he says: "I, the Lord God, will hear them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the mountains and springs in the midst of the plains; I will turn the desert into marshes of water, and the thirsty land into watercourses." If you turn your mind to it, you will see how these things were fulfilled and are still at work even now in the churches of God founded in every place through the apostles of our Savior. Among the nations there were souls that were once utterly destitute and lacking the knowledge of God. They did not have even a drop of life-giving drink, so their tongue, and the speech it uttered, had dried up, because they had no share in any moisture of the saving word. These souls have received an extraordinary blessing: through heavenly grace they have been filled with springs and rivers and every kind of life-giving water. They enjoy the water of which it was said above: "And they will draw water from the springs of salvation." They drink from the springs of Israel, which were mentioned by the passage that says: "In the churches bless God, the Lord, from the springs of Israel." This would be the Holy Spirit, which wells up in the church of God and pours out living waters, sometimes from the old covenant and sometimes from the new teaching of the gospel. Ever-flowing rivers also run and flood the old desert. They take their source from the great river of which it is said: "The streams of the river make glad the city of God," and: "The river of God is full of water."

In the land that was once waterless, the church of God, one can see souls that have grown lush from so much water and have risen to a height. They are like plants that grow only where there is abundant water, such as the cedar and box and myrtle, the cypress and white poplar, according to the Seventy, or, according to Symmachus: "cedar and smokeless olive wood, cypress and elm and box together." All these are fed and grow only in abundant water, and so they have been taken as an image of the flourishing souls in the church of God, raised to a height by the great abundance of the divine waters of the Word. When the text wishes to present the fruits of the church, it uses the image of the olive or the palm or the vine. Here, however, it shows the lushness and vigor, the youth and full bloom of those who are advancing in the church, and so it has used the image of the plants just named, which by nature grow only from abundant water and firm, fertile soil. It has presented this as a marvel: in a waterless, parched and thirsty land it promises such a supply of water that plants like those listed will spring up. The same will happen in the once desert and waterless land of the nations that were once foreign and godless. For it prophesies that the same great change will take place among them too, as a demonstration of the saving blessing.

That is why he adds: "so that they may know and recognize and consider and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done these things, and the Holy One of Israel has shown them." For if it were not God, the hand of the Lord, that brought about so great a change among the nations through his apostles, how could churches of God have been established in such a desolation of the nations? How could the waters of the Word within the church have multiplied everywhere on earth, so that the souls of nations once desolate and parched are cultivated by the word of godliness? How could they put forth tall and lofty shoots, rooted below on the earth, that is, in mortal human life, yet rising above to such a height that they reach even to the kingdom of heaven and hang their hopes there? That is why they are compared to fragrant plants that rise to a height.

The text has now completed its account of how the once desert, fruitless and waterless land was changed into fertility, by which it hinted at the change of the church of God from worse to better. It now moves on to another group, those who remained in their former error of idolatry. So it turns to them and says: "Your judgment draws near, says God." For you are without excuse, he says, you who, after so great a grace had accomplished such things, remained in the error of many gods. You did not consider that it was truly the hand of the Lord that accomplished these things and testified before they happened that they would come to pass, "so that they may know and recognize and consider and understand that the hand of the Lord has done these things." So to those who did not pay attention, did not recognize and did not consider, the text fittingly utters a threat, saying: "Your judgment draws near, says the Lord God." For their condemnation comes on them at once, since they are without excuse. That is why he adds: "Your counsels have drawn near." In place of this Symmachus has "Bring near your strong things," Theodotion "Bring near your strongholds," and Aquila "Bring near your bones." Bring out into the open, he says, the things you consider strong, your strongholds. It is as if he were saying more plainly: bring your gods out into the open. "Let them draw near and declare to you," or, as Symmachus has it, "let them come forward and announce to you what will happen. Or tell us what the former things were, and we will turn our minds to them and know the last things; and tell us the things that are coming. Declare to us the things that are coming at the end, and we will know that you are gods."

And truly this is enough to convict the demons of powerlessness. Long ago they pretended to give oracles and claimed to foretell the future, yet none of them ever divined or foretold that the Christ of God would one day come and dwell among men to put an end to their god-making. None foretold that the temples raised to them in the cities would be left desolate, and that their divinations and oracles would be exposed. Yet these things were accomplished at the end of days through the coming of our Savior. The evil demons, who pretended to give oracles and to know the future, ought not to have been ignorant of these things. If there were any divine power in them, they should at least have foreknown and prophesied them. That is why the text says, as if speaking to them: "What are the last things, and what are the things that are coming? Tell us. Declare to us the things that are coming at the end, and we will know that you are gods." The prophets of God shared in the divine Spirit and foretold the last things. They prophesied plainly that the waterless, barren and fruitless land of the nations would change for the better. They foretold the coming of Christ, the preaching of his apostles, and everything else contained in their prophecies. From this it is known that the one who prophesied these things in them and through them is truly God. But how could the evil demons know the counsel and purpose of the God over all, or what he had decreed about the coming of Christ and about their own overthrow and destruction? So they did not know the things to come, or what was going to happen in the last times concerning the calling of the nations and their own desolation. It is no surprise, then, that they did not know the former things either. That is why none of them has been able to prompt their own prophets with the things that those counted worthy of the Spirit of God have handed down in writing. Moses was one of these, writing about the former things and saying: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth. And the earth was invisible and unformed." These things, and others like them, were the former things. The last things concern the conversion of the nations, the exposure of demonic error, the end of the age, and the righteous judgment of God that will follow it. How then could they be gods, when they can neither know nor tell the last things?

Then he moves on to another refutation, saying: "Do good, or do harm, and we will see and marvel together." For even if you are perfectly able to do harm, since you are evil demons, that does not give you any mark of divine activity. You must first show what belongs properly to God, that is, doing good. Then you must show whether you will judge justly and punish those who deserve harm. As it is, you welcome without distinction all who come over to your error. You promise good things to everyone, but only in words and in phrases twisted so as to hide your ignorance under the veil of ambiguity. And you hand out your oracles without distinction even to shameful men and licentious women. How then could you be gods?

That is why he adds next: "For where do you come from, and where does your workmanship come from?" And he goes on to expose the material they are made of by saying: "From the earth. They have chosen you as an abomination." For whether it is gold or silver, iron or bronze or stone, all these are the leavings of the earth. When they are taken up to make gods, they become an abomination, though they are not such by nature, since every work of God is good. But when worthless men take them up with their wicked craft for the sake of godlessness, they become foul, abominable and hateful. And since they are lifeless, they can neither do good nor do harm. This shows that the so-called divine workings and oracles are the deceptions of sorcerers who exploit the foolishness of the many.

Having said this, and having as it were demonstrated their error to those who still cling to idolatry, the text goes on: "But I have raised up the one from the north," or, as Symmachus has it, "I will rouse from the north," "and the one from the rising of the sun, who," he says, "will be called by my name." By the one from the rising of the sun he means Christ and his righteousness. He showed this in the earlier words too, when he said: "Who raised up righteousness from the east?" and he showed there that it had been given to the nations as well. By the one from the north he means the people from the nations, who were once in the north, according to the words: "From the face of the north evils will be kindled upon all who dwell on the earth." So he says: I have raised this people from the nations out of the north, so that it may no longer remain there; and I will also call the one from the rising of the sun, that is, the Christ of God. In addition he says: "They will be called by my name." Who these are he teaches next, saying: "Let rulers come." By this name he means either the angels who stand guard about his kingdom, through whom, he says, godless error was overthrown, or else the rulers and leaders of his church. When the people from the north has been gathered, and the one from the rising of the sun, and the rulers just mentioned have come together, he adds what will happen next: "And like a potter's clay, and like a potter treading clay, so you will be trampled." He means you, the ones to whom it was said: "For where do you come from, and where does your workmanship come from? From the earth. They have chosen you as an abomination."

That is why he turns to them again and says: "Who will declare the things from the beginning, so that we may know, and the things before, and we will say that it is true?" Having said this to those just mentioned, and having brought the same refutation against them, he adds: "There is no one who foretells, nor anyone who hears your words." Here again the text means two things: the disappearance of the oracles, and the return to their senses of the men they had long led astray. The words "There is no one who hears your words" also have a double meaning. First, the idols themselves have no word, since they can do nothing and know nothing. Second, those who were once led astray by them do not remain in their error. Having been helped by the word of truth, they no longer lend the idols their ears, because they have condemned the old deceit.

After this he continues: "I will give rule to Zion, and I will comfort Jerusalem for the way." What he means is this: Know, O men, that I myself will give rule over all to my church, which was also called Zion and Jerusalem in the earlier passages. I will comfort my church and make it a way. For among the nations that remained in unbelief no god has been found, and among their idols there was no one who declared anything. They were exposed as being nothing, and for that reason able to do nothing. Even if I ask them where they come from, none of them will give an answer. It is plain that their makers are craftsmen, since all the idols of the nations are the work of human hands. So all of you have gone astray in vain. That is why I want you to know that I myself will give rule over all to my own church. I will bestow the authority of my kingdom on my Zion alone, and I will comfort my Jerusalem and appoint it as a way, so that all who travel on it may journey to the thrice-blessed end that leads to the God over all and to his heavenly kingdom.

Very fittingly he has set the prophecy about Christ, and the calling of the nations that goes with it, alongside the refutation of the idols. But before considering the passage itself, it is worth noticing that neither the name Jacob nor the name Israel appears in the present prophecy. That is why neither the other translators nor the Hebrew text mention them. Symmachus rendered it this way: "Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in whom my soul delighted," and Aquila: "Behold my servant, I will take hold of him." In the earlier passages the apostolic band was called Jacob and Israel, where it was said: "But you, Jacob, my servant, Israel, whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham, whom I loved." In the present passage, however, a greater person is introduced. So that he would not be thought to be the same as those mentioned before, he is called neither Jacob nor Israel nor seed of Abraham. The passage is clearly spoken of the Christ of God, as the Evangelist testified when he quoted the words: "I have put my Spirit upon him, and he will bring forth judgment to the nations," and, after all this, "in his name the nations will hope." It would not have been fitting to say these things of the apostolic band. So it is fitting that the names Jacob and Israel are left out of the present prophecy, for the one called the servant of God and his chosen one here is someone else. That is why the words are added: "My soul has accepted him." For he alone was the chosen one of God, and he was accepted by what is called the soul of God. Divine Scripture regularly uses the word "soul" loosely of God, just as it is accustomed to speak in human terms of God's feet and hands and fingers and eyes. "I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations." You will find that these words agree with what was prophesied earlier about the one who would come forth from the root of Jesse. He is not chosen in the same way as the apostles, since to him alone it is said: "whom my soul has chosen." The Spirit of God also rested on him alone, for in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. The Spirit given to the one who came forth from the root of Jesse was the only-begotten Word of God himself, as the Apostle also showed when he said: "Now the Lord is the Spirit." So, as the only one who contained the Father's Spirit, he accomplishes everything that follows. He announces to the nations what concerns the universal judgment, so that all may prepare for the coming judgment of God. That is why it is said: "He will bring forth judgment to the nations."

Then, since he passed through human life so quietly and gently that he did not even allow those he healed to make him known to everyone, for this reason it is said: He will not cry out or raise his voice, nor will his voice be heard outside; and he will not even break a bruised reed. For he will pass through his life among men so noiselessly and quietly that he will not grieve even an ordinary person, the lowliest and weakest of all, who is likened to a reed because of its weakness. Nor will he quench smoking flax; or, according to Symmachus: nor will he quench dim flax; according to Aquila: and dim flax he will not quench; and according to Theodotion: and dim tow he will not quench. The smoldering flax, you might say, is the person puffed up by the mind of his flesh, someone exalted and swollen with conceit, whom the one prophesied was said not to hinder or stop in his pride. And this the Christ of God fulfilled in deed when he sojourned in mortal life: he neither grieved anyone lowly and weak among men, nor went after any of the exalted and arrogant, but toward all people he was gentle and lowly in heart.

With truth and boldness he declared to all what concerns the judgment of God, and he did not cease until he shone forth like a light through his resurrection from the dead, which the prophetic word hinted at when it said: He will shine forth and will not be broken. For those who contrived his death tried to break him and put him out, since the whole mortal race is by nature broken by death. But him they did not break; he alone, of all since the beginning of the ages, was shown to be stronger than death, and so he is fittingly attested by the prophecy that says: He will shine forth and will not be broken. Then it adds: until he establishes judgment on the earth; and in his name the nations will hope. Therefore, after his resurrection from the dead, having shone like a light into the whole world, he did not cease until he had ordered on earth the government and judgment of his church, which he handed over to his disciples.

After these words there follows next: Thus says the Lord God, who made the heaven and set it fast, who made firm the earth and what is in it, and gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread on it. Notice how he said that the heaven was set fast, since according to Moses' account of the making of the world it is said to have been formed when waters set solid—not, as the Greek natural philosophers would have it, who supposed the ether and the heaven itself to be made of fire. The earth, on the other hand, he says was made firm, and fittingly so, because, lying at the center of the universe, it is immovable—something that would not have been suitable to say of the heaven. In place of 'and what is in it,' Symmachus says: You made firm the earth and the things that go upon it. What these are he makes clear by saying next: who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread on it.

For we must learn from whose person the things said about Christ were spoken. Since the prophetic word launched in abruptly, saying at the beginning: Jacob my servant, I will help him; Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him; I have put my Spirit upon him—but did not first explain who it was that said these things, it must now make clear who uttered these oracles. That is why it adds: Thus said the Lord God; for it was he who said both the first words and those that follow. 'For even if,' he says, 'you humans are wholly unable to behold the invisible and incorporeal being of God, yet look up at the greatness of so vast a heaven and reckon what sort of being he is who set so great an expanse fast. Look also at the earth itself, how great it is and how immovably it has been seated through all the ages, rooted and founded so as never in any way to be moved, and consider of what unspeakable power he is who made it firm and rendered it fertile and fruitful, so that it brings forth so many animals and plants.' He, then, the Lord and God of the universe, who fashioned such beauties and such magnitudes—he it is who pronounced the oracles spoken before about his Christ.

Very consistently and carefully it is said that he has given breath to the people on the earth in general, that is, to all people whose lot it is to dwell on the earth, since at the first creation of man God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul, so that from him all people share in life—but not also in the higher Spirit; for the Spirit is said to be given only to those who tread the earth underfoot. These would be the ones who trample down an earthly way of thinking. One might also say, in another sense, that every kind of living creature on the earth, both rational and irrational, is indicated by these words.

In addition to what has been said, the same Lord and God also addresses the words that follow to his Christ, saying: I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand and strengthen you. He addresses these words to his servant mentioned above, to whom he was said to give his own Spirit. First he calls him in righteousness, making his calling according to his worth and in perfect justice; then he promises to hold his hand and strengthen him; and third, to bestow him as a gift, like a great light, on all the nations, saying: And I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations. Long ago, then, he gave the old covenant to the Jewish people through Moses; but here he says he has bestowed the one prophesied as a covenant for the human race and as a light of the nations. Fittingly, then, since the Christ of God was himself the covenant, he published no writing or book as Moses did; for he himself was the covenant, being the first mediator between God and humans. And he is also given as a light of the nations, so that, enlightened in him, the eyes of those who had long been blind in their souls might be opened, and they might regain their sight and perceive the knowledge of God, so as no longer to pay the honor due to God to stones and wood and lifeless matter.

And since these very people were bound tight with the cords of their own sins and shackled in the darkness of wickedness, but were destined through the grace of Christ to be granted forgiveness of sins and released as if from prison, set free and delivered from the devil's jail, for this reason there follows next: to bring out from their bonds those who are bound, and from the prison house those who sit in darkness. All these things the bountiful God promises to give through his Christ, not to Israel or to the Jewish nation, but to all the nations together.

And he adds: I am the Lord God; this is my name; my glory I will not give to another. Observe how in the other translators and in the Hebrew reading itself the words 'my glory I will not give to another' are said in the same way. If the words of the Lord are refined by fire, and one must not read them carelessly, it is worth noting that it is not said, 'My glory I will give to no one.' For 'to no one' would have excluded everyone, whereas 'I will not give to another' shows that the grant has been made to one alone—namely, the one being addressed. And this was the one to whom it was said: I have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand and strengthen you, and I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations. 'Since, then, I have given you my glory,' he says, 'you should know that I would not share it with another as well.' What the glory of the speaker was he taught beforehand by saying: I am the Lord God; this is my name. The name, then, by which he is glorified as Lord and God of the universe, 'I will not give to another,' he says, 'but only to you, whom I have bestowed as a light of the nations.' Hence, in keeping with the promise, the Christ of God too is proclaimed Lord and God among all the nations, since the Father has granted this glory to him alone. Next he adds: nor my excellences to carved images; or according to Aquila: and my hymning to carved images; and according to Symmachus: nor my praise to carved images. Through these words, I think, he teaches all the nations to hymn none of the gods they formerly believed in, but to glorify only the Christ of God and the Father who sent him. That is why Christ alone is himself spoken of as God, since the God who is over all has granted his glory and his excellences to him alone and to no other.

After this it is said: Behold, the things from the beginning have come, and new things which I declare; before they were declared, they were made known to you. According to Symmachus: The first things, behold, have come, and new things I declare; before I declare them, I will make them heard by you. 'For just as the first things were fulfilled in deeds,' he says—'for as I promised Abraham concerning his seed, so I also did, and the things foretold through Moses and the other prophets were fulfilled—so now I too announce good news to all,' he says, 'and before declaring them and before they came into the open, I have made them heard by you through this prophecy.' What these things are he goes on to explain next.

Having said in the preceding words that he would do new things, he teaches in these words what the new things would be. He commands that a new hymn be sung to the Lord, or, according to the other translators, that a new song be sung. All people must do this, since his rule, he says, and his royal authority are glorified in all the earth, and his name has reached to the ends of the earth, so that the whole world has been filled with Christians, named after the title of Christ. According to Symmachus: his praise from the ends of the earth. Having urged them to sing the new song and the new hymn to the Lord, he next teaches to whom he addresses the proclamation, saying: you who go down to the sea and sail it—plainly indicating the Savior's apostles, whom, as he passed along by the sea, he saw casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen; and likewise the rest of them. To them, then, the prophetic Spirit called out, saying: Sing to the Lord a new hymn, you who go down to the sea and sail it. These same men, sailing around our sea, at times preached the gospel in the islands, and at times crossed over beyond to Spain and Italy, so that in a short time they filled even the imperial city itself with the teaching of Christ. In another sense, too, these words signify those who sail the sea of human life and preach the gospel to all the nations in the midst of the islands; for they too announced the new hymn to all people, preaching and teaching in the midst of the churches.
