That is why he next commands the islands to sing the new hymn—clearly meaning the churches of God, which are washed round by the sea just mentioned and buffeted on every side by the winds from outside. Therefore he adds: the islands and those who dwell in them, indicating in this way those who are gathered in the churches.

Then again he brings good news to the desert, about which countless things were said earlier, saying: Rejoice, O desert, and its villages; or, according to the other translators: and its cities. For many cities are conceived of within the church of God, according to the different ways of life, as was shown in the vision concerning Egypt, in which it was said that there would be five cities in Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue and swearing by the name of the Lord of hosts. He also promises that the hamlets and the inhabitants of Kedar, and besides these the inhabitants of Petra, will rejoice. Kedar lies beyond Arabia, in the farthest desert, which they say is held by the race of the Saracens; through them the word meant to indicate all who inhabit the deserts and the ends of the earth, since God's spiritual joy was destined, through the grace of Christ, to reach even them. And Petra is a city of Palestine, of superstitious men steeped deep in demonic error; its inhabitants too, he says, will partake of grace, saying: Those who dwell in Petra will rejoice. The outcome of events has confirmed the truth of these words, since in our own time churches of Christ have been founded both in the city of the Petraeans itself and throughout its territory, and in the deserts of the Saracens. In another sense, Kedar is interpreted 'darkening,' on account of those who have turned from darkness to the light proclaimed to the nations. The word says that those who dwell in Petra will likewise rejoice; and the rock was Christ. And all those whom the prophecy has listed, having come to be on high and standing as if upon mountains among the lofty words of God—from where they will hymn God and give him glory it foretells, saying: From the top of the mountains they will shout and give glory to God. So too it was said above: Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem.

But having promised these things to the desert and the islands and Kedar, which were admittedly foreign to the Jewish nation, the word next adds an indication of the rejection of Israel, saying: The Lord God of hosts will go forth and shatter war; according to Symmachus: The Lord will go forth as a mighty one, as a man of war. You see how he says that the Lord himself will come in the form of a man and, like a warrior, will make war on his enemies. Then he adds: he stirs up jealousy—the jealousy about which Moses also taught when he said concerning the Jewish nation: They made me jealous with what is no god, they provoked me with their idols; and I will make them jealous with what is no nation, with a senseless nation I will provoke them. This, then, is the jealousy he says he stirs up, adopting and making his own Kedar and the islands and the foreign nations, while shaking off and thrusting away the Jewish people—and doing this with reason and with a well-grounded defense. Therefore he adds: and he will shout against his enemies with strength.

For he will not make war on them without reason, but will make the cause plain by stating it, and with a great shout; and this cause he also teaches, saying: I have kept silent; shall I also keep silent forever? 'For while they broke the law and acted impiously, I bore with them patiently and endured them in my long-suffering, not bringing my wrath upon them at once; I kept silent.' In another sense, too, at the time of his passion, he kept silent when slandered, and when false witness was borne against him he answered nothing. 'But then,' he says, 'I kept silent; yet I will not keep silent forever. Then I endured like a woman in labor; but now it is the time of recompense. Therefore I will bring amazement and dry up together'; or according to Symmachus: I will breathe in and blow out together.

Then he adds, according to the Hebrew reading and the other translators: I will lay waste mountains and hills and dry up all their grass—hinting by mountains and hills at the rulers of the people, and by grass at their sins. He threatens to bring down their pride and the heights of their rulers, and to dry up their grass. That these things are said about them the word will show as it proceeds, before long. 'Moreover, the rivers among them'—the teachings once supplied to them like rivers—'I will turn into an island,' he says; 'and also the places among them where spiritual waters stood in pools, so that they could be likened to marshes—these too I will dry up.'

And having threatened these things against them, he passes again to the grace that would be given to the nations. Therefore he adds: And I will lead the blind by a way they did not know. Who these were he taught earlier, when he said in the person of Christ: I have given you as a covenant of my race, as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind. It is these very people, then, who were formerly blind among the nations, that he promises to make walk on a way they did not know. For how could we have known the way that leads to God except through his divine grace? And since, according to all the translators, it is said in the singular—And I will lead the blind by a way they did not know—and the Savior confirms this when he says, I am the way, see how he promises to us, the blind, Christ, whom we did not know before, and his saving word. He says, moreover, that we will understand paths which we did not know—namely the prophetic scriptures and the ways of life set before us by divine teaching—and that he will turn darkness into light for us and crooked things into a straight road. For he promises to change into the light of knowledge the ignorance of God that formerly lay over our souls, and to make smooth the oracles of God that we once thought crooked and obscure. And he adds: These words I will do for them—very precisely promising not to speak the words to them, but to do them. For long ago these things were spoken among the prophets, but he undertakes to accomplish them in deeds. And I will not forsake them, he says.

Then, having said these things about those formerly blind, he turns his discourse back again to those who were once near to God but turned back, hinting at those of the circumcision, about whom he says: But they turned back. Then, as if showing them the change in the nations, and from what error they had changed, coming from darkness into light, he adds reproachfully to those people as idolaters: Be ashamed with shame, you who trust in carved images, who say to molten images, You are our gods. And truly, when the nations that were formerly idolaters changed to godliness, the Jewish nation was put to shame. Thus, although in the times when these things were prophesied they were devoted to idolatry, now they have ceased, being ashamed because of the change in the nations. Hence this was indicated prophetically in the words: They will be ashamed with shame. 'For when they see those formerly blind changed to light,' he says, 'then they too will be ashamed and will cease saying to molten images, You are our gods.'

Having said this, the word, as though sending out a cry into the ears of the deaf, shouts: You deaf, hear; and you blind, look up and see. And so that no one should think these things are said about the nations who were formerly blind and deaf, he necessarily clarifies and interprets the meaning, adding next: And who is blind but my servants, and deaf but those who rule over them? Then, according to Symmachus, there is added: Who is blind like the perfect one? And he interprets the saying still further, declaring: And the servants of God have been blinded. According to Symmachus: 'You blind,' he says, 'look up, and you deaf, hear. Who is blind but my servant, and deaf like my messenger whom I sent? Who is blind like the perfect one, and deaf like my servant?' What the other translators have amounts to the same. And whom does he call his servant but the people of the circumcision? The same people he also names messenger and perfect one and servant of the Lord, to their condemnation, as if saying: 'For I wished to have this people as my servant and my perfect one and my messenger, but they were blinded.'

How they became blind and deaf he explains, saying: You have seen many times, and you did not take heed; your ears were opened, and you did not hear. Of the same kind were the words spoken earlier: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not perceive; for the heart of this people has grown dull. According to Symmachus: You have seen many things, he says, and you will not keep them; his ears were open, and you will not hear. The Lord willed, in order to justify him, to magnify the law and make it wonderful. But he is a people plundered and despoiled. You see that all these things are said about the people of the circumcision. The Lord wished to justify them and to magnify praise; but they were handed over to those who wage war on their souls, and became a people plundered and despoiled. For the snare was within, in the inner chambers of their souls and in their houses alike. For in the very thoughts they kept hidden, plotting against Christ—in those very thoughts lay the snare against them; and there was no one to rescue, no one to deliver, no one to say, Give them back.

Then, since he was speaking as if to the deaf and was at a loss for hearers among them, he says: Who among you will give ear to these things, and who will listen for what is to come? For even if the outcome of events has not yet arrived, it will be accomplished in the times to come. And who among you, then, will be the one to understand these things? Who will seek out the cause of the plundering of the people, so as to say: Who gave Jacob up for plunder, and Israel to those who despoil him? If anyone should ask who did this, he would find that none other gave them up for plunder than he himself against whom they sinned and in whose ways they would not walk. For when they were called to the ways of the gospel they did not obey, nor were they even willing to hear the law of the new covenant. Therefore he brought upon them the wrath of his anger, and war prevailed against them. For long ago, when warred against for a time, they would recover themselves again, so that Jerusalem and their kingdom in it survived; but now the war has prevailed against them—not only the war from outside, but also the war of those who besiege their souls. That is why it is said: and those who set them ablaze round about; and though they suffered these things they did not understand, nor did they lay it to heart, so as to reckon the cause of the evils that had overtaken them.

Let us remember what was said just now about the people of the circumcision. Scripture called them blind and deaf, saying: "And who is blind but my servants, and deaf but those who rule over them? And the servants of God were blinded"; and again: "And the people became plundered and despoiled," and the words that follow, in which he threatened to bring wrath, anger and war upon them. If we remember this, we will never suppose that the present words are spoken about the same people. So the prophecy passes over to the better group: those of that people who received the saving word. It addresses them, saying: "And now thus says the Lord God who made you, Jacob, and who formed you, Israel." For even if the unbelievers among you became completely blind and deaf, did such things and were handed over to the wrath of God, you must still listen, even now. And by "you" I mean those who have not been ignorant of their own Maker and Former, but have kept what was made and formed in them safe and unharmed. So it is to you, the true Jacob, worthy of the name of Israel, that he who made you sets out what follows, and to you he says this: "Many will begrudge you your salvation and will try to hinder the gospel message that you proclaim, but I urge you to fear none of them. For I myself am the Lord God who made you and formed you. I made you as to the soul, which was made in the image of God, and I formed you as to the body, which was taken from the earth and shaped by me. I gave my own blood as a ransom for your salvation; I redeemed you and called you. More than that, I made you my own possession, so that you are my people and I am your God. Take courage, then, since I have counted you worthy of so much, and walk the road you were commanded to walk. Boldly proclaim the gospel message to all the nations everywhere on earth. Even if blazing fire comes upon you, even if waters and rivers overwhelm you, none of this will harm you, because I am with you everywhere. For I made a promise that cannot lie: 'Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.'"

"Know this too: just as I redeemed you, my own people, by giving my precious blood for your salvation, so you too will be the exchange for others. I mean the nations who will be saved through you, among them the Egyptians, the Ethiopians and those who live in Syene." Where the text has Syene, the other translators have rendered "Seba." Symmachus has: "I gave Egypt as your propitiation, and Ethiopia and Seba in your place." "For you have become so precious to me, so glorified in my sight, and I have loved you so much, that the salvation according to God which is provided through you to all people will reach to the ends of the earth. Even the Egyptians, the most superstitious of all people, will be counted worthy of the calling that comes through you." By the Egyptians, then, he hinted at all the superstitious and the idolaters, and by Ethiopia and Syene at those who live at the farthest edges of our inhabited world. If Seba is also mentioned, we should know that there is a nation of Sabaeans, from which the queen of Sheba came on a visit in the time of Solomon. "These, then," he says, "I have acquired in your place," or "on your behalf," "all as my own. But those who make war on you because of the word you proclaim I will hand over to destruction."

"For this reason I urge you to take courage, since I am with you always. And the seeds that you have sown across the whole world, the many children you have begotten according to God, I will gather into my heavenly city. I will take them up on high through the air, borne aloft as if by winged winds, by which I mean the angelic powers. I will take some from the north and others from the southwest," or, according to the other translators, "from the south." "For I will command the angels to do this, because those whom you have sown and who have been born again in my church are my sons and my daughters."

"And if I must show by name who these are, I here and now make it plain to all: they are the ones who will be called by my name." And where else did the name "Christians" come from, if not from the title "Christ"? It was he who was uttering these things through the prophet. In place of "For I prepared him in my glory," the other translators have: "I created him for my glory." "For I created this new people for glory, so that I might be glorified through them. I also formed them, when they were unformed in their way of life."

"And I brought them out," he says, "when they were formerly in darkness and were a blind people." For even if they seemed to have the eyes of the soul and a certain human wisdom, they were nevertheless sightless, caught in the error of idolatry. Next it is said: "All the nations have been gathered together, and rulers will be gathered from among them." The actual course of events shows the fulfillment of this saying as well. Through the seeds sown by the apostles and through their teaching, those who were once blind and deaf were changed and gathered into the church of God, and now rulers from these very nations have been appointed over the people of God. Having said this, the prophet was filled with wonder and astonishment at what he had foretold, and cried out: "Who will declare these things? Or who will declare to you the things from the beginning? Let them bring their witnesses and be justified, and let them speak the truth." Who, then, he means, will one day see with their own eyes the outcome of these words? Let those who are witnesses of the fulfillment come forward and be justified by bearing witness, since I, God, will also be their witness, and so will the servant whom I have chosen. Of him he said earlier: "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my elect; my soul has accepted him."

"I, then, God himself, and this servant, my chosen one." The Savior made this plain in the Gospels when he said: "Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father in heaven." "I will bear witness for my witnesses, so that you may know and believe and understand that I am. Before me there was no other god, and after me there will be none." For the reason for Christ's coming, and for the witness of his apostles to all the nations, was nothing other than to proclaim the knowledge of the God who is over all, faith in him and understanding of him. They proclaimed it to those who had formerly been senseless, faithless and unbelieving, who did not know him and were therefore blind in the eyes of the mind and wandered about in the error of godless idolatry. That is why, after prophesying, "Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and so is the servant whom I have chosen," he added: "so that you may know and believe and understand that I am. Before me there was no other god, and after me there will be none." For since there is one first principle, there is one Godhead, and the doctrine of his only-begotten is included with it.

Continuing the same teaching, the text goes on: "I am God, and besides me there is no one who saves." He says this after having said earlier, "I am the Lord God, and so is the servant whom I have chosen." So one would not go wrong in the present passage either by joining the phrase about the servant whom he chose to the statement about God set out here: "I am God, and besides me there is no one who saves, and the servant whom I have chosen." For just as he himself was called a witness, and the servant whom he chose was too, so he would also be the God who saves, and so would the servant whom he chose. When he says, "Besides me there is no one who saves," he would not be saying it to deny that the servant whom he chose is the Savior. Indeed, this very prophet knows him as Savior, where he says: "And the Lord will send them a savior who will save them; judging, he will save them." Rather, he means: "Even if the servant whom I have chosen saves as Savior, he does not save apart from me, but with my will and at my bidding. For without my counsel and apart from me there is no one who saves."

"And these things," he says, "I myself, God, announced in advance through my prophets, and in keeping with my own words I saved those worthy of salvation through my servant." In place of "I reproached," all the other translators have said, "I made it heard." "For I made these things heard beforehand, since I alone was God among you, and there was no strange or foreign god. And you are witnesses of this, that there was no stranger or foreigner among you when these things were being foretold through my prophets. And I too was a witness, the Lord God, and so was the servant whom I have chosen." So when he was foretelling these things, the servant was with him; these things were from him and with him, and the servant whom he chose was bearing witness through the prophets.

In these words the text shows explicitly that Christ existed before he became man and was with the Father. "But from the beginning," he says, "having determined these things, I establish my own counsel, and there is no one who can set it aside or turn it back. For since no other god exists, it is clear that there will be no one who can deliver out of my hands, or overturn what I have determined." These things are said in the person of Jacob and Israel, but they refer to the company of the apostles. And the saying extends also to all those of the Jewish race who have received the Christ of God.

The sense of the passage is this: "Long ago I bestowed my benefits on the Jewish nation. To discipline and correct them I handed them over to the Babylonians, but before long I set them free from the captivity in Babylon, since I am God and Lord of all. And I overthrew the Babylonians themselves, who had attacked Jerusalem, so that the Chaldeans among them were put to flight. Some of them were even put in ships and carried off in chains on their own sea by other enemy powers stronger than they. I, God, brought this about, showing my kingdom to men." In place of "who showed Israel your king," Symmachus has: "I am the Lord, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King."

"These things I accomplished against the Babylonians and the Chaldeans." God was speaking prophetically, going through things that had not yet happened but were going to happen, as though he had already done them. "But even earlier," he says, "in the most ancient times, I showed my divinity to those in Egypt. I led my people through the Red Sea, making a passage in mighty water and a dry path through the sea itself. Then I hurled Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea, so that they sank to the bottom and lay there asleep, never to rise again. Those who had earlier been like blazing fire became like a quenched wick. These were the things I did in times remembered from long ago, and these were the wonders that the people of old admired and spoke of. But now, in the present, I urge you no longer to marvel at those things, neither at what was done in Babylon nor at what was done in Egypt. That is why I say: 'Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the things of old,'" or, according to Symmachus, "do not ponder."

"And why do I no longer want you to marvel at those things? Only because other, newer wonders, in no way inferior to those of old, will rise like light upon all people, and you will come to know them in their time." And what are these? "I will make a way in the wilderness," he says. Here again he means the church that was to be established among the nations, which was a wilderness empty of the knowledge of God before the Christ of God came, who said, "I am the way." "But in that former wilderness," he says, "I will make a way, just as I made one earlier in the Red Sea." And rivers of divine oracles will flow from the teaching of the Holy Spirit into the land that was once dry, just as rivers flowed in the wilderness in the time of Moses. But there it was bodily water, a flowing and perishable substance; now it is rational and spiritual water, supplied from a divine source.

"And when a way has been made in the wilderness, and rivers from my springs flood the dry land" (the springs of which it was said earlier, "And you will drink water from the springs of salvation"), "then the beasts of the field," that is, souls that have become savage, "will be changed from their bestial state, transformed by the power of the river. Even those who were once wild beasts will bless me, a thing that has never happened since the world began." For nothing of the kind is recorded to have happened, neither in the case of the former people, nor in Egypt, nor at the exodus from Egypt, nor during the stay in Babylon. "And if there were sirens who bewitched people's souls with pleasure and demonic song, adorned with eloquent words in the inventions of poets, these too will be changed and will bless me. Even the daughters of sparrows" (or, according to the other translators, "and ostriches," a creature found in deserts and uninhabited regions) "will be tamed and will learn to bless me, God." The cause of all this will be the water given by me in the wilderness and the power of the rivers that flowed in the wilderness. "And when the wild beasts, the sirens and the sparrows have drunk my water and been changed into a gentle and rational nature, they will learn to recount my excellencies, since they will have become my people and my chosen race"; or, according to Symmachus, "my praise."

"When these things have been so marvelously accomplished, know, Jacob, that you will not be worthy of my calling then"; or, according to Symmachus, "Nor did you call upon me, Jacob"; and according to Aquila and Theodotion, "And you did not call me, Jacob." "For the wild beasts, the sirens and the daughters of sparrows will bless me. But you, Jacob, did nothing of the kind; you did not even think fit to call upon me. Instead you grew weary of me" (according to Symmachus), or according to Aquila and Theodotion, "because you toiled in me," "even though I did not make you toil. Indeed, all the things that were thought to burden you with toil I had already rejected long before, when I said: 'What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs or the blood of bulls and goats.'"

"Nor did I ask you for incense or frankincense or sacrifices, or anything else of the kind, in the laws of the new covenant, which I ordained through my servant whom I have chosen. And you did not offer these things to me either. If the truth must be told, you did quite different things. For in your sins I stood before you," or, according to the other translators, "in your sins you called me, and in your iniquities." You see how in this passage too he proclaims good tidings of hope to the wilderness and the beasts in it, but rebukes the people of the circumcision for their impiety. He now calls them Jacob and Israel in this plain way, with bare names, without calling them his servant or his chosen one, as he did in the case of the better group.

Yet after rebuking those who stand accused, he spurs them on and urges them to turn back, and promises to forgive their sins if they do. That is why he says: "I am the one who blots out your sins, and I will not remember them. But you, remember what you were in." For the remembrance of former sins is good when it is spoken out in confession. That is why he adds: "State your sins first yourself." "For if you do this, you will be justified, since a righteous man is his own accuser in his opening speech."

"But know that you have been a sinner since your fathers, and your rulers in each generation have acted impiously against me." In place of "and your rulers acted lawlessly against me," Aquila and Symmachus have rendered "and your interpreters." Then he says: "And your rulers defiled my holy things." Here he names three groups: fathers, interpreters and rulers. By rulers he means the leaders of the nation, by interpreters the expounders of the divine Scriptures, and by fathers those among them who are older in age and years. Having said that all of these acted impiously, he shows that they were responsible for the destruction of Jacob. For because of them, he says, "I gave Jacob over to destruction and Israel to reproach," or, according to the other translators, "to blasphemies."

Here again he named those who stand accused "Jacob" and "Israel" without any addition, but those who are introduced next he names differently, with the customary addition. That is why he goes on: "But now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen." With these words he calls the company of the apostles back once more. He addresses them, saying: "Thus says the Lord God who made you and formed you from the womb: You will yet be helped"; according to Symmachus, "helping you still from the womb." What, then, does he say to them? "Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and beloved Israel whom I have chosen, for I will give water in thirst to those who walk in a dry land." And he makes clear how, saying: "I will put my Spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children." For through the Holy Spirit he was going to supply rational, fruitful and spiritual water to the dry land and the wilderness. The seed of the apostles is the churches of God, and their children are those who have been born again through the Holy Spirit everywhere on earth and among all the nations. They, he says, "will spring up like grass amid water"; according to Symmachus, "and they will spring up amid green grass like willows by flowing water"; according to Theodotion, "amid green grass by flowing water." Here too he took up the willow because the plant is evergreen and fresh, to represent the abundance of rational waters that would flow in his church.

Such will be the progress and achievement in piety at that time among those who once lived in the dry land and the wilderness that all will run to God, and, as if in a race, snatch up the grace of God ahead of one another. One will say, "I am God's," and another will take the name of Jacob for himself. Although he is not descended from him but comes from the wilderness and the dry land, he will nevertheless call out the name of the people who were once called God's. That is why it is said: "This one will say, 'I am God's,' and this one will call out the name of Jacob" (or, according to Symmachus, "will be called by the name of Jacob"), "and another will write on his hand, 'I am God's,'" and yet another will call out the name of Israel, taking pride in calling himself Israel. One may truly marvel and be amazed at the power of the prophetic words, since we have seen their fulfillment in actual deeds. In the persecutions of our own time we saw many from the foreign nations claiming for themselves the names of holy men. One called himself Jacob, another Israel, another Jeremiah, another Isaiah, and another again Daniel. Taking such names for themselves, they went to martyrdom for God with great courage and boldness. This is what the prophecy signifies when it says: "This one will say, 'I am God's,' and this one will call out the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'I am God's,' and another will call out the name of Israel."

The text has now concluded its earlier theme, which was a gospel theme, since it foretold the shining forth of God's chosen one upon mankind and announced the best of news to the land of the nations that was once dry and desolate. Here it makes a fresh start, addressing the idolaters of the Jewish nation, to whom it says: "Thus says God, the King of Israel." Of what Israel he calls him king he makes clear next, adding: "and the God of hosts who rescued him." He teaches that he is king only of the Israel that was rescued, not of those accused of idolatry. To these people, who were low-minded and still infatuated with idolatry at that time, he presents a refutation of their error. He urges and teaches them to consider no other god but him alone, since there is no other, neither beside him nor after him. That is why he says: "I am first, and I am after these things; besides me there is no God." Here again it is fitting to set alongside and join to this the phrase "and the servant whom I have chosen." For once that phrase has been said in the earlier passage, we must remember it and include it along with every statement about God. What has once been said and attested by God has been said truly, and what has been truly said is true wherever it is applied. And who was the servant whom he chose, if not the one of whom it was said: "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my elect; my soul has accepted him. He will bring forth judgment to the nations, and in his name the nations will hope," and the words that follow, by which the text clearly presented the Christ of God? But this has already been established earlier by all kinds of proofs. To those who persisted in the error of idolatry and supposed that there were many gods, the present passage sets out the teaching that they should consider no other god but one. For the unbegotten is one, and the sovereign authority over all things is one. And even though the Word of God is included in the doctrine of the Father (for "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"), it was not the right time to reveal the mystery of the only-begotten Son of God to those still infatuated with carved images, statues and lifeless matter. So this was held in reserve for the coming of the Son himself and for the grace given through him to all who no longer worship idols. But to those still wandering in the belief in many gods, to the point of approaching lifeless statues and all kinds of carved images as gods, [?]. Such were the Jews in the prophet's time.

The text fittingly presents the refutation when it says: “Who is like me? Let him stand, let him call, let him declare and set it before me, from the time I made humankind forever.” Let him say, that is, whether anyone is a god, and what work of his own among the things in the universe he can point to. For if the world is one, of a single nature and joined together with itself, its maker too must be one; and he is recognized from the greatness and beauty of created things as the author of the whole. If anyone brings in another god, let him prove it by presenting another such world in the same way. But there is no other world besides the one we see, and so there will be no other god either. If there is, “let him stand” first, it says — I mean, let him show that he exists: that he is a real, substantial being, and that he abides and stands on his own. Then let him utter a rational voice befitting God and declare what will happen afterward in life, or what came to pass long ago from the beginning, from the time I placed humankind on the earth up to the present; for from this we shall know that there is some reason in him.

“But do not pretend, hiding your faces,” as though you knew something but would rather not say it. For you have neither given ear to any of these things nor known them from the beginning. I, however, both foretold and announced them in advance through my own prophets, and I also displayed in deeds the works of divine power. Of these you are witnesses, you to whom I am speaking, who have learned the oracles of Moses, so that you must confess, even if unwilling, that there is no other god besides me. For at the time when I allowed you to see the mighty works of my divinity — those in Egypt, say, or those at the Red Sea, or those in the wilderness, where I displayed countless wonders — no one was with me in them. Nor was anyone with me still earlier, “not from the beginning,” it says, that is, before the times of the flood, when there were not even any craftsmen of lifeless wooden images. And you are witnesses of this too, that at that time — I mean at the beginning, when mortal life was first established — there were none who molded and carved gods, since the arts of sculpture and modeling had not yet been discovered among men. And if, late in the times that followed, a great many such people sprang up, they will all be put to shame and will cease from their error from then on, blushing and hiding their faces; but if they persist in their error, they will be handed over to destruction at the time of vengeance. Meanwhile, though, it is you, for the present, to whom this discourse is addressed.

Why ever do you not consider within yourselves what the nature is of the things you make into gods in lifeless statues? Is it not plain for all to see that they are the works of carpenters, fashioned with adzes and drills and other such tools, the invention of a poor and needy man who, for lack of food [?] and bread, devised this engine of error? And why do you not consider what the nature of God is: whether God needs food, and whether he will go hungry if you do not sacrifice — will God then grow weak if he is not fed? Or, as Symmachus has it: “He will be hungry, and weak, and faint, and will not drink water.” For why, it says, will he not also drink water, if he is in any need of drink at all? But if he partakes of none of these things, as a dumb beast does [?]. Why ever have you gone astray, you fools? These things and others like them serve to expose the impotence of wooden idols.

Having dealt with the idolaters of the Jewish nation, he adds: “Remember these things, Jacob and Israel.” He says this as to people who have forgotten and need to be reminded of them because of the dullness of their minds. Then he reminds Israel, saying: “For you are my servant; I formed you to be my servant.” Therefore you ought to remember your own dignity, and since you are God's handiwork, do not disgrace yourself by preferring to yourself, and making into a god, lifeless matter shaped by the hands of common craftsmen. Then, urging them to hasten to repentance, he promises that if they turn back he will grant them forgiveness of their former sins. So he says: “I have blotted out” — meaning “I will blot out” — “your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like darkness.” And he adds: “Return to me, and I will redeem you,” as one who had turned away and been handed over to enemies.

Having said this, the prophet then foresees that many of them will heed the prophetic word, and, fixing his gaze on them, he calls on the heavens — I mean the heavenly powers — to rejoice at their salvation, saying: “Rejoice, O heavens, for God has had mercy on Israel,” since there will be joy in heaven over those who are going to repent of their former evils. “And sound the trumpet,” it says, “you foundations of the earth,” or, as the other translators have it, “Shout aloud, you lowest parts of the earth.” For if there are certain divine powers that hold up the earth itself, let them too send up a shout and a hymn to God. It is likely, though, that the prophets themselves and all righteous and God-loving men are called the foundations of the earth; this at any rate is what the Apostle taught when he said: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.” And “let the mountains cry out,” it says, raising voices of gladness, and let the hills and all the trees on them likewise glorify God for the repentance and salvation of those just mentioned. By the mountains he hints at lofty and exalted souls, by the hills those more modest than these, and by the trees those that bear fruit. But in another sense he also commands the whole world and its parts to sing hymns to God, adding: “for God has redeemed Jacob, and Israel shall be glorified,” or, as the other translators have it, “and he shall be glorified in Israel.” This was in fact fulfilled in deed among those of the former people who were benefited by the teaching of the prophetic words and turned from the error of idolatry to godly piety.

Having first set out, in the preceding passages, its refutation of idolatry, as though idolatry were going to cease among those who were benefited by the prophetic teaching, the text now makes promises of a return from the captivity in Babylon. For since they had been handed over to the Babylonians for practicing idolatry, and Jerusalem itself had endured a siege and utter overthrow in the time of the Assyrians because of the outrages its inhabitants had dared to commit in it, he foretells to those who had suffered these things a deliverance from their evils, if they would cease from their error. These things were fulfilled in the time of Cyrus, the first to reign over the Persians. That is why, quite wonderfully, he even mentions Cyrus himself by name, though Cyrus lived some two hundred years later — the man who freed the Jewish people from captivity and ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be rebuilt.

It was for this reason, in view of so great a promise of good things, that in the preceding verses he called on the heavens and the foundations of the earth, and on the mountains and the hills and all the trees, to sing hymns to God and glorify him. In keeping with this he adds, in the passage now before us: “Thus says the Lord, who redeems you and forms you from the womb.” Who it is that forms from the womb, the scripture of Jeremiah will teach, where it is said: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you.” Here the prophet plainly presents the Word of the Lord as a real being and teaches that he is the one who forms the bodies conceived in the womb. Then, since he was hinting at their return from captivity, he fittingly called him the one who redeems. And since those to whom this was said were rather carnal-minded, he naturally reminds them that it was he who had formed them from the womb. And he adds: “I am the Lord who accomplishes all things,” or, as the other translators have it, “who made all things.” First, he says, “I alone stretched out the heaven”; then, “I made the earth firm.” For “all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.” He alone stretched out the heaven and made the earth firm at the nod and will of the Father; for “he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created.” That is why it is said in Proverbs, in his own person: “When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him.” For he was present with the Father as the Father prepared it by willing and ordaining, and when the Father brought it forth into actuality, he served him, carrying out in deed what the Father had determined. Therefore he says: “I stretched out the heaven alone and made the earth firm.” The earth, being solid and compact so as to be fixed immovably for all ages, is rightly said to have been made firm, while the heaven, being spread out over everything, is said to have been stretched out. So it is said elsewhere too: “stretching out the heaven like a skin.”

What it is that so great a Lord teaches, he next sets out, saying: “Who else will scatter the signs of mediums and divinations from the heart?” He indicates that there will come a time afterward when all the divinations and oracles of those formerly regarded as gods will be scattered by his power. “And those who are reckoned wise in this age,” he says, “I will turn back,” showing their supposed wisdom to be foolishness. These things, then, I will dispose in this way; but as for my beloved and chosen servant — I mean my Christ, about whom a great many things were said in the preceding passages — I will establish his words, and I will make the counsel of his messengers — I mean the apostles, disciples and evangelists — come true. I, then, who am going to do these things, foretell and promise already from this point that after the first destruction, which will take place at the hands of the Babylonians, I will cause Jerusalem to be renewed, so that the cities of Judea too will be inhabited, and their desolate places restored as they were at the beginning.

Moreover, the great mass of wickedness, which is called the deep, I will make desolate, and I will dry up the rivers of the great multitude of the cities, so that Babylon will no longer stand, nor will its rivers, which held great power in their multitude, endure. All these things I will do using as my servant a man of the Persian race, the first to reign over it. And if his very name must be foretold as well, the one prophesied is called Cyrus. I will set him up as the minister of my words, granting him a pious understanding, so that he will do everything that is pleasing to me and will order Jerusalem to be built and the temple in it to have its foundations laid. Or, as Symmachus has it: “who says to Cyrus, ‘My shepherd,’ and ‘He shall fulfill all my will,’ and who says to Jerusalem, ‘Let it be built,’ and ‘The temple shall have its foundations laid.’”

For when I have brought this about and willed it, Cyrus king of the Persians will carry it out in deed. That is why I have also called him anointed, as one advanced by me to the kingship; for among the Hebrews all kings advanced by God were called anointed. Having found in the man thus named a good servant of my will, I promise from now on to hold his right hand, so that he will not be turned aside nor overcome by anyone stronger. I am subjecting to him a great many of the kingdoms among the other nations, and through him I will break the strength of every dominion among the other nations. Having made everything smooth and level before his feet, I will deliver into his hands the gates of cities and the cities themselves entire, so that none will stand against him.

Let Cyrus himself also hear what is said to him, since he has been deemed worthy of this foreknowledge. Know, then, sir, that I will go before you, and I will level mountains, and I will shatter bronze doors, and the [?] that are impossible for others to undo, being shut as with iron bars; and the treasures stored within them, which were hidden and invisible to the kings before you, I will open up to you, so that you may know from the deeds themselves who I am, who so many years beforehand engraved your name in my prophetic scriptures as on everlasting pillars. I am the God of Israel, whom it is fitting that you too should not fail to know, O Cyrus; for I will grant you all that has been foretold for no other reason than for the sake of my people, whom I chose for myself out of all the nations out of regard for their fathers. Already, then, having called you by name and proclaimed you anointed, I have received you as my own, even though you did not know me but were devoted to other gods whom you received from your fathers, and did not know that there is no other besides me. But even if you did not understand this before, learn it now at least from what I am about to accomplish, through which all who inhabit the whole world will know that there is no other god besides me. For they will learn this from the deeds themselves. When I had to bring painful things on my people for their conversion and correction, I gave them up to their enemies, handing them over as if to darkness and wrath because of their impieties. But when it is fitting to take them back again, now that they have turned and been benefited, it follows that the light of peace and of all good things should rise upon them. For it is from me that light is supplied and all that belongs to peace, and by my judgment that the things of wrath are brought on as well. Learn this doctrine from me, then: that I myself am both the creator of light and the giver of peace, and likewise of darkness and of what are thought to be painful things. These are commonly considered evils, and I might be called their maker in that I bring on the deserving what corresponds to them by just judgment. I, then, am the one God, and there is no other besides me who does all these things — even if they seem to be opposites, they are not opposites by nature. For even the things thought to be evils brought on by me can contribute greatly to the benefit and salvation of those who are brought to their senses through them.

Having, as it were, proclaimed this good news and foretold the return of the people from the enemy's land that took place in the time of Cyrus, the text again calls upon the heavenly powers, saying: “Let the heaven above rejoice, and let the clouds sprinkle righteousness.” For just as there was once a time when I commanded the clouds not to send rain upon the vineyard, so now, at the proper time, I command my clouds, which are rational beings, to sprinkle not physical water but righteousness itself from on high upon those who dwell on the earth. And let the earth, which long ago was made desolate because of the people's sins, be renewed and sprout forth the fruits of godliness, producing mercy and righteousness — and by “earth” I mean those who will inhabit the earth. And all this will come to pass, he says, since I, the Lord who created you, have commanded it to happen. For just as I brought you into existence out of nothing and led you forth into the light when you did not exist before, so by my creative power I will bring all that has been foretold to completion, renewing you and creating you, as it were, from the beginning. Through all these things the prophetic word addresses exhortations to the people to turn away from the error of polytheism, and at the same time enables its readers to know beforehand what is to come. And it is likely that Cyrus took courage from this scripture and became more eager to do what had been declared, once he had learned what God had said about him beforehand. For since such a book was preserved among the Jews in Babylon, it was nothing surprising that they should disclose the prophecy to King Cyrus once he had been moved, at God's prompting, to show them kindness. Josephus bears witness to this account in his Histories, writing word for word as follows: “King Cyrus says: Since the greatest God has appointed me king of the inhabited world, I am persuaded that he is the one whom the nation of the Israelites worships. For he foretold my name through the prophets, and that I would build the temple in Jerusalem in the land of Judea.” Cyrus learned these things by reading the book of his prophecy that Isaiah had left two hundred and ten years before. This is said in the eleventh book of the Antiquities.

In place of “What better thing have I made?” and the words that follow, which are obscurely expressed in the Septuagint, Symmachus gives a clearer sense, saying: “Woe to him who contradicts the one who formed him, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth! Will the clay say to the one who formed it, ‘What are you doing?’ and to your work, ‘They have no hands’?” In Aquila it is put this way: “Ah, you who contend with the one who forms you, an earthen vessel with the craftsmen of the ground! Will the clay say to the one who forms it, ‘What will you make?’ and of your work, ‘It has no hands’?” And in Theodotion it reads thus: “Woe to him who goes to law with the one who forms him, a plowman among those who plow the earth! Will the clay say to the potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and your work, ‘You have no hands’?” It seems to me that through these words the text rebukes those who, after all the benefits he has listed concerning the return from captivity and the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem, do not run to God or confess that he alone is God over all — who disciplines his own people when he wishes, and takes them back again and restores them to their own land when he judges that this should happen. For it is as if addressing those who speak against his universal providence and governance that he says: “Woe to him who contradicts the one who formed him.” For when there was need of discipline and conversion, I both shattered Jerusalem like a potsherd and handed the people over to foes and enemies; but when, after sufficient discipline, it is again time to show my love for humankind, then I made the temple of that day better than the former one, and the city too, reshaping it like a potter's clay and renewing what had long ago been shattered. Similar things are said in Jeremiah, somewhat as follows: “And I went down to the potter's house, and behold, he was working at the wheel. And he broke the vessel that he was making in his hands, and he made it again into another vessel, as it seemed good to him to make it. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not do with you as this potter has done, O house of Israel?”

And so in the present case he says that "now I have formed, better than before, like a potter's clay, the people that was once shattered." Instead of "Shall the plowman plow the earth?" Theodotion rendered it thus: "he who plows those who plow the earth." For I myself, God, who cultivate and plow the human beings who inhabit the earth as with a plow, that is, my word, have myself formed the people like potter's clay, and the temple too, producing a work better than the former. Can the clay, then, give orders to the potter, or contradict the one who shaped it, or find fault with him and say, "What are you making?" or "Why do you not work, and you have no hands"? But just as the clay would not say these things to the potter, so it is not right to find fault with God, the maker and creator of all, before whom we are all reckoned as clay. Let every human being, therefore, who was taken from the earth and is clothed in an earthly body, and who differs in no way from clay when set beside the one who created him, be taught not to dare to contradict God's governance nor to find fault with the reasons of providence; for "woe to him who contradicts the one who formed him."

Above all, let the people dedicated to God, who claim him as their Father, beware of uttering anything rashly; for "woe to him who says to his father, What will you beget? and to his mother, Why are you in labor?" Or, according to Symmachus: "What have you begotten?" and to the woman, "Why are you in labor?" For there are many who love to complain and are in the habit of laying blame, saying: "Why was it necessary to come into life in the first place?" "Why do these things happen this way?" "What need was there of such things?" "It ought to have turned out like this." But for such people the "woe" is reserved.

Next the same Lord, the Holy One of Israel, adds: "Ask me about my sons, and concerning the works of my hands command me", as though you were advising me either about my sons or about the works of my hands. The intellectual and rational nature is indicated by "sons," while the parts of the world are represented by "the works of his hands." Concerning these, he says, if anyone has anything to say by way of correction, let him bring it forward and speak; but if anyone has nothing to teach, let him ask, if he wishes, and by inquiring let him demand from me an account about my sons and about the works of my hands, and let him learn in what way I order and govern, providing for and caring for all things on earth, and especially for those who, because of the rational nature in them, have been deemed worthy to be called my sons, and for the works of my hands, for which I never cease to exercise providence. If you are ignorant of any of these things, learn them from me by inquiring through my prophets.

Having said this, he next presents a pious teaching that sets forth his providence, saying: "I made the earth and man upon it; I with my hand established the heaven; I gave command to all the stars." What fault, then, could be found with these? What beauty do they not surpass, or what greatness do they not overshadow? In what respect do they not contribute both to the ordering of the present world and to a life that benefits human beings? For I made the earth not as a desolate or useless element, but as a dwelling place for human beings. That is why I also prepared the other living creatures and the plants for the use and service of human beings; and I established the heaven, adorning it with stars, which I commanded to keep an orderly and harmonious motion, so that at times they give light to those on earth, and at times serve for signs and for seasons and for days and months and years.

I, then, the creator of such great works, together with my other good deeds, also accomplished this for the sake of my people: "and I raised up a king with righteousness." Who is this, and of what kind? One person will say it is Cyrus, king of the Persians, whom the text also mentioned earlier, so that it is of him that it says, "and all his ways are straight," or according to Symmachus, "and I will make all his ways straight." "And he will build my city": for in effect it was he who built the city of Jerusalem, by permitting those who wished to go up from Babylon and to rebuild the place. Moreover, he says, "he will turn back the captivity of my people, not with ransom nor with gifts, said the Lord God", and according to history this too was fulfilled by the Persian king just mentioned. Another might say that these things are spoken about Zerubbabel, who, sprung from the royal line of the tribe of Judah and from the succession of David, led the return from Babylon of those who came back to Judea, and built the temple while Haggai and Zechariah were prophesying, so that it was said of him: "The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it." But someone else, beyond these, will refer the present passage to the Christ of God, whom the Father raised from the dead, loosing the pangs of death, and whom he appointed king with righteousness, so that he truly says: "But I was appointed king by him on Zion, his holy mountain." Of Christ alone were all the ways truly straight, and he built the true city of God, according to the promise he made when he said: "On the rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." For this is truly a city, built of living stones, the indestructible city of God, extending from the rising of the sun to its setting and filling all the nations through its God-fearing way of life. Moreover, the Christ of God alone turned back the captivity of souls, freeing them from demonic error and slavery. And he did this "not with ransom nor with gifts," as the Apostle teaches when he says: "By grace we have been saved." One might also say that what happened historically in the case of Zerubbabel or of Cyrus contains images and symbols of the true realities, while what concerns the true Lord and the true Christ of God has been fulfilled spiritually, so that the word that says, "Thus says the Lord to my Christ, Cyrus," is more truly verified in him. For according to the obvious sense of the words, the Persian king, who was not the Christ of God, does not appear to have built Jerusalem; indeed, the work of building made no progress at all during his lifetime. They only began the foundations in his time; then, when the work was halted, the place remained desolate until the reign of Darius. And what is said next would fit the Christ of God better than the Persian king, and our Savior better than Zerubbabel.

For thus, he says, "says the Lord of hosts: Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, tall men, will cross over to you and will be your slaves, and will follow behind you bound in manacles." He says that Egypt has labored through idolatrous error, when it had been enslaved to the devil and the wicked demons around him; nevertheless he promises that Egypt will find rest from its labor, hinting through it at the whole race of idolaters. "And the merchandise of the Ethiopians," he says, "and the Sabeans, tall men, will cross over to you", that is, to the king who is prophesied, "and will be your slaves." By these he seems to signify certain barbarous and savage nations dwelling in the remotest parts of the earth, which he foretells will serve Christ. That is why he adds: "They will follow behind you bound in manacles, and they will bow down to you." Saba is an Ethiopian nation, from which the queen of Sheba came to hear the wisdom of Solomon. Yet to these too a good end is promised: that they will worship the one who is prophesied and pray in him, since God was in him, and because of the God who dwelt in him he too was God.

Those who worshiped him did not know this long before, yet once they came to know it, they benefited greatly. He was also the Savior of Israel; that is why the name Jesus is rendered as "Savior." When, therefore, the souls of idolaters and of savage and barbarous men, made subject to the Christ of God, worship him, as indeed they have worshiped him, knowing him to be God because of the one who dwells in him, then "all who oppose him will be ashamed and confounded, and will walk in shame." How all who at various times have set themselves against Christ have been put to shame and confounded, both those of the circumcision and all those among the nations who kindled the persecutions against his church, the testimony of actual events shows better than any words.

Instead of "for God is in you, and there is no God besides you," Theodotion's version runs as follows: "only in you is the Mighty One, and there is no other besides him"; for there is no other than the God who dwells in you. Again, instead of "for you are God, and we did not know it," Symmachus says: "Truly you are a hidden God"; Aquila: "Surely you are a Mighty One who hides himself"; and Theodotion: "Therefore you are a hidden Mighty One". In naming him a hidden God, he makes clear the ineffable mystery of Christ's divinity.

Next he adds: "Be renewed toward me, O islands. Israel is saved by the Lord with an everlasting salvation; they will not be ashamed nor be confounded forever." These words too follow fittingly and concern the apostles, disciples, and evangelists of our Savior. For they were the Israel that is saved, and through them were renewed the islands so often mentioned earlier. These islands were the churches of God, surrounded by the wickedness of life as if by a sea. These, then, he says, are renewed and turn to him through the calling of his apostles, who were "Israel saved by the Lord with an everlasting salvation." To them the words "they will not be ashamed nor be confounded forever" clearly applied, as the work accomplished through them throughout the whole world by means of the churches of God bears witness.

Observe with me through these words how greatly the human race is honored by God, the maker of all. That is why he deemed it worthy of the saving call and of everything promised in the present prophecy. For just as I necessarily established the heaven as the abode of angels and holy spirits, for the constitution and adornment of the universe, in the same way I did not make the element of earth for idleness or uselessness; rather, I made it a dwelling and abode for those who live in it as rational beings, who were able both to know God and to live godly lives, inasmuch as they were made in the image of God. What the angels, the ministers of God, are in heaven, men who are dear to God are on earth. Since, then, the human race has been deemed worthy of such great honor by me that I established the whole earth for its sake, it was fitting that I proclaimed the gospel message openly to all human beings, so that not only the Jews but all the nations on earth might obtain the salvation that comes from me. That is why he adds: "I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth." For since the whole earth and all the people in it are mine, he says, I did not allow my words to be hidden or to lie concealed as in darkness; rather, I brought them into the open and spread them out before all, so that the saving gospel might be proclaimed to all nations. That is why the sound of my apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. These words fit very consistently with "Be renewed toward me, O islands. Israel is saved by the Lord with an everlasting salvation; they will not be ashamed nor be confounded forever." In these words the text mentioned the churches of God and the apostles of our Savior, and then consistently added: "I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth." According to Symmachus it reads: "I did not speak secretly, nor in a dark place of the earth."

These words would plainly fit the gospel message alone. For if anyone wishes to examine the oracles of Moses, he would find that they were spoken in secret, in the Hebrew tongue and in characters peculiar to it and not known to all. Moreover, if anyone considers that the law of Moses was given in a desert land, trackless and waterless, he would find that it was spoken in a dark place of the earth. Not so the gospel of Christ: the sound of his apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. It has been handed down in every tongue and every language, and in the scripts of each nation, so that all the nations may hear it. Therefore, if anything was ever proclaimed wonderfully and aptly, it was this, I mean: "I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth." Next he adds: "I did not say to the seed of Jacob, Seek a vain thing"; according to Symmachus: "I did not say to the seed of Jacob, Seek me in vain"; or according to Aquila and Theodotion: "I did not say to the seed of Jacob, Seek me to no purpose." For I called them first, he says, through the gospel message, and to them first I promised the kingdom of heaven, pledging it to them as a reward for their faith in me, so that they would not think that their service of God was in vain. That is why I also promised eternal life and good things "which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man." But since I am God who speaks righteousness and declares truth, in keeping with the principle of righteousness I called all people to myself after them.

From that point on I proclaim to all, saying: "Gather together and come; take counsel together, you who are being saved from among the nations." Instead of "take counsel together," Symmachus has: "Draw near to me, you who have escaped from among the nations." You see how he invites those from the nations who wish to be saved. But since they were not going to obey the message or accept the grace of the call, but would remain in their own godless error, he fittingly adds a mention of them as well, saying: "Those who carry the wood, their carved image, and pray to gods who do not save them, did not know." If they have anything to say on behalf of their own gods, let them come to me and draw near to me; for once they have come near they will know the true God. A great proof of his divinity is that he prophesied these things through my prophets and announced them in your hearing from the beginning. That is why he says: "Who made these things heard from the beginning? Then it was announced to you." Instead of this Symmachus says: "From the first I spoke them then." For if you think anyone else is God, tell me: what other god knew these things and foretold them? Who announced beforehand the things that were to happen? No one else knew, no one foretold them, since there was no other god; I alone decreed these things. That is why I say: "I am the Lord God, and there is no other besides me." And I decreed and foretold them because I am righteous and a Savior; therefore, in keeping with the principle of righteousness, I call all the nations to the salvation that comes from me.

Following this he adds: "Turn to me and you will be saved, you who are from the end of the earth," or according to Symmachus: "Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth." You see how he announces a universal message to all the nations. And he adds: "I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear: surely righteousness shall go forth from my mouth." Once again he puts forward righteousness, adding an oath to confirm the promise, so that, as the divine Apostle says, "through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong encouragement." And through the righteousness that comes from him he promises salvation to all people. "And these words of mine," he says, "will not be turned back." What words, if not those in which he said: "Turn to me and you will be saved, you who are from the end of the earth"?

And he adds: "For to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess to God," or, according to the other translators, "and every tongue shall swear by God." Through these words too he foretells that every knee shall bow to him, not that of the Jews alone but also those of the other nations, and nothing could be more blessed than this. The outcome of this prophecy too was fulfilled at the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, after which all the peoples gathered in his church throughout the whole world were taught to bend the knee to God in their prayers, even though the Jews did not know to do this. That is why it is said: "For to me every knee shall bow." No longer to other gods, nor to the error of idolatry, but to me, he says, every knee shall bow, to the God who foretells these things, and by me every tongue shall swear. And this followed naturally: for those among all the nations who have come to know me, God, in every tongue and speech, both barbarian and Greek, will call on me as witness in their oaths when they confirm their pledges.

These same people will say: "Righteousness and glory will come to him," or according to Symmachus: "Righteousness and strength will come to him." All the virtues found among human beings will have him as their goal, and all the strength of those who have contended for godliness will come to him, and they will receive the fruit of their labors and the reward of virtue; but those who separate themselves from him will be ashamed. That is why it is said elsewhere too: "All who worship carved images, who boast in their idols, shall be ashamed." And when will they be ashamed, if not when every knee bows to God and every tongue confesses to him?

Next it is said: "All the seed of the sons of Israel shall be justified and shall be glorified in God." Observe the precision of the language: he did not say "Israel," nor "the seed of Israel," but "the seed of the sons of Israel." The sons of Israel were the first heralds of the saving gospel, and it is their seed and their succession that are said to be destined for justification and glory. At the beginning of the prophecy too it was said concerning the same people: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah."

Having outlined the conversion of the nations and the election of the seed of the sons of Israel, the prophecy turns its discourse back to the Jews and signifies the complete overthrow of idolatry, saying: "Bel has fallen, Dagon is shattered; their carved images have become wild beasts and cattle." Bel was an idol, which the Greeks call El, interpreting him as the god they call Kronos. The ancients were so frenzied about him that they slaughtered their dearest ones to him and offered him countless other human sacrifices in every place. Dagon too was a wooden image belonging to the Philistines who inhabited Ashkelon and Gaza. Having mentioned these individually, the text then adds a more general statement about all the things deified everywhere: "their carved images have become wild beasts and cattle." This can be seen throughout the whole of Egypt, where they are accustomed to revere every kind of wild beast and cattle as gods. According to Symmachus: "their idols have been given over to animals," since they have been cast away and reduced to utter desolation. Next it is said: "You carry them bound like a burden for one who is weary"; according to Symmachus: "and for your beasts of burden, loads to carry, to the point of exhaustion. They were weighed down, they sank down together; they could not rescue the burden." These things were fulfilled word for word by actual events in our own time. In the deeper sense, too, the heavy, hard-to-bear, and diabolical burden of idolatrous error lay upon human souls long ago. That is why it is said: just as if someone were to lay a burden on a man who is hungry and no longer has any strength but is faint from lack of food, so the demonic burdens weigh most heavily on those enslaved by their error, people who are lost and unable to be saved from the war that has seized their souls, in which, like captives, they were bound in collars and diabolical chains and led away. That is why he says: "who will not be able to be saved from war, but they themselves were led away captive."

Teaching these things to the Jewish nation to turn them away from the idolatry that held them fast, the text next addresses them directly, saying: "Hear me, house of Jacob and all the remnant of Israel." Yet he neither calls them Jacob nor names them Israel, but only the house of Jacob, because of their kinship according to the flesh, and the remnant of Israel, as if they were its leftovers and dregs. Then he reproaches them for their study and learning of the divine readings from their earliest years: learning them from childhood even to old age, they studied them in vain, so that it was for this reason that it was said: "and peoples studied vain things." The greatest proof that their study of the divine Scriptures had been empty and in vain is that even then they were still practicing idolatry and needed prophetic words to refute them and turn them from their error. But even if you are such as this, he says, I, being God, will remain the same and will not cease to devote my effort to saving you.

These words too are addressed to the people of the circumcision, whom he no longer called his servant, nor chosen and beloved Israel; for in the earlier passages these added titles indicated the elect among them. So he says to them: "You who from childhood and, so to speak, from the very womb have been instructed in the divine oracles and have grown old in them have reaped no benefit for the soul from them. But I, even after so many of your lapses, still bear with you even now and call you to repentance, since you are my handiwork. For I made you, and therefore I also bear with you; and I promise to grant forgiveness for your sins, if you change. That is why I say: I will pardon you, and I will take you up again and save you."

Such, then, is my exhortation. But consider into what fighting against God and what impiety you have fallen, daring to liken me to things that do not exist and to count my divinity as nothing. You made me equal in honour to the lifeless matter that you shaped. You collect gold and silver from your contributions, have human hands make them into idols, and are not ashamed to worship them. Yet they can neither walk nor move. They are carried on shoulders and pushed along by others, and they can neither hear nor save themselves. You reckoned that I too am like these, you whose souls are crippled.

But look up a little and consider into what a depth of impiety you have run aground. Remember these very things, repent, and with right reasoning turn back to the knowledge of my divinity. Consider within yourselves that I am from boundless ages and before any time that can be conceived, and there is no God besides me.

I have set before men the greatest testimony of this through my own prophets. I declared what was to come and foretold what would happen long ages later, and I have accomplished these things in deeds and will accomplish them again in times to come. All that I have planned and determined will certainly come to pass when I bring my words to fulfilment. Whenever I wish, I do this by calling my servants, who are carried through the air like birds and winged creatures. I mean the angelic powers and the ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. So, calling from the east a winged creature (or 'a bird', according to Symmachus), and from a far land the divine powers that serve me, I will accomplish through them in deeds what I spoke beforehand through my own prophets. But according to Symmachus and the other translators he says: 'I will do all my will, calling a bird from the east, from a far land, the man of my counsel. Yes, I have spoken, and yes, I will bring it about; I have formed it, and I will do it.' And whom would you call the man of his counsel but his Christ? God says he calls him back from a far land, that is, from the recesses of Hades. All that I promised before this, I will make pass into deeds through him.

These words too are addressed to the people of the circumcision, and they should be joined to what was said above. There the word addressed them, saying, 'Hear me, house of Jacob and all the remnant of the house of Israel,' and went on, 'To whom have you likened me? See, devise, you who go astray.' There he called them those who go astray. Here he says, 'Hear me, you who have lost your heart,' for which Symmachus translated 'hard-hearted.' And he adds, 'who are far from righteousness.' You, he says, have removed yourselves far from my righteousness. Yet I have not dealt with you as you deserve. In my love for humanity, as a good and just God, I have brought my righteousness near, and I will not delay the salvation that comes from me. And I will do this without hesitating or delaying; from now on I will give salvation in Zion and glory to Israel. For so Symmachus translated it: 'I will give salvation in Zion and glory to Israel.' Acting in my love for humanity, then, I will give these things to Zion and to Israel, and I will display my righteousness by punishing those who besieged them.

These were the Chaldeans and Babylonians. He now turns to them and addresses them, foretelling the overthrow of their kingdom and the humbling of the height in which they boasted, having held sway over the nations for long ages. In these words he personifies their kingdom, naming it 'daughter of Babylon.' He also calls her 'virgin,' because she adorns and beautifies herself like a virgin, wanting to look young and to be thought a girl. Then, as to one seated on high, he commands her to get up, come down from her throne, sit on the ground, and hide the disgrace she will suffer from this change for the worse. This is what he means by saying, 'Go into the darkness.' Then, still personifying the kingdom as a virgin, he says, 'You shall no longer be called tender and delicate.'

That is what you once were, living in such luxury that all those you ruled used names like these of you. So put off that royal luxury and, like a hard-pressed maidservant or mill-girl, prepare yourself to serve your own masters. Take a millstone, that is, and grind with it, exchanging your former luxury for this hard and toilsome servitude. Take off your veil too, the veil with which you covered your head, adorned with gold and precious stones and all the rest of the hairdresser's elaborate art. You grew old over long ages in your tyranny over the nations, yet you hid your old age and your years, covering your grey hairs with your finery so as to be thought a tender and delicate virgin. Hear now, as you are exposed, that you will have to uncover the grey hairs on your head and display your age to all. According to Symmachus he says: 'Cover your ears, uncover your leg, cross rivers; let your shame be uncovered, for your disgrace has appeared. I will take vengeance on you, and no man will stand against me.' That is Symmachus. With these words the passage describes a deportation into a foreign land, a kind of captivity under enemies and foes, for her who is thus enslaved. Comparing these readings will make our own text clear as well. Instead of 'I will take what is just from you; I will no longer hand you over to men,' Symmachus has 'I will take vengeance, and no man will stand against me.' Instead of 'he who rescued you, the Lord of hosts,' Aquila has 'the Lord, who acts as our kinsman'; Symmachus has 'our redeemer, the Lord of powers'; and Theodotion has 'he who redeems us, the Lord of powers; his name is the Holy One of Israel.'

This, he says, is what our Lord has decreed against you, he who redeems us and frees us from the misery we suffered under you. Therefore he says, 'Sit pierced with sorrow' (or, according to Symmachus, 'silent'). You were once exalted and boastful and gave orders to the other nations as if they were household slaves. Now sit humbled on the bare ground, as one who repents of what she did and is pierced to the soul.
