Or, if you can, hide yourself and give yourself over to darkness, so that you may not be put to shame. Then, according to Symmachus, it says: 'For you shall no longer be called mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people; I profaned my inheritance.' I acted justly when I handed my own people over into your hands, to discipline them, to turn them back, and to bring them to their senses. But you went far beyond what was needed and showed no humanity toward people who shared your own nature.

The rest, being clearer, depicts the arrogance of the Chaldean kingdom and the boastfulness of the men who reigned there, and how they promised themselves deathless power and a rule that could never be overthrown. But at one and the same time, he says, two things will come upon you: the loss of a husband and the destruction of children. The husband is the one who reigns in you, and the children are those who would be ruled by you. These things will come upon you all at once, so that you will be shown to be both widow and childless. And this will befall you not only for the reasons already given, but also because of the multitude of your sorceries and enchantments. You placed your hopes in them and grew proud, all but saying, 'I am, and there is no other.' Instead of 'Know that the understanding of these things will be,' Symmachus has: 'And this knowledge of yours deceived you; therefore you said in your heart, "I am, and there is none after me."'

When the wrath of God comes upon you, use the enchantments and sorceries you are used to, and see whether you can somehow obtain help. These were your studies, which you learned from ancient times and from your youth. The book of Daniel shows how, among the Chaldeans who lived in Babylon, certain magi, soothsayers and sorcerers, men skilled and wise in these and similar arts, held a prominent place. They were in high repute with the king, as if the kingdom owed its success to them. But they did not busy themselves only with sorceries and enchantments. They also prided themselves on their knowledge of astrological theory, claiming to understand the heavens, the motions of the stars and the effects they produce. So use these too in the present crisis, when the time comes, and learn what is about to overtake you. But no one will be able to foretell the future from studying these things. The punishment by fire will seize above all those who pride themselves on such knowledge. When the whole city is about to be burned, then indeed they will be exposed, unable even to defend themselves. And this end awaits you as a whole as well: I mean being burned with coals and fire. And then your coals will be better for you than your former luxury, because they will turn you back and do you good. The words 'they will be a help to you' are not found in the other translators. You will be clothed with this end, he says, O Chaldean, because you gave yourself up to error for long ages and, so to speak, laboured in your trade from your very youth. The other translators have: 'Your merchants from your youth have each wandered off to his own side,' and none of them has been found to save you. Or, according to Symmachus, 'therefore there is no one who saves you.'

Having foretold what would come upon Babylon, its inhabitants and its kings, the word now rebukes the Jewish people in this passage. It says: It is because of my justice that I will bring these things on the Chaldeans, not because you deserved help. And I foretold these things before the events happened, declaring them by divine foreknowledge. I did this so that, when the predictions against the Chaldeans are fulfilled and carried out in deeds, you will not credit those you think are gods, or say, 'It was my gods, to whom I devoted myself in idolatry.' The Chaldeans have received this punishment at the hands of their enemies because I had already prophesied what would happen and threatened, through my prophets, to bring these things on the kingdom of the Babylonians. When these things come about in deeds, just as I declared, you will be compelled to confess that I alone am God, who made my own words come true. He calls them 'house of Jacob' as though they were not worthy of their forefather's name. And he says 'those who are called by the name of Israel' because, although they were not Israel and did not live up to that name, they were still called by it. Then he adds, 'and who came forth from the water of Judah.' They had nothing worthy of the patriarch's soul and came into being only from his water, that is, his bodily seed. So they were his sons only in body and flesh, not true children of his soul. By 'the water of Judah' he means the royal line descended from David and from the tribe of Judah, which still remained in Jerusalem at that time, in the age of the prophets. These people now accused were called Jacob and Israel and Judah only in pretence, not being truly worthy of these names. In the same way, when they swore by the name of the Lord and made mention of the God of Israel, they did it with their lips and mouths alone. They did not take their oaths in truth. They clung to the city dedicated to God and thought they were relying on God, but this too they did in hypocrisy.

Having addressed these words to the Jewish people, he next makes this declaration to them: Do not think, you people, that I foretell the future idly. All of this is done so that the unbelievers among you may learn from the outcome of events that the words of my prophets were not human, for it is not in human nature to know the future. It is I, God, who declare these things. Already in former times I foretold certain things, and certain words went out through the mouths of my other prophets, so that what was foretold reached the ears of many, and the events that followed agreed with the predictions.
Yet you, the Jewish people, seem to carry an unbending neck of iron, and you are now so shameless that no one would be wrong to say you have a brow of bronze.

That is why I have now announced to you beforehand what will happen. I did not want you, when the events came, to deceive yourself into thinking that those falsely believed to be gods had brought them about. Yet my foreknowledge also sees that you will not profit even from these words. Nevertheless, holding to my love for humanity, even now I solemnly declare to you what will happen to Babylon and to the Chaldeans who are going to make war on you. See, I have announced in advance the destruction that will overtake them, so that you may know it. Then, when the enemy arrives from Babylon and stands over you, you may recognize the God who prophesied these things to you and call on him as your helper, since he has already declared the end that awaits them. I granted you knowledge of these things through my words, for you had received no knowledge of them from anywhere else. Do not deceive yourself or say that you knew them before my prophecy. Where could you have learned them? Yet I am convinced you will not profit at all from these words.

For I know, and knew even before this, that you will surely deal treacherously. So in my eyes, as God who foreknows all things, you were called lawless and a transgressor even before you were born. Hence Symmachus has: 'and you were called a covenant-breaker from the womb.' Nevertheless, not for your sake but out of my own love for humanity, I have already foretold and shown you the destruction that is to come upon your enemies, because I am eager for you to be saved by every possible means.

So when I handed you over to your enemies, I did not sell you for silver. I did this too for your benefit, so that you might be brought to your senses in this way, since you had not accepted correction through words and exhortations. I did not sell you to the enemy for silver, but because of your sins and impieties; for you were sold for your sins. And yet even so I did not leave you to serve your enemies forever. I will redeem you again and set you free once more from your affliction under the Babylonians, as from a furnace of poverty.

And I will do all these things for my name's sake, because the enemy went too far and blasphemed my divinity. They did not believe that I had handed you over to them. Grown insolent and proud of themselves, they supposed I was nothing, and they glorified their own gods as the authors of their victory over you. Therefore I do not give up my glory, nor would I yield to another my divinity, which consists in a righteousness that extends to all people.

The word goes on to address these words also to the same people and about the same things. It says: 'Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call' (or, according to Symmachus, 'my called one,' and according to Aquila, 'O my called one'). Here he calls on those who do what is right. In the preceding passage he named others, those among the people who stood accused, but here he speaks to the better ones, whom he names his called. For among that people many were called but few chosen, and those meant here were not chosen but called. He reminds them of the truth about his divinity, saying that he is first and last. Hence the other translators have: 'I am first and I am last.' And it is said somewhere of the only-begotten of God that he is the first and the last, and 'the Alpha and the Omega.' How he is first and how he is last is made clear next, where he says, 'the living one, and I became dead.' He is the beginning of life, because he was the life. And again he is the last, because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father, humbling himself to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Next he presents his surpassingly great power, saying: “My hand founded the earth.” This is why it is said in Proverbs: “God by wisdom founded the earth.” And further he says, “my right hand made firm the heaven” — or “the heavens,” according to the other translators — that is, the divine and heavenly powers. And he adds: “I will call them, and they will stand together.” For the powers just mentioned will obey him as a master giving commands, and they also gather in one place and stand to hear his words. This is what the word indicated at the beginning of the book as well, when it said: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken.” By these words he puts his hearers to shame: if the divine powers show such reverent obedience to him as the Master of all things, how much more should you, who are only human, take up the fear of God? In place of “Who announced these things to them?” Symmachus rendered: “Who declared these things to them, whom the Lord loved, who will do his will?” How did human beings come to know that the heavenly powers obey when they are called and are brought to hear the counsel of God? If you long to know, learn that the Lord himself declared it and made it plain to you because he loves you. In Aquila it is put this way: “Who among men declared these things? The Lord loved him.” This is like Symmachus, who said: “Who declared these things to them, whom the Lord loved?” So it is this very one whom the Lord loved who made these things known to human beings. And this same one whom the Lord loved will carry out the Father’s will: he will bring upon Babylon what was foretold in the preceding passages, call his own people back from the enemy’s land, bring them home to their own country, and guide them on their way. “These things, then, I will do at the appointed time. But you have learned them beforehand, and they were not spoken to you in secret but announced to you openly, so come to me in haste. For when the Father was planning these things, I was with him; and now he who is himself Lord, the God over all, together with his Spirit of holiness, has sent me to accomplish what he once for all determined.”

“Hear, then, O Israel, what the Lord who rescued you is teaching you, and with every word remember that I am your God and there is no other. I show you all these things so that you may find the way of salvation. If you had obeyed me from the beginning, you would never have been handed over to your enemies. So great an abundance of peace was being kept for you that the peace flowing to you from me would have been like the stream of a river. And your righteousness would have become famous, resounding in the ears of all like a wave of the sea.” Notice here how he compares the abundance of peace to a river, and the people’s righteousness to a wave of the sea — or “waves of the sea,” according to the other translators. He does this so that if such things are ever said in other places too, one may not simply fall back on the obvious sense and suppose that they are said about a physical sea and physical rivers. “Moreover,” he says, “your seed would have multiplied into a countless multitude, so that it could be compared to the sand, and the offspring of your womb would have been likened to the dust of the earth for their number, if you had kept my commandments.” In place of “as the dust of the earth,” the other translators have said “as its grains.” Now if someone should take these things in a rather bodily sense, since they were addressed to Jews who were fleshly and bodily-minded, he might say that the promise was made to flatter their pride in having many children, because they could conceive of nothing lofty or worthy of God. But if you look at God’s promise in light of the dignity of the one who speaks, then understand, I pray, the seed from Israel to be the seed that was spoken of earlier in the words: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom.” This signified the company of the apostles and all the disciples of our Savior who came from the Jews. They became the fathers of the churches throughout the world, and of the multitude of those reborn in them according to God, who “were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.”

“But these things,” he says, “would have happened to you if you had listened to my commandments.” With regard to the Jews, someone might object that even though they disobeyed and did not keep the commandments, and even worshiped idols and killed the prophets, their begetting of children according to the flesh has nonetheless been very abundant. How, then, can the word hold this out with reservation as a special promise, saying: “If you had done these things, your peace would have been like a river and your righteousness like the waves of the sea, and your seed and your offspring” would have been so many? Now if they had had an abundance of peace while they acted righteously, and many children along with it, there would be nothing more to say. But in fact, by acting wickedly they have been cut off far from peace. Even now they are still enslaved to their enemies. The place that was once venerable and holy lies desolate and closed to them. Their laws and their kingdom have been dissolved. And while faring so badly, they multiply like worms in bodily begetting alone. It is time, then, to accept the meaning of the prophecy in no other way than according to the interpretation we have given. “But even now,” he says, “when you have not kept the commandments, nevertheless, because of my love for humankind, you will not be utterly destroyed, nor will your name be blotted out before me” — or, according to Symmachus, “from my presence.”

“This is why, promising from this moment on that I will not destroy you or blot out your name, I told you to go forth from Babylon, released and set free from fear of your enemies. Now that you have received leave to return to your own land, do not make the journey carelessly or sluggishly, but with all eagerness. For a voice of gladness will meet you, which can already be heard from here, and all who hear these words of mine will rejoice with you in your salvation. They will cry out so loudly that the news will reach all who dwell at the ends of the earth, as they say: ‘The Lord has rescued his servant Jacob. And if they thirst, he will lead them through the desert; he will bring water out of the rock for them; the rock will be split, and water will flow, and my people will drink. There is no rejoicing for the ungodly, says the Lord.’” Historically, these things were not fulfilled at the time when those who had been freed by Cyrus and Darius, kings of the Persians, returned from Babylon. As to their deeper sense, since history records no literal rock gushing water at the people’s return, we shall say that the promise comes true for those freed from the spiritual captivity, about whom Christ said of God: “He has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives.” For it is for them that the spiritual drink pours forth from the true rock, “and the rock was Christ,” according to the Apostle. Our Savior himself shows this when he says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly, springing up to eternal life.” Such, then, is God’s promise. But the word foresaw that many of those who heard the prophecy would prove unworthy of the promises. So that the children of the Jews would not suppose without distinction that what was said applied to them, it had to add to the promises: “There is no rejoicing for the ungodly, says the Lord.” For the godly will receive all the delight that comes from God, and joy and gladness, and everything else that has been promised; but the ungodly have no claim to what has been promised.

Having said enough of what was fitting for the Jewish people, the word now makes a fresh start in the passage before us and turns again to the calling of the nations, while at the same time prophesying the appearance of our Savior among human beings. So at the outset he summons the churches of God that are established throughout the earth among the unbelieving nations, and are washed on every side, as if by a sea, by the salty waves of wickedness. That is why he calls them islands and says: “Hear me, O islands.” But so that no one may slander our interpretation as wrongly given, he makes the meaning of the passage clear by adding next: “and give heed, O nations.” He all but states outright that these words are not directed to the Jews, nor to just any islands understood in the obvious sense, but to the nations and to the churches of God set in the midst of the nations. Hence Symmachus renders it this way: “Hear me, O islands, and listen, O nations.” Then he adds what he wishes to teach his churches: “After a long time it will stand, says the Lord.” First we must observe that these words are spoken in the person of the Lord, and so are those that follow. In them the Lord who began the speech teaches what follows as if about another, and yet he also confesses that he himself was born, calls himself a servant, and sets forth all the other things in the passages that follow.

We must listen, then, to what the Lord who speaks in this passage teaches when he addresses the islands and the nations. "Do not expect," he says, "now, while I am setting these things out, to see the words fulfilled. A long time will pass in between, during which what is prophesied will be made good in deeds." Where our text has "after a long time it will stand," the other translators said "from afar," joining "from afar" to the thought before it. This is why Symmachus rendered it "and listen, nations, from afar." Then he added: "The Lord called me from the womb, and from my mother's belly he remembered my name." Learn this, O nations, and you islands too. And what is it, if not that the Lord, the master of all, called me, the Lord, even before I came forth among human beings, while I was still being carried in the womb, and that he himself gave me a name? For now that name is known, as it were, to him alone; but in due time it will become plain to you as well, I mean to all the nations.

Moreover, the same God and Father made my mouth (the mouth of the Lord who says these things) like a sharp sword, able to cut so as to divide and separate those worthy of God from those who are not. He himself bore witness to this in the Gospels, saying: "Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth. I came not to bring peace but a sword." So here too he says: "And he made my mouth like a sharp sword." And he adds: "And under the shelter of his hand he hid me." By this he hints at the hidden plan of his coming in the flesh, which escapes the notice of the many. Just as he called his tongue a sharp sword, so he says that the Father made him a chosen arrow, so that he might wound, whenever he wished, those worthy of his goads. Such was the soul that said: "For I am wounded with love." Yet the God and Father hid this arrow too, as in a quiver and a case for arrows, so that not everyone might see it or understand it, but only the worthy. Fittingly, having called him an arrow, he uses the word "quiver." And you would not be wrong to call the flesh which the Word of God took on when he came to dwell among human beings a quiver and an arrow-case.

"Having made me such, me the Lord who says these things, my God and Father said to me: 'You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified.'" Since you came forth from a mother's womb and underwent birth from the seed of Israel, you did not take on human nature in some other race or among foreign nations. You were born in Israel, from the seed of David according to the flesh and from the tribe of Judah. So it is natural that you yourself should be called Israel, and also servant, because you took the form of a servant, though you are the only-begotten Son. As in the earlier passages, here too he conceals the name of Son and calls him servant, keeping the title of Son in reserve for his coming and for the grace revealed through him to all people. Then he says that what never belonged to any servant who ever lived will come about through you: "for in you I will be glorified."

These, then, are the words of the God and Father. "But I, the Lord who says these things, on hearing these words answered and said: 'And how will you be glorified in me, Father, when I have toiled much and endured countless labors for the salvation of human beings and have achieved nothing? For most of them have remained in unbelief, and above all the nation of the Jews.' So I say: 'I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength on what is futile and for nothing.'" Then he adds: "Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my toil before my God," or, as Symmachus has it: "my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God." "For even if people do not do what is right, and do not profit as my labors deserve, the labors I endured for their sake, I have nevertheless done my part and fulfilled the Father's will before my God."

"For this reason I first preached the Father's grace to those of the circumcision. He who formed me from the womb as his own servant, and prepared my body from Israel, willed that I should preach his grace to them first, in order to gather Jacob and Israel to him." Fittingly, then, he gives the instruction: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." "The Father, then, was pleased that I should make my passage among human beings in order to gather Jacob and Israel, and he said: 'In you I will be glorified.' But I, seeing the unbelief and hardness of heart of Israel, said earlier: 'I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength on what is futile and for nothing.' And elsewhere, making this same point, I said: 'What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to corruption?' But now I say that even if many people disbelieve and persist in their hardness of heart, still 'I will be gathered before the Lord, and my God will be my strength.' For the glory that comes from him alone is reserved for me, and he is my strength." Indeed, the wonderful and extraordinary works done through him were proof of the Father's power.

After this he goes on: "And he said to me: 'It is a great thing for you to be called my child'" (or "my servant," according to the other translators) "'so as to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to turn back the dispersion of Israel.'" And truly it was a very great work of our Saviour to take on the form of a servant and to undergo birth among human beings. That is why it is said to him: "It is a great thing for you to be called my child," or "my servant," according to the other translators. And the reason the Saviour became a servant was this: "to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to turn back the dispersions of Israel." For this reason he preached first to them, proclaiming release to those who were captives in their souls and recovery of sight to those who were blind. But since they did not accept the grace, it naturally follows next: "Behold, I have made you a light of the nations, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth."

After this the prophetic Spirit addresses the nations, saying: "Thus says the Lord." Then, since they did not know who this Lord was, he adds: "who rescued Israel"; Symmachus has "who redeems Israel," and Aquila and Theodotion "who acts as kinsman to Israel." "For he himself," he says, "who long ago rescued Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, he it is who addresses these words to you, the nations, and commands you, saying: 'Sanctify him who holds his own life cheap.'" The more he humbled himself, even to death, death on a cross, the more you are to glorify him. I mean the one who is abhorred by the unbelieving nations, who serve the rulers of this age, that is, the evil demons. Those still enslaved to these demons blaspheme and abhor the Christ of God, disparaging, mocking and belittling his death. But you, whom the word addresses, sanctify him by glorifying him, since every knee shall bow to him, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Then indeed, then kings will see him, and rulers will rise up and bow down to him, when he comes in the glory of the Father with his angels and sits on the throne of his glory, judging the living and the dead. For then all will worship him for the sake of the Lord his Father, because the Holy One of Israel, who chose him, is faithful. Where our text has "and I chose you," Symmachus said "who chose you."

These words, then, are addressed to the nations, while what follows is prophesied with reference to the Saviour himself. The prophetic Spirit speaks to him as the Saviour: "At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you, and I formed you and gave you as a covenant of nations." The words "At an acceptable time I heard you" are put most wonderfully, for this was the time of his resurrection. At the time of his passion the Saviour cried out: "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?" that is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" He also prayed: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." Then, seeing the Father refuse, he added: "Father, if it is not possible for it to pass, your will be done." So the Father accepted this prayer for its proper time, after the passion and the descent into Hades, and pointing to the time of his resurrection he says to him: "At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you." Where our text has "and I formed you," the other translators said "and I preserved you." Having hinted at his resurrection with these words, he adds: "and I gave you as a covenant of nations," fittingly mentioning the new covenant. Then he makes his meaning clear: "to establish the land and to inherit desolate inheritances." Long before, ahead of the passion and before those of the circumcision laid hands on him, it was said: "to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to turn back the dispersions of Israel." But since they did not accept the grace, they are no longer mentioned; here instead he speaks of the nations: "and I gave you as a covenant of nations, to establish the land and to inherit desolate inheritances," or, as Symmachus has it: "to raise up the land and to apportion inheritances that had been wiped out." Such were the souls of the godless and of those who worshipped many gods: desolate of God and truly wiped out altogether.

"And also," he says, "to say to those in bonds, 'Come out.'" These were bound fast by the cords of their own sins. He proclaimed forgiveness to them, handed on the way of rebirth, and by his very deeds said to those in bonds, "Come out," "and to those in darkness, be revealed." For we were all children of wrath, and we were once darkness, but now we are light in the Lord. Then he brings good news to those set free from their former bonds and their former darkness: "In all the ways they will graze, and in all the paths will be their pasture." The ways and paths along which the men of God of old travelled are the divinely inspired Scriptures. Grazing in them, those who have obtained the promise enjoy the divine delight that nourishes the mind, for they have found this good pasture, so that they can say: "The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of green grass, there he made me dwell; beside the water of rest he nourished me."

Nourished in this way, with food for the mind, "they will not hunger or thirst, nor will the scorching heat or the sun strike them." By the scorching heat and the sun he means the burning heat of mortal life and the passing enjoyment of what people consider light. "But not even these will touch them," he says; rather, "he who has mercy on them will comfort them and lead them through springs of water." Many are the springs of Israel and the springs of salvation, some belonging to the Old Covenant and others to the New.

"And I will make," he says, "every mountain a road," so that nothing may be uphill for them, or hard to pass and rough. And he promises also to make every path a pasture for them. We have said before that Zion and Jerusalem are to be understood in three ways. In one way they are understood in a lowly and Jewish sense. In another they mean the whole God-fearing commonwealth, understood as a community of souls. In the highest sense they mean the angelic commonwealth in heaven, of which the Apostle says: "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother," and: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." This being so, the present passage foretells what lies before us concerning the God-fearing commonwealth. Long ago it was established among the Jews; but it was torn down among them and, as it were, suffered a fall, and so it has been transferred to the church from the nations.

He makes clear next to whom he brings all this good news: "Behold, these will come from far away, these from the north and the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." The four regions of the earth are indicated here. One is indicated by the words "Behold, these will come from far away" (or, according to the other translators, "Behold, these will come from afar"), where the region is left unnamed. The other three are presented in what follows, for he clearly means north, west and east when he says: "these from the north and the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." If some come from the north, others from the sea, that is, from the western parts, and others from the land of the Persians, by which the interior regions are meant, it follows that the first, said to come from a distant land, are to be understood as people of the south. And since the southern land, lying in the southern parts of the world, is beyond human reach, he fittingly said that they will come from far away. In any case, the passage foretells that people will come to God from everywhere, from all four regions, and will receive the promises spoken of earlier.

Then, over the salvation shared by all people, he cries out: "Rejoice, heavens," for there is joy in heaven even over one sinner who repents, "and let the earth exult," he says, like a mother rejoicing over sons who are saved. Where our text has "let the mountains break forth into gladness," Symmachus has "the mountains will be made cheerful over all things," and Aquila and Theodotion said "resound with praise, you mountains." So the mountains too, as though they were rational beings, are commanded to rejoice and exult over the salvation of human beings. The mountains might be souls still living on earth but raised very high by their success in the virtues, or else divine and heavenly powers. He urges them to rejoice, "because God has had mercy on his people and has comforted the lowly of his people." And who were these, if not those mentioned before, namely those called back from the four regions of the whole earth?

Having spoken earlier about the calling of the nations, as we have shown, as though addressing islands and nations, he went on in the present words to add, consistently, that even if Zion among the Jews has been torn down (that is, the God-fearing commonwealth that once existed among them), still let her not say: "The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me." For it is impossible for God to forget the God-fearing commonwealth among human beings. And he uses an example from nature: "Just as it is impossible for a mother to forget her own child, and impossible for her who gave birth not to have pity on the offspring of her womb, so it is impossible for me, who brought the rational souls of human beings into being as my children, to forget the God-fearing commonwealth among human beings. Therefore let Zion not say: 'The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me.' A mother would sooner forget her own flesh and blood than I would forget the human race, which must by all means be gathered into this commonwealth, whether from Jews or from Greeks or from any nations whatever."

He develops the thought further, and quite necessarily, when he says: "Behold, I have painted your walls on my hands, and you are before me continually." With these words he plainly shows that the true Zion cannot fall and cannot be torn down, but remains forever and stands firm continually. So if anyone longs to contemplate it, let him not look around here below or search for it in the land of Palestine. Let him rather hear God saying to it: "Behold, I have painted your walls on my hands, and you are before me continually." For the hands of God truly build such a city. Or rather, they shape and paint it, tracing its site as if in a picture on a panel, and setting up the outlines of the godly way of life in human souls. The builder of his own city himself, that is, the Word of God, taught this when he said: "On the rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." For the God-fearing commonwealth, the city of God called Zion that cannot fall or be torn down, is understood to include both those who lived rightly among the former people and those who excel in the church of God. That is why it was said to her: "Do not say, 'The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me.' For I will not forget you, said the Lord. Behold, I have painted your walls on my hands, and you are before me continually."

The church from the Gentiles was established in a short time after the God-fearing commonwealth among the Jews fell away. So he next adds: "And quickly you will be built by those by whom you were torn down." For just as the Jews caused its demolition, so the workers on the new building came from them too: the apostles of our Savior, his disciples and evangelists, through whom the church of God from the Gentiles has been raised up. These same men tore down the self-made worship of the Jews, as Paul teaches when he says, "For if I build up again the things I tore down," and they established the new Zion according to the way of life of the gospel. Next, others besides these are indicated, men who laid Zion waste but did not build it. Of them it is said: "And those who laid you waste will go out from you." It is remarkable how the word was fulfilled not only in its deeper sense but also in history. After the church from the Gentiles was established, the whole Jewish nation was cast out of the physical city in Palestine, besides falling away from the God-fearing commonwealth.

After this he uses personification. He presents a kind of bride who takes pride in a multitude of children, and he addresses her: "Lift up your eyes all around and see them all. Behold, they have gathered and come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall put them all on as an ornament." He does not say who "all" are, because he has already told us who they were and where they came from, when he said: "Behold, these will come from afar, these from the north and from the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." All these, he says, "have gathered and come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall put them all on as an ornament, and wear them like a bride's ornament." Indeed the bride of the Lord, that is, the church, is honored by the comely souls who excel within her. She is made bright and beautiful by the multitude of virtues and of the gifts supplied to her by the Holy Spirit.

Then he says: "And your desert places, your ruined and fallen places, will now be too narrow for those who live in you." For the great multitude of the church throughout the whole world has been brought in from all the nations to take the place of those cast off from the people of the circumcision. These, then, were taken in. "But those who swallow you up," he says, "will be removed far from you." Such were, long ago, the powerful men among the people of the circumcision: the false prophets, the Pharisees and Sadducees, and those of whom it was said, "who devour the people with their whole mouth." He foretells that they will be driven out and removed far from the new and fresh city of God. And he prophesies that so great a multitude will come to the city he has described that it will need wider and larger buildings.

This very thing is shown in the words: "For your sons whom you lost will say in your ears, 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me so that I may live here.'" For those who ran to the commonwealth of God through saving grace were once lost. When the church of God sees them she will marvel and say, "Who has borne me these?" She is amazed at the strangeness of the calling of the Gentiles, and she will admit the childlessness that came upon her from the Jewish nation. That is why she says: "But I am childless and a widow. Who has reared these for me? I was left alone. Where were these for me?"

Then, since she was at a loss, God answers her: "Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and to the islands I will raise my signal, and they will bring your sons in their bosom and carry your daughters on their shoulders." He is teaching that he will gather to her, from those chosen among the nations, the sons and daughters about whom she said, "Where were these for me?" "I will lift up my hand," he says, "to the nations," and to the islands, that is, the signal of the church. And what is this signal but the gospel proclamation of the Savior's passion and of his resurrection from the dead? After this, he says, they will bring your sons carried in their arms. For that is how Aquila and Theodotion translated it. The one says, "and they will bring your sons in their arms"; the other, "and they will carry your sons in their arms, and lift your daughters on their shoulders." And who will do this, if not those who lead by the hand the childish minds of people being brought into the church of God? Paul was such a one, when he said to the Corinthians: "I gave you milk to drink."

Next he presents kings as foster fathers of the church of God, and says that their princesses will become her nurses. We have seen this too fulfilled to the letter with our own eyes, as those who hold the highest rule carry the church of God like foster fathers. Their "princesses" are the governments and authorities in each nation and each province, which serve the supreme imperial power. Like nurses, they will serve the needy of the church, supplying them with grain allowances at the emperor's command. That is why they were called her nurses, or, in Symmachus' version, her wet nurses, for he says: "and their princesses your wet nurses." Who can see with his own eyes these governments and authorities bending the knee in the church of God and pressing their foreheads to the ground, and not admit that this prophecy too has been fulfilled literally and historically? For it said expressly: "With their faces to the earth they will bow down to you and lick the dust of your feet." And when these things, he says, come to pass in deed, "then you will know that I am the Lord, and those who wait for me will not be put to shame." For it is good not to grow careless or give up the hope of what has been promised before events turn out. Those who wait for him will not be put to shame.

Having said this, he next teaches how the nations that were subject to the devil were set free from him through the power of our Savior. For he says: "Will anyone take spoils from a giant?" By "giant" he means the devil and the opposing power. Can just anyone, he asks, draw up for battle against a giant and despoil one so strong? And even if someone should attempt to take such a one captive, will he then be saved, even if he acts justly? Will he not be overpowered by the giant, as by one stronger than himself, and be in danger of losing his own life? In place of "unjustly" the Hebrew reading has "justly," for anyone who takes a giant captive would do so justly, and likewise anyone who despoils him. So Aquila and Theodotion translated "just," since it is just to despoil the tyrant and anyone who holds possession unjustly, and to make him a captive. But who is this who can draw up for battle against such a one and come out safe? No human being. Yet hear how what is impossible for humans is possible for God: "Thus says the Lord: Even the giant will be despoiled, and the one who despoils him will be saved." So Symmachus' version reads: "But even the captives of the mighty one will be taken, and the plunder of the terrible one will be rescued." He shows at once who it is that will do this, when he says: "But I will judge my judgment, and I will rescue my sons." He clearly teaches that he himself is the only one able to take the spoils away from the one described.

Then he goes on to explain what the spoils are, saying that they are his sons. So he adds: "I will rescue my sons." Once they are rescued, those who had seized them out of malice "will eat their own flesh and drink their own blood like wine." For since they can no longer eat the flesh of others, they will eat their own. Since they can no longer drink up the blood of human souls, they will drink their own blood, until they are drunk with it. When these things have been done, "all flesh will perceive," that is, all people, even those who are still fleshly, "that I am the Lord who rescued you and who help you." And who is "you," if not my own city, the restored Zion, to whom all these things were spoken? This, then, he says, all without exception will know and confess: that the achievement of so great a salvation of the nations did not belong to mortal nature. It was the power of God that rescued its own sons from the giant mentioned earlier and from those with him. In another sense, these words can be applied to those who at various times persecute the church of God. Then the word is describing their end and overthrow, and how they will eat their own flesh and drink their own blood. At that time all will know and confess that it was no mortal power that rescued the church of God, but that the one who helped her was the God of Jacob. In place of "God of Jacob" the other translators have given "Mighty One of Jacob." The word fittingly mentions the God of Jacob, or the Mighty One of Jacob, for it sends us back to the God who appeared in human form to the patriarch Jacob. We must take him to be none other than the Son of God.

The divine is incorporeal, immaterial, intangible and simple, and no one who thinks rightly about it would form any bodily image of it. Yet sacred Scripture speaks to us about it in human terms. Those who live in bodies, and gross bodies at that, could not understand it in any other way unless things from our own condition were brought in as examples. In this way, starting from things that can be perceived and seen, we may be able to understand at least in part what concerns the divine essence.

The word has gone through the gospel proclamation and the calling of the nations that came about through it, the founding of the God-fearing commonwealth and the overthrow of the giant described above. Now it turns again to the people of the circumcision. It is as though he were trying to persuade them and defending himself, explaining why, after visiting all the nations, he gave them up. So he says, speaking as if to their face: "Let none of you find fault with me as though I had forgotten the care I once showed you long ago. Let no one accuse me of having given a certificate of divorce to your mother, who once held the place of my wife. Nor let anyone think that I was forced, as a debtor to certain people, to sell you to pay off the debt. None of these things came from me. If the truth must be told, you sold yourselves by your sins. And you would admit yourselves that this is so, since I, who am God and Lord of all, did not shrink from coming down below my own greatness and coming to be present even among you."

That is why I came, lived among you, and shared your life as a man. I called all of you to myself, and I did all this out of my boundless love for humankind. Yet no one came to meet me. No one listened when I cried out and called all of you back to myself. Instead you dared to do things that the ear could hardly bear to hear. I bore even these things patiently, although I could have suffered nothing at all and need not have allowed anyone to dare such things. Or do you yourselves not remember how once I made the Red Sea dry land, because I wished to lead your forefathers through it? And when the Jordan River ran back against its current, those who were then guided by my power crossed it as though over dry ground. Surely you also know about the ten plagues against the Egyptians, and how I threw darkness over the sky like sackcloth and made it last three days.

I showed such power in the time of your forefathers. Why, then, could I not now rescue myself, and the bodily instrument I took on for the sake of humankind, from your hands? I could have, but this was the will of the supreme Lord who is over all, who is also my own Lord and Father. That is why I too call him Lord and say: "The Lord, the Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word." So it was fitting that I kept silent when I was accused and gave no answer when you bore false witness against me. I did this at the Father's command, since I had to become obedient to him even to death. For this reason I kept silent and accepted the insults on your behalf, knowing well that a time will come when I will no longer be silent. Then, having received a tongue of instruction from the Father, I will use it at the right moment, when I must speak a word. That time will come when I establish my churches throughout the whole inhabited world of humankind. Then I will no longer keep silent. I will cry aloud in the hearing of all the nations and make my Father known. At that time he will give me ears that can hear and understand the meaning of my teaching. These ears will wait upon me in the early hours of the morning and will receive my instruction. For my Lord himself will open my ears, that is, the ears that wait upon me and learn as my disciples. That is why I say: "He appointed for me early," or in Symmachus, "He appointed for me early, round about [?]," or in Aquila, "He wakes, morning by morning he wakes my ear to hear." For when I called you, I found none who would listen.

That is why I said: "Why did I come, and there was no one? I called, and there was none to answer?" But in due time I will speak with the disciples the Father will give me. The Father's grace will then supply me with speech and a tongue of instruction, and will supply my disciples with ears able to understand the instruction my words contain. I know that these things will happen in their time. For the present, though, when I made my coming to you, I looked among you for those who wished to be saved and did not find them. I called all of you back, and I found none who would listen. And when the time of your outrages came, I kept silent because the Father willed it, and I gave no answer even when I was slandered.

So I gave my back to those who wanted to strike it. To those who shamefully insulted me and struck me in the face I gave my cheeks. I did not turn my face away when it was covered with your spittle. I remained unmoved, handing over my bodily humanity to every kind of dishonor and outrage, and I defended myself against no one in anything. The Father's will was enough for me. I obeyed it and endured everything, knowing that the Lord who rules all things was present to help me. That is why I set my face like a solid rock, sure that obedience to the Father brings me no shame. I saw him at all times standing near me, presiding, as it were, over the contest as it unfolded and vindicating my endurance. If anyone can claim that the insults against me, and death itself, were justly brought upon me for some wrongdoing, let him come forward and show whether I gave any cause or pretext for such great outrage against me.

If anyone wishes to go to law with me and prove some such thing against me, let him come near to me, step forward, stand up, and make his case. But no one can bring any charge against my teaching or against the deeds I have done. So it is fitting that my Lord will be present to help me. For he says: when God the Father defends me, does away with all your abuse, and establishes my glory, who among you will be great enough to oppose his invincible will and be able to harm the one he helps? So if the scribes and Pharisees had had any sense, they would have refrained from their plots and attempts against him. They had learned beforehand from the holy prophets that they would never be able to harm Christ, who is God and Lord and the true Son of the Father.

"All of you will grow old like a garment, and the moth will devour you"; or "mould," in Symmachus; or "the devourer," in Aquila. By these words he signifies that their bodily worship has grown old, for everything that grows old and ages is close to vanishing away. The moth that devours them stands for their conscience over what they have dared to do, which eats away at the soul like a worm. For when they see the nations turning to God, and see their own fall, which they suffered because of their impiety, they are wounded and devoured by their conscience. That is why, at the end of the book now before us, the same prophet declares about these same people: "Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a spectacle to all flesh."

After going through all these things that happened to him in his Passion, the Lord himself goes on to address the same people: "And now, if there is anyone among you who fears the Lord, let him listen to the voice of his servant." By calling himself God's servant, he lets us understand that even after becoming man he is the true Son of God the Father. And listening to his voice was no breach of the Law. It confirmed the Law, which by type and shadow had described the truth in advance, and that truth is God and his decrees. "For I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance." So even now I call you back, you who are in the darkness of ignorance, and I say: "You who walk in darkness and have no light, trust in the name of the Lord and lean upon God." Only come and listen, and believe me when I promise you salvation.

But as I see, you shut yourselves out from every good hope. You heap up your own fire and make your own flame stronger, persisting in your unbelief and kindling all the more, by your blasphemies against me, the fire of eternal punishment that awaits you. That is why "you will lie down in grief," or in Symmachus, "you will lie down in pain," or in Aquila, "you will lie down in torment."

So that you may not suffer these things, I urge you even now to turn back and listen to these words of mine. Listen, then, you men who pretend to honor the Lord but act against the Lord's will by driving out what is right and treating the truth itself as an enemy. In their great folly the crowds of the Jews saw the only-begotten Word of God in a form like ours, that is, made man, and did not understand the mystery concerning him. In their lack of understanding they very often grieved him wickedly with words of abuse. So, as I said just now, he makes his most fitting glory and power plain to them and draws some away from wanting to think little of him, saying: "Trust in the Lord." In this way he declares most plainly that he himself is Lord and God, drawing them away, as I said, from wanting to think and speak of him in a lowly way. What, then, is it that I say? "Look to the solid rock which you hewed, and to the hollow of the pit which you dug." Instead of "to the hollow," Symmachus has "to the hole," and Aquila "to the cutting." Through these words the passage seems to hint at that very rock which received the Savior's body, in which Joseph dug out the chamber in his new tomb.

From there he passes on to the example of Abraham and Sarah. Like a rock, they were barren, fruitless, and childless, and remained sterile into old age, yet they grew to be as many as the stars of heaven. That is why he says: "For he was one, and I called him and loved him and multiplied him." Just as I did for Abraham, then, do not despair. From this rock too, which you yourselves hewed, there will be a hope of salvation for all people, so that they will not miss the promise made to Abraham, that is, the grace I will give to all the nations through this rock. The chamber that Joseph hewed out as a tomb was indeed a rock. But the divine Apostle also knows how to call Christ himself a rock, when he says: "And the rock was Christ." Those who contrived his death laid hands on the body of Christ and maltreated it in the Passion. So it is fittingly said to them: "Look to the solid rock which you hewed, and to the hollow of the pit which you dug." The Savior himself teaches this in the Psalms, when he says: "They dug my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones." And perhaps by "the hollow of the pit" he was hinting at the pierced side of his body, from which blood and water came out.

In the case of Abraham and of Sarah, who was barren, childless, and sterile by nature, they grew by a wonderful and divine power to be as many as the stars of heaven. In the same way it will happen now through the rock that you hewed and dug. For it will happen through Zion itself, by which I mean the God-fearing commonwealth, the Zion that had been given up for lost: "And you too, Zion, I will now comfort." By "I will comfort" he means the God-fearing community, which because of you had become a desert [?]. "But I myself will take up her desolation, and I will make her desert places like a garden, and her western parts like the garden of the Lord." The church from the nations is called a desert here in contrast with the one who once had the husband, just as in the passage where the same prophet declares: "Rejoice, you barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate one are more than those of the one who has the husband." And who was the one who had the husband, if not the one who received the certificate of divorce? In the desert, he says, there will be a garden like the garden of God that Moses wrote was planted at the creation of the world. That is why it says "like the garden of the Lord," and he says that it will be toward the west. For on those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death the light of salvation has dawned, and so has the garden of God, filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. There, he says, they will find joy and gladness, and besides these, confession and the voice of praise. Those who do what is right will raise the voice of praise, and those who turn back from their former sins will be cleansed through confession.

He has gone through the charge against the Jewish people, the proof of their impiety toward Christ, and the evils that came upon them for what they dared to do against him. Then he has foretold the change for the better of the church that was once a desert: that the garden of God will be in her, and that those in her will find joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise. Having prophesied these things, he very fittingly calls people to listen to his words. He no longer calls the Jewish nation, which was usually named Israel. He plainly calls the people gathered to him from the nations and the kings of the nations, in these very words: "Listen to me, listen to me, my people; and you kings, give ear to me; for a law will go out from me, and my judgment will be a light to the nations." No one could be so foolish as to think that "his people" here means the people to whom it was said: "See, you were sold for your sins, and for your lawless deeds I sent your mother away." It must be the present people from the nations, saved by the grace of God. This, then, is whom he addresses in the words before us: "Listen to me, listen to me, my people." He also wants the kings to pay attention to what is said, that is, the rulers of the nations, or else the kingdoms of the earth, for he evidently sometimes refers to kingdoms in this way [?]. He sets out teaching suited to them, saying: "For a law will go out from me," which the other translators have rendered in the same way. For a new people that was to be gathered from the nations had to be given a new law as well. The law given through Moses did not suit the life of the nations, since it confined all bodily worship to one place, the one in Jerusalem. So, necessarily hinting at the new covenant and the preaching of the gospel, he says: "For a law will go out from me, and my judgment will be a light to the nations." Here again he promises light to the nations, not to Israel. Instead of "and my judgment," all the other translators have "my decree." For he says: I have judged, and I have determined by decree that this law of mine and my decree shall become a light to the nations.

And these things, he says, will not be far off: "My righteousness draws near quickly"; or in Symmachus, "Suddenly I will hasten; righteousness is near." For the grace given equally to all the nations was full of righteousness. This was the Christ of God, whom Simeon took in his arms. Scripture records that he said: "Now, Master, you let your servant depart, for my eyes have seen your salvation," and the rest. Here the prophecy signifies the divinity of the Word. Just as it indicated his humanity by "salvation," so in this way it hinted at his divinity. "Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt." For, he says, those who wish to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted, reproached, and despised by men, and they will endure all kinds of persecutions and trials. So, to fortify them from this point on, he commands them: "Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt."

Rather, he says, they should look to the end that awaits those people. He describes it, saying: "For as a garment will be eaten by time, and as wool will be eaten by the moth," so clearly these people too will be handed over to corruption and destruction. So there is nothing to fear. They should take courage in their own Savior, whom he has already taught to be immortal, ageless, enduring, and the bringer of salvation. And once more he repeats this teaching about God and seals it with the words before us: "But my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to generations of generations."

The addition "Jerusalem" is found neither in the Hebrew text nor in the other translators. Aquila says: "Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of the Lord." Symmachus has: "Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of the Lord." And Theodotion likewise has: "Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of the Lord." So according to all the translators and the Hebrew wording itself, the passage addresses not Jerusalem but the arm of the Lord. It follows that we too should take these words as addressed to the arm of the Lord, of which it was said above: "And the nations will hope in my arm." We said that the divinity of the Word is signified in this way. He had just urged the people not to fear the reproach of men and not to be overcome by their contempt. Fittingly, then, a prayer of entreaty is now sent up in the person of the people to the arm of God, begging it to awake and fight for its own people. For, they say, we are nothing unless you shield us and fight for us. So you yourself, arm of the Lord, awake, awake, and put on your own strength and your own might. And awake, he says, as you did in former times. That is why Symmachus has: "Awake as in the days of old, the generations of ages." For it was you who wounded the great dragon in Egypt and brought down his arrogance, when you hurled Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea. Now too, arm of the Lord, awake, so that you may do the same for us and bring us safely through every trial. That is why Aquila has: "Was it not you yourself who hewed down the onrush?" or "arrogance," in Symmachus, and also: "You wounded the dragon." Or, in Theodotion: "Was it not you yourself who dried up the sea, the water of the deep, who made the depths of the sea a road for those rescued and redeemed by the Lord to pass over?"

So bring about in our own time the very things that you, the arm of the Lord, did in the days of old. Then the enemies and foes of your people will suffer what the ancient tyrants suffered, while your servants and your household will come to Zion with gladness, that is, to your heavenly city. When they arrive there with gladness and everlasting rejoicing, they will be crowned like victors with the prizes that come from you. Upon their head, then, will be praise, which they will wear in place of a crown, and gladness will take hold of them. Then they will also be beyond all fear, no longer on guard against enemies or foes, for in the heavenly Zion pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away.

When the prophetic Spirit had offered this prayer in the person of the new people and of the church from the Gentiles, the arm of the Lord, having been called upon, answers and says: "I am he who comforts you." For he is our propitiation and the one who comforts the lowly. Then he fittingly reminds the rational nature, made in the image of God, saying: "Know who you are, that you were afraid." For you have been thought worthy by me of the greatest honor, so that you are comforted by me. That is why I say: "I am he who comforts you." But somehow you forgot your own worth, gave way to cowardice, and were afraid of a mortal man and of a son of man. He says this to the more timid and weaker members of the church, for those who have been made perfect and adorned with the crowns of martyrdom have obtained the glory that is with him. But since all are one body, and when one member suffers all the members suffer with it, he fittingly brings comfort and healing also to the more timid and weaker, and to those who faltered in the time of the persecutions, calling them to repentance. That is why he says: "Know who you are, that you were afraid of a mortal man and of a son of man, who have withered like grass." For you ought to remain fearless and untroubled, as my people, looking to the end of humanity's perishable nature and to the destruction that awaits the very people you feared.

"But you feared them, and you forgot God who made you, who made the heaven and laid the foundations of the earth. And all your days you were continually afraid of the face of the fury of the one who oppressed you, who planned to do away with you." Yet even if you were afraid out of weakness, now at least observe their end, consider within yourself how they have vanished from among humankind, and reckon: where then has that fury of your oppressor, which you feared, been quenched? For when you are being saved, those who once made war on you will neither stand nor appear, while you who were humbled for a little while will rise up from the fall into which you have fallen.

These things will happen for you because I am your God. Long ago I handed Pharaoh over to the depths of the sea and saved my own people, and I also always display the same power of my divinity. For when I will, I allow the sea to rise for a little while, so that it roars and its waves are tossed; then I calm it again, soothe it, and bring it to stillness. So too I let the persecutions against my church take place and allow them to happen in order to test my athletes. "For I am he who stirs up the sea and makes its waves roar"; but when I so will, it is calmed again and all is at peace.

"Yet while the sea is stirred up and its waves are rising, I will put my words in your mouth and shelter you under the shadow of my hand," so that you may suffer no harm from those who make war on you. And so that you may become still bolder, unshaken and unfalling, learn that I promise to shelter you in my hand, in this very hand with which I established the heaven, founded the earth, and brought the whole world out of non-being into being. Why then should you be anxious or fear with a merely human fear? You ought to run under my shadow and never withdraw from it, and to carry my words in your mouth at all times. The words "I will put my words in your mouth" are like what our Savior said to his disciples: "But when they bring you before courts, do not be anxious about how or what you will say, for what you are to say will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you." For this reason I have shown human beings my own hand, by which I established the heaven and founded the earth, so that I might tell Zion, that is, my people, to take courage and no longer be anxious or afraid of mortal man. Therefore Symmachus renders it: "And in the shadow of my hand I will shelter you, the hand with which I planted the heaven and founded the earth, in order to say to Zion, 'You are my people.'" Aquila renders it: "and to say to Zion, 'You are my people.'" So the whole people of God may rightly be called Zion, and Zion will be nothing other than the people of God. Throughout the present passage these words are addressed to the people from the Gentiles, as was shown from what came before.

In the earlier passage the Word foretold the calling of the Gentiles in these words: "Hear me, hear me, my people, and you kings, give ear to me; for a law will go forth from me, and my judgment as a light to the nations." In the present passage he moves on to another subject and addresses fallen Jerusalem, urging her to rise up from her fall. By these words he seems to mean her final fall, which she suffered after the crimes committed in her against our Savior, for which she also experienced the wrath of God. But the Word is kind and loves humankind, and does not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance. So he urges her to hasten to repentance and holds out good hopes if she should repent. That is why he says: "Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury." So it is Jerusalem that has drunk the cup of wrath. But there is another Jerusalem, about which most of the prophecies are spoken. Therefore we must not confuse them or suppose that contradictory things are said about the same city. One is in heaven; God is said to reign over it, and neither wrath nor fury touches it, for pain and sorrow and sighing have fled from it. Another is the city of God established on earth, which, as we showed, signifies the godly commonwealth among human beings. And besides these there is the one that has experienced the fury of God because of the transgressions of its inhabitants. In place of "the cup of falling, the bowl of my fury," Symmachus rendered: "the cup of his fury, the bowl of convulsion, she drank and drained, and there is none to console her." A person drinks the cup of fury and falling, and drains it to the bottom, when he undergoes all the punishments and chastisements brought upon him for the wrongs he has done. Physicians give bitter antidotes to the sick in order to purge the disorder already present in the body. In the same way it is said of God: "In the hand of the Lord there is a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, and he has tilted it from one side to the other; yet its dregs have not been emptied; all the sinners of the earth shall drink." For the physician of souls applies punishments to the soul in proportion to the passions present in it, like healing antidotes, to cleanse the evil already within it.

He teaches, then, that this happened to Jerusalem and to the people in her. And he says that not one of the sons born in her could be found who was able to comfort her and free her from her troubles. This too was fulfilled at no other time than after the passion of our Savior, when neither prophet nor priest nor any man dear to God was found in her. For they drove the disciples, apostles and evangelists of our Savior out from among themselves, killing some and tormenting others with blows and chasing them far away. In the time of the Babylonians, when the city was besieged and the people taken captive, righteous men and prophets were still left among them who could comfort them. But now the prophecy says: "There was none to comfort you from among the children you bore." In place of "These two things are set against you," Symmachus says: "These are the two things that have come upon you; who will grieve for you? Misery and ruin, famine and sword; who will console you?"

And according to Symmachus he adds: "Your sons went off, led at the head of all the nets, like an oryx in a net." The other translators also have, in place of "like a half-cooked beet," "like an oryx caught in a net," or "captured." The oryx is a bird by that name, and he compares to it the sons of Jerusalem, who were caught in the devil's net and for that reason were also handed over to fury. Hence Symmachus adds: "those who are full of the wrath of the Lord, of the rebuke of God."

And he goes on: "Therefore hear this, you who are afflicted and drunk, but not with wine." And according to Symmachus he continues: "Thus says your Lord, and your God, who will fight for his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of convulsion, the bowl, the cup of fury; you shall not drink it again." The Word promises Jerusalem that he will take the cup of fury from her if she repents, for "Behold, I have taken" stands for "I will take." The promise holds if you do what you are commanded and obey the word that says to you: "Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem." For these promises are made to her once she has been awakened and has risen. But if she does not obey, is not roused, and does not rise from her fall, but remains disobedient and deaf, she herself will be to blame for not obtaining what was promised. These words were spoken to the whole nation of the Jews. They were not addressed to the stones and buildings, nor to the dust of the ground and the desolation of the place. You will grasp the meaning of the passage from what is said elsewhere in the same terms: "Does not one who falls rise up again? Or does not one who turns away turn back? Why do you turn away in shameless turning? says the Lord." So he promises to raise her up, so that she will no longer drink the cup of fury, for it will be given to her enemies. Therefore Symmachus renders it: "And I will put it into the hands of those who carried you into exile, who said to your soul, 'Bow down, so that we may pass over'; and you made your back like the ground, and like a road for those passing by."

It is likely that these words also refer to the opposing powers, to which every soul that has turned away from God subjects itself. The soul that draws near to God stands upright, looking up and lifted toward him. But the soul that has joined itself to the wicked demons who work sin is forced to bend down, like the woman in the Gospel who was bent over completely and could not straighten up, of whom the Savior said: "And this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound for eighteen years." In the same way Jerusalem, which had fallen wholly to the ground and lay stretched out on the earth to be trampled by those who humbled her, is commanded to rise up. And the Word addresses her a second time, saying: "Awake, awake, Zion; put on your strength, Zion." For the rational soul has very great power and strength, and has great glory, since it was made in the image of God. He wants her to take this up again and become a holy city, so that no uncircumcised or unclean person will pass through her any longer. By "the uncircumcised" he means the foreigner and the alien, and by "the unclean" the idolater. So, the Word says, if you obey the command, rise up, and become the holy city of God, he promises you that neither idolater nor foreigner will pass through you.

And he urges her to do yet another thing, saying: "Shake off the dust and arise, Jerusalem." For it was in her power to rub off the dust caked on her, to rise up from the fall that had befallen her, and to loose the bond laid on her neck, with which the opposing powers had tied the soul as with a noose, with the cords of sins. That these words were spoken not to the buildings or to the visible city but to the unbelieving people, he makes clear by what he adds next: "Loose the bond from your neck, captive daughter of Zion." For by plainly saying "captive" he meant nothing other than the people, taken wholly captive by the power of the devil. That is why he addresses the same people more plainly and says: "You were sold for nothing." And earlier it was said to them: "Behold, you were sold for your sins, and for your iniquities I sent away your mother. Because I came and there was no one; I called and there was none to answer." In these words the Word plainly indicates the Lord's coming among human beings, after which they were sold by their sins for nothing, receiving nothing in exchange for their own destruction. Nevertheless, even after so much, the Word calls them back to salvation and promises to redeem them, if they are willing to run to him and receive the grace of Christ. And he promises to redeem them not with silver. Their captivity was not bodily, so that they might gain freedom by a bodily ransom, since it was their souls that had been sold. Therefore they were to be redeemed not with silver, but clearly with the precious blood of Christ.

Next he accuses the Jewish people, who long ago went down into Egypt of their own choice and afterwards were carried off to the Assyrians by force and compulsion. In place of "they were led by force," Symmachus says: "And Asshur carried him off for nothing." Long ago, he says, he became subject to the Egyptians and then to the Assyrians, but now, at my coming, they were sold for nothing in a different way. That is why it is added: "And now, what will there be here?" Or, according to the other translators: "And now, what is there for me here?" For, he says, I find nothing here among them. This was also shown earlier, when he said: "Because I came and there was no one; I called and there was none to answer." Long ago they were enslaved by force and compulsion, first to the Egyptians and then to the Assyrians, and were handed over because of their sins. Now, however, they were taken for nothing, "like an oryx in a net," caught by the hunter of souls in the nets of wickedness. That is why he adds: "Because my people were taken for nothing, marvel and wail." Symmachus says: "Those who rule over him wail"; Aquila: "Those who rule over him weep"; and Theodotion: "His rulers wail." So the rulers and leaders of the people, having become the cause of its destruction, wail when they are handed over to punishment. For it was they who stirred up the crowds to shout godless cries against our Savior. This was also shown earlier in the words: "The Lord himself will come to judgment with the elders of the people and with its rulers. But you, why have you set my vineyard on fire, and why is the plunder of the poor in your houses?" After this the Word resumes and says: "Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations." Or according to Symmachus: "Continually, all day long, my name is blasphemed." The words "among the nations" are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators. By these words the prophecy refers to their blasphemies against Christ, which the rulers of the Jewish nation utter all day long, always and continually.

You, he says, are like this. But another people, from the Gentiles, has been formed for me, and of it the earlier words say: "It will know my name", the name that you blaspheme because you do not know its power. My people will know my name, having learned by experience how great a saving and divine power it shares in. And this will happen "on that day." Which day? When, he says, I myself, who now speak these things through the prophets, make my own coming among human beings. Symmachus renders it: "Therefore my people will know my name on that day, because I myself am the one who speaks: Here I am." It is as if he were saying more plainly: when I myself, who now speak these things through the prophet, have shown myself to human beings and say that I myself am the one who speaks: I am here.

Having foretold the coming among human beings of the one who long ago spoke through the prophets, the Word very fittingly adds the gospel proclamation that was spread to all the nations through his apostles, whom he mentions in the present passage. The divine Apostle took up the sense of these words in the Epistle to the Romans and paraphrased it in this way: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, who bring good news of peace!" Symmachus rendered the passage this way: "How comely upon the mountains are the feet of one who brings good news, who makes peace heard, who brings good news of good things, who makes salvation heard." Where we have "salvation," the Hebrew has the word yeshua. So if the translators had kept the Hebrew word unchanged, nothing would have kept them from saying: "who makes Jesus heard." According to Aquila: "How beautiful have become upon the mountains the feet of those who bring good news of good things, of one who makes salvation heard." According to Theodotion: "How comely upon the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news of good things." In these words the prophetic Spirit marvels at the feet of the heralds of the gospel, by which they ran their course as they made their circuit to all the nations.
