Their feet were beautiful also because they had been made clean, for the Savior had washed them. They ran upon the mountains because the gospel proclamation is lofty and exalted. They announced peace to human beings as they brought the good news of peace with God. This was the very peace they proclaimed to those far off and to those near, showing that the Christ of God has made both one and broken down the dividing wall of the partition, the enmity, in his flesh. That is why Paul, when he wrote to the churches, wrote: "Grace to you and peace." They also brought good news of good things, the truly good things, announcing the beatitudes that the Savior gave through his gospel teaching. And the proclamation said to Zion, that is, to the godly commonwealth and to the company of the apostles: "Your God shall reign." That is why they proclaimed the kingdom of heaven to all people.

Instead of “The voice of those who guard you has been lifted up,” Symmachus has said, “The voice of your watchmen raised its voice,” and he went on: “Together they will give praise, for they will see with their own eyes when the Lord turns Zion back.” Here again the God-fearing commonwealth is called Zion. According to Aquila: “The voice of your watchmen,” he says, “raised its voice; together they will exult, for they will see eye to eye.” And according to Theodotion: “The voice of your watchmen raised its voice, about which they will give praise, for they will see eye to eye.” Here the text calls the disciples and apostles of our Savior watchmen. The prophets who arose among the people of the circumcision were called that people's watchmen. In the same way, the apostles of our Savior have now become watchmen and guardians of the new and fresh Zion, that is, of the church of God and the God-fearing commonwealth. They saw the Savior with their own eyes and heard him with their own ears, and they raised their voice so that it could be heard by all the nations. And they were filled with every spiritual joy, because God was showing mercy to the Zion restored to us, and its places that had long lain desolate were being saved through the redemption that brings salvation.

Instead of “Let the desolate places of Jerusalem break forth in gladness together,” Symmachus has: “Be cheerful and exult together, you desolate places of Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is to be understood as the city of God, by which I mean the God-fearing commonwealth. The text now announces the good news that its places, long desolate, will be filled with exultation and gladness through the mercy of God.

Quite consistently, he goes on to show what was meant by the words spoken to Jerusalem, saying next: “The Lord will reveal his holy arm before all the nations.” According to Symmachus it reads: “The Lord has revealed his holy arm before all the nations, and all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God.” You see how here too the gospel proclamation promises the nations what had been foretold. For he says that God will reveal his holy arm, which was God the Word himself, to all the nations, and that all the farthest parts of the earth will see the salvation that comes from our God. So whenever he addresses Zion and Jerusalem, what he says refers to the calling of the nations. For the God-fearing commonwealth, which has been named Zion and Jerusalem, was at one time among them and at another time among the nations. That is why such a city of God has always existed among human beings. So it makes no difference whether the chosen portion set apart for God among human beings is called Zion or named Jerusalem.

This, as we have often said, is the God-fearing commonwealth among human beings. Next, addressing the company of the apostles, the prophetic Spirit says: “Depart, depart, go out from there”—clearly meaning from the unbelieving people—“and touch nothing unclean; go out from the midst of her and be set apart, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.” The vessels of the Lord were their bodies, chosen by the Lord and set apart for God in holiness and honor. Or the vessels of the Lord may be the gospels of the new covenant. He commands those who carry them to leave behind the unbelief of the Jewish people and to separate themselves from them.

And he adds: “For you will not go out in confusion, nor will you go in flight.” For they did not set out on their circuit of the nations like men driven out. They went with complete eagerness and of their own free choice, because they had been commanded to make disciples of all the nations in his name. That is why it is said to them: “For you will not go out in confusion, nor will you go in flight.” So they made their journey in complete peace, having with them the one who had said to them, “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” This is what the present passage also means when it says: “For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel is the one who gathers you.”

“Behold, my servant will understand, and he will be exalted and glorified and lifted up exceedingly.” For he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name. This is exactly what the present prophecy shows. Here it says, “Behold, my servant will understand, and he will be exalted and glorified and lifted up,” and by these words it signifies his resurrection after death and his taking up and exaltation into heaven. In what follows it sets forth his humiliation even to death, where it says: “We saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honor and fell short of the sons of men.” And again: “He was dishonored and not esteemed. This man bears our sins and suffers pain for us.” And again: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth; because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death.” Since these passages set forth his humiliation and death, it was fitting that his exaltation after death should also be foretold. The prophetic Spirit announces the happier events before the grim ones, and sets them forth when he says: “Behold, my servant will understand,” or, according to Aquila: “Behold, my slave will be made knowing.” He rightly calls him a slave because of the form of a slave that he took on. For God the Word, who existed in the form of God, emptied himself, and, as the holy Apostle says, took the form of a slave and was found in appearance as a man. But this servant and slave of God was filled with all wisdom and knowledge, because he had received God the Word into himself. That is why it is said: “Behold, he will be made knowing,” and also, “he will be exalted and glorified and lifted up.” All these things were fulfilled in the human being of our Savior through his union with God the Word.

Then he adds: “Just as many will be astonished at you.” According to Theodotion it reads: “Just as many,” he says, “marveled at him, so your appearance will be without glory among human beings, and your glory among the sons of men.” This above all is what astonished many and left them at a loss: I mean the lowliness and obscurity of his coming among human beings. Indeed, even now the account of him produces astonishment, perplexity, and bewilderment in most people. Yet many nations also marveled at him. Those who believed in him worshiped his divinity, while those who remained in unbelief marveled at his power, seeing how it proved higher and stronger than those who tried to make war on it. Kings, too, uttered many blasphemous, godless, and impious words against him and persecuted his church. Then, able to accomplish nothing, they at last shut their mouths after their futile labors and gave way to his teaching. They were defeated in one way or another at various times and seasons, because they were driven about by scourges sent from God. We who are writing these things have learned this from our own experience. Some of them shut their mouths, while others even recanted, ordering by laws and edicts that houses of prayer be built and that his church carry on its customary practices. Next he explains why kings were stirred up over him: “For those to whom nothing was announced about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.” This was what stirred up the kings: his gospel message had spread even to the most distant nations. Quietly and indirectly, the text also exposes the Jewish nation's ignorance about him. The things concerning the one who was prophesied were announced to them first, and they learned the prophecies about him from childhood, yet they did not understand him when he came. For this reason he says that it is not they who will see, nor they who will understand, but on the contrary those to whom nothing was announced about him and who had not yet learned anything concerning him. These, he says, will see him with the eyes of the soul, and these will understand his teaching. These things were foretold in words long ago and fulfilled in deeds at our Savior's coming among human beings. The children of the Jews saw him with their eyes and heard his voice, yet they neither understood nor listened when he called. So the earlier prophecy was fulfilled in them, which said: “You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed look but never see.” They neither saw nor understood. But, as the Savior himself said, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” Those from all the nations who had never learned anything about him and did not know the scriptures concerning him nevertheless saw him and understood him and received the knowledge of his divinity.

This filled with wonder and amazement those who long ago beheld these things by the prophetic Spirit. That is why it is said next: “Lord, who has believed our report?” God's prophets said this in wonder, as they saw the unbelief of the Jewish nation and beheld the conversion and obedience of the nations. “And to whom,” he says, “has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” The preceding prophecy taught to whom the arm of God was revealed, where it said: “And the Lord God will reveal his holy arm before all the nations.” We have often shown that his only-begotten Son is called the arm of God. He became known to all the nations that believed in him, just as the prophetic utterances had said. After marveling at these things, God's prophets go on to foretell, in the form of a narrative, the coming among human beings of the servant or slave of God mentioned before, saying: “We made announcement as of a child before him, as of a root in a thirsty land.” According to Aquila: “And he will come up,” he says, “like a nursling before his face, and like a root from untrodden ground.” For he says that before his face, meaning the face of the arm just mentioned, he will come up like a nursling. This was the one born of the virgin, of whom it was said earlier: “Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel.” The text makes clear next that this was the nursling who came up before the face of the arm of God, when it says, “like a root from untrodden ground.” By untrodden ground it hints at the virgin, on whom no one had trodden. By root it means that very root of which it was said: “A rod will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will come up from the root.” There too it was shown that he would come up; but there it was from the root of Jesse, here from the untrodden ground just described. According to Symmachus it reads: “And he came up like a shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground.” Here too the text calls the untrodden ground thirsty. According to Theodotion: “And he will come up,” he says, “like a suckling before him,” that is, before the arm of God, “and like a root in thirsty ground.” The child spoken of here, according to the Seventy, who said, “We made announcement as of a child before him,” was the very one of whom it had been said earlier: “For before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness.” And again: “For before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take the power of Damascus.” And again: “For a child has been born to us, a son has also been given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder.” We showed in the proper places that these passages refer to the Christ of God. After foretelling the birth among human beings of the one who was prophesied, a birth from untrodden or thirsty ground, he next describes his life among human beings, saying: “He has no form or glory,” meaning that he had no glorious appearance. “And we saw him,” he says, “and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honor and fell short of the sons of men.”

Yet we—here the prophet speaks in common, out of love for humankind counting himself among those who did not esteem the Savior—did not esteem him, nor take him to ourselves, nor perceive who he was. Yet he was the Savior of our souls, healing them himself and cleansing them of every sin. That is why he adds: “This man bears our sins and suffers pain for us, and we reckoned him to be in trouble, under a blow, and in affliction.” According to Symmachus: “Truly he took up our diseases and endured our pains, yet we reckoned him to be stricken, struck by God and humbled.” And Aquila: “Yet we reckoned him wounded, struck by God and humbled.”

We held this opinion of him like infants, while he was suffering all these things for our sake, to free us from all punishment. That is why it continues: “But he was wounded because of our sins and made weak because of our lawless deeds.” And Aquila: “And he,” he says, “was profaned by our transgressions, crushed by our lawless deeds.” For he was truly profaned when he became a curse for us. Indeed, he was crushed and profaned and endured all the worst things, not for any sins of his own, but for ours. “And the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him.” What we ought to have suffered as chastisement for our sins came upon him for the sake of our peace with God. “And by his bruise,” he says, “we were healed.” For he was bound to bear bruises and wounds on his body, since he was beaten and scourged, slapped in the face, and struck on the head with a reed. Yet these bruises were our saviors, for by his bruise we were healed. And who are “we” but those who long ago went astray and neither esteemed him nor understood who he was? That is why it says: “All we like sheep have gone astray; each has gone astray in his own way.” For each traveled a different road of error, holding various and contradictory opinions about him. But what happened to him did not happen without God. For the Lord himself handed him over for our sins, so that he might become a life given for our lives and a ransom for us. In this way he also became the Lamb of God, taking away and cleansing the sin of the world. That is why Symmachus renders it: “But the Lord caused the lawlessness of us all to fall upon him.”

Then, instead of “And he, because he has been afflicted, does not open his mouth,” Symmachus says: “He was brought forward, and he submitted.” Brought before whom, if not Pilate? And since he kept silent when accused and answered nothing when false witness was given against him, Symmachus therefore says: “And he did not open his mouth.”

Then, after describing his sufferings, he turns the minds of his hearers to the contemplation of his generation, adding: “Who will tell of his generation?” For a person will marvel all the more at his endurance of such things when he comes to consider who and what kind of being it was that underwent all this: the only-begotten Son, begotten of God. That is why Aquila renders it: “Who will recount his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” And Symmachus: “For he was cut off,” he says, “from the land of the living, and because of the injustice of my people a blow fell upon them.” And Theodotion: “For he was cut off from the land of the living; because of the faithlessness of my people it touched them.” For rather it laid hold of them, and his death became a very great blow to them. Indeed, immediately afterward the wrath that came upon them and the blow that struck them proved incurable. In these words the prophet clearly showed that he was prophesying these things neither about himself nor about the people, as one might suppose, when he said: “Because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death.”

Instead of “And I will give the wicked in return for his burial,” Symmachus has: “And he will give,” he says, “the ungodly in return for his burial.” Who will give them, if not the Judge of all? And whom will he give, if not those who did the things described? He handed them over immediately, before long, to enemies, foes, and besiegers. And he says that he will also hand over the rich of former times, with the advantages in which they excelled, in return for his death. This too came about at once, so that the memory of those who had once wielded great power among the Jews vanished from among men: the Pharisees, scribes, and Sadducees, and besides them the priests and high priests and those honored among them with royal rank. These were the “rich” spoken of here. The wrath of God overtook them before long, because they had subjected the Christ of God, who was without sin, to such punishment. That is why he adds: “Because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” And this was the extraordinary thing about our Savior's more divine virtue: that throughout his whole life he was sinless and blameless in word and deed. For no one has ever been pure from stain, not even if his life lasted a single day, except him alone. So he died for all, to cleanse and take away the sin of the world. That is why God his Father also decided to cleanse him of the blow, that is, of the suffering inflicted on him. Or according to Aquila: “And the Lord willed to crush his sickness”; and according to Symmachus: “The Lord willed to thresh him in his wounding.” After this it is said: “If you give an offering for sin, your soul will see long-lived offspring.” The meaning of what he says is this: after all that has been described, if any of those who acted impiously against him should wish to offer a sacrifice for their sin, that is, to show confession and repentance for their sins, he will not be disappointed of the good hope in him. For even though it was said in the strongest terms, “I will give the wicked in return for his burial and the rich in return for his death,” nevertheless, if you who dared such things give the offering for sin, you will obtain forgiveness and your soul will be saved. And it will not merely be saved; it will also see the long-lived seed. This was the seed sown by him among human beings, about which he taught in parables, saying, “The sower went out to sow,” and again, “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his own field.” So if you give an offering for sin, your soul will see this rational and heavenly seed. Instead of “And the Lord wishes to take away from the toil of his soul,” Symmachus has: “And the will of the Lord,” he says, “will prosper in his hand”; and according to Aquila: “and the purpose of the Lord in hand.” This fits our Savior alone, for the Father's will always prospered in his hand.

He also gave him light, so that those justified through him might be enlightened. He also granted him understanding, for the spirit of wisdom and understanding rested upon him, so that he might make people understanding and justify those worthy of being justified. Who these are, he goes on to say: “And he himself will bear their sins,” or according to Symmachus: “And he himself will carry their impieties.” For he took upon himself the impieties of those who had long been sinners and ungodly, stripped them of the tunic of sin, and made them righteous. That is why it continues: “Therefore he will inherit many.” Because he took upon himself the sins of the many, he has been able to make all of them his own inheritance. If he had not been able to forgive sins, they would have remained in their offenses and would not have obtained salvation. But now, since he himself took up their sins, he has received them from the Father as his inheritance. He himself teaches this when he says: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.’” “And he divided the spoils of the strong,” that is, of the opposing powers and the wicked demons. He snatched from them the souls they held captive and made them his spoils, and he distributed these spoils to his disciples, forming various churches from them. That is why it was said above: “And they will rejoice before you like those who rejoice at the harvest, and like those who divide spoils.” He is able to do all this and will do it, “because his soul was handed over to death.” He received this from the Father as a kind of reward: I mean the power to forgive the sins of those who had sinned before and to bring them into his own inheritance. For since his soul was handed over to death and he was reckoned among the lawless, and since he himself took up the sins of many and was handed over because of their lawless deeds, therefore he will inherit many and will divide the spoils of the strong. How he was reckoned among the lawless, the Gospel teaches: it says that the prophecy was fulfilled when the robbers were crucified with him, one on either side. So it is said in Mark: “And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘And he was reckoned with the lawless.’”

Following on from the prophecy about our Savior, which described his birth among human beings, his life afterward, his death and the cause of his death, the word now uses the present passage to proclaim the good news of the church he founded throughout the whole inhabited world. That church was once desolate, childless and fruitless, and so the word calls her "barren," because the souls of the unbelieving nations were formerly like that. But now the word announces to them a change for the better and bids her who was once barren to rejoice. As though she had now received seed, was pregnant at last, and was about to bear the saving and good offspring, it adds: "Break forth and cry out, you who formerly did not give birth." In place of "Break forth and cry out," Aquila has: "Sing out praise and neigh, you who were not in labor." Symmachus says: "Be cheerful with exultation and neigh, you who do not give birth." Theodotion says: "Break forth in gladness and delight, you who were not in labor." And it adds: "For more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has the husband." According to Symmachus: "For many are the children of the woman made desolate, more than the children of the married woman." And indeed the church from the nations was formerly made desolate and deserted, since she did not yet have the heavenly bridegroom. Yet she is promised greater fruitfulness and more children than the woman who has the husband. And who was that woman but the Jewish nation, and Jerusalem, which they once honored as the city of God? She had the heavenly Word as her husband, but in the earlier passages she was shown to have given him a bill of divorce and to have played the harlot away from him. Those passages said: "How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot! She was full of justice, and righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers." So, set beside the woman who once had the husband, the soul among the nations that was formerly desolate of God is granted a gracious promise. The word announces to her many offspring and many children, so that her children will be multiplied beyond the people of the circumcision. That is why it says: "For more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has the husband."

Then it addresses the same woman, saying: "Enlarge the place of your tent and of your curtains; fix them firmly, do not hold back. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes." This is said with the tabernacle that Moses built in mind. The word uses that tabernacle as an image and urges the church from the nations not to keep her own building as small as it was, but to widen the pitching of her tent and stretch it to an untold length and breadth. The tabernacle Moses built was a hundred cubits long and fifty wide. But here it says: Do not hold back in this, and do not confine yourself to set measurements. Stretch out, lengthen and strengthen, and spread out even more to the right and to the left. You will understand the length, breadth and size of this new tabernacle, which no human being pitched but the Lord, if you consider how large the one Moses built was, and how large Jerusalem was, whose temple was sixty cubits long and twenty wide. So if the temple set up in a single city of Palestine deserved wonder, how much more do the number, the size and the beauty of the churches of God raised up in every place! The oracle shows clearly that these things are prophesied for the church from the nations when it goes on to say: "And your seed shall inherit nations, and you shall inhabit desolate cities." The seed of the church of God would be the word of the gospel, of which it is said: "The sower went out to sow," and: "Did you not sow good seed in your field?" This same seed also established the desolate cities. Symmachus has: "And your seed shall inherit nations, and they shall inhabit cities that were made desolate." The seed of the church can also be the succession of the apostles and disciples of our Savior, through whom the godly way of life was established in the churches that were once made desolate and deserted by God.

After this it adds: "Do not fear because you were put to shame, nor be confounded because you were reproached." For when she was barren, neither giving birth nor in labor, and without the husband, she was reproached and full of shame. But now it says to her: Even if you once did things that deserved shame and reproach, take courage now, for "you will forget the eternal shame, and you will no longer remember the reproach of your widowhood." Here it calls "widowhood" her lack of the bridegroom, the Word. You will not remember it, it says, because "the Lord of hosts is the one who makes you." Your foundation did not come from human beings or through a human being, but through the Lord himself. That is why the Savior himself makes this promise: "On the rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." So the one who makes you is himself the Lord of hosts, who was formerly the God of Israel and is now known to all the earth. That is why Symmachus has: "He shall be called God of all the earth."

Continuing with the promises to the desolate woman, the word adds: "The Lord has called you not as a woman forsaken and faint-hearted, nor as a woman hated from her youth, said your God." According to Symmachus: "For the Lord called you as a woman deeply grieved and forsaken in spirit, and as a wife of youth when she is cast off, said God." "For a brief moment I forsook you, and with great compassion I will gather you. In a burst of anger I hid my face from you for a little while, and with everlasting mercy I have had compassion on you."

Then it adds: Just as in the time of Noah I swore that I would never again destroy those on earth by a flood, so now too I assure my people with an oath concerning you that I will never again be angry with you. "For the mountains shall be shaken and the hills shall be disturbed, but my mercy shall not turn away from you, nor shall the covenant of my peace be overturned, said the Lord who has compassion on you." The mountains will be moved from their foundations and the hills disturbed sooner than my mercy will be removed. The word promises these things, too, to the godly commonwealth. That commonwealth was once among the Jews, but it lapsed among them and has passed over to the church from the nations. And the word promises her a covenant of peace, saying: "Nor shall the covenant of my peace ever be removed."

Then it recalls what the godly commonwealth was formerly like among the Jews, and what change for the better it will receive. So it says: "Lowly and unstable." Among the Jews, worship was truly lowly and bodily, consisting of circumcision of the body, animal sacrifices and similar things. That is why it called her lowly and unstable. Then it adds: "You were not comforted." None of the prophets and none of the men dear to God was great enough to take her up and restore her. But even if no one did these things for you, it says, "behold, I myself am preparing carbuncle as your stone." In place of this Symmachus has: "Behold, I set your stones in antimony," and Theodotion: "Behold, I will lay your stones in antimony." Just as a woman adorning herself paints her eyes with antimony, so I myself, it says, will arrange the stones of your building with a beauty and adornment surpassing all others. According to the Seventy, it is said that he will prepare for her carbuncle, a precious stone. Perhaps this carbuncle, which is literally a "coal," hints at the cleansing of the soul, since one of the seraphim cleansed the lips of the prophet Isaiah with the coal from the altar. It says that he will make every stone of your building like this, that is, cleansed, so that no stone in the building will be unclean. "And I will lay your foundations of sapphire stone." That is why the other translators have: "And I will found you on sapphires."

"And I will build your battlements of jasper stone." According to Symmachus: "And I will make your houses of carbuncle, and your gates of engraved stones." According to the Seventy: "And your gates of crystal stones, and your enclosing wall of choice stones." We should understand all these as precious and costly souls, from which God promises to build the godly commonwealth. He compares them to sapphire because sapphire resembles the color of the sky. Their way of life has also become heavenly and angelic, as Paul teaches when he says: "But our commonwealth is in heaven." The prophet Ezekiel also says that the place beneath the throne of God was like sapphire. All the prophets and the apostles, then, were foundations, as it were, of the godly commonwealth: firmly set and steadfast, and likened to sapphires because of their heavenly commonwealth and because they bear the image of the heavenly one. That is why it says: "And I will make your foundations sapphire." The battlements of this new Jerusalem were jasper stone, or carbuncle according to Symmachus, a choice and translucent stone. These would be the people in the church of God who have fortified the faith with reasoned preparation. They are like the ramparts of the godly commonwealth, because they can tear down every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God and refute every false word that is the enemy of the truth. On city walls the battlements are ramparts prepared for battle against the enemy, and in the same way those in the church who are powerful in speech and wisdom may fittingly be called battlements. With these he lists others and likens them to crystal stones, from which he prophesies that the gates of the city will be built. He uses this image to show the clear and pure quality of sound faith, that is, the first, elementary and introductory teaching given to believers. In addition to these, he promises to build the enclosing wall of the new city of God from choice stones. These would be the people who surround the whole building of the city and, better than any fence, secure it through their prayers to God. So much for the great, costly and honored buildings of the city:

that is what they are like. But the rest of the multitudes who will live in that city will claim God himself as their teacher. The oracle shows this when it says: "And all your sons taught by God." For the one who said in the Gospels, "Do not call anyone on earth teacher, for you have one teacher in heaven," will make the sons of the once-barren woman taught by God. Moreover, her children will live in great peace. He promised them this when he said: "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you."

To these words it adds: "And in righteousness you shall be built." The builder of all things, the Wisdom of God, acted with perfect justice when he fitted the living, well-set stones into the building. He made some into battlements, laid others as foundations and placed others in the enclosing walls. He set some apart for the temple of the city and others for the innermost parts of the sanctuary, while others adorned the rest of the city. That is why it says: "And in righteousness you shall be built." Such are the things God has promised to his church. Next he gives her a charge, saying: "Keep away from what is unjust, and you shall not fear, and trembling shall not come near you." What has already been provided for you will be yours by my grace. But if you are anxious that fear might come upon you from some enemy attack, take courage from my command. If you do these things, those things will not befall you. If you do not keep the command, blame yourself when you fall into human fears. Therefore I solemnly charge you and say: "Keep away from what is unjust, and you shall not fear, and trembling shall not come near you." Moreover, if you stay with me and worship God in the proper way, proselytes will come to you, though not without my counsel, for these too will sojourn with you through me. By "proselytes" you might understand, after the ranks of the church already described, those who join the crowds without genuine or pure intent. It says that they will sojourn in her but not dwell in her, because they come in as if only passing through. That is why it is put so well: "Behold, proselytes will come to you through me, and will sojourn with you, and will flee to you for refuge." People like this come as if in need of refuge: some need protection, others need help, and others come for some other reason. That is why it called them proselytes and said that they would sojourn, a fitting description of these men's intentions.

"And I myself, the Lord," it says, "will do all these things, since I myself became your creator when I built my church on the rock. I created you not by any human craft but by divine and ineffable grace. So I also say: 'Behold, I created you, not as a smith who blows on the coals and brings out a vessel for use.'" Human contrivances, which come into being through human effort, are like that, and so they decay and are destroyed. But my work is by nature incorruptible. "So I say: 'But I created you, not for destruction, nor shall any vessel fashioned against you serve to destroy you.'" For nothing will be found against my work that can corrupt and destroy it. Moreover, it says, "every voice that rises up and everyone who plans to contend with you shall be defeated," and it adds: "You shall defeat them all." Next it says: "There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord." This follows very naturally, for after all that had been said, it was necessary also to recall the inheritance laid up in the age to come. And what could this be but the kingdom of heaven? The words found in the Seventy, "but those who are liable to you shall be in it," are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators. Next it adds: "And you shall be righteous to me, says the Lord." The other translators join this to what comes before. So Symmachus has: "This is my inheritance of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is from me, says the Lord."

The prophecy now before us points to the Christ of God himself when it says: "You who thirst, go to the water." Then, hinting at the grace given freely to human beings through the Savior, it says: "And you who have no money, go, buy and drink without money." The Seventy have: "and the price of wine and fat, so that you may value with silver [?]." In its place Symmachus says: "and without exchange, wine and milk," and Aquila likewise translated "wine and milk." So the oracle promises the thirsty not only water but also wine and milk. The water from the spring of salvation stands for the preaching of the gospel, while the wine and milk hint at the mystery of rebirth in Christ. Those who are born again of water and the Spirit are nourished like newborn infants with spiritual milk, and they share in the wine of the new covenant. We should be aware that in ancient times mystical milk was offered to those reborn in Christ together with the body and blood of the new covenant. It is said that this custom is still kept even now in some churches. But even where it is not done physically, the mystical blood of Christ is offered, at least in meaning, in place of both wine and milk to those who have been found worthy of rebirth in Christ. If, following the Seventy, the word "fat" is read, it hints at the rich, nourishing and sustaining quality of the spiritual food in Christ. The Savior himself made the same point when he said: "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in yourselves." Just as he spoke of flesh there, he speaks of fat here; and just as he spoke of blood there, he speaks of wine here. The fat and the flesh signify his incarnate dispensation, while the wine and the blood signify the mystery of his passion. These, then, are the things he promises to provide without payment and to give freely to those who thirst for salvation in God.

Why do you spend your labour, busying yourselves with other things, from which the soul cannot be nourished nor enjoy food to its fill? This is why Symmachus renders it: “Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread, and your toil for what does not satisfy?” You will understand who buys the bread of the soul with silver if you consider those who bring money to the wise men of this age who promise some rational teaching, or else those who sell to their pupils, for a fee, the tradition of the Jewish readings. Next he urges them to incline their ears by understanding, and to make the hearing of their souls obedient to what is said. So he says: “Listen, and you shall eat good things, and your soul shall delight in good things.” For he says that, besides the former things, a hope of other good things and a divine delight has been stored up for the souls of those who obey. He does not hold out the gift of the good things to come to bodies, but expressly to souls.

To this he adds: “Give heed with your ears and follow my ways,” or according to Symmachus: “Incline your ear,” he says, “and come to me”; and also: “Listen to me, and your soul shall live in good things.” All these things too he promises to souls. Then, having urged them on by these words and roused their hearing, he begins his teaching, saying: “And I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the holy and sure things of David.” For the old covenant, being temporary, has passed away and come to its end. And since in many places in the Scriptures promises were given to David that the Christ of God would come forth from his seed: Rouse yourselves and hear the word about these things. For know well that if you give yourselves to my words, I too will give you the fruit of your obedience. The promise I made to David I will grant to you. So I will make with you the new covenant, which will not be temporary like that of Moses, but lasting and everlasting, and will endure until the consummation of all things. And the holy things of David, which I promised him, I will make sure, fulfilling my promises.

Then, since the prophetic Spirit has foreknowledge and foresees the future, it was not unaware that the Jews would keep these words among themselves, yet would gain nothing more from them for the benefit of their souls. So he turns his discourse to the foreign and alien nations, to whom he also promises to give the promises, saying in these very words: “Behold, I have given him as a testimony to the nations, a ruler and commander to the nations. Nations that do not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who do not understand you shall flee to you for refuge, for the sake of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.” By these words he refers his readers back to the one made known in the preceding passages, where it was said: “For those to whom nothing was announced about him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand,” and: “We saw him, and he had no form or beauty.” It is that very one, then, about whom all these things were said, of whom he says: “I have given him as a testimony to the nations.” This is why I also brought good news to the barren woman who of old bore no children, and to her who had no husband, and bade her stretch out and widen her tent: since the one who had been promised came to suffer these things because of the sins of my people, it is fitting that I have given him as a testimony not to the people of the Jews but to all the nations, and as ruler and commander to the nations. For it is plain to me, God, that all the nations will obey him rather than the people of the circumcision. And his testimony was the preaching about him, just as he himself taught when he said: “This gospel must be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all the nations.” Then the Spirit cries out to the very person of the one prophesied, saying: “Nations that do not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who do not understand you shall flee to you for refuge.” And all these things, he says, will come to pass “for the sake of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.”

Next he urges them to seek the Lord, joining to the command a promise that they will find him. So he says: “Seek the Lord, and when you find him, call upon him.” Then he exhorts them, saying: When you find him standing near you, and not dwelling somewhere far away, set your lives in order as people standing in his presence. And since he is addressing these words to the nations, who were formerly godless and impious, he goes on fittingly to exhort them: When the Lord draws near to you, “let the impious forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels.” For repentance and turning away from evil are good. Even if you think your condition is beyond healing, even if it is despaired of as far as human beings are concerned, yet with me it is not beyond cure or healing; for I abound in forgiveness.

“For my counsels are not like your counsels, nor are my judgments and my ways like your ways, the ways of men,” says the Lord. “For as the heaven is high above the earth, so shall my ways be exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts. For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and will not return there, but will drench the earth and make it bring forth and sprout, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth: it will not return to me empty, until it has done all that I willed and accomplished all for which I sent it.” Having said all this to confirm the promise he had made to the impious and lawless man who turns to him from among the nations, he clearly presented God the Word, who was in the beginning, coming down from above from the Father like rain and snow, to descend to humanity in order to water their souls and make them bear fruit. He also made known his return to the Father, saying: “It will not return to me empty, until it has done all that I willed and accomplished all that I commanded it”; for when it has first done these things, then it will return to me. And if it is said to come forth from the mouth of Christ [?], one must not suppose it to be a word that merely signifies, like the spoken word among us, since no one [?] would attribute a bodily mouth to God either, unless he had fallen away from sound reasoning. For how could the word of anyone else, having no substance of its own, be sent forth and come down, and, having done and accomplished certain things, return again to the one who sent it? No, these things plainly agree with the teachings of the Gospels, in which God the Word is presented as sent from the Father, carrying out the dispensations among human beings, and ascending again to the Father.

After this the prophecy says to those from the nations who come to the saving word: “For you shall go out in gladness and be taught in joy.” For you will go out from the error handed down from your fathers, and you will receive the teaching of the saving gospel, which will indeed produce divine joy in you. Symmachus has: “You shall go out in gladness and be led in peace.” Then he says: “The mountains and the hills shall be [?] before you with exultation, and all the trees of the field shall clap with their hands.” By this, I think, divine powers are meant, rejoicing with those on earth who repent, as the Saviour also taught when he said that there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. And the trees of the field clapping with their branches might perhaps be the fruitful souls rejoicing with the souls of the lawless as they turn to God; so they gave signs of joy by clapping with their branches. But he also says: “Instead of the brushwood the cypress shall come up, and instead of the fleabane the myrtle shall come up.” Through these words too he hinted allegorically at the fruitfulness of souls passing from worse to better. Formerly, when they lived in godlessness, they bore nothing productive or nourishing, but, as in a desert, barren and untilled land, they grew brushwood, useless stuff, and fleabane, a most foul-smelling and altogether useless plant. But now, when they have shared in divine grace, they bore the most fragrant myrtle and the very tall and likewise fragrant cypress. According to Symmachus: “Instead of brushwood,” he says, “juniper shall come up, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall come up”; as though it were said more plainly: instead of vice, righteousness shall come up; instead of licentiousness, self-control; instead of rashness, courage; instead of folly, prudence; and, in a word, instead of wickedness, virtue. Besides these he promises something else marvellous to the nations that have turned to God: “The Lord,” he says, “shall be to them for a name and for an everlasting sign, and it shall not fail.” And who would not be amazed at the fulfilment of this word, seeing people throughout the whole world called Christians after the Christ of God? And this will be for them an everlasting sign of salvation with God: to bear the name of the Lord inscribed upon them, which will remain with them forever and will never fail. For the gifts of God are irrevocable.

The people of the Jews did nothing good, neither keeping judgment nor doing righteousness, yet they honoured the Sabbath day alone, as though they were doing God some great favour. So he fittingly speaks as if to them: Listen, you people! Since you neglect what is essential and think you must keep the Sabbath day, and that this is the great achievement of piety, you ought to know that first of all you must keep judgment and do righteousness. For whoever does these things would be worthy of blessing from God. Along with these it is necessary also not to profane the Sabbaths, and this will be so if you keep your hands pure of every wrongful deed. But if, without doing these things, you spend the Sabbath day in leisure and idleness, know that you are accomplishing nothing.

Next he also calls the proselytes among them, who were foreigners and alien to the race but had been joined to the people by coming over to God. He urges them to hold to the word of piety, and teaches the children of the Jews not to think highly of themselves because of their race or to pride themselves on their forefathers. This is why it is said, in Symmachus's version: "Let not the son of the foreigner who has attached himself to the Lord say, 'The Lord will surely separate me from his people.'" And since the Jews also held that having many children was a blessing from God, and took a large family to be the reward and fruit of piety, he puts down this opinion of theirs as well. Showing it to be mistaken, he now makes the promise to those who are childless and unable to beget children because they have been castrated, declaring that nothing will stand in the way of eunuchs obtaining the good things that come from God, if they choose to live according to God. So to the eunuchs too, who in the childlessness of their bodies resemble a fruitless tree, he holds out the same hope as to Israel. For if they too keep what was said before, abstaining from all injustice and pursuing through godly works the life that pleases God, and in addition keep the strict law about the sabbaths, they too will obtain what has been promised. In their case also he draws a careful distinction, saying that besides keeping the sabbaths they must choose "the things that I will"; but "it is not the sabbaths that I will," he says. That is why I said at the beginning of the book: "Your new moons and sabbaths and great day I cannot endure." So if they accept "the things that I will" and hold fast to my covenant, which I pointed out just now when I said that one must keep judgment and do righteousness, and: "Blessed is the man who does these things, and the person who holds fast to them, and who keeps his hands from doing wrong" (for how could he not be blessed who has received such promises?). These, then, were "the things that I will." If the proselytes and the eunuchs do them, even keeping the sabbaths for the sake of the law's command would do them no harm.

So to the eunuchs who keep what has been said, and who have no fruit by way of human succession, he promises to give, in place of a large family, "in his house and within his wall a renowned place," or, in the other translators: "a hand and a name better than sons and daughters." "And I will give them an everlasting name," he says, "which shall not be taken away." For just as I once gave Jacob a name, calling him Israel instead of Jacob, and in fact made him a man who beholds God (for that is how "Israel" is rendered in the Greek tongue, being interpreted "a man seeing God"), so too to those who are childless according to the flesh, if they choose to be godly, I will grant a name that will be theirs above any abundance of children. And if, according to the saving teaching, there are also eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, it would follow that this should be understood all the more of them, as when it is said: "I will give them in my house and within my wall a renowned place." For if there are many dwelling places with the Father, and there is a heavenly Jerusalem, the city of God, and a place for them within the house of God among the many dwelling places, they will also be given a portion in the wall of God's heavenly city. And a name better than sons and daughters will be given to them, or, in Aquila: "and a good name beyond sons and daughters; an everlasting name I will give them." Through these words, I think, the passage refutes the opinion of the Jews, since they considered themselves dear to God because they had many children; for they supposed that God's blessing consisted in this.

To the proselytes from the nations too, if they keep what was said before, and resolve not only to serve God but also to love him and hold fast to his covenant, he promises to bring them into his holy mountain, to gladden them and to accept their sacrifices, even if they seem to be of another race and foreign. For his house does not belong to some and not to others, but is open to all the nations, so overflowing is his love for humanity that he receives both eunuchs and proselytes. And the sacrifices which he says he will accept from these people are surely those offered through prayers and praises.

But if someone should say that bodily sacrifices are meant, he will not be wrong, since these things were said to those who lived under the law of Moses before the new covenant. All these things, he says, have been promised by God, who is going to gather the dispersed of Israel, or "the outcasts," in Aquila. I think that by these words, as regards the letter, God would be said to gather the dispersed of Israel because of the people's return from Babylon that took place under Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes. For it was under these Persian kings that those recorded in the history of Ezra returned from captivity, and at that time it was likely that a multitude of foreign nations also became proselytes among them; these the passage called "beasts of the field" because of their different condition and the foreign and wild character of their ways. And he said that these would be gathered together with Israel. But as regards a deeper sense, the Israel gathered from the dispersion would be the choir of the prophets and all among the former people who succeeded in living a godly life, and also the evangelists, disciples and apostles of our Savior, all those from Israel who received the Christ of God. Of them the Savior himself taught, setting his seal on the prophecy of Isaiah which speaks in his person: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind." And the beasts gathered together with Israel would be those from the nations who come to the word, whom he calls next, saying: "Come, eat, all you beasts of the forest." We have often observed that the multitude of the foreign nations is called a "forest." So he deems these beasts worthy of God's calling and summons them to a feast. That is why in Aquila, instead of "all the beasts," it says "every living creature of his," and again, "all his living creatures." Whose, if not God's? So he does not simply call the beasts, but his own. Then, since he had mentioned foreign nations and beasts of the forest, and perceived in the Spirit that these would obey the call while the mass of the Jews would remain in unbelief, he turns back to them and reproaches them with blindness. For if wild beasts and creatures of the forest were to change over to a godly life, these were dying in their own wickedness.

How then could what follows not rightly be said against them? And what does he add? "See that they have all been blinded" (Symmachus says: "his watchmen are blind"), "all are without understanding, all are mute dogs, unable to bark." The rulers of the Jewish nation are called blind watchmen, senseless, and dumb dogs unable to bark. For they ought to have defended God's flock and, like hunting dogs, driven the wolves away from the sheep. But like dumb dogs they did not even get as far as barking; they were no different from sleepers, and paid attention only to fancies, as if they were dreaming. That is why Symmachus has: "seers of visions, lying down, loving to slumber," and Aquila: "imagining things, loving to slumber." Such were the rulers of the Jews toward those outside, against whom they should have been wakeful and sober and barked at the enemy. But toward their own people they were shameless, devouring the sheep they were supposed to shepherd. That is why he adds next: "And the dogs are shameless in soul, never knowing when they have had enough; and they are wicked, without understanding; all have followed their own ways": not the ways of God, but their own, by doing whatever pleased them.

Very consistently, having mentioned blind watchmen and called them dogs, in one respect slumbering in their dumbness and not knowing how to bark, in another shameless and wicked, he goes on to their boldness against righteous and God-loving men and their threats against the prophets, saying: "See how the righteous man is taken away, and no one takes it to heart; righteous men are taken away, and no one considers it." And how were those who were blind in their souls to consider it? If they had not been so, they would have seen the righteous man and understood God's dispensation concerning him. But while they, being blind and shameless dogs, dared such things against the righteous, the righteous were received by God in peace. "And his burial was taken away from the midst." One might say that these words can also fit the Savior and his disciples, who were plotted against by the Jewish nation; and indeed the oracle, it is said, also hints at the resurrection of our Savior: his death is indicated by his burial, and his resurrection by his burial having been taken away from the midst. For he was taken away from the midst of injustice and came to be in peace, and his burial vanished from the midst because he did not remain in the place where he was buried. Hence the angel, standing by the women, said: "Whom are you looking for? Jesus? He is not here; come, see his place."

"But you," who long ago dared similar things against the prophets of God, who are truly blinded, dumb and shameless dogs, "come here" (or "draw near here," in the other translators), "you lawless sons, seed of adulterers and of a harlot." For it is not fitting to call you children of Abraham and Sarah: if you were children of Abraham, you would be doing the works of Abraham. Scripture is accustomed to call "adulterers" those who practiced idolatry long ago, of whom it is said, "and they committed adultery with wood and stone," and to call Jerusalem a "harlot," as the present prophet showed earlier when he said: "How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot!" Hence Symmachus has "seed of adulterers and of her who played the harlot," so that even if the children of the Jews do not practice idolatry at present, they are nonetheless the seed of adulterers and of a harlot. That is why the passage says to them: "Seed of adulterers and of a harlot, come here," and when you have come near, say: "In what have you taken your delight?" Or, in Symmachus: "Whom have you mocked, and against whom have you opened wide your mouth and stuck out your tongue?" For he chiefly accuses their tongue and mouth because of what they said against the Savior and the blasphemies they still utter against him even now. That is why he says: "Against whom have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you let loose your tongue? Are you not children of destruction?" For he was taken away from the midst of injustice and came to be in peace, and his burial was taken away from the midst; but you, then, were children of destruction and a lawless seed.

"You who call upon the idols under leafy trees, slaughtering their children in the ravines among the rocks. That is your portion, this is your lot; to those you poured out drink offerings, and to these you offered sacrifices." Or, in Symmachus: "under every flourishing tree, slaughtering the offspring in the ravines beneath the overhanging rocks." For you deserved these things, he says; therefore "that is your portion, and this is your lot." These words clearly show that the present prophecy fits the idolaters of the time of Isaiah the prophet. Having listed their transgressions, it goes on: Is it not right, then, to let loose wrath against you for these things, especially since "on a high and lofty mountain, there is your bed, and there you brought up sacrifice, and behind the posts of the door you set up your memorials"? And you did these things, he says, practicing your impiety not in secret but openly, so as to perform demonic sacrifices even on the very highest mountains. And behind your doors, as if in place of an amulet, you even set up the memorials of your own idolatry, that is, lifeless statues; and you did these things thinking you would gain some advantage by turning away from me. These words are addressed to the blind watchmen and dumb dogs already mentioned; what follows he addresses to Jerusalem itself and the congregation of the Jewish people, saying: "You loved those who lay with you," or, in Symmachus and the other translators: "You loved their bed." Whose, if not that of your watchmen and shameless dogs just mentioned?

"And you multiplied your harlotry with them." That is why it was said of them: "dreaming of a bed, loving to slumber." They, then, were like this, dreaming of beds and loving to slumber; and she who is reproached in these words, as one who delighted in those very men, hears: "You loved those who lay with you, and multiplied your harlotry with them, and made many those who are far from you." For many men devoted to God fled Jerusalem because of the godless deeds being carried out in her. That is why it is said: "and you made many those who are far from you." But also, he says, "you sent envoys beyond your borders," or, in Symmachus: "and you multiplied your perfumes, you sent your hostages far away." All these things he personifies as addressed to a courtesan who adorns herself and does everything to please those who come to her. That is why, because of these things, he says: "You were brought low to Hades; you wore yourself out with your many ways." For you did not walk the one royal road, but many wandering ones. Therefore you wore yourself out, and even so you did not stop, nor did you say, "I will stop and regain my strength"; but as if you were strong and full of youthful recklessness you did worse than these things, persisting in your own outrages. Hence you neither turned back nor besought me (or, in Aquila: "you did not supplicate") so as to obtain forgiveness.

You remained from of old without fear and without reverence; and if you ever seemed to be godly, even then you were false to what you professed. But even before this, he says, you did not remember me, nor did you take me into your mind or into your heart. So it is right that I too should overlook you for these reasons and leave you desolate; for not even now do you take up the fear of God.

So learn what awaits you. And what is that? The wrath of God will overtake you, avenging everything you have dared, at the time when your evils are exposed; and at the time of the wrath that will come upon you, no one will stand by you, nor will those whom you take to be your gods hear your voice. Instead of "let them deliver you in your affliction," Symmachus says: "let your synagogues deliver you," the passage teaching plainly and clearly that their synagogues will do them no good. Then he adds: "For the wind will take all these, and a storm will carry them away. But those who hold fast to me will possess the land and inherit my holy mountain. And they will say, 'Clear the ways before him, and remove the obstacles from the way of my people.'" So all who have been accused, he says, the wind will take and a storm carry away. Such is the end that will overtake those reproached for the things mentioned. But those who have chosen the good portion, namely me, God, and who hold fast to me genuinely and purely, will receive my reward: they will possess the land promised to them and inherit my holy mountain. And they will also be teachers of others, urging them to level the ways of the people by making their teaching to the people pure and smooth, with nothing crooked or tortuous in it. As regards the people of old, "land" and "holy mountain" could mean Jerusalem and Mount Zion and the country of Judea; but according to the true sense, the holy mountain, as he has often indicated before, is the heavenly Jerusalem, and the land is the life in the heavenly realms and the whole heavenly region, where those who hold fast to God will receive the inheritance they deserve. And in Symmachus: "But he who has put his confidence in me," he says, "will inherit my holy mountain. And he will say: Build a road, clear a way, lift the stumbling blocks out of the way of my people." For whoever has lived uprightly before God will not provide for his own salvation alone, but will also make himself useful to the people of God, directing that the way of piety be leveled for them and that the apparent stumbling blocks in the divine readings be removed by interpreting them more clearly.

The passage had directed the preceding prophecy at the rulers of the Jewish nation, whom it called dumb dogs, blind watchmen, lawless sons, and seed of adulterers and of a harlot, and had declared what was fitting to the people under them. Now, in what follows, it brings encouragement and consolation to those among them who were devout, who had the fear of God and repented of their sins, whom the present text calls broken in heart and faint-hearted. For there were among them, even if few and easily counted, men nonetheless devoted to God: not only the prophets, but also others who zealously followed them, who were taught by the prophets and attended to their teachings. These, lamenting the ruin of the multitude, spent their lives in humiliation and hardship, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes in the ground. And there were others again who lamented their own evils, humbling themselves and chastising their own lives for the sins they had committed. That is why the present passage calls them broken in heart and faint-hearted, or, in Symmachus, crushed and humble in spirit. And it introduces the God who is over all, who is beyond the universe, the Most High, who dwells on high forever, the Holy One who rests among the holy, speaking to the humble and faint-hearted. For even though he is supremely exalted and has his dwelling on high, he nevertheless does not disdain the humble, but gives them grace, raises them from their humiliation and makes them exalted. That is why it is said: "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble," and "whoever humbles himself will be exalted." Thus, having exalted the humble, he will also dwell in them; for being Most High he dwells on high forever. So he speaks to the humble in order to exalt them, so that he may dwell in them too; and in the same way, being holy himself, he chooses those who are holy among men in order to rest in them. That is why it is said: "Holy, resting among the holy." Moreover, being long-suffering himself and mindful of human weakness, he gives long-suffering to those who are worn down in this mortal life for the sake of piety and who lose heart under afflictions, so that they may endure vigorously and steadfastly the afflictions that piety brings. And further, God, being himself life and having the fountain of life with him, grants [?] the eternal and immortal life that comes from him to the broken in heart, since a broken spirit is a sacrifice to God, and a broken and humbled heart God will not despise. So it is God himself, the giver of such great goods, who addresses these words to the humble and faint-hearted, and he says that he will rest in them.

I will not punish you forever. For I will not exact punishment in full for all the sins you have ever committed. As human beings, you need some brief punishment, even if it happened that you too shared in the consequences of the people's sins, so that you too were carried off with the multitude and handed over to punitive justice because of the sins of others. Nevertheless, you ought to know this: eternal wrath will overtake all the others, those among the people who are truly ungodly and sinners, but you I will not punish forever, nor will I be angry with you continually. For I care for my own spirit, which went forth from me and came to dwell in you, since I am also the maker of every breath that is able to praise me, as it says: "Let every breath praise the Lord." And at the making of the world, when God breathed in the breath of life, man became a living soul. Accordingly it is now said: "I have made every breath." Job too teaches this when he says: "It is the spirit of the Lord that made me, and the breath of the Almighty that teaches me." It is fitting, then, that with those who have kept this spirit that comes from me, and the breath that I made, through which man became a living soul, I will not be angry forever.

For even if, for some brief time, I grieved and struck those who had sinned, because of certain sins that arose from human weakness, as a father disciplines his sons (for "whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives"), yet you came to perceive my discipline, were grieved with godly grief, and went about downcast and repentant. For this reason, having seen your turning and your repentance, and your later deeds and the ways of your life, I healed you and comforted you, giving you true comfort. For everything that I bestow on those who are my own is true. Therefore to those who have been brought to their senses by my discipline I gave true comfort, and a peace that is not simple and temporary but multiplied, so that it is enjoyed both by those who are near and by those far off, settled at a great distance. After promising these things, the Lord, who is declared to be God, adds: "I will heal them," promising his healing to those afflicted in soul and heart. And he added this as the crowning end for those who have profited from God's discipline.

"But those who are not such," he says, "but remain unjust and ungodly, will be tossed by the waves and will not be able to rest." Then, since it is not in the nature of things for those estranged from God to share in joy, he adds to it all: "There is no rejoicing for the ungodly, says the Lord." Or, in Symmachus's version: "But the ungodly are like a churning sea; for they will not be able to be still, and they will be cast up beside its waters, a trampling and mire. There is no peace, said my God, for the ungodly." Here again it should be noted how he has compared the multitude of the ungodly to a churning sea, a sea that surges and is troubled. That is why he says, "like a churning sea; for they will not be able to be still," and he says that the waters of so great a sea are like trampled mud. Aquila likewise said: "And the ungodly are like a churning sea, for they will not be able to be still, and it churns up its waters like trampling and mire." So if anything is ever said, for instance, about the sea of Egypt or about certain waters, one should remember the present passages, since they are useful for interpreting those.

Having healed those among the multitude of the people who were humble and contrite of heart, the discourse passes again to the class of the ungodly among them, against whom it pronounced the sentence already mentioned, when it said: "There is no rejoicing for the ungodly, said God." For we needed to be taught who these ungodly people were and the reasons for the sentence against them. These very things, then, he commands the prophet to bring into the open with all boldness and with a strong voice, not shrinking from God's proclamation or hiding it out of fear of death or of any other human threat. Therefore he commands him to cry out like a trumpet, the loudest of all musical instruments, so as to be heard by the very people being reproved, and to speak out the words of God. To the evangelists of the saving word it was said in the earlier passages: "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not be afraid." Here, however, the prophet is not told to go up on a high mountain, for those he was addressing were not on high. He is commanded only to cry aloud with strength and not to hold back, as one speaking into the ears of the deaf, and to lift up his voice like a trumpet. A trumpet is a signal of war. He bids him use his cry against the ungodly and sinful man as against an enemy, so that it may lay hold of the minds of the hearers and wound them with a most stinging word. Next he says: "And declare to my people their sins." He calls the sinner his people in order to condemn him: "I adopted them," he says, "and did not disdain to call them my people; but they removed themselves far from me, giving themselves over to their own wickedness."

In vain and to no profit they pretend to seek me, God, day after day, hurrying to attend their synagogues and even lending their ears to the divine readings. In vain, he says, they make a show of wanting to know my ways and busy themselves with these things, as though they had set everything else right and fulfilled in deeds all the fruits of righteousness. Yet their very deeds prove that they have forsaken the judgment of God. Then, in their utter insensibility to their own evils, as though going to law and contending in court with me, they ask for rewards for their good conduct and demand a just judgment from me. They act as though they themselves longed to worship God and to draw near to me, while I was unwilling and was even turning away from them most unjustly.

That is why they find fault and lay charges, saying: "Why is it that we fasted and you did not see? We humbled our souls and you took no notice?" Since, then, they shamelessly dare to say such things, you, my prophet, answer them with a great cry and refute them. Show how they have forsaken my judgment, and that nothing they assert is true. If they pride themselves on such a fast, it would be far better for them to spend their time eating than to dare such things. That is why, at the beginning of the prophecy, it was said to them: "My soul hates your fasting and idleness and your feasts." Right away they put forward their fasting, and now they speak of the humbling of their souls that takes place on the day of their fast. Expose how they actually behave, taking this one example and showing from it the manner of all the rest of their conduct. Tell them, then, and show them that on these very days of fasting in which they take pride they do not seek my will. Instead they devote themselves to their own pleasures and misdeeds, at one time beating those under their control, at another wearing themselves out in quarrels and disputes with one another, so that those they beat utter cries of weeping and unseemly shrieks.

So he says: "I have not chosen this fast, nor such a day of humbling." Not even if they bend their necks like a ring, bowing down and putting on a show of humility, nor if they wrap sackcloth around their very flesh so that its roughness causes them pain and distress, nor if they spread ashes beneath them to punish their own bodies. For when joined with the sins already mentioned, all this effort will be in vain. But if anyone wishes to be taught the manner of a true fast, one pleasing to me, God, let him do this. Following the Savior's instruction, let him make his face bright and anoint his head with oil, keep his fast in secret, and show the humbling of his soul only to the Father who sees in secret. But in the open let him allow everyone to see, through his deeds, the fruits of the reverence in his soul, by loosing every bond of injustice. For even if some people are bound in matters arising from contracts and human dealings, it is right, when the season of worship through fasting arrives, to dissolve these and to shake off the knots of forced agreements. In this way one fulfills in deed what was said by the Savior: "If you are offering your gift and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there, and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." Moreover, free from their debts those brought low by loans and debts, and tear up every unjust contract. But even if you have not been involved in any such tangled dealings and are clean of such sins, it is still necessary for you, if you wish to make your fasts pleasing to God, to do at least this:

Break your own bread, which you would certainly have eaten if you were not fasting, for the hungry, for there is no lack among people of those in need of food. In this way your going without food will not turn into a gain for you. Instead you will be nourished in your soul in another way, by restoring with your own bread the one who is in need and lacks food. Yet one must not stop there. Into your own house invite not the rich, nor those able to repay you in kind the very next day, but the poor, those who are found to be truly destitute, who are cast out because they do not even have a roof over their heads. Become a roof to them yourself by receiving them into your own house. And to complete this good fast that pleases God: when you see someone naked, do not pass by on the other side, nor overlook him as a stranger. For the God of all has made some well supplied with food and money, and others needy and poor, as a test for both. The rich are to have the fruit of their abundance by providing for the needy, while the poor, trained by poverty, are to receive the provision of the well-off in place of a fruitful field. Further, in addition to what has been said: "And you shall not overlook those of your own seed." For first of all one must share generously with everyone, but give special portions to those of the household of faith. The apostolic ordinance also enjoined this, saying that we should be kind toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith. Once you have kept these sayings in your deeds as though they were laws, do not humble your soul, nor bend your neck like a ring, nor spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you. Instead, cheerful and looking up to God, receive the rewards he gives.

Learn now from what follows what these rewards are. When night and darkness suddenly give way, the light of day breaks out and displays the sun's far-shining radiance. In the same way, for you too a light will break forth early: something heavenly and divine, coming suddenly and driving far from your soul the darkness that formerly lay upon it, so that you live as in the day of God and in the light of knowledge and truth. So too the healings of your soul will spring up together with that light, so that it is set free from every disease and infirmity and every defilement. And once you have become such a person, you will be a light to others as well; for your righteousness, shown through works of virtue, will go before you, shining out to the many who see it. These are the things your fruits will win for you. And over and above them, the glory that comes from God will adorn your soul from above with all kinds of blessings, as with a crown, so that you will be glorified both among men and before God himself.

Besides these, you will also have these special gifts. As soon as you cry to God, you will find him listening; he will all but speak aloud and say, while you are still speaking, "Here I am." All this will be yours if you keep what has been said and remove from yourself the yokes of sin. (There is no harm in mentioning the same things a second time.) This will be so if you remove from yourself the bond of sin, the unjust gestures of the hand, the reproaches of your words, and your grumbling against God.

Further, if, as was said before, you give your bread to the hungry, know that you have bestowed great things on yourself. Likewise, if you fill the soul brought low by want with what you have in plenty, the word again makes you the same promises: "Your light will rise in the darkness, and your darkness will shine like noonday. And your God will be with you continually, and he will fill you just as your soul desires." He promises you food for the soul and the enjoyment of the good things that are with him.
