"And your bones," he says (that is, the powers of the soul), "will be made fat" by spiritual and divine food. And there will be in you a spring of living water and an evergreen garden, bearing fruit from the plantings of the Holy Spirit.

And the long-desolate places of the soul will be built up in you and filled through divine teachings and words, so that you become your own builder, building up the thoughts of your mind with divine instruction. You will also put a fence around your soul, hedging it in on every side and securing it against troubles from outside. These things are said to each one of the hearers, but in the person of the whole people. For if you do these things, O people who were reproached at first, the promises will be yours: "Your light will rise in the darkness, and your darkness will be like noonday. And your God will be with you continually, and you will be filled just as your soul desires, and your bones will be made fat." The bones of the people may fittingly be taken to mean the powerful among them, who support the whole body. "And you will be like a well-watered garden and like a spring whose water has not failed. And your everlasting wastes will be built up for you": what has long lain desolate because of sin will be built up. "And your foundations will be everlasting, for generations upon generations." You will understand the foundations if you attend to the apostolic writing, where it is said: "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets." "And you will be called Builder of fences." He builds fences who hedges in and walls around the doctrines of the Church with reasoned demonstrations. And whoever removes what seem to be stumbling blocks in the divine readings by making clear what is said is the one who removes the stones from the middle of the paths.

In addition to all these things he says: "If you turn your foot away from the Sabbaths, so as not to do your own will on the holy day, and call the Sabbaths delightful, holy to God, you will not lift your foot to work, nor speak a word in anger from your mouth, and you will trust in the Lord." For if, along with all those other things, you also keep the Sabbaths as the word directs, then these too will be of real use to you. The word suggests that they should not do their own will, spending their time in drunkenness and carousing. Instead, living in holiness and purity, they should sanctify the day as well, and keep it delightful and free from grief through the godly rest observed on it. They should not move their foot even slightly toward other activities, nor defile their lips even with a word, but should devote themselves throughout the whole day to leisure for divine things alone.

All these things taken together will make the Sabbath not unprofitable for you and will make your fast acceptable. In this way you will trust in the Lord, confident for the rest of your life, holding fast to his promises, which do not deceive. In addition to these, he promises to give you this as well: I mean that he will raise you from your sojourn here to what is called the land above, and grant you those good things "which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him." And he will feed you with the food of that place and give you the inheritance he promised to your father Jacob. Now the promises made to the fathers were heavenly and spiritual. Even if all these things were spoken through a man, they were not human words; it was God who uttered them through the prophet. Therefore it is added to all of it: "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." One could, however, take what is said about the land and its good things in a more Jewish sense, since all that has been said has been shown to be addressed to the people of the circumcision.

In the preceding passages the word set out, as to the people of the Jews, what must be done. To those who carry out in deeds what must be done it set forth the fitting promises, and to those who choose the opposite it threatened corresponding punishments. In the present passage it brings a reproof against them as people who chose what was contrary to God's will, which is why they have fallen into misfortunes. So he says to them: It was not impossible for me, God, to recover you even when you were perishing, nor was my hand too weak to save you even though you were unworthy. And my ear, which hears all things, was not so hard of hearing that it could not hear you when you cried out. But though my part is such, your sins are such that they pile up a heap of evils and raise a dividing wall between God and you. To save you while you are such is neither just nor in your interest. The Apostle says somewhere about the Savior: "who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the fence, the enmity, in his flesh." But the Savior is said to have broken down the dividing wall of the fence through the forgiveness of sins, while the present prophet teaches that each person's sins, thrust in between God and human beings, drive the sinning soul far away from God, since it is impossible for sin to be joined to God. Therefore he adds: "And because of your sins I turned my face away from you." Your lawless life does not allow you to enjoy divine providence, because sin is abhorred as foul-smelling, shameful and dishonorable.

He has taught, then, that the cause of the people's falling away, and of their being cast off far from God, is nothing other than their sins. Next he lists what kind of sins these are, saying: "Your hands are defiled with blood and your fingers with sins, and your lips have spoken lawlessness." And notice that here he does not reproach them with idolatry or any other unlawful act, but with murder done by the hands and lawlessness spoken by the mouth. By these he hinted at their uprising against the Savior and their plotting against righteous men. He had already made this plain in the earlier passages, when he said: "See how the righteous one is taken away, and no one considers it; and righteous men are taken away, and no one takes it to heart. For the righteous one has been taken away from the presence of lawlessness; his burial will be in peace; he has been taken away from the midst." And even if they did not kill the Savior with their own hands, yet by asking that his blood be on them and on their children, and by raising godless shouts, they showed in deed that their hands were defiled with blood, that their lips had spoken lawlessness, and that their tongue had practiced injustice.

That is why the prophet says: "No one speaks what is just, nor is there true judgment." Then, since they deceive themselves and wait for another Christ, telling human myths about him, he adds: "They trust in vain things and speak empty words." This is why the divine Apostle urges us not to pay attention to Jewish myths and the commandments of men who turn away from the truth. These same people devise clever arguments for themselves and compose blasphemous words against the Christ of God out of their own reasonings, and so they conceive toil and give birth to lawlessness. For they do not know how to say: "Through fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and were in labor, and gave birth to a spirit of salvation." What they conceive is the kind of thing spoken of elsewhere: "Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived toil, and brought forth lawlessness; he dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole that he made." Such too would be the impious and godless doctrines that each person fabricates, inventing them out of his own mind.

Such people have also "broken asps' eggs," having conceived within themselves the seeds of the opposing powers. That is why it was said to the sons of their wickedness and evil: "Serpents, brood of vipers." By analogy with the divine seed, he called the seed of the opposing powers "eggs," taking his example from the reptile kind, since asps and snakes and the like lay eggs. And since, after such great wickedness, they profess the teachings drawn from the divine Scriptures but fall away into old wives' tales and human traditions that contain nothing sound or useful, he fittingly adds: "and they weave a spider's web," comparing the flimsiness and worthlessness of their zeal to a spider's weaving. "And whoever is about to eat of their eggs," he says, "crushed one and found it addled, and in it a basilisk." What eggs? The ones of which it was said: "they broke asps' eggs." Those who are perfect in wickedness broke these eggs open and took into themselves what had come to full term, while the less advanced, eating of them before they were broken open and brought to term, perish. Hence the other translators read: "Whoever eats of their eggs will die." But if a man of understanding should be found who can crush them with a word that refutes and convicts, he would find in them what is windy, addled, foul-smelling and corrupt, and, crawling and hidden in all of it, the creature that of all reptiles kills by its very glance, I mean the basilisk. According to Aquila: "and what was warmed split open, a viper"; according to Symmachus: "and what was coiled up, breaking out, will be an asp"; according to Theodotion: "what was warmed burst open, an asp." Such are the eggs among the people in question, because they conceive toil and give birth to lawlessness.

Then, since it had been said before, "and they weave a spider's web," he sets out its meaning more fully, saying: "Their web will not become a garment, nor will they clothe themselves with their works." What the "web" is may be learned from the prophet Isaiah himself, who said earlier: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." For by cherishing the traditions of their elders they disregarded the law of God, weaving and stringing together the commandments of men who turn away from the truth. That is why he says: "Their web will not become a garment, nor will they clothe themselves with their works; for their works are works of lawlessness." Those who compare spiritual things with spiritual by means of the divine words spoken by the Holy Spirit weave a divine tunic. But those who wear themselves out to no purpose on Jewish mythologies imitate nothing more than the spider's web, hunting for worthless souls, which are caught in their mythologies as in snares. Next it is said: "For their works are works of lawlessness, and their feet run to evil, swift to shed blood; and their thoughts are the thoughts of fools." All these things they weave for themselves on their own web, imitating the spider, running to wickedness and growing swift to shed innocent blood, as the other translators have it. That is why it was said to the same people above: "For your hands are defiled with blood and your fingers with sins, and your lips have spoken lawlessness, and your tongue practices injustice." Moreover, he says, "ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known." That is why the Savior wept over them, saying to Jerusalem: "If you had known, even you, the things that make for your peace! For days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a palisade around you and surround you and dash your children to the ground." So they did not know the way of peace. Nor is judgment found in their ways, but only utter lack of judgment and injustice; all their paths are crooked, and they do not know peace. For they did not receive the Prince of peace, of whom it is said: "For he himself is our peace." That is why he secured it in advance for his disciples, saying: "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you."

"But because of all these things," he says, "judgment has departed from them, and righteousness will not overtake them." By "judgment" here he means the one spoken of above: "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul delights; he will bring forth judgment to the nations." This judgment, then, which was given to the nations, departed from them; and the righteousness bestowed on all the nations through saving grace also left them and withdrew. Then, since they were waiting for the Christ of God proclaimed to them through the words of the prophets, yet did not receive him when he came, it is fittingly said: "While they waited, the light became darkness for them; waiting for brightness, they walked in the dead of night."

And since, groping at the divine Scriptures, they did not understand the sense hidden in the depths of the words, but busied themselves with the letter alone, they seem to be groping, as it were, at a wall. For this reason he next adds: "They will grope like the blind for a wall, and as those who have no eyes they will grope." And to this he joins: "They will fall at noon as at midnight, and like the dying." For at the time of the noonday light of the nations, when the church of God is lit up by the saving rays of the gospel, they alone, as people who have sinned unto death, have fallen and live as if at midnight.

"And they will groan like a bear," he says, "and like a dove they will go together." Had their groans been reasonable, over what they dared to do against the Savior, they would have done them good. For they ought to mourn and groan and lament and weep over the blood they shed. But since they make no show of this, but instead bewail the city of sense, I mean Jerusalem, and groan senselessly over its fall, they were fittingly compared to a wild beast. Hence it was said: "and they will groan like a bear," and elsewhere: "like a bear robbed of her cubs." They were called a bear because the beast eats men, since they too devoured men, committing murder and killing the prophets; and they were likened to a bear robbed of her cubs because of the loss of their children.

In place of "and like a dove they will go together," Symmachus and Theodotion said: "like a dove we will meditate with meditation," and Aquila: "and like doves we shall utter a sound." For after all these things, even now they still try to meditate on the divine Scriptures, and this alone is left to them: to learn them by heart and recite them by mouth, chanting them aloud, so that they differ in no way from a senseless dove, which seems to be doing something by the sound it utters, yet produces no articulate speech. Hence Aquila, rendering the Hebrew word in its proper sense, does well to say: "and like doves we shall utter a sound." And the other translators set out everything that follows as spoken in the person of the accused people. Thus Symmachus has: "Therefore judgment has become far from us, and it will not overtake us. For we will wait for righteousness, for light, and behold, darkness; for brightness, and we will walk in gloom. We will grope like the blind for a wall, and as those who have no eyes we will grope." In the Seventy too what follows is spoken in the person of the people; at any rate it says: "We waited for judgment, and there is none; salvation has stood far off from us; for great is our lawlessness before you." The prophet says these things in the person of the people, teaching them to confess their sins to God and to accuse themselves, so that, stricken in soul even in this way, they may lift up their heads and turn back, having been taught to repent. And how did they wait for judgment, "and there is none"? Because they did not find the judgment proclaimed to the nations, as was said before, for it had departed far from them. And why? They themselves teach this, saying: "For great is our lawlessness before you, and our sins have stood against us; for our lawless deeds are within us, and we have known our iniquities."

And what all these things are of which they accused themselves, they will again teach, saying: "We have acted impiously and lied"; according to Symmachus, "we knew," he says, "how to do wrong and to lie against the Lord"; according to Aquila, "and to deny in the Lord," the text plainly presenting their denial. "But also," he says, "we have turned away from following our God; we have spoken slander." You see how he nowhere accuses them of idolatry, but of slanders, false words and the like. "And we disobeyed," he says, "and conceived and meditated unjust words from our heart"; according to Aquila: "to speak slander and apostasy; they conceived and uttered from the heart words of falsehood"; according to Symmachus: "to speak slander and turning aside, to conceive and meditate false words from the heart."

Next it is said: "And we have turned judgment back." For it did not abandon us, he says, but we turned it away. "And righteousness has stood far off, because truth was consumed in their ways, and they could not pass through by a straight road"; according to Symmachus: "because truth grew weak in the street, and uprightness could not come, and truth became lacking." Observe how often in these words he accuses them of denying the truth and exposes the false reasonings they invented. To this he next adds: "And the Lord saw, and it did not please him that there was no judgment; and he saw, and there was no man." Above too it was said: "Why was it that I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one to answer?" And here too he says: "And he saw, and there was no man; and he looked, and there was no one to help. And he defended them with his arm and supported himself with mercy," or, according to the others, "upheld himself with righteousness." "And he put a helmet of salvation upon his head, and clothed himself with righteousness as a breastplate, and put on a garment of vengeance, and his cloak, as one who will repay recompense, reproach to his adversaries." This is the conclusion of the present indictment against the Jewish people, and it plainly signifies a war of God rising up against them, which indeed overtook them: the war they suffered in the final siege, in the Roman times.

Having gone through the impieties of the Jewish people against the Savior, and, after all the charges against them, having foretold that God himself would be their enemy, the prophetic word in the passage before us passes once more to the calling of the nations, to which it joins the coming of Christ. For it was fitting that the prophecy about Christ should also include the grace he secured for the nations. Beginning, then, it says: "And those from the west will fear the name of the Lord." Now the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. So it is not Israel that he declares will partake of this wisdom, but those from the west, that is, those whose lot is to dwell in the western regions, "and those from the rising of the sun." Likewise they too "will fear the glorious name." Above too it was said: "Behold, these will come from afar, these from the west and these from the north, and others from the land of the Persians. Rejoice, O heavens." Much has been said about those who fear the Lord: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord," and "Those who fear him lack nothing," and "The fear of the Lord is instruction and wisdom," and "The fear of the Lord adds days." All these things, then, the prophet announces as good news to the nations when he says: "And those from the west will fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun the glorious name." The cause of so great a salvation of the nations he presents next, saying: "For the wrath of the Lord will come like a violent river; it will come with fury." But neither the Hebrew reading nor the other translators mention wrath or fury here; for there was no reason to bring the fury and wrath of God into promises of good things.

Hence Aquila has: "For the spirit of the Lord will come like a river, a signal for itself"; Symmachus: "The spirit of the Lord will come like a pressing river; it hastens and will come"; and Theodotion: "For the spirit of the Lord will come like a besieging river; it was signaled in it." Nowhere in these is the wrath of the Lord mentioned, nor fury. So then, the spirit of the Lord will come like a violent river, so that those from the west and those from the rising of the sun may fear him; for it is for this purpose that the spirit of the Lord is said to come. We shall understand how it is said that it will come like a violent river when we look at the fulfillment of the word, which was fulfilled in the Acts of the Apostles, when, as they were gathered together, "suddenly there came from heaven a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit." In this way, then, the spirit of the Lord is said to come like a violent river; and he also says, "a sign for itself." This was the sign of our Savior's ascension, as he himself taught, saying: "If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come," and again: "When I go away, I will send you the Spirit of truth."

Next it is said: "And the deliverer will come for the sake of Zion"; according to Symmachus: "and he will come to Zion as kinsman-redeemer"; according to Aquila: "and he will come to Zion acting as kinsman-redeemer." The Savior himself made this plain when he said: "I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Here again the God-fearing commonwealth is signified by Zion, which has been shown in various ways to be the church of God. It is for the sake of this city of God, then, that the deliverer, or the kinsman-redeemer, is said to come. And what will he do? He will forgive the iniquities of those who come to him. Hence it is said: "He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob," that is, for those of Jacob who turn back. And if they do not turn back, they have only themselves to blame that they did not share in the grace as the nations did, although they were called first.

"And this," he says, "will be my covenant with them." What it is he adds next: "My spirit, which is upon you." This spirit, then, was the covenant. That is why our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, gave the Spirit to his disciples, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven him." This, then, would be the new covenant and the sum of the mystery: the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said: "And this is my covenant with them, said the Lord: my spirit, which is in you." He addresses these words to the kinsman-redeemer, the deliverer, the one who forgives sins; and he gave a share of this Spirit to his own disciples, so that they in turn might impart it to the worthy. "And my words," he says, "which I have put into your mouth," the words to be handed down through the new covenant, these too would be my covenant. For "my spirit and the words which I have put into your mouth" are already your covenant, which "shall not depart from your mouth and from your seed, said the Lord, from now and forever." For these words remain both in the present age and in the age to come, as the Savior himself taught when he said in the Gospels: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away."

Having announced the good news of Christ's coming, the prophet urges Jerusalem first to partake of the light, that is, the whole Jewish nation, which had long been bound to Jerusalem. Since the Christ of God was himself the light and the truth and the life, and "the light that enlightens every man coming into the world," the word fittingly called upon Jerusalem to enjoy his coming, saying: "Be enlightened, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come." He says the light is hers because the promises about Christ had been proclaimed to her by the prophets. If, then, she had obeyed the command and partaken of the light by receiving the Christ of God, she would have remained in peace to the end. For he says: The light that was announced to you long ago through the prophets has now, behold, come. So do not delay, but be enlightened, be enlightened, and partake of grace; for once you are enlightened, this and that will be yours. And everything that follows, as I said, might perhaps have been fulfilled for them even in a bodily sense, had they obeyed the command and received the Christ of God when he came to dwell among them. But as it is, by denying Christ they deprived themselves of the light as well, and so of all that was promised through the prophecy at once. So much for the bare letter. As for the sense: according to the other translators the name of Jerusalem is not added. Aquila translated it this way: "Arise, be enlightened, for your light has come," and Symmachus: "Arise, be enlightened, for your light is here." Nor is Jerusalem named in the Hebrew reading. So it is fitting to understand these words as addressed to those who received the redeemer, or kinsman-redeemer, who had been promised to come. These were the ones of whom it was said: "And those from the west will fear the name of the Lord, and those from the east the glorious name."

We have often explained that the godly commonwealth, understood as existing in the souls of godly people, is called the city of God and Jerusalem. Long ago this commonwealth existed among the Jews, at the time when prophets and righteous men and a great company of godly and God-loving men flourished among them; and the godliness practiced among them according to the will of God was truly a city of God. But all those among them who had been made perfect departed this life while still awaiting the coming of Christ announced by the prophets, and they hoped that he would descend even as far as death for their salvation. For this reason the word brings them, as to people sitting in darkness, the good news of the coming of the light, saying: "Shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come." These things could be fulfilled at the first coming of our Savior, and they will also reach their completion at his second and glorious appearing as God. This is fitting, since then there will no longer be sun or moon or stars. Instead, the Christ of God himself, the true light and the sun of righteousness, will be enough to give light to the souls of those counted worthy of his kingdom. For then, according to the holy Apostle, "the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command and with the voice of an archangel, and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are left will be caught up together with them in a cloud to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord."

So when he makes his glorious coming, the word then addresses those who are worthy of it and says: "Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come," or, according to the other translators: "Arise, be enlightened, for your light has come." See whether he has not clearly foretold the resurrection of the dead by saying "Arise." The cause of the resurrection of the dead was the coming of the light, for the souls of the saints who died long ago will be rekindled by its life-giving rays and will obtain what was promised. That is why, according to the Apostle, "the Lord himself will descend with a command and with the voice of an archangel, and then the dead in Christ will rise." Then, once they have risen, they will see his glory. So he adds: "And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you." It will not rise upon everyone, but only upon the worthy. Those who are not worthy will be seized by the outer darkness, the eternal fire, and everything else threatened against the ungodly. But upon you, he says, the city of God and the new Jerusalem, the glory of the Lord has risen; share in it and shine. For darkness is laid up for those who have not recognized the Lord or kept his coming before their eyes, and this is what he means when he says: "Behold, darkness will cover the earth, and gloom will be upon the nations; but upon you the Lord will appear," or, according to the other translators: "but upon you the Lord will rise, and his glory will be seen upon you." Those who are to see his glory must first receive light and a dawning, so that they may come into the day of the divine light and become beholders of the glory of the only-begotten Son of God.

Then, he says, "nations will walk by your light, and kings by your brightness." To my mind he has two ranks of the saved in view here. The first is the company of those in the Jewish nation who excelled in godliness. For prophets and patriarchs and priests and God-loving people and high priests, countless men and women, lived among their ancestors and preserved the commonwealth of godliness, so that they form no small part of the city of God. Yet all of these, though made perfect through faith, "did not receive the promises," according to the holy Apostle, "since God had foreseen something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us." That is why they were held in the regions of death, waiting for Christ's coming there. John the Baptist teaches this too, when he asks Christ: "Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?" Since all the saints who had fallen asleep earlier were waiting for him, the present passage fittingly brings good news to their souls and makes known the Savior's descent all the way down to them, saying: "Arise, be enlightened, for your light has come." This, then, was the first rank of the saved, made up of the former people. The other rank is the church from the nations, called second through the grace of Christ, and about it he goes on to say: "And nations will walk by your light." The light you once enjoyed, by which the prophets and patriarchs and all among the Jews who lived godly lives had the eyes of their souls enlightened, will also enlighten the foreign nations of other races. And the brightness you enjoyed, you the former city, scoured clean by divine words, polished and made bright, and cleansed of all filth and every stain, will be enjoyed also by the kings of the foreigners, as they are cleansed and scoured by the power of the divine mysteries.

It is amazing and utterly astonishing to see how the prophecy was fulfilled in our own day, when the very highest rulers were counted worthy of the grace of the washing of baptism. Then, since he has mentioned nations and kings, he very consistently teaches the former city of God to regard as her own children all those from the nations who come over to the godly commonwealth. So he says to her: "Lift up your eyes round about and see your children gathered together; all your sons have come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on shoulders." That is why all who have believed in God through Christ from among the nations have received the promise that they will rest in the bosom of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, as his Savior taught. In many other places too, the church from the nations is called daughter of Zion and daughter of Jerusalem. The mother of the new Jerusalem, made up of the nations, was therefore the one that long ago flourished among the former people, and we are all her children. That is why it was said: "All your sons have come from afar." For we were somewhere far off, "alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world." But "you," he says, "who were once far off have been brought near." That is why it was said: "All your sons have come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on shoulders." These souls are tender and still infants, longing like newborn babies for the pure spiritual milk. Having become children of Abraham through rebirth in Christ, they are borne up, lifted on the shoulders and carried lightly by the teachers who lead them by the hand, as Paul did when he said: "As a nurse cherishes her own children, so, longing for you, we were pleased to share with you not only the gospel of Christ but also our own souls."

When the ancient mother sees this, she is filled with joy: "Then you will see and rejoice, and be afraid, and be amazed in heart." The words "and be afraid" are not found in the other translators. For if there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, how could the souls of the saints who went before, who began this same godliness and were made perfect in it, not rejoice over so many nations turning back? Such souls will rejoice even more when they see the wealth of the sea, and that of the nations and of all the foreign peoples, transferred to her. That is why Symmachus renders it: "when the multitude of the sea is turned toward you, the strength of the nations." Notice here too how he likened the vast multitude of the saved to the multitude of the sea. The strength of the nations would be those who excel, who do not grow weak before the rigors of the life that is according to God but are strengthened, so that they can say: "I can do all things in Christ Jesus who strengthens me."

First, then, she will rejoice over their strength, and after that she will also see the remaining crowds of those who are less mature and less rational in godliness. He likened their ways to herds of camels, saying: "And herds of camels will come to you, and the camels of Midian and Gephar will cover you; all will come from Bashan bringing gold, and they will bring frankincense." I think these words hint at those in the church who are well off and abound in great wealth. In the same way the Savior compared the rich man to a camel when he said: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." Yet the marvel was this: what is impossible for human beings becomes possible for God. That is why Jerusalem is amazed and filled with joy as she watches souls likened to camels being changed and entering eternal life by the narrow and hard way, as if through the eye of a needle. And they did not come without a load: they brought gifts to God, fittingly, as the ransom for their souls.

"Camels will come from Sheba": from the barbarian nations, all the other barbarian nations being signified by the one nation of the Sabaeans. And that such camels were rational, observe carefully how it is said of the same ones: "Herds of camels will come to you, and the camels of Midian and Gephar will cover you; all will come from Bashan bringing gold, and they will bring frankincense and will proclaim the good news of the Lord's salvation." So the camels proclaim the good news of the Lord's salvation as well as bringing the gifts already mentioned: frankincense, that is, the spiritual fragrance of theology, and gold, that is, bodily wealth. Midian and Gephar are barbarian lands that breed camels, as is Sheba, lying beyond Arabia, where camels are very numerous. That is why the passage uses them as an image.

But the most extraordinary thing of all was this: the brutish and rather irrational souls of the rich of this world, likened to camels because the animal is a beast of burden, [?] and crooked, would be changed and come to such profit that they would proclaim the good news of the Lord's salvation. And this salvation was Christ himself. He also says that the sheep of Kedar will be gathered, and that the rams of Nebaioth will come and be offered up on the altar of God. It seems to me that with such words the passage charms and sweetens the childish ears of the carnal Jews, so as to draw them in and urge them to hasten toward the commonwealth that is according to God. Since they could not do it any other way, they might at least in this way come to desire God's promises, just as someone stoops down and lisps along with an infant child, promising the things familiar to childhood and thought to be most delightful, in order to encourage the child toward whatever he wants to teach him. In the same way, I think, the word hands on mystical and divine meanings in veiled form to those whose souls have been enlightened, while it addresses the Jewish people as minds still in infancy, holding out the promises in words and expressions familiar and customary to them. And perhaps all these things would have been fulfilled for them in this bodily way, if they had received our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, as we have already said earlier. At any rate, after urging them to shine, the passage added the promises that follow, which are joined to the condition that they be enlightened by the light of saving grace.

But since they did not share in the light when it first shone upon them, it followed that they would not enjoy what came after either. So they fell away from what they had hoped for, while God, fulfilling his promises, showed them to be true, with their meaning established in a way befitting divine pledges. For divine Scripture is accustomed to use sheep for the simpler rational souls among human beings, as can be seen from the Gospel saying: "Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." So he adds: "And all the sheep of Kedar will be gathered to you, and the rams of Nebaioth will come." Again, Kedar is interpreted as "darkening," and it is said to lie around the desert of the barbarians called Saracens. And Nebaioth would be some other land foreign to the land of Israel. So just as he said that strange and foreign camels would come from Midian and Gephar and Sheba, so too with the sheep and rams from Kedar and Nebaioth he hints at the foreign and alien character of such nations. By the camels, then, he signified the well-off and rich among people; by the sheep, the gentlest and simplest; and by the rams, those of the converts from the nations who are more fit to lead. These, the passage says, will be offered up as gifts on the altar of God. One can see the oracle being fulfilled whenever one sees such souls from the conversion of the nations dedicating themselves to the word of godliness and attending to the service of God's altar. For it is then above all that the church of God is glorified, through the conversion and salvation of such people. That is why it is said next: "And the house of my prayer will be glorified." These things, then, were promised to the ancient Jerusalem, the mother of the new city. I said she was the company of prophets and patriarchs, of righteous and God-loving men, who excelled among the former people, the very ones to whom the word first announced the good news of Christ's coming.

What follows is spoken in the person of these same people, in the words: "Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves with their young, to me?" We will understand this too by attending to the words of Paul, who teaches that "we who are alive, who are left until the coming of Christ, will be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord," joined, that is, and gathered together with the company of those who excelled among the former people. So, marveling at the grace of Christ poured out on humankind, at the multitude of the saved from the nations, and at their flight up to heaven after their departure from this life, they say: "Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves with their young, to me? The islands have waited for me." Earlier too the passage often hinted at the churches under the name of islands. Since the churches of God, as they read through the prophecies, were waiting for the promises made to the fathers, he fittingly says: "The islands have waited for me, and the ships of Tarshish among the first, to bring your children." By the ships of Tarshish he hints at the bodies in which souls sailed through mortal life. Tarshish, again, was a land of foreigners, which is why it is said somewhere about the unbelieving foreigners: "With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish." But those ships were shattered, while here the children of the ancient Jerusalem, who were added to her from the nations, will come to her from afar in the ships themselves, that is, in their very bodies, changed for the better. For "this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality." So those already mentioned will come in their very bodies, bringing with them their virtuous deeds, which are called silver and gold; for the Apostle knows deeds as gold and silver. That is why it is said: "Their silver and their gold with them, and the holy name of the Lord will be glorified."

Besides this it is said: "And foreigners will build your walls." You will see this too fulfilled in fact if you turn your mind to how men from foreign and alien nations who preside over the church of God fence it about with reasoned teaching. They secure the word of godliness as if with ramparts and walls, so that those who are strangers to the faith cannot slip in or find room to plot against the doctrines of truth. "And their kings," that is, the kings of the foreign nations, "will stand by you," he says, and this too we can see with our own eyes. At any rate, the commanders of the Roman forces and the fear of the ruling emperors contribute greatly to overthrowing those who try to plot against the church of God. That is why it is said: "And their kings will stand by you." And he adds: "For in my wrath I struck you, and in mercy I have loved you." It is as if he says: Just as once I struck you, the city of God that professed to be godly, because of the multitude of those in you who were not godly, handing you over to enemies and to captivity, so that even prophets and teachers shared in the wrath against the ungodly, so now, because of those who have recently excelled, you will be counted worthy of my love, whose fruits are great freedom of speech and peace.

That is why it is said: "And your gates will be open continually; they will not be shut day or night." What would the gates of the city of God be but the elementary and introductory teachings? He says these are open night and day to all people, to receive everyone from all the nations who has chosen to be godly. That is why it is said: "to bring into you the strength of the nations." And he promises that the kings of those same nations will also be received through these gates. The strengths of the nations are those who can say: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me," and their kings are those who are outstanding and worthy of the heavenly kingdom. And now that we also see Roman emperors and kings in the bodily sense passing in under the gates of the church of God and being counted worthy of the mysteries within the gates, how could we not bear witness that the prophecy is true? These, then, the gates of the kingdom of heaven will also receive. But as for the nations that remain in unbelief, and their rulers and kings who died in idolatry, the passage goes on to show what end they will have, saying: "For the nations and the kings who will not serve you will perish." For it must be one or the other: either the worthy of salvation serve, with the saving and most noble service, the city of God, I mean the church and the godly commonwealth within it, or those who have acted impiously toward such service are handed over to destruction.

To you, the church of God and the godly commonwealth, will be brought the finest and loftiest of the trees of Lebanon, so that through them "my holy place" may be glorified. Lebanon, again, is a mountain of foreigners, where the tallest and largest trees grow, the most useful for building. Such would be the learned men from the nations who have had a share in the wisdom of this age. When you see them distinguished in the church of God and adorning it with their equipment in eloquence, you would not be wrong to say, by the rule of allegory, that they are the timber of Lebanon, the cypress and pine and cedar, through which the holy place of God is glorified, the place of his feet, that is, the church.

In addition to all this, many who envy the people of God are cut to the heart but can do nothing. They humble themselves and play a part, pretending to honor the saving word and accepting it with irony. The prophet did not pass over them either. So he says: "And the sons of those who humbled you and provoked you will come to you in fear." And in another sense, we know of many who once blasphemed the church, provoked it, and persecuted it, but changed and came to worship the God who is in it. "And then," he says, "you will be called City of the Lord, Zion." For then truly, "when the fullness of the nations has come in, then all Israel will be saved." For the company of God's ancient saints, united with the people of the nations who have been joined to them through Christ and becoming one body, will form one united city. That is why the body made one out of all of them will be called "the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel."

Then he adds: "Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was no one to help." For since, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, they became forsaken and hated because of those of the former people who transgressed, the natural branches of the cultivated olive that were cut off, and there was no one to help them. But now, in place of the branches that were cut off, those from the wild olive have been grafted in and have filled up the lacking part, the place of those who were cast away. And so, by the power of the Savior, the fullness of the saved has been formed: one perfect company of God out of both peoples, and one city out of both ranks, called the Zion of God. To her, once she is made complete, he promises what follows, saying: "And I will make you an everlasting exultation, a joy from generation to generation."

And again he prophesies that he will provide her with the milk of the nations, saying: "And you will suck the milk of nations." What could the milk of the nations be but the new mystery of the gospel teaching and the elementary teaching of the new covenant, in which those reborn in Christ share? He also promises the wealth of kings to the people he has been describing. Here again we should understand the kings to be none other than those worthy of the beatitudes, to whom the Savior has promised the kingdom of heaven. Yet who, seeing grain allowances supplied to the church of God by those in power, and rich gifts and offerings brought to her, would not say without hesitation that these words have been confirmed even literally? And from all that has been said, "you will know," he says, "that I am the Lord who saves you and the God of Jacob who delivers you."

But in addition to what has been explained, learn this as well: there will no longer be any need of useless wood, for such things are food for fire; nor will you have any need of stones, that is, of foolish souls. Therefore, in place of these I will bring you things more precious than they. Those who were once men of bronze and unyielding, harsher than any iron and hard in their ways, will be changed into gold and silver and will be fitted into your building according to God. And the foolish, more senseless than dry wood, will also be changed and will serve you in place of bronze and iron. They will become better than they were and more useful for God's building, after the pattern of the first, who exchanged bronze and iron for the worth of gold and silver. And when things have gone forward in this way, your rulers will spend the rest of their lives in peace, presiding over and leading the church of God. If, by prophetic foreknowledge, one must address them in advance by their proper name, God has already named them bishops here, saying: "And I will appoint your rulers in peace and your bishops in righteousness."

To this he adds: "And injustice will no longer be heard in your land" (that is, in your dwelling place), "nor ruin nor misery within your borders." So no enemy or adversary will be left then, nor will there be any memory of wickedness; instead, "pain and grief and sighing have fled away." "And then," he says, "your walls will be called Salvation." In place of "Salvation," the Hebrew reading contains Jesus himself, in the very letters and characters in which our Savior's name is written. So the very power of our Savior Jesus will become this for those worthy of these things, in place of an enclosure and a strong wall. These things can be seen here in part, but they will come to pass in the new age, after the consummation of the present one. He goes on to say: "And your gates will be called Carving"; but according to Aquila: "and your gates," he says, "hymning," and according to Symmachus, "praise." You see how the word leads us away from the more bodily interpretation, so that we do not fall into the obvious and Jewish interpretations. That is why he names the gates of this new Jerusalem hymning and praise. For it is chiefly through these that the entrances to the godly commonwealth are formed, since those who are brought in are taught to hymn and praise God.

But the sun will no longer give you day, nor will the moon light you through the night, because those who will be counted worthy of the new age will be neither in night nor in sensible and bodily light. For above any sun they will have the Lord himself as their everlasting light and God as their glory. That is why the prophecy next says: "And the days of your mourning will be fulfilled." In deed, he means, the beatitude will be confirmed that says: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted."

"And the whole people," he says, will then be shown to be righteous, since no unrighteous person will then be found among it. Therefore, as a chosen people, it will inherit the land promised to it. The Savior taught this too when he said, "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth," hinting in this way at the heavenly dwelling place. In it lies the city of God, the heavenly and true Jerusalem, which according to the Apostle is our mother. In place of "guarding the plant, the works of his hands," Symmachus has: "a shoot of my planting, the works of my hands, to be glorified." For such is my people: a shoot of my planting. "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted," but this shoot, which comes from God's planting and has become the work of his hands, will inherit the promised land, so as to be glorified with such great blessings.

Then the one who is fewest in the present life will also become thousands, in keeping with the Savior's promises. In these he promises to appoint rulers, and he will then say to them: "Have authority over five cities," and "Have authority over ten cities." In this way, then, they will become thousands, as though each of the saved were to become a commander of a thousand. And the one who is now least will then become a great nation. Paul is an example of this, for he said: "To me, the very least of all the saints, this grace was given." Then he will be the ruler of some great heavenly nation, counted as such before God. "All these things," he says, "will come about when I, the Lord, gather them at the time I have appointed." For even if the things promised have not yet arrived, the time appointed once and for all will come, and in it all these things will take place through my gathering. For then "he will send out his angels, and they will gather to him all the saints from one end of heaven to the other."

In the preceding section, after the gospel promises, he said at the end of the passage: "I the Lord will gather them in due time." Quite consistently, then, he now cries out in the present passage: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." Then, in what follows, he teaches how he carries out the gathering. The one who said, "I the Lord will gather them in due time," goes on as though he were someone other than the speaker: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." How this can be would be clear to those who hold that the Christ of God is neither a mere man nor a Word without flesh or body that had no share in mortal nature. Rather, they say that he is at once both God and man. He is God inasmuch as he is the only-begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father, and man inasmuch as he is understood to have been born of the seed of David according to the flesh. So God the Word, whom the prophecy calls Lord in the strict sense, added this to the other promises he had made, saying: "I the Lord will gather them in due time."

Then he presents the man whom he had assumed, introducing him as saying: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." It has also been shown many times in the earlier sections how the Spirit of God rested upon the one from the root of Jesse: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness. Hence the Gospel according to Luke fittingly records that our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ taught that the prophecy had been fulfilled in him. He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, went into the synagogue on the sabbath day as was his custom, and stood up to read. The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him, and when he opened it he found the place: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the broken away in release, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." Then he rolled up the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down, and the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." And all bore witness to him and marveled at the words of grace that came from his mouth. If you pay attention to the time indicated by "Today this scripture has been fulfilled," you will find that it was at that very time, after he had been baptized in the Jordan, that the Holy Spirit came down in the form of a dove and remained on him. Then he was led up into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. Then he came to Nazareth and read the prophecy just quoted. That is why he added, with precision: "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." For at the very time when the Holy Spirit came down upon him in the form of a dove, the prophecy spoken in his own person was being fulfilled: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." It would not be said of him that he was anointed with a bodily anointing like those of old, for he would have had nothing exceptional if he had been anointed in the same way as other men.

But as it is, he received his anointing by the Holy Spirit, and so he is shown to be the Christ of God, exceptional beyond all and only-begotten. The words "he has sent me to bring good news to the poor" were being fulfilled at the time when he preached the kingdom of heaven and set the beatitudes before his disciples, saying: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." He also healed the brokenhearted, treating them with the promises in which he said, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted," and, "Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh." The souls of the nations had been taken captive by invisible and spiritual enemies, and already he was proclaiming release to them when he commanded his disciples, saying: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Through this he secured the forgiveness of their former impieties. In this way, then, he proclaimed release to the captives. He also proclaimed recovery of sight to those who suffered from blindness, in that they were enslaved to the error of polytheism. And he called "the acceptable year of the Lord" the whole time that he made his own year, during which he lived among men and gave days of light to those who came to him. But perhaps he was hinting at the age to come, which follows the consummation of the present one, when he said: "to call the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense for our God." According to the other translators, it is "the year of good pleasure." That time and age which is pleasing to the Lord would be the same age as the day of recompense, for at that time he will repay those who have labored in the present life.

That is why it says: "to call the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense for our God," and also "to comfort all who mourn." He who said, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted," promised them comfort for now, but on the day of recompense he will restore them by his own words and comfort them. To those who mourn for Zion he will also give glory, and the oil of gladness instead of ashes. Paul and those like him mourned for Zion, weeping over the fall of the Jewish nation and of the godly commonwealth among them. To these, then, he will give glory instead of mourning. They sprinkled ashes on themselves and afflicted themselves in their supplications to God on behalf of the people, and instead of these ashes he will give the oil of gladness. In a spirit of despondency they wore themselves out from their surpassing love for humanity, and instead of that spirit he will give a garment of glory. He promises to give these things to these same people: at his first coming the Savior promised that he would do so on the day of recompense. So it was fitting that, having read that part of the prophecy, he added: "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." Next after these words it says: "And they shall be called Generations of righteousness, the Planting of the Lord for glory." When will they be called this, and who will be called this, if not those who will be counted worthy of the acceptable year and of the day of recompense? According to Symmachus: "And they shall be called Mighty ones of righteousness, the Plant of the Lord, so that he may be glorified."

"And they shall build up the everlasting desolations": this clearly means the souls of the nations that had long been desolate. Therefore he adds: "They shall raise up what was formerly laid waste, and they shall renew desert cities laid waste for generations." Indeed, through all these words the prophecy foretells the change from worse to better.

Then next he adds: "And foreigners shall come, shepherding your flocks." So the prophecy promises the oversight of shepherds to foreigners as well. "And aliens," it says, "shall be your plowmen and vinedressers." Indeed, strangers and foreigners shepherd the sheep of God. Certain strangers and aliens cultivate the vineyard, that is, the church, as plowmen. They were once idolaters, alienated from the covenant of God and strangers to the promises, having no hope and without God in the world. Then he addresses these very people, saying: "But you shall be called priests of the Lord, ministers of your God." And who are "you" but the plowmen, vinedressers, and shepherds of the church? These same people will also eat the strength of the nations, or, according to Aquila, "you shall eat the wealth of the nations." For no food is so fitting for the priests of God and for the shepherds, vinedressers, and plowmen of the church as the strength of the nations that are saved through them. You will understand the strength of the nations when you look at God's martyrs throughout the whole world and at the strong and invincible endurance of those in every nation who contend for the truth. "And in wealth," he says, "you shall be admired." You will understand the wealth of the nations from the testimony of Paul, who wrote to the Corinthians: "I thank my God through Jesus Christ that in everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge, just as the testimony of God was confirmed among you, so that you are not lacking in any spiritual gift."

These same people inherited the land a second time. Indeed, they inherited the whole inhabited world, about which it is said in the Psalms: "The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession." This inheritance of the Savior, then, the leaders of his church have inherited, and everlasting joy has come upon their heads. All these things have been received in part in the present life, but the fullness of the promise was deferred to the hope of the age to come.

"These things will come about," he says, "because I am the Lord who loves righteousness and hates plunder gained by injustice." For the opposing powers, the evil demons, were enslaving the souls of men, and they did so by violence and injustice. "Therefore, because I hate this plunder and myself love righteousness, I have poured out my grace not on the Jews only but on all the nations as well." "And I will give their labor to the righteous," he says. Whose labor, but that of those who inherit the land a second time? Instead of "to the righteous," all the other translators have "in truth." This means that their labor will not be disappointed but will truly be kept for them. "And I will make an everlasting covenant with them": he will no longer hand down to them the temporary commandments of Moses, but the mystery of the new covenant, which will endure and be everlasting.

Further, it says: "And their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of peoples. Everyone who sees them will recognize them, that they are a seed blessed by the Lord." And who would not admit that it is precisely by God's blessing that the seed of the church has multiplied, so that it is known throughout the whole world? By "their seed" we should understand either the word and teaching of the gospel, or those who are genuinely their disciples in word and in life. They are plain to see, so that they are indeed a seed blessed by God.

Quite consistently, after the promises just listed, which the Son of God himself made at his first coming, the prophecy now speaks in the person of the church of God. She has obtained such great blessings and gives thanks for what she has experienced. She has received the full number of the saved as her own members. She is like a bride made up of one comely and beautiful body, clothed in the adornment her bridegroom has given her. So she says: "Let my soul rejoice in the Lord." And she adds the reason: "For he has clothed me with a garment of salvation." The body of the resurrection, which is called the garment of salvation, will be like a pillar of light flashing with divine radiance. It will no longer be a body of death, such as Paul meant when he said, "Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" That body too will share in salvation. It will be put on the soul as a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness, for each person will be clothed in his own adornment through the righteous deeds he has done. She will have attained to the perfect man and to the measure of stature, and will have been made like her bridegroom. Then, because of the perfect within her, who have been formed in the image of the bridegroom, she will say: "He has put a mitre on me as on a bridegroom." And because of those who are not yet such, who stand in the second rank of the good, she will say: "And he has adorned me with ornaments like a bride." This same bride, who is the bride of the Word her bridegroom and has received his seeds, yields beautiful and blossoming fruits. Therefore she says: "And like the earth that makes its flower grow, and like a garden, it will make its seeds spring up." Then next, so that the children of the Jews may not snatch these things for themselves, the prophecy draws a distinction: "So the Lord, the Lord will make righteousness and gladness spring up before all the nations."

Having uttered these oracles, the prophet is then moved by what has been said and cries out: "For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not let up." According to the other translators: "And for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until her righteousness goes forth like light and her salvation burns like a torch." According to Aquila: "And her salvation is kindled like a torch." "For I shall not be able," he says, "to be still and keep quiet. I must cry out night and day and give myself to prayers and supplications, until I see with my own eyes the fulfillment of these very things that have been spoken." That will be when the righteousness of Jerusalem and her salvation shine forth like light on all people. For the light that is to shine upon her will not be confined to her alone, but will share its radiance with all the nations as well. Therefore he adds: "And nations shall see your righteousness, and all the kings of the earth your glory." Here again he gives the names Zion and Jerusalem to the godly commonwealth that once existed among the Jews, to the choir of righteous and God-loving men who were distinguished among them, and to all the prophets who were worthy of salvation. He promises that their light will shine forth to all the nations more brightly than any torch, so that all the kings will see their glory, meaning in this way the kingdoms on earth. Then he adds: "And you shall call it by the new name that the Lord will give it." For the name of the Lord adorns his church.

Then, he says, "you shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord." She will receive this crown at that time, saying: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness." "And a royal diadem in the hand of your God." For all who achieve virtue through Christ are truly his crown. The holy martyrs who have contended in the contests on his behalf are the diadem of his kingdom. The Father chooses them with his own hand and places them around the Son, crowning him and honoring him with a royal diadem through the multitude of those saved by him and through him. When these things are fulfilled, she who has received the new name will no longer be called Forsaken or Desolate Land, even if she was once like that. Now that she has been counted worthy of such great blessings, she will be called, he says, My Will, that is, she will be named according to my will, and your land will be called Inhabited.

In the new age of Christ's kingdom she will be established, and her only inhabitants will be those who are counted worthy of God's promises. They will live in such delight and gladness that they will be like a holy young man living with a pure virgin, who in no way defiles her virginity but rejoices in her virginal chastity and in their pure companionship and shared life. In this way your sons will rejoice. And the Lord himself will receive you as his own bride: the holy church made up of perfect members, both from the former people and from the new people drawn from the nations. He will rejoice over you as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride. He will also appoint watchmen, that is, divine angels and holy powers, to guard and keep the walls and ramparts of this new Jerusalem, so that he himself may rule in peace through the whole age. And these watchmen just mentioned, he says, will not cease all day and all night to sing hymns and doxologies to the author of such great blessings and to give him thanks for the salvation of so many.

Instead of "For there is none like you, if he sets right and makes Jerusalem a boast on the earth," Symmachus says: "Do not keep quiet, and do not let him keep quiet, until he prepares and until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth." To whom are these words spoken, if not to those who said above, "For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not let up, until her righteousness goes forth like light"? When the choir of prophets had said this, the Holy Spirit encouraged them and urged them to persevere in their prayers for the things spoken of. Therefore it says: "Do not keep quiet, and do not let him keep quiet." Clearly this means the Lord who promises these things: "until he prepares and until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth." With these words he commands those who are able to intercede for the whole people not to fall silent or keep quiet. They are not even to give God himself any quiet, but to rouse him with unceasing shouts and cries until he brings what has been promised to completion.

While they cry out and do not allow the Lord to delay, he who made the promise and said, "While you are still speaking I will say, Here I am," counts them worthy of an answer. Therefore he adds next: "The Lord has sworn by his glory and by the strength of his arm: I will no longer give your grain and your food to your enemies, and foreign sons shall no longer drink your wine, for which you have labored." These things did happen in the past, when they offered their own fruit as food to the enemies of God, doing and practicing such things that their deeds became food for demons. But now the Lord swears an oath to those who will be counted worthy of the new age and will obtain what has been promised. He swears that he will no longer give their fruits to enemies, but that they themselves will enjoy them. For it is right that those who achieve the virtuous life and live in godliness should enjoy their own fruits, as it is said: "You shall eat the labors of your fruits." "And they shall eat," he says, "and drink in my holy dwellings." These would be the many dwelling places with the Father. And since he has mentioned dwellings, or, according to the other translators, courts, it is fitting that he also mentions the temple.

Therefore he adds next: "Go, go through my gates, and make a way for my people, and throw the stones out of the road." With these words he leads us to understand the heavenly city of God, its gates, and the courts within the city. All these will be thrown open to the worthy in the promised age, and it will be said: "Go, go through my gates." Then come the words about clearing the way: let no hindrance or obstacle, no envy or malice, no pretext, no demon, no evil spirit, no opposing power prevent my people from entering the kingdom of heaven. These words will be spoken to certain angelic powers. Then next he adds: "Raise a signal to the nations. For behold, the Lord has made it heard to the end of the earth." Let no one think, he says, that these things are said about the Jewish people. For he commands that the signal be raised to all the nations, and he announces the things foretold as good news to everyone, as far as the end of the earth. Then he teaches the daughter of Zion, which is plainly the church, to expect her Savior, saying: "Tell the daughter of Zion." He has named the new church of God, which has received the new name, the daughter of Zion, since she is the daughter of the former godly commonwealth among the Jews. He also addresses her, saying: "Behold, your Savior has come, bringing his reward." Notice how these very things were also indicated in the earlier passages, where it was said: "Behold, the Lord comes with strength; behold, his reward is with him and his work before him." And now it says: "Tell the daughter of Zion, Behold, your Savior has come to you, having his reward with him and his work before his face." Earlier, at his first coming, this same one was a Savior. By what he did and suffered for the human race, he secured salvation from God for those who believe in him, and for this reason he was also named Jesus, as the angel testified. But here, in presenting his second coming, the prophecy introduces him as judge and rewarder.

"And he shall call it a holy people, redeemed by the Lord." Instead of "and he shall call it," the other translators have "and they shall call them," meaning, clearly, those who are to be saved. These, then, will be called a holy people redeemed by the Lord. But you, the city of God, to whom so much has been said, will be called a city sought out and not forsaken. Jerusalem both became forsaken and was called so. But this city, which the whole discourse is about, will be sought out, he says, and not forsaken. For he who came to seek and to save the lost has found it and saved it, and he no longer allows it to be lost.

To those who had succeeded in godliness, the Saviour was said to come bringing his reward with him, so as to give recompense and the prizes of the upward calling to those who had contended for piety. In the same way, it is foretold that he will come to the ungodly, and to those who walk the opposite road, as one to be feared and as an avenger. So above it was said: "And as a bridegroom will rejoice over a bride, so will the Lord rejoice over you," together with everything else that the word promised to those who do well. The present passage, however, describes the judgment against the ungodly, in which he will put all his enemies under his feet. This is what the divine Apostle taught when he said: "Then comes the end, when he abolishes every rule and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death." The present prophecy therefore signifies the overthrow of these opposing powers, rules and authorities. The passage dramatizes the questions of certain people who see the Christ of God appearing in the guise of a warrior, his clothing stained with blood. Astonished at how strange he looks, they say to one another: "Who is this who comes from Edom, with crimson garments from Bozrah, so beautiful in his robe, with force and might?" Symmachus has: "Who is this who comes from Edom, his clothing reddened from Bozrah, so comely in his robe, striding in the greatness of his strength?" Edom and Bozrah belonged to the land of foreigners and were always enemies of Israel, so with these names he fittingly hints at the opposing powers. Because these have been destroyed and, as it were, slaughtered, they say his clothing is stained with blood. Seeing him so greatly changed by the punishment of the ungodly, they seem not even to recognize him, for they know him as bright, serene and gentle. So they ask: "Who is this who comes?" And he answers them: "I speak of righteousness and of saving judgment." Symmachus has: "I speak in righteousness, fighting to save." For he fought on behalf of those unjustly oppressed by the opposing powers. He pursued the one as enemies, and he saved the others by freeing them from the enemies' dominion.

After this answer they ask him a second time: "Why are your garments red, and your clothing as if from a full winepress that has been trodden down?" Symmachus has: "Why is your clothing reddened, and your garments like those of one treading a winepress?" He does not refuse to explain how this came about. So he goes on, according to Symmachus: "I trod the winepress all alone, and of the peoples there was no one with me. I trod them in my anger and trampled them in my wrath, and their victory was spattered on my garments, and I stained all my clothing." Notice how he is said to have trodden the winepress all alone: the Father has given judgment to him alone. Scripture usually calls the exacting of the penalty for sins a winepress. So Jeremiah says in Lamentations: "The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah. For these things I weep." The combined accounting for sins and the conviction that follows them, the exaction and the punishment, have been called a winepress. In the same way there are also winepresses dear to God and pleasing to him, for the good fruits gathered from the good vine, and for these the Psalms speak of "hymns for the winepresses." But in the passage before us, he alone, with no one working alongside him, trod the winepress and swept all his enemies out of the way at the time of vengeance, abolishing every rule and every authority and power: "For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet." Having thus subdued his enemies and crushed their seed, when no enemy remains any longer, and there is no longer any devil or demon or vice or sin, he will bring to the Father those who are to be ruled by him in the new age. Then, as the Apostle says, he will also hand over the kingdom to God the Father. He stains his clothing, and it is said to have turned red. This is a vivid figure of speech, a personification, as is the blood of the enemies, of which he says: "And I brought their blood down to the earth." We must not suppose that the opposing powers have physical blood. Must not these words too, then, be taken figuratively?

Then he mentions again a day of recompense and a year of redemption, as was said above about the happier things: "to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense for our God." The whole new age has been called the acceptable year of the Lord, since it will have the Lord himself as its everlasting light, and the same age is also called the day of recompense. So he says: "The day of recompense has come upon them, and the year of redemption is at hand." At one and the same time he will redeem his own and repay the others, as Moses said: "And he will repay justice to his enemies, and repay those who hate him."

Then he says: "And I looked, and there was no one to help; and I considered, and no one gave support; and my arm delivered them." We will understand what this means if we observe that he alone emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross. What no one ever endured, whether among human beings or angels or the divine powers, he alone took upon himself for our salvation. That is why the Father granted to him alone the name that is above every name, and entrusted to him the judgment of all. Having received this authority from the Father, he delivered those who were worthy of salvation, and routed his foes and enemies. So he says: "And my wrath came upon them, and I trampled them and brought their blood down to the earth." Instead of "blood," the other translators have rendered "their victory." These powers once seemed to be beyond subduing and to yield the victory to no one. So to hint at their defeat and humiliation, he fittingly says that he has brought their victory down to the earth.

The prophecy about the second coming of Christ has now been completed, and the passage begins another subject, in which it proclaims God's benefits to the Jewish people. Speaking in the person of the people, it brings a charge against them, and through their own confession it shows that their rejection and the final desolation of Jerusalem came about by God's just judgment. So he says: "I remembered the mercy of the Lord," and adds: "I will recall the excellent deeds of the Lord." That is: I will never let the marvelous benefits of his mercy be forgotten, but I will always remember both his mercy and the wonders he has shown us at any time. Grim things did overtake us at the last, and the nation and the city of Jerusalem, with its temple, were handed over to the wrath of God until they were torn up from their foundations. Where the Seventy have "in all that he renders to us," Symmachus says "concerning all the good he has done us." Again, where they have "The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel" and what follows, Symmachus has: "The Lord, out of the abundance of his goodness to the house of Israel, who did them good according to his compassion." "All these things, then," he says, "I will recall, as I count up the abundance of his goodness." Among these, God bestowed this greatest gift: he deigned to call the people his own children, provided they did not reject his grace. So Symmachus has: "Surely they are my people, sons who do not break the covenant."
