Yet at the beginning of the prophecy he had rebuked them, saying: "I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me."

He himself, then, took the initiative and hastened to save his people. He came in person, as his own messenger, and he provided them with good things himself, not through others. So he says: "Not an envoy nor an angel, but he himself saved them, because he loved them and spared them," and so on. Such were the works of his love for humankind. But they showed themselves unworthy of his benefits and tried to make him their enemy. And at once he who had given them so many good things became their foe. He recalled that this was not the first time they had behaved this way. They had always, from his very first visitation of them, been harsh and blind to God's benefits.

In the time of Moses, for instance, they were granted countless marvelous benefits. Yet they never kept their benefactor before their eyes, or reckoned among themselves who it was, and what kind of being, that had shown them so many wonders. Instead they made a calf, and again worshiped idols, and committed countless other impieties in the desert itself. They never stopped to consider how he had led them through the Red Sea, setting Moses over them like a shepherd of sheep, and how he had shown Moses to be a great prophet and his servant by filling him with his own Spirit. Where the Seventy have "he strengthened the water before him," Symmachus says "who split the waters before them, to make for them an everlasting name." So, having split the waters of the Red Sea, he led them like a horse through the desert and over dry land, and like cattle across a plain. But the people this passage refers to kept no memory of these things. They disobeyed and provoked his Holy Spirit, and so he turned and became their enemy, and he himself fought against them.

He who had once been their champion judged this with right reason and justice. Nevertheless, since he is loving toward humankind and good, as God is by nature, we must not lose heart or despair of the salvation that comes from him. By devoting ourselves to supplication and confession we can win his favor. So let us all say together, both I, the prophet who speak these words, and you among the people who have chosen to fear God, as we beseech him and plead with earnest appeals: "Turn from heaven and look down from your holy and glorious house." If indeed we show him our change from worse to better, we can say, "And look." And this too, O Lord, must be recalled: often you acted for us, not for our own sake but for the sake of your zeal, unworthy as we were, and you granted us your mercies. Where, then, is that zeal of yours, and your strength, and the abundance of your mercy? Many times before, when we sinned, you bore with us. This is no wonder, since you once deigned to say: "My people are children," and "My people are sons." As a father with his children you bore with us before, so bear with us now again. For Abraham was not our father, even if he seemed to serve as the means of our birth according to the flesh. In truth you are our father, since you are the father of all spirits and of the souls made in your image. We plead with you, then, to deliver us, since your name adorns us. For the sake of your own name, so that it may not be blasphemed among the nations, count us worthy of your mercy.

The prophet said these things in his own person and in the person of the more devout among the people. Now he adds the following words in the person of those among the people who love to find fault and bring accusations, and who often do not hesitate to blame even God himself. So they say: "Why, Lord, have you made us stray from your way, and hardened our hearts so that we do not fear you?" He says this as if in the person of the people: "Just as you once hardened Pharaoh's heart, so now you have hardened us too, judging us unworthy of the fear of you. Indeed, O Lord, you yourself have led us astray, so that we did not know your way. Nevertheless, even if we are such people, you are God; so turn back for the sake of your servants, for there are likely to be some such in the whole multitude. And since we were counted worthy to be called your portion, we beseech you: 'Return for the sake of your servants and for the sake of the tribes of your inheritance.' Then, if only for the sake of your servants and the tribes of your inheritance, we too, unworthy as we are, may obtain some small share in the holy mountain you promised. We have now fallen away from it completely, since our adversaries have trampled your sanctuary.

"They did this because you turned away from us. So now, abandoned and without your care, we are just as we were before you ruled over us. There was once a time when we had no prophets, no priests, no kings, and none of your gifts, and in the same way we have now fallen back into that desolation. That is how we were in Egypt, where we spent a long time before Moses was set over us. At that time your name did not adorn us, and we were not called your people or the portion of your inheritance. And now, likewise, we have come round to the same end." All this seems to refer to the time after the coming of our Saviour, when they were utterly abandoned because of what they dared to do against him. For now they have truly become as they were at the beginning, when God did not rule over them.

Where the Seventy have "If you open heaven, trembling will seize the mountains before you" and what follows, Symmachus translated it this way: "We have become as we were from of old, people over whom you do not rule, upon whom your name has not been called; nor did you tear open the heavens and come down. Before your face the mountains flowed down; as at the kindling of fire the sea melted, the waters were terrified." "We have become," he says, "like people who never experienced your wonders, to whom you never showed the marvels you performed in the time of Moses." According to the Seventy he says: "We have become such as we were before you ruled over us. Nevertheless, we know for certain and are convinced that if you choose to open heaven, being God and all-powerful, trembling will seize the mountains before you." The mountains are, of course, the opposing powers that exalt themselves against the knowledge of you. "They will melt like wax before fire, and fire will devour the adversaries of your Godhead. The power of your name will be shown in deed to all your enemies. If you should only choose to open your heaven and visit those on earth, the nations that do not know you as God will be thrown into confusion, and trembling will seize the mountains just mentioned before you."

"Such is the power you have. So from all eternity we have not heard of any other God like you. Nor could we say, without bearing false witness, that our eyes have seen anyone else who performs such works. We have seen no other god besides you, and no other divine deeds. Nor do we ascribe to anyone else the things you have let those who wait for you see." At this point, notice how the prophetic word presents God as one who is seen, saying in the person of the people: "Nor have our eyes seen a God besides you." And yet: "No one has ever seen God," and "No one shall see my face and live." It seems, then, that these words hint at the Christ of God. He spoke with Moses in the desert, and all the people saw him through the glory displayed to all, of which it is said: "And all the people saw the glory of the Lord."

Next he adds: "Behold, you were angry, and we sinned." It is as if he were saying more plainly: because we sinned, you were angry. "And we went astray," he says, "and we have all become like something unclean. And if any righteousness or righteous action was thought to be found among us, it too has been shown to be filthy and worthless. So we have become like a barren tree that has shed its fruit. We have all fallen away like leaves, and been scattered like dust before the wind."

"No one among us is said to be the kind of person who calls on your name and is able to move you by prayers. For no one holds fast to the help that comes from you, or keeps it in mind. So you were right to turn your face away from us. Even after all this, however, we know you as Father. Nor are we ignorant of what we ourselves are. We are no different from clay, of which you alone are the potter, and we are in no way different from earthenware, a fragile vessel, broken and shattered now in one way, now in another. So we beg you to look on the frailty of our weakness and grant pardon for our sins, recalling that we were once called your people, and that this was your city, now desolate, and your sanctuary, now torn down. Recall that the house of your holiness has become a curse, and the place our fathers blessed has been given over to fire." Symmachus has: "Jerusalem has become desolate, the house of our sanctuary has gone to ruin; where our fathers praised you, it has become a blaze of fire, and all that we treasured has become a disgrace." "Will you hold back at all this, Lord, and keep silent, and humble us exceedingly?"

The preceding words offered up supplications and confessions in the person of the people. They also contained something like reproaches from those who said: "You have made us stray, Lord, from your way; you have hardened our hearts so that we do not fear you." To these words an answer is given through the prophetic Spirit, with this meaning: "How could I, who do not desire the death of the sinner but rather his repentance, disregard those who pray and confess such things? I wish all people to turn from error to the truth, and I summon even the fallen to rise. How then could I lead you astray from my way, or harden your hearts so that you do not fear me? Indeed, if anyone wished to consider my love for humankind with a mind that loves the truth, he would find that my benefits reach even those who stand far from knowledge of me before they seek me. For instance, out of surpassing love for humankind I made myself manifest to those outside, who had never asked for me. So now foreigners and people of other nations have received knowledge of me, though they contributed nothing toward it. Indeed, I gave my grace to those who did not seek it, before others could even plead for it: before they prayed, before they made supplication, I said, 'Here I am.'"

How then could I, who am by nature so kind and good even toward those who were strangers to the knowledge of me, have appeared cruel, harsh and utterly unjust toward you? In fact, it was with you that I began my grace, and to you first that I stretched out my hands, calling you and embracing you as my own true sons. But you went on disobeying, while I called you and urged you to hasten to the salvation that is with me.

You went the opposite way and multiplied your own evils. Are you not the ones who have provoked me from all time? You forsook the temple consecrated to me and gave yourselves over to idolatry and the error of many gods, so that you sacrificed in the gardens and burned incense to unclean spirits and wicked demons on altars you had built of brick, and even slept in the tombs and the caves. Such were the places held to be shrines of the gods, [?] where you devise oracles for yourselves. For what else are you doing but making yourselves like the utterly lawless and the foreigners? You now gorge yourselves on swine's flesh, and you do not shrink from defiling all the vessels in your houses with polluted sacrifices.

And worst of all, the thing that most deserves wrath and indignation, is that you prided yourselves on these very things as if they were good deeds and considered yourselves purer than all other people. You would not even come near ordinary folk or deign to touch your neighbours, but said to those who approached, "Do not come near me, for I am pure." For these things, then, will not what is called the wrath of God, that is, his avenging power, be most justly stirred against them, and the fire that will be kindled against them?

For this is written before me, and these things cannot be passed over until they pay the penalty for them. And not only for their own sins, but also for the impieties of their fathers, who at one time burned incense on the mountains and practised idolatry on the hills themselves, and at another mocked my laws. In due time these things will be repaid into their bosom.

What has been said was spoken against the ungodly among the people, so that anyone in the multitude who is found to have hope of salvation will be free of these words. For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, the house of Israel, produced thorns instead of grapes, lawlessness instead of justice, and not righteousness but an outcry. For these reasons desolation and utter destruction have been decreed against it. Even so, if amid the destruction of so many anyone should be found to be like a sound and healthy grape in a withered cluster, he will not fall when I am judge, nor perish with those who perish, because he shares in a blessing. And this grape will be as precious to me as it is rare. On this pattern I will deal with the whole nation, if anyone among them should be found worthy of salvation. Therefore I will not destroy them all, but I will lead out the one among them who serves me, separating him from those who perish. He will be a seed from Jacob, a living and useful seed, able to serve for the fruit-bearing of others as well. Such also was what was said earlier: "And unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed." This good and rare seed, that is, the band of apostles set apart from the multitude of those who perish, will inherit my holy mountain. They confessed that they knew this mountain when they said, "We have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." And that heavenly inheritance, he says, "my chosen ones and my servants will receive, and they will dwell there." Here again he means by his chosen ones and servants the apostles, who were found to be the sound grapes. Having chosen them, he called them a kind of safeguard for others and a holy and chosen seed.

Through them what follows was also fulfilled. And what is that? "And there shall be," he says, "folds for flocks in the thicket." Scripture usually calls the multitude of foreign and alien nations a "thicket". It foretells that there will be folds for flocks among them, hinting at the churches of God's sheep. There is also the Valley of Achor, which was once placed under a ban. There, as the history of Joshua, the successor of Moses, relates, Achan perished with his whole family because of the transgression he had committed. He was stoned in the valley and became accursed. The land of the godless, that is, of the foreign nations, who were themselves under a ban, was of the same kind. But this too "will become a resting place for herds, for my people who have sought me." And the people who sought him were the grape and the seed spoken of above, his chosen servants. Through them, he prophesies, herds of cattle and flocks of sheep will be gathered, not in Israel or in the land of the Jews, but in the thicket and in the Valley of Achor just mentioned.

So much for these matters. The word then turns again to the multitude of the Jews and says: "But you who forsake me and forget my holy mountain," the mountain we have often explained. You who join in the idolatry of the nations, so that you prepare a table for what they call Fortune and set out a mixed cup for the demon that lurks in the statue of so-called Fortune: hear what awaits you. You will all be handed over to the sword of war. And if any of you should ask, "Why?", I say that it is for this reason, to pass over the rest: I myself counted you worthy of my presence and called you first to myself, but you did not obey. I made this charge before as well, when I said, "Why did I come and there was no one? Why did I call and there was no one to answer?" And now I say again: "Because I called you and you did not obey; I spoke and you would not listen; you did evil before me and chose what I did not desire." Since, then, I called you first and counted you first worthy of my grace, while you were deaf and disobedient, how can you complain, accusing and charging me, and dare to say, "You made us stray from your way, Lord"? That is why I refuted this impious saying long ago, when I said, "I became manifest to those who did not ask for me, and I was found by those who did not seek me," and then, "Behold, I said to those who did not call on my name, 'Here I am.'" You did the very opposite. You were called and given preference, yet you did not obey at all, but treated with contempt the grace that I had granted to you first.

The word has announced the good news about those of the Jewish nation who would be chosen and kept like good seed for the planting and fruit-bearing of others. It has told how these very people would set up folds for flocks in the thicket and make resting places for herds in the Valley of Achor, as interpreted above. Then, assigning what follows to the remaining multitude of those who perish, it turns again to them and brings the charges set out above. It teaches that God, who does everything by the scales of justice, will never overlook those who serve him, wherever they are and from whatever nation they come. For he will receive all without exception who have once chosen to serve him, and he will provide them with heavenly food: the saving Word, who said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." These, then, will be nourished and filled with that bread. "But you," he says, "who did not accept my grace, will hunger for lack of spiritual food." Again, those who serve me will be filled with the drink of immortal life, of which it is said, "Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, it will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." But you who rejected my grace will thirst, because you abandoned the fountain of life. And again, those who serve me will share in divine gladness, as befits the drink and food they were found worthy of. But you who spurned my grace will be put to shame, because you are again deprived of these things. Moreover, besides what has been said, those who serve me will exult in gladness and rightly rejoice in their souls, since they have been found worthy of such great blessings. But when you see them enjoying these things, you will cry out from pain of soul and wail from brokenness of spirit. For the pain of the body is small compared with the pain of the heart. So you will suffer not in the body but in the heart itself, grieving and all but letting out cries and shrieks, as if over your own ruin.

In place of “For you will leave your name for satiety,” the other translators all agree in rendering “for an oath.” People commonly swear by those who have suffered terrible things: “May we not suffer what these have suffered!” In the same way, your name will become an oath for my chosen ones. Because of what will happen to you, your name will become something to shun, and so your name and the memory of your misfortunes will serve my chosen ones as an oath. The end of the evils that will overtake you will be the death that will come upon you from God himself. This death is a separation, not of the soul from the body, but from immortal life, and the loss of God himself. This, then, is what awaits you. But what was promised will be granted to those who serve me, whatever nation they come from. And if you are curious to learn who these future servants of mine are, and what their name is, know that God does not yet wish to bring their name into the open. He indicates only this much: they will be called neither Israel nor Jacob nor Jews, nor by any name already known among people.

For a new and fresh name will be given to them, a strange name never yet heard. It will be blessed on the earth, growing and multiplying beyond every bodily blessing. If there is any other blessing from God that brings increase, the name to be given to those who serve me will receive it. So for the present let no one be overly curious before events come to pass. Those spoken of continue to be blessed, and they themselves bless the true God.

In place of “the true God,” Aquila has: “and to his servants he will call another name, by which the one who is blessed in the earth will be blessed faithfully.” Symmachus has: “but to his servants he will call another name, in which the one who is blessed upon the earth will be blessed in the God Amen.” For he means that just as they will bless the true God, so they will be blessed faithfully, or, as Symmachus puts it, “Amen.” Moreover, when those who will serve me swear on the earth, they will swear by the true God. They will no longer swear by the beings they wrongly took for gods, for they will have learned from the Savior to know him as the only true God, together with the Lord Jesus Christ whom he sent. Having received these things, those who will serve him will forget their first affliction, which they once endured while subject to the evil demons. The misery of idolatrous error will not come up into their heart. Having passed as from darkness into light, they will forget their former condition.

And so the heaven will be new for them, and the earth new. For once, when they looked at the heaven, they worshiped the creation rather than the Creator. In the same way they made gods of the earth and of the fruits that spring from it. But now, when they see heaven and earth as new, they confess that these are the works of God's hands and no longer think them gods. Therefore he adds: “They shall not remember the former things, nor shall these come into their heart.” Instead they will find gladness and exultation, for they have received the fountain of good things. “Then I will make Jerusalem an exultation for them”: I myself, God, who am able to do all things. For exultation itself, the gladness that accords with God, and pure piety will be their Jerusalem. “And my people I will set in gladness”: that very new people to whom I promised to give the new name.

“And I myself,” God, “will exult” as I behold that Jerusalem, that is, the godly commonwealth of those who will serve me, which I have judged within myself to be far better than the bodily Jerusalem. Therefore, “I will exult over it and be glad over my people.” The godly community of my servants will then live in such a way that no deeds or actions deserving weeping and outcry will be heard among them any longer. “Nor will there be there one dying untimely, or an old man.” For at the time of the promises all will receive the resurrection from me and will come “to perfect manhood, to the measure of the stature.” All will be in the prime of their souls, so that no untimely, immature infant will be found among them, and no one past his prime and grown old. All will be of the same age, since they will receive the resurrection at one time and share in one rebirth. Therefore the young man who is saved will be complete and in his prime, as though a hundred years old, and the sinner who perishes will again be the same age as he. For they will return to life at one time and become equal in age through the simultaneous resurrection. Then some will receive eternal life, while others will be handed over to the second death and subjected to the punishment and retribution of the soul. It is a remarkable thing that he calls the young man who is saved a hundred years old, and likewise says that the sinner is a hundred years old. In this way he shows that the resurrection from the dead takes place at one and the same time. So the sinner too will be a hundred years old, “and he will be accursed.” He will be in his prime and, as it were, perfect in wickedness, dying in his own sin. And the young man in turn will be a hundred years old, himself perfect among the perfect, and received into salvation.

These same people “will build houses and will themselves dwell in them.” For by their own works and their own deeds they will gain for themselves the dwelling places with the Father. And they will eat the labors of their fruits. So whatever they have gathered by their farming they will find, and they will be nourished by it, no longer anxious that strangers might seize their labors. That is why it is said: “They shall not build and others dwell; they shall not plant and others eat.” Instead they will live in immortal well-being for endless ages. That is why it is said: “For like the days of the tree of life shall be the days of my people.” The tree is said to have been planted in the paradise of God, so this shows that the promises are not found outside the paradise of God. And he clearly pointed to eternal and immortal life when he said, “For like the days of the tree of life shall be the days of my people.” In another place Solomon taught that the tree of life is the wisdom of God, saying: “She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her, and for those who lean upon her as upon the Lord she is secure.” The wisdom of God is everlasting and the fountain of eternal life, and the word promises that the days of the people will be like this. What else, then, does it foretell for them but the highest blessedness? “These things I will do for my people,” he says, “and I will be glad over my people; for like the days of the tree of life shall be the days of my people.” In all these words he clearly brings in for himself another people distinct from the nation of the Jews. Moreover, he says, “they will make the works of their labors grow old.” For they themselves will not grow old. Nor will they have to leave their labors to others as they depart this life. Instead they will take the works of their labors back for themselves and delight in their own fruits.

God promises all these things not to just anyone, nor to the called, “for many are called, but few are chosen.” Therefore he proclaims in advance to the chosen: “My chosen ones shall not labor in vain, nor bear children for a curse.” There will indeed be labors at the time of the promises. They will be saving, good, and pleasant, surely of the kind the angelic order also undertakes. Yet their work will not be in vain, for a worthy reward has been stored up for them. Their offspring too will not be for a curse. Let us understand “offspring” as the thoughts of the soul and the fruits of the mind, which he foretells will be strangers to the curse and worthy of blessing. “And their seed is blessed by God.” These things can also be taken to refer to the present life. On this reading the word again hints, right from the start, at the band of the apostles: “My chosen ones shall not labor in vain, nor bear children for a curse.” For one can see with one's own eyes that the apostles' labors were not in vain, from the church they founded throughout the whole world. And we will understand their children to be those reborn in Christ through the washing of regeneration. We see how these were not born for a curse when we set beside them the curse pronounced upon Adam and the words spoken to the woman: “In pain you shall bear children, and your turning shall be to your husband.” Adam and Eve had children in that way, begetting them according to the flesh, but God's chosen ones did not. Their gospel seed, which they sowed in all the churches of God, has been blessed for these very people, namely God's chosen apostles, and the disciples and evangelists of our Savior.

He promises something more, saying: “And it shall be that before they cry out I will hear them; while they are still speaking I will say, ‘What is it?’” This was indeed fulfilled in the Acts of the Apostles. Many signs and wonders were worked because God stood beside them, and as they worked such things, the conversion of the foreign nations followed. Some had once been so rapacious and savage that they could be compared to wolves. Now they changed to gentleness and grazed together with lambs and oxen, sharing one and the same rational food from the divine readings. Others, whose ways had been no different from a lion's, no longer resembled flesh-eating beasts that devour raw meat. Like oxen, they too ate the grass of inspired teaching. And the man who had once been snakelike and full of venom spat out the wickedness within him and “will eat bread.” He uses rational, human food instead of the earth he ate before. These beasts will be tamed so completely that they wrong no one and harm no one on the mountain of God. They themselves will make their home there because their ways have changed. The Jews expect these things to happen in a more bodily way in the earthly Jerusalem. To them it is worth saying first that these passages make no mention of good things concerning them, only reproofs, reproaches, and accusations of their impieties. Next, what need is there for lions, wolves, and snakes to be on the holy mountain and in Jerusalem itself? What use will they be to the people of that time? And what would be worthy of God's promise in having snakes, lions, and wolves live alongside the blessed on God's holy mountain? These things clearly refer to human characters.

Then, since he has mentioned his holy mountain, he must add: “Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me? says the Lord. And what is the place of my rest? For my hand made all these things, and all these things are mine, says the Lord.” With these words he clearly rejects the earthly Jerusalem. He indicates that the promises will not be given to the worthy on the bodily mountain either. The same was said earlier: “For the heaven will be new and the earth new, and they shall not remember the former things, nor shall these come into their heart.” If the heaven is to be new and the earth new, and the former things are no longer remembered, then there will be no memory either of a bodily mountain or of an earthly Jerusalem. So it was fitting for him to add, as a refutation of the Jewish assumption: “What house will you build for me? says the Lord. And what is the place of my rest? For my hand made all these things, and all these things are mine.” Why, then, should anyone expect a house of God on earth? And why again imagine the lower Jerusalem? For if the heaven is to be new and the earth new, it follows that we should picture Jerusalem as being of the same kind, so that there will no longer be any memory of anything that came before. Clearly the present passage introduces a new heaven, a new earth, a new people, a new name, and a new Jerusalem, and likewise gates and temples built anew. Of these it is added: “And they shall not remember the former things, nor shall these come into their heart.”

The children of the Jews took great care to offer sacrifices by slaughtering animals, so God shakes these off as well and turns away from them. He says that he accepts the one who is reverent, humble in soul, and sincerely devoted to him, but rejects the offerings made through sacrifices. Therefore he says: “On whom will I look but on the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? But the lawless one who sacrifices a calf is like one who kills a dog.” In the Hebrew reading and the other translators, the words “But the lawless one” are not included. Without them the text simply goes on: “He who slaughters a calf is like one who strikes a man; he who sacrifices from the flock is like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents an offering is like one who offers pig's blood; he who burns incense as a memorial is like one who blesses iniquity.” These words are fittingly joined to “What house will you build for me? And what is the place of my rest?” For when he does away with the house on earth, he naturally does away with what is performed in it as well. To these he adds: “And they have chosen their own ways and their abominations, which their soul desired.”

“For these are not my wishes,” he says, “nor are these my ways; they are what pleases their own choice. Therefore I too will choose their mockeries,” or, as the other translators have it, “their mockings.” For they will be mocked when they are handed over to those who punish them. “And I will repay them for their sins.” He testifies once more that these things will come upon them, not [?] but because, he says, “I called them and they did not obey, and they did evil before me and chose what I did not wish.” Note that this has now been said a second time in the same prophecy, since a little earlier it was said: “Because I called you and you did not obey me; I spoke and you paid no heed; you did evil before me and chose what I did not wish.” When did they refuse to obey when he called, or fail to understand when he spoke to them, if not when he lived among them and cried out: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest”? Because they did not come to him when he called, when the promises are bestowed the worthy will enjoy them, but these people will be handed over to their own sins.

The word has foretold that all things will be new at the time of the promises. In keeping with that, in the following passage it addresses those who have learned these things in advance during the present life: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word.” Who these were he taught earlier, when he said: “On whom will I look but on the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” So it is to those who have shown a reverent and godly character by trembling at his word that he speaks: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Say ‘You are our brothers’ to those who hate you and abhor you.” In this he gives them a gospel command that is no different from: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, so that you may become sons of your Father in heaven.” So the prophecy also urges what the gospel teaches.

Trembling at the divine oracles and treating them with all reverence is not enough for perfection. To reach the height of virtue we must carry forbearance so far that we call brothers the enemies who hate us, and do not regard as foes those who abhor us, but cherish and love them as true friends. "For so you will be sons of your Father in heaven," says the Savior, "who makes his sun rise on the just and the unjust, and sends rain on the wicked and the good." And the prophecy says this: "Do so, that the name of the Lord may be glorified and may appear in their gladness"; or, in Symmachus' version, "and we shall see in your gladness." For if you do these things, at the end, when the rewards are given, your gladness will be plain for all to see; but they will be put to shame when they see your end, and at the time of God's righteous judgment they will learn by experience their own destruction. For the day of recompense is all but upon them, the day on which every kind of cry will be heard from those being punished: some from the city itself, as its inhabitants cry out, and others from the temple itself, as the priests and the other ministers lament. Then the voice of the Judge himself will also be heard, rendering recompense to his adversaries. Since, then, these things await those who hate and abhor you, bear with patience the hatred and insults directed at you in this present life, and say to those who hate you, "Our brothers"; love your enemies and do good to those who hate you. The prophetic word seems to say this in the person of the apostles of our Savior, as men who were about to be persecuted by the Jews, and above all by those who lived in Jerusalem. And the promise to the apostles was fulfilled when churches of God were founded through them throughout the whole world, while the wrath of God pursued those who hated and abhorred them without delay, so that everyone in the city itself raised cries of mourning, and those who served in the temple raised other cries, as the enemy surrounded them and God brought recompense upon them. That is why it is said: "A voice of crying from the city, a voice from the temple, the voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his adversaries."

That is their lot. But the God-fearing commonwealth, the new and fresh Zion, that is, the church of God that will be established through you, will give birth all at once to so great a multitude of peoples that whoever hears of it will be astonished. Just as a pregnant woman carrying a child in her womb might suddenly give birth, with no labor pains at all, and to a male child at that, in the same way the new Zion will bring forth a new people, a whole nation, all at once, in a single moment, so that the whole thing is utterly beyond belief, such as was never heard before. For the Jewish nation, Israel itself, did not come into being all at once. First there was their forefather; to him were born twelve sons; then from each of these came sons and daughters, and sons of sons, offspring and descendants. In this way, through the succession of parents over many years and through various generations, their whole nation was formed. One would find that the other nations likewise grew to great numbers over time. But the people of the church of God filled most parts of the world all at once, at a single moment and, as it were, in a single day. This is a strange thing, beyond all wonder, such as eye has never seen nor ear heard. "I, the Lord, am the cause of these things," he says, "the maker of wondrous works, who have already given you this expectation from here, foretelling through my prophecy what was to come, so that when the events themselves take place you may have firm faith in my words. I foretold all these things for your salvation; but you, the people to whom I am speaking, did not remember me, nor did you believe even when you saw with your own eyes."

The words "You did not remember me, says the Lord" are not found in the other translators. In Symmachus the passage runs this way: "Am I one who brings a woman to the birthing seat and does not deliver? says the Lord. Or shall I who deliver also shut the womb? says your God." For how, he says, will a nation be born upon the earth, except by my power? It is I who bring women with child in the womb to the point of giving birth, and who become the cause of their bringing a human being into the light and bringing into existence one who did not exist before. Shall I, then, who do these things in bodily birth, not deliver her who is to give birth to a whole nation together and all at once, so that this divine offspring may come forth straightway, without harm or pain? Shall I, the Lord, who am accustomed to deliver what has been conceived, shut up the birth so that the child in the womb perishes?

And how could I do such things, I who by divine and saving power bring into existence all who come from nonbeing into being through birth in the flesh? For not those individually [?] ... But in view of all this, what remains except that all who hear of these things should rejoice and be filled with gladness together with that new Jerusalem? She must no longer be thought of as built of lifeless stones, but as made up of holy souls; and it is fitting to be glad with her and to celebrate with her, keeping festival not outside her but within her. "And rejoice over her," he says, "all" who see her new and fresh constitution, and who have long mourned from afar in longing to receive her. Such was Paul, who says: "We who are in this tent groan, being burdened, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven." But now that you have received her whom you long desired with groaning and mourning, rejoice and exult, for you are about to be filled with the milk that is in her. For it follows that she who has all at once given birth to a male people for God should also be filled with milk to nourish her infants. This spiritual milk will flow from her two breasts, namely the Old and the New Testament. From both these breasts of hers, of which it is said in the Song, "Your breasts are better than wine," she will water her infants with the spiritual and pure milk and bring them to full manhood. So words of exhortation and consolation are properly called the milk of less mature souls, while solid food is understood to lie in the mystical doctrines and in the contemplations stored up in the divine Scriptures. But you, the children of the new Jerusalem, newborn infants, rejoice as you hear these things, since you are going to enjoy them and delight in the promises of God.

Next it says: "For thus says the Lord: Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent overflowing with the glory of the nations." Here again he joins the glory of the nations to the new Zion and the new Jerusalem already mentioned, and he compares the peace that will be given to the nations to a flooding river, the river he also presented elsewhere, saying: "The river of God is full of water," and "The streams of the river make glad the city of God." And indeed, when the deepest peace waters the church of God like a river with its abundant stream, "their children," he says, "will be carried on shoulders and comforted on knees." Earlier too he had used these same promises, indicating that those in the church who are still infants, being fed on milk, are carried by certain nurses, whether the genuine teachers and leaders of the church of God, or divine and heavenly angels. This is what our Savior made clear when he said: "Do not despise one of the little ones in my church; for their angels always behold the face of my Father in heaven." So the stronger will carry the weaker on their shoulders and comfort them on their knees. "As a mother comforts her own children, so I myself, the Lord, being the Father of them all, will comfort those who comfort the weaker."

"When these things are thus accomplished," he says, "you will see, and your heart will rejoice." And what will you see, if not, clearly, God? "And your bones will spring up like grass"—or, in Symmachus, "will bloom like green herbage"—"and the hand of the Lord will be made known to those who fear him." This will be the end of the promises: "You will see God." That is why the Savior also called them blessed, saying: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." In this way it will also become known to all that it was not a human hand or human power that accomplished such great things, but truly the hand of God himself, which will be made known to those who fear him. For having taken to themselves the fear that comes from God's wisdom—"for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom"—they will understand that so great and so wondrous a grace could not have come to humankind without the hand of God [?]. These, then, will have knowledge of these things; but to those who are not such, the word that follows threatens what is coming upon them.

To those described above he promises what has been foretold; but having said that he will threaten those who have taken the opposite path, he goes on to teach the manner of the threat, presenting the second and glorious coming of the Savior, when he will come with the glory of the Father and with his angels to judge the living and the dead. That is why he says: "Behold, the Lord will come like fire." Instead of "will come like fire," all the other translators have "will come in fire." "And his chariots like a whirlwind": his chariots are the angels and the powers around him, which, he says, will fall like a whirlwind upon those who deserve punishment. He is said to come in this way because of the ungodly, upon whom he is about to let loose his wrath; and the powers that chastise and punish are usually called his wrath. "And he will let loose his utter rejection with flaming fire" against these same people. Instead of "utter rejection," the other translators have rendered "his rejection." Such, then, will be his wrath, as has been said. But toward those worthy of his kingdom he will be as has often been shown in what went before: how he will show the glory of his kingdom to his elders, how he will appear like a bridegroom and receive his bride, and all the other things the word has announced as good news to those who will share in the promises.

Then he threatens, saying: “For by the fire of the Lord all the earth will be judged, and all flesh by his sword; many will be wounded by the Lord.” He speaks of a “sword” in rather bodily terms, and of “the wounded” in the same way, because the hearers were Jews and could not have understood him otherwise, being unable to follow the meaning of the words. The Apostle, however, makes the sense of these words plain when he says: “By your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. He will repay each one according to his works.”

Next the prophet rebukes the Jews who were acting impiously in that same period, saying: “Those who sanctify and purify themselves in the gardens and in the porches, eating swine’s flesh and abominations and the mouse, shall be consumed together, said the Lord.” Here the passage does not accuse them of eating pork themselves. It accuses them of doing the things he was charging them with while they lived among people who ate pork and the rest. For they lived among the nations and conducted their lives among foreigners, and in their way of life they were no different from them. That is why he says they will perish along with them, handed over to the same punishment as the nations. He said they purify themselves “in the gardens” because they no longer purified themselves according to the law that Moses handed down, with the ashes of a heifer, with seven days of sprinkling, and with the purifications that came through sacrifices. Instead they went about in the gardens and thought that purification by water was enough for them. They washed themselves in the waters of the gardens and supposed that they no longer needed anything the law prescribed. Or else it means that after foul and unclean deeds and lawless obscenities they thought they could cleanse their souls with mere water.

That is why he adds: “And I am coming to gather their works and their thought.” The passage moves on to the universal judgment, saying: “I am coming to gather all the nations and the tongues, and they shall come and see my glory. And I will leave a sign upon them, and I will send out from them those who have been saved.” The Savior teaches this more clearly in the Gospels, saying: “When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father, and all the angels with him, they will gather all the nations before him. He will separate them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, and he will set the sheep on his right and the goats on his left.” And he will say one thing to the first group and another to the second. The prophecy also presents this in the words: “And I am coming to gather their works and their thought, all the nations and the tongues, and they shall come and see my glory.” Here again the nations are promised that they will be counted worthy to behold his glory. So that this may come about, and the promise may reach a good end for the nations, he says, “I select some from them.” From whom? Clearly from those who were perishing, of whom it was said, “they shall be consumed together.” For some who are left over from these very people will receive my sign and the calling of the nations who are to see my glory. Hence it is said: “I will leave a sign upon them and send out from them those who have been saved.”

These were the remnant chosen by grace, of whom it had been said: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed.” This seed, then, preserved from those very people who were perishing, “I will send out,” he says, to the nations of other races and foreign stock: “to Tarshish and Put and Lud and Meshech and Tubal, and to Greece, and to the islands far off, who have not heard my name nor seen my glory.” Earlier, too, it was said: “Those to whom nothing was announced about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.” And again: “I became manifest to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me; I said, ‘Here I am,’ to those who did not call on my name.” The present words are akin to these. In them he promises to send his own apostles to the nations that are strangers to Israel, the ones farthest from Judea, and to the islands, where no one had ever heard the name of a prophet. He says that his apostles will come to these people bringing a sign with them. What is this sign, if not the saving sign? Trusting in it, they proclaimed the glory of the only-begotten God to all the nations. Among these nations they will set free those long enslaved by the error of idolatry and lead them, and having shown them to be their own brothers, they will bring them as an offering to God. This they will do for the present. But at the time of the consummation they will bring them to the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and so bring them to this good end. Then they too will be taken up as Elijah was, riding on angelic chariots, while heavenly light flashes around them.

Hence it is said: “With horses and chariots, in mule-litters with canopies, to the holy city Jerusalem, and they will bring your brothers from all the nations.” You will understand that the horses and chariots are angelic if you look at the prophecy of Zechariah. There the text describes dappled, piebald and white horses and certain chariots, and by them it hinted at angelic powers. The mule-litters seem to signify the bodies of the resurrection. Riding in these, souls will be taken up into the heavenly city. They are fittingly called lampēnai because of the glory that shines out in them. In place of “in mule-litters with canopies,” Symmachus translated “on horses and in chariots and in litters and in carriages and in sedan-chairs.” All these things were said in this coarse and bodily way to suit Jewish ears. In their meaning, though, they signify the lofty journey through the air that carries these people to heaven. The divine Apostle explained this more clearly when he said: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.” In this way they will enter the heavenly city of God. In this way those saved from all the nations will come to the heavenly Jerusalem, just as the sons of Israel once went up on earth and brought their sacrifices. He means this when he says: “as the sons of Israel would bring their sacrifices to me with psalms into the house of the Lord”; or, in Symmachus: “just as the sons of Israel would bring the offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.” At that time, under the bodily law, those who performed the worship did these things at the earthly Jerusalem. In the same way, following the earthly pattern, those who go up to the heavenly Jerusalem will come with their own fruits, and with the gifts that each one carries in the soul from the fruit borne by the virtues.

Then he adds: “And from them I will take.” From which ones? From the nations he named a little earlier: “Tarshish and Put and Lud and Meshech and Tubal, and to Greece, and to the islands far off, who have not heard my name nor seen my glory.” From these very people, he says, “I will take priests and Levites, said the Lord.” Then he adds an argument showing that the statement is reasonable: “For as the new heaven and the new earth, which I make, remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand.” For if the heaven will be new, and the earth new, and Jerusalem new, it would follow that the priests and Levites will also be new. That is why it was said earlier too: “They shall not remember the former things, nor shall they come into their heart.” I will take, then, priests and Levites from those very people I mentioned before. It was not plausible that “I will take priests and Levites” was said of the Jewish people, since they already had these. Nor was it even possible to take Levites from Levites or priests from priests, because all those of the tribe of Levi without exception were priests and Levites. But now he promises to make a selection from the calling of the nations. And this will happen because the heaven will be new and the earth new, “which I make” to remain. The first ones did not remain. Hence it was said: “Heaven and earth will pass away”; and again: “The heaven will be rolled up like a scroll”; and: “The earth will be utterly destroyed.” But of the age to come Christ is the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming. After that come the new heaven and the new earth, of which he spoke in the Beatitudes: “Blessed are those who are such, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” This new heaven, then, and the new earth of the new age remain and endure for a boundless and endless age. But understand with me that there are differences among the places in the kingdom. There are many mansions with the Father. Some of them will stand to the others as earth stands to heaven, while others, compared with the lower mansions, will hold the glory of heavens. These will indeed remain forever and will no longer pass away, for “the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.” Hence he says: “which I make to remain before me”; and your name, too, will likewise abide forever before me. The word “forever” hints at eternal, immortal and boundless life.

Then he adds: “And it shall be that from month to month and from sabbath to sabbath all flesh shall come to worship before me in Jerusalem, said the Lord.” The words “in Jerusalem” are not found in the other translators, nor in the Hebrew reading. Still, their presence in the Seventy does no harm, for clearly it signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, where the kingdom of our Savior will be established. And if what Moses laid down in the law consisted of types, symbols and images of heavenly things, it follows that we should take in a spiritual sense the feasts in heaven, the true sabbaths there, and the months there. Much could be said on this subject, but it is hard to interpret and would need long leisure and a treatise of its own. Yet consider the Jerusalem below. There the great multitude of the nation lived in various cities, while the place of the sanctuary was set apart, and at appointed times those who lived in the rest of the country gathered there to carry out the worship of God. The same holds for the heavenly city as we understand it spiritually, and for the special sanctuary there, which no one may enter except the high priest alone, that is, the Son of God. He alone may approach the Godhead of the Father, and he passes into the Father’s very bosom. Those who will inhabit the many heavenly mansions will cross over at appointed seasons to the heavenly city, which is set apart and reserved for the kingdom of God and for those who have reached the summit of blessedness. Even those of lower rank will not be deprived of that blessedness. We must imagine the seasons and years there in a way suited to that place. One of the prophets was contemplating them when he said: “And I remembered eternal years and meditated on them.”

They too will arrive at certain periods, as if at heavenly festivals. They will share in an unceasing, divine gladness and enjoy the ineffable good things there, of which it is said: “What eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and what has not entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him.” Filled with these things, they will return to their own mansions, and each will receive the dwelling that is proper and suited to him. Then the true sabbath rest, the perfect and true repose of souls, will be granted to those who are worthy of it. Hence it is said: “And it shall be that from month to month and from sabbath to sabbath all flesh shall come to worship before me in Jerusalem, said the Lord.” By “all flesh” he means all the nations, naming them in this way. So it was also said earlier: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God”; and elsewhere: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and they shall prophesy.” He had to widen the sense and speak universally of “all flesh,” and so refer to the whole human race, so that the Jews would not think these things were said about them alone. Some will come at appointed times, but others are citizens of Jerusalem itself. These are myriads of angels, as the Apostle also taught, and the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. They will not come at intervals. They will be its inhabitants and citizens continually, as ministers and priests under the high priest, the Son of God, and will enjoy the good things there without ceasing. All these will see the destruction of the ungodly and will reflect on how great the good things are that those people have lost.

Hence it is said: “And they shall go out and see the limbs of the people who have transgressed against me”; or, in Symmachus: “and they shall see the last end of the people who rejected me.” He showed who these were at the beginning of the prophecy, when he said: “I begot sons and raised them up, but they rejected me.” So he was hinting at those of the Jewish nation who rejected the saving grace. Those who go out from Jerusalem and depart to their own mansions will see them from far off. This is what the text presents when it says: “They shall go out and see the limbs of the people who rejected me, whose worm shall not die and whose fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh.” This, then, would be the worst of all punishments: to have their own worm within them without end. By the worm he means conscience. Like a worm, it devours the souls of those who know they have done nothing good, as they repent of their impieties and see themselves shut out from such great good things. Each of them, as he confesses, will become his own accuser. He will go over what he did in his mortal life and be stung by his conscience, and so their worm remains without end. Surely this was not said of a physical worm, as though one too were going to come into being. Their fire will also be unquenchable. Our Savior also set out this end of the ungodly in the Gospels, when he said to those who will stand on his left: “Depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” As the fire is called eternal there, so it is called unquenchable here, and both scriptures present one and the same nature of fire. Moreover, while they are in such punishment, they will be a spectacle to all flesh. To what flesh? Surely to the flesh that will not be punished but will be counted worthy of the heavenly vision. Of this flesh it was said above: “All flesh shall come to worship before me, said the Lord,” and “they shall go out and see.” This flesh, then, which has been counted worthy of better things, will see the end of those who are being punished. But those who will be handed over to the eternal fire, carrying their own endless worm in their souls, will be set out as a spectacle for those who will be counted worthy of divine blessedness.
